#11. The China Price

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

Beijing’s Green Path to Ending Dollar Dominance

In 1971, as the international monetary system was on the brink of collapse, U.S. Treasury Secretary John Connally told a group of worried European finance ministers that the dollar was “our currency, but your problem.” The dollar had become that system’s official reserve currency in 1944, under the Bretton Woods agreement, making signatories subject to the whims of U.S. monetary policy. Even after Bretton Woods collapsed and many currencies floated freely, the dollar continued to dominate. In the last half century, U.S. currency power has only expanded, as more countries have integrated into the global economy and therefore grown to depend on the dollar. China, reliant on export-driven growth, is foremost among them.

Reckoning with the possibility that Washington could someday make the dollar China’s problem, Beijing is now crafting its own solution. In a January 2024 speech, Chinese leader Xi Jinping made this effort explicit, instructing senior provincial and ministerial officials to accelerate China’s transformation into a “leading financial power.” A strong currency, he specified, was one of the essential foundations of that power. When Qiushi, the Chinese Communist Party’s flagship journal, published the full text of the speech in 2026, the standard Xi had in mind became clearer: for a currency to be considered “strong,” it must be widely used in international trade, investment, and foreign exchange markets and be recognized as a global reserve currency.

Xi’s call is the latest episode in a long history of efforts by major powers to reduce their dependence on the dollar-centered global financial system. In 1965, French Finance Minister Valéry Giscard d’Estaing famously described the disproportionate advantages that dollar dominance confers on the United States as “exorbitant privilege”; the same year, France began aggressively converting a substantial share of its dollar reserves into gold, contributing to the collapse of the Bretton Woods system. In 1999, the Japanese government released a report on how to promote wider international use of the yen. That same year, the launch of the euro gave Europe what would become the world’s second most important international currency, affording it greater monetary autonomy even as the European Central Bank carefully danced around any suggestion that it might challenge the dollar.

What distinguishes Xi’s ambition is that China, unlike Europe or Japan, possesses the economic heft, military capability, and political will to rival the United States’ geopolitical power. Not since London commanded a global empire has another country’s currency stood a realistic chance of competing with the dollar. A global financial transition from “In God We Trust” to “Where the Party Leads, We Follow” can no longer be dismissed as fantasy.

The internationalization of the renminbi would afford China a measure of financial survivability should the United States ever choose to wield the dollar as a punitive weapon, as it did against Russia after the country’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, in 2022. The United States controls both the supply of the dominant global reserve currency and many of the critical financial infrastructure chokepoints through which it circulates. Washington, if it so desired, could severely restrict China’s access to dollar liquidity by making the cost of doing business with Chinese institutions prohibitive, for example by indicting or sanctioning a major Chinese bank. Any such measure would shock the Chinese financial system, raise transaction costs for trade, and deliver a major competitive blow to China’s export sector, which accounts for roughly one-fifth of its GDP.

Survivability, however, is only a prerequisite for credible deterrence. To deter the United States from using the dollar weapon, Beijing requires a financial second-strike capability. It must be able to redirect a substantial share of global trade and finance to a renminbi-based network. The durability of that shift depends on healthy global demand for an anchor asset priced in renminbi. For China, the most likely source of such an anchor asset lies in its dominance of the green economy.

Xi does not necessarily want the renminbi to replace the dollar. His 2024 speech advocated strength, not hegemony. Placing a respectable second, or even a consequential third, would suffice to break the dollar’s effective monopoly and constrain the United States’ ability to impose financial sanctions unilaterally, while saving China the effort and cost of sustaining currency supremacy. From Beijing’s perspective, the mission is to establish the renminbi as the Pepsi to the dollar’s Coca-Cola: never the market leader, but serviceable in a pinch and more than capable of keeping the dominant incumbent honest.

The near-universal acceptance of the U.S. dollar arguably benefits China more than any other country. The Chinese economy relies on exports, and Chinese goods priced and financed in dollars can reach ready buyers almost anywhere. The resulting profits can then be invested almost anywhere and converted into liquid funds on short notice. This suits Beijing: China enjoys the benefits of global liquidity without bearing the burdens of sustaining it. To preserve the global dollar system, the United States must tolerate foreign ownership of an ever-expanding volume of dollar claims as countries conduct ever more business in the currency. U.S. markets are exposed to international volatility, and foreigners hold some influence over U.S. corporations. The Federal Reserve, which issues the dollar, backstops the system, expanding its balance sheet during periods of financial stress, when governments and private companies hoard dollars to ensure they can continue to pay their debts and buy goods. This openness and exposure has posed little threat to the U.S. economy because foreign shareholders have generally sought to operate within, rather than change, U.S. business norms, and U.S. banks have earned tidy profits intermediating the world’s capital flows through New York and London.

China’s leaders have no desire to make any such tradeoff. Maintaining a global renminbi system would be fundamentally at odds with China’s state-led economic model. For the renminbi to replicate the dollar’s functions, China would have to create broad, two-way financial channels through which foreign holders of renminbi could reinvest that money into the Chinese economy. The resulting capital inflows would fundamentally reshape China’s domestic financial markets. It would be impractical for Beijing to confine foreign investors to a narrow group of approved assets, as it does now. Once foreign investors were allowed into China’s markets in force, they would arbitrage the distortions created by financial repression and politically directed capital allocation. Such competition would undermine one of Beijing’s most effective means of securing the loyalty of China’s business class: controlling who gains access to capital, on what terms, and for what purposes.

For many wealthy Chinese citizens, including some members of the Communist Party itself, the dollar is an indispensable form of political risk insurance. Domestic political rivalries can lead to asset seizure or even imprisonment with little due process. Offshore dollar deposits and foreign corporate structures allow elites to diversify their holdings across currencies and jurisdictions. Control of a company listed overseas, especially in the United States, offers wealthy Chinese more than prestige and access to global capital; disclosure obligations, duties to shareholders, and international visibility, which extend beyond the party’s control, can give Chinese executives leverage against arbitrary demands from officials at home. These constraints cannot prevent interference by senior authorities determined to pursue their targets, but they can raise its cost, slow its implementation, and create room for negotiation. The dollar-based system is a refuge for Chinese elites who fall from grace, and because no one’s position is ever entirely secure, few wish to see that refuge disappear.

China is perfectly willing to go on living in a world that the dollar makes go round. But it cannot abide the dollar’s weaponization, and the renminbi still has a long way to go before it is strong enough to blunt that threat. If more countries and businesses are to adopt the renminbi, there must first be a global financial infrastructure for its use. China has already laid the foundation by facilitating renminbi use among firms in more than a hundred countries and across a growing array of commodity markets to settle transactions, obtain financing for trade and investment, and hedge their risks. Here, breadth matters far more than depth. Even modest daily volumes of renminbi transactions can keep payment channels operational, preserve financial relationships, and maintain the legal and administrative expertise needed to run an alternative financial system.

Because China’s relative economic strength lies in the flow of manufactured goods—it accounted for 20 percent of global manufactured exports in 2025—Beijing has concentrated its efforts on building a payment network that facilitates the commercial flows generated by its manufacturing machine. In 2005, Zhou Xiaochuan, then governor of the People’s Bank of China, publicly encouraged the already increasing use of local currencies among China’s trading partners. In 2009, the PBOC launched a pilot program for settling cross-border transactions in renminbi, followed in 2015 by the creation of the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System, the backbone of China’s international renminbi network. CIPS began with 195 participants spanning 50 countries; by June 2026, it had 1,829 participants and could route payments to more than 5,200 banking institutions in 191 countries. But CIPS remains much smaller than the mature wholesale payment systems supporting the dollar and the euro. In 2025, the U.S.-based Clearing House Interbank Payments System processed an estimated 19 times as much value in international payments as CIPS, and Europe’s real-time gross settlement system, called T2, cleared about 14 times as much.

But payments alone are a misleading measure of currency power. An international transaction entails far more than a transfer of economic value; it requires a package of financial services that unfolds across five linked stages: pricing, financing, risk transfer, payment, and reinvestment. The dollar dominates international trade and finance because it is the default currency at every stage, with its strength in each reinforcing its position in all the others. For the renminbi to supplant the dollar, it would have to become competitive at every stage of the transaction cycle, not just in payments.

China’s leaders recognize that the influence of financial centers in London, New York, and Tokyo rests not only on their ability to move money but also on their institutions’ ability to create credit, set prices, insure shipments, and recycle savings. That is why Chinese state-owned enterprises are driving the expansion of the renminbi network. By denominating invoices, contracts, and overseas project financing in renminbi, these enterprises create a base of recurring demand for the currency around which Chinese banks, insurers, and other financial institutions can build competing business lines under Chinese control. To reinforce that base, the Communist Party laid out an action plan in 2025 that instructs state-owned enterprises to prioritize settlement in renminbi, rather than dollars, whenever they deal with foreign suppliers and customers. That strategy is already fostering a regional network for renminbi use in Southeast Asia. In 2024, renminbi payments involving economies in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations rose 19 percent, with two-thirds of those transactions occurring between ASEAN countries.

Beijing has largely completed the first phase of its strategy, establishing a foothold in payments, and it is now expanding upstream into pricing, financing, and risk transfer, and, cautiously, downstream into reinvestment. Only recently has Beijing begun to appreciate how much the currency in which goods are priced influences the subsequent stages of the transaction cycle. Historically, China has been content to price the goods it imports and exports mostly in dollars. According to International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates, only 6.5 percent of China’s exports were invoiced in renminbi in 2023. Chinese government statistics show that nearly 30 percent of China’s trade in goods is settled in renminbi, but much of that is essentially a dollar transaction masquerading as a renminbi one: Chinese exporters invoice in dollars, buyers obtain dollar funding and are debited in dollars, and the funds are converted into renminbi only just before reaching the mainland.

The government is seeking to reverse that pattern by promoting what it calls “China prices”: renminbi-denominated benchmark prices listed on local exchanges for major commodities that China imports. Greater autonomy over pricing means that Chinese firms can buy raw inputs and manage their exposure to commodity price swings in global markets without acquiring dollars. It also gives Chinese authorities greater influence over the reference prices used to set the terms of supply contracts for the physical delivery of those commodities. This leverage is vital for China because the steady flow of raw inputs is essential to the smooth running of its manufacturing machine.

Price autonomy matters especially for critical minerals, which feed the green industries that in Xi’s view are central to China’s economic future. China produces more than 80 percent of the world’s batteries and consumes over 75 percent of its lithium, 70 percent of its cobalt, and about 60 percent of its nickel. But the country’s position in global markets for each of these minerals does not yet reflect its dominance in production and consumption. To date, China has made the most progress in lithium; more than 90 percent of global trading in lithium-carbonate futures occurs on the Guangzhou Futures Exchange, where contracts are denominated in renminbi. In July, the exchange allowed foreign traders to trade the lithium-carbonate futures contract directly, announcing with fanfare that several overseas “leading enterprises” had joined the market. China is now poised, perhaps for the first time in modern history, to become the principal financial center for a globally important commodity. Nickel and cobalt, on the other hand, remain tied to dollar benchmarks in London and Chicago. Although China is the largest consumer of these two minerals, it is not yet the financial reference point for their markets. That is the sort of mismatch that the push for China prices is meant to resolve.

The financing stage of Beijing’s renminbi strategy is gaining momentum. In 2023, Beijing instructed Chinese financial institutions to expand their renminbi funding abroad. State-backed lenders such as the Export-Import Bank of China have increased their renminbi lending for overseas trade and infrastructure projects, and commercial banks increasingly supply renminbi trade finance. Between 2023 and mid-2026, Chinese financial institutions more than doubled their renminbi lending to overseas borrowers from 1.3 to 2.9 trillion yuan ($428 billion). The PBOC, for its part, has adopted currency swap agreements with 32 foreign central banks and monetary authorities, including those in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, as well as the European Central Bank. In their early years, after the global financial crisis, these swap lines were largely symbolic and only lightly used, but in recent years, some have provided direct support for commercial activity. In 2025, Turkish companies borrowed four billion yuan ($557 million) to pay Chinese suppliers using a facility backed by a PBOC swap line, 70 percent more than they had borrowed a year earlier. This effort to turn the renminbi into a funding currency is starting to gain traction: in May 2026, the renminbi accounted for seven percent of the value of trade-finance messages on SWIFT, the leading global platform for exchanging payment instructions, up from 5.1 percent two years earlier and enough to overtake the euro for second place, although the dollar remained leagues ahead with an 82.5 percent share.

Beijing has also taken steps, if more modest ones, to increase the renminbi’s presence in markets for insurance and reinsurance. In 2025, Bank of China, a state-owned bank, and PICC, a state-owned property and casualty insurance company, developed new terms under which premiums and claims for cargo shipments could be settled in renminbi. The terms also specified Shanghai as the preferred venue for arbitration, part of a broader effort to shift the maritime-insurance market away from its traditional reliance on dollar settlement and English commercial law, long the standard framework for international shipping and maritime insurance contracts.

The final stage of the transaction cycle, reinvestment, completes the loop through which goods and value circulate through the global economy. Recipients of payment must decide what to do with the proceeds: hold them in a short-term account, invest them in longer-term assets, or convert them into another currency. A strong currency ecosystem becomes sustainable at scale only when recipients are willing to hold and reinvest their balances rather than routinely convert them.

Beijing has, over the past decade, given foreign holders of renminbi more ways to reinvest their balances. The Stock Connect and Bond Connect programs, which took their earliest forms in 2014 and 2017, respectively, have since expanded to allow a much broader mix of investors outside China to use renminbi to buy some mainland equities and bonds. Before these programs began, licensing and quotas restricted direct access to Chinese markets, with only about 228 large institutional investors receiving quotas in 2013; today, about 1,000 investors have that status. In 2025, foreign trading through Stock Connect averaged 212 billion yuan ($29.5 billion) per day, and Bond Connect averaged 39 billion yuan ($5.4 billion) per day. The tools available to manage the risks associated with these investments have also expanded. Swap Connect, launched in 2023, allows offshore investors to hedge against movements in onshore renminbi interest rates.

Access to China’s financial markets is no longer the biggest problem facing foreign investors, but the risk that Beijing’s unpredictable capital controls could someday trap their funds remains a worry. A 2023 survey by the Insurance Asset Management Association of China and J.P. Morgan Asset Management found that roughly two-thirds of chief investment officers at insurance companies outside China cited controls on capital moving in and out of the country as a top concern for investing there. Despite greater access than ever, foreign investors remain reluctant to hold Chinese assets at scale. In March 2026, they held only 3.2 trillion yuan ($448 billion), or 1.6 percent of the Chinese bond market, compared with roughly $15.5 trillion, or 27 percent, of the U.S. bond market. Reserve holdings recorded with the IMF reveal an even wider gap: in the first quarter of 2026, the renminbi accounted for just under two percent of global foreign-exchange reserves, compared with 57 percent for the dollar. Without a far larger pool of renminbi assets that foreigners can freely buy and sell, the renminbi cannot come close to replacing the dollar.

For China to wield anything approaching the currency power of the United States, the renminbi must dominate trade in a good that China controls and the rest of the world cannot easily do without. In the dollar system, the global oil trade has long played this role—hence the term “petrodollar.” In a renminbi-ascendant system, the corresponding anchor could be the critical minerals, clean energy equipment, and electrical infrastructure that are central to green energy technology. If China consolidates its dominance over that industrial ecosystem, using its scale and cost advantages to prevent competitors from catching up, it could gain enough leverage to price those essential, hard-to-substitute exports in renminbi, creating the foundation for a “green yuan” that might eventually replace the petrodollar.

China has spent decades methodically assembling the supply chains that have made it the world’s dominant producer of green energy technology and equipment. Beijing is now on the verge of taking a commanding position across a set of goods that the world has decided it cannot do without. China’s strategy rests on vertical integration of nearly the entire clean energy supply chain. It is the leading refiner of 19 of the 20 energy-related strategic minerals tracked by the International Energy Agency, with an average market share of 70 percent. It accounts for roughly 85 percent of global solar panel manufacturing capacity, and it supplies 78 percent of the wind-turbine capacity installed worldwide. In 2025, it produced about 70 percent of the world’s electric vehicles.

After decisively seizing the first-mover advantage, Beijing is now consolidating its market position, using economies of scale to undercut prospective rivals and promote technical standards built around technologies owned by Chinese firms. The green energy economy is more diffuse than the fossil fuel system it seeks to replace and therefore more difficult to command. But China is already beginning to turn its market-share lead into structural advantages that could lock out competitors and entrench its dominance.

Until recently, Beijing focused more on extending its industrial lead in green energy than on converting that advantage into financial power. But that is beginning to change. The proliferation of carbon-neutral investment mandates has unintentionally created a green finance industry almost tailor-made for China. In 2022, Beijing published its “Green Bond Principles,” which require green bond issuers to allocate 100 percent of proceeds to eligible green projects.

By the end of 2025, funds dedicated to sustainable investment were worth $4.13 trillion worldwide, and assets managed according to sustainability criteria were projected to reach $40 trillion by 2030. Chinese entities, meanwhile, already had 47.2 trillion yuan ($6.7 trillion) in green loans and bonds outstanding, far exceeding any other country’s green lending, but largely confined to its domestic renminbi system. In 2024, foreign institutions held only 3.2 billion yuan ($445 million) of China’s 2.2 trillion yuan ($306 billion) green bond market, a minuscule 0.15 percent.

That meager foreign participation is likely to increase. Chinese authorities are working to turn more of the country’s vast pool of green debt—a term for loans and bonds issued for projects with a positive environmental impact—developed primarily for a domestic investor base, into tradable securities that foreign investors can hold in compliance with international sustainability mandates. Their objective is to create a broad class of renminbi-denominated assets that are internationally investable, tied to green projects, and integrated into the broader renminbi ecosystem for pricing, settlement, and other financial services.

About 17 percent of China’s green bond market has already been screened against technical criteria aligned with European green finance frameworks, making those bonds easier for foreign investors and index providers to recognize and include in their portfolios. The Ministry of Finance has begun issuing renminbi-denominated sovereign green bonds outside China, with its first bond issuance raising six billion yuan ($834 million) in London in April 2025, followed by a second six-billion-yuan issuance in Hong Kong this past May, where orders were ten times the amount on offer. These issues are tiny compared with China’s domestic market, but they establish pricing reference points that make it easier for other entities to issue renminbi-denominated green debt in the future. Pakistan’s issuance, in May, of a 1.75 billion yuan ($258 million) green Panda bond—the term for renminbi-denominated debt issued in China by foreign borrowers—offers a glimpse of a future in which foreign borrowers routinely raise renminbi in China to finance their green development.

This is how industrial dominance begins to grow into financial power. The Chinese government has no formal plans to create a green yuan, but the constituent pieces of such a system are nevertheless starting to come together. The anchor asset for a green yuan would not be green technology itself, but an expanding family of renminbi claims on the green economy. Green bonds would form this economy’s tradable core, connecting China’s industrial advantage to the growing global demand for sustainable assets.

Much of the world has set deadlines for replacing fossil fuels that cannot be met without China’s green economy. Even if the political will to combat climate change fades, global dependence on imported energy has created geopolitical vulnerabilities that will likely continue to buoy demand for renewables, which almost any country can deploy to produce more energy at home. For countries and firms seeking entry into the green economy, accepting renminbi financing and Chinese technical standards may eventually become part of the ordinary price of admission. The result would be a self-reinforcing circuit of green goods and green finance, much of it denominated in renminbi.

For Washington, the prospect of a green yuan should not set off alarms about an imminent renminbi takeover. It should instead prompt a harder question: whether the petrodollar is no longer fit for purpose and what asset class, technology, or industrial system might anchor the dollar’s currency power in the future. The dollar rests on far more than the United States’ ability to secure global energy flows and its ties with major oil-producing states, but policymakers would be mistaken to treat its supremacy as permanent.

Beijing is not plotting to dethrone the dollar, and the Communist Party almost certainly does not want the financial openness such a victory would require. Whether or not the green yuan becomes a reality someday, the more immediate value to the party of an internationalized renminbi is its potential to deter China hawks in Washington from weaponizing China’s current reliance on the dollar.

As China’s renminbi-based system becomes stronger, so will Beijing’s ability to withstand the shock of potential U.S. financial sanctions. Washington’s threat to impose those sanctions will, in turn, lose some of its potency. That shift in the economic power dynamic would likely make Beijing more willing to call Washington’s bluff—which it may already be doing. In May, China issued its first-ever blocking order, instructing firms in China not to comply with U.S. sanctions on five Chinese oil refiners alleged to be major purchasers of Iranian oil.

If the reign of King Dollar ever ends, it probably won’t be because China usurped the throne but rather because the United States surrendered it. Washington must take note that the strategic asset underpinning the next monetary order may not be a barrel of oil but an industrial ecosystem. The danger is that financial markets may provide little warning that such a transition is underway. Markets can go long stretches ignoring the mounting evidence of change before a catalyst—such as a political stalemate over raising the U.S. debt limit—finally causes models to adjust and prices to snap up or down. U.S. officials are reluctant to plan for the erosion of the dollar’s dominance for fear that doing so would signal to markets that such a decline is inevitable. Their eagerness to point to price charts as proof of the dollar’s resilience, however, suggests that the lessons of the last financial crisis may already be forgotten. The United States must make contingency plans before the dollar’s exorbitant privilege is visibly tattered and signs of hedging against it become clear. By that time, the damage may no longer be possible to contain.

Zongyuan Zoe Liu is Maurice R. Greenberg Senior Fellow for China Studies at the Council on Foreign Relations and Senior Research Scholar at the Institute for Global Politics at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs. She is the author of Sovereign Funds: How the Communist Party of China Finances Its Global Ambitions.

#13. Midwest pro-Trump state could hold key to Republicans' midterm hopes

Fox News Digital attended a fundraiser House Majority Whip Tom Emmer spoke at on behalf of Rep. Zach Nunn in Des Moines, Iowa.

DES MOINES, Iowa — House Republicans are pinning hopes of keeping their majority on a state that President Donald Trump won by roughly 13 points in November 2024.

And while Iowa has leaned red in recent years, Republicans are now finding themselves defending three of its four congressional districts as polls give Democrats more hope by the day that the key to a blue wave runs through the Midwest.

But Republicans are dismissing public perception surveys as a political cudgel used by the media and the left to discourage GOP voters, while insisting the results will come down to one thing.

"Nobody knows what's going to happen on November 3. But I'm here to tell you, if our people show up, we win. If our people don't show up … then we're going to be scratching and clawing to hang on to every inch that we've got," House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., told a room of GOP supporters in Dubuque, Iowa, on Thursday.

MEDIA NARRATIVE PREDICTING BLUE WAVE IN KEY BATTLEGROUND STATE NOT MESHING WITH LOCAL REPUBLICANS: 'FIRED UP'

President Donald Trump arrives to speak at a rally at the Iowa State Fairgrounds, on July 3, 2025, in Des Moines, Iowa. (Alex Brandon/AP Photo)

Fox News Digital joined Emmer and several other House Republicans on a two-district swing in Iowa late last week. The No. 3 House GOP leader spent his afternoon at an event for congressional candidate Joe Mitchell in Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, followed by a fundraiser for Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa, in Des Moines in the evening.

At both events, he argued that polling showing Democrats with a growing advantage was incorrect, but he and others are still warning that getting Republicans out to vote will be key to the party’s success.

"Republicans do not like to participate in surveys," Emmer told people Thursday evening in Des Moines. "We are very suspicious of the people who are giving the information to and the databases they’re putting us in. By the way, there are Republicans who answer these surveys who may tell exactly the opposite of what they actually stand on, because again, we don’t trust them."

CRITICAL HOUSE RACE THAT COULD DECIDE CONTROL OF CONGRESS HITS HOME STRETCH AS GOP REP WARNS WHAT'S AT STAKE

Fox News Power Rankings show all but one of Iowa’s four congressional districts are in play. Nunn’s district and the one represented by Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa, both "lean Democrat." The seat Mitchell is vying to take over from retiring Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, is ranked a "toss-up."

Republicans across the country are privately worrying that Trump’s low approval numbers coupled with some of his more unpopular policies could drag down the GOP. Add in the overall high cost of living and gas prices, some on the right are bracing for a 2018-style blue wave.

TRUMP’S BEEF IMPORT SCHEME WREAKS HAVOC ON FED-UP RED STATE CATTLE RANCHERS

Two of the policies that could sandbag Republican candidates in Iowa in particular are Trump’s tariffs and his decision to import foreign beef. The agriculture-heavy state has been hit particularly hard so far, with tariffs making farm equipment and other materials more expensive, while Trump's trade war with China has hit American farmers hard with Beijing's retaliation.

Trump has sought to mitigate the impact of his steel tariffs in particular, announcing plans last month for a $15 billion steel plant in Lee County, Iowa.

Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa, speaks during a news conference at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 15, 2025. (Eric Lee/Bloomberg)

But both Nunn and Mitchell are confident in the races they are running.

TRUMP-LINKED SUPER PAC PULLS FUNDING FROM 2 HOUSE REPUBLICANS AS GOP FIGHTS TO KEEP MAJORITY

"We feel very confident about the race. And that's because we've talked to every voter we can, asked for their vote on November 3, and we've been traveling the district for the last 13 months — all 22 counties, rural and suburban and urban, telling people, this is an election of common sense versus crazy," Mitchell told Fox News Digital. "We have the hardest workers on the ballot."

Nunn told attendees at his event, "Not only is Iowa at the front line of the entire country when it comes to making sure we've got three competitive House seats, Des Moines, Iowa, the third district, our proud district, is now one of the most competitive in the country."

"So not only are we on the front line, we get to be at the tip of the spear," Nunn said, weeks after he led a bipartisan bill aimed at curbing Trump's imports of foreign beef.

And despite the national-level outlook on Trump, turning out the president’s supporters could be the difference between narrowly keeping the GOP majority and losing control of the House.

TRUMP SAYS POLLS 'DON'T ACCOUNT FOR ONE THING,' AS HE PLEDGES TO DEFEAT COMMUNISTS 'ONCE AND FOR ALL'

Trump, for his part, is doing what he can to motivate the base.

Nunn kicked off his Thursday evening event shortly after a phone call with Trump, during which the president said he "is committed to making sure we remain here in Iowa," the congressman said.

Trump is also set to descend on the state later this week for a rally in Sioux City, though it’s taking place in the only safe district for Republicans in the state.

"I'm always competing. I don't care if it's Iowa, I don't care if it's Pennsylvania, Ohio, Nevada, Texas, Florida, they're all important to this midterm," Emmer told Fox News Digital. "This midterm, to me, will come down to about 10 seats. Everybody talks about 20-plus. No. It's going to be a very narrow end, and for Republicans, Iowa is a great example. If the Republicans come out to vote, we're going to be just fine."

House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., speaks during a press conference with members of the Republican Study Committee and other members of House Republican leadership in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 28, 2025. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)

If the fate of the House majority did come down to the results of just 10 seats, that would mean Iowa would be responsible for roughly one-third of that success.

And while not all Republicans are as confident in the GOP’s chances in Iowa, they do agree that the final results will come down to turnout.

"This goes one of two ways — and both aren’t great for Republicans. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, Joe Mitchell, and Zach Nunn either win by the skin of their teeth or it’s complete and total obliteration on November 3," a GOP operative familiar with campaigns in Iowa told Fox News Digital. "There is no in-between. If Republican voters turn out to the polls, there’s hope. If not, it’s going to be bad."

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

#14. The Conciliator

On the night of Sept. 30, the last day that the U.S. Senate was in session before breaking for fall recess, Sen. Jeanne Shaheen strode onto the chamber’s floor and made an unusual request.

The 79-year-old Democratic lawmaker sought to force a vote to confirm 10 new ambassadors. The nominees weren’t the big campaign donors who typically get glitzy posts in Paris and Rome. They were career diplomats, tapped to represent Washington in places such as Benin, Sierra Leone, Malaysia, and Kyrgyzstan, whose nominations are frequently held up for political horse-trading. And sure enough, despite having had successful confirmation hearings, their nominations had stalled amid partisan fighting.

On the night of Sept. 30, the last day that the U.S. Senate was in session before breaking for fall recess, Sen. Jeanne Shaheen strode onto the chamber’s floor and made an unusual request.

The 79-year-old Democratic lawmaker sought to force a vote to confirm 10 new ambassadors. The nominees weren’t the big campaign donors who typically get glitzy posts in Paris and Rome. They were career diplomats, tapped to represent Washington in places such as Benin, Sierra Leone, Malaysia, and Kyrgyzstan, whose nominations are frequently held up for political horse-trading. And sure enough, despite having had successful confirmation hearings, their nominations had stalled amid partisan fighting.

Fed up with the lack of progress, Shaheen—the top Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee—made her move. She played the China card. Shaheen gave a speech highlighting the dearth of confirmed U.S. ambassadors while Beijing makes diplomatic inroads around the globe.

As she spoke, she gestured to two world maps juxtaposing where the United States and China have ambassadors. While the map of China’s top envoys appeared to be almost filled out, the U.S. map showcased gaping white spaces across most of Africa, with many other unfilled positions in Latin America, Asia, and Europe. Empty posts in Russia and Brazil loomed particularly large.

U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen points to a map of filled U.S. ambassadorships as Secretary of State Marco Rubio testifies during a Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington on Jan. 28. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

Shaheen finished her remarks and requested the confirmation of the nominees. None of the other 99 senators objected—an almost unheard-of result in today’s polarized Senate.

“I think this is very uniquely Jeanne Shaheen,” said Naz Durakoglu, the Democratic staff director on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and a longtime staffer for Shaheen, recalling how other Senate staff for both Democrats and Republicans laughed when they realized what the senator was doing and that she was going to get away with it. “Because she was the one doing it, no one objected.”

Shaheen, who is retiring at the end of the year, has spent nearly two decades on Capitol Hill working in a bipartisan manner to strike modest compromises. That hasn’t always made her popular with the Democratic base, which has been hunting for its own flamethrowers to meet the challenge of U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term.

Flamethrower she is not. Rather, Shaheen operates as a conciliator, doing the often-unglamorous work of trying to build consensus. No matter how outraged she may be over Trump’s latest norm-defying move, she always speaks in measured, even tones.

“You can’t just say ‘I’m going to give up.’ You’ve got to keep at it. I believe in persistence,” the senator said during a June interview in her office in the Senate’s Hart Office Building.

In her two final years in office, Shaheen has had to watch some of her signature foreign-policy achievements—such as securing initiatives to advance women’s rights, which she spent years painstakingly building bipartisan support for—come undone. Will her legacy be defined by Trumpism, or does her story still have a twist in the tale?

Rubio stands between Shaheen and Republican Sen. Jim Risch during Rubio’s Senate Foreign Relations Committee confirmation hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington on Jan. 15, 2025.Jabin Botsford/The Washington Post via Getty Images

Prominently featured in Shaheen’s office is a large wood-and-glass display case full of the challenge coins that the senator has received throughout her long public service career, including from the New Hampshire Air National Guard, the U.S. Navy, and various U.S. embassies around the globe. On the walls is a series of framed woodblock prints by New Hampshire artist Matt Brown, who loaned them to the office.

New Hampshire is not just the state that Shaheen represents—it’s a place whose politics deeply shaped her.

She was the state’s governor for six years, from 1997 to 2003. Because of the moderate nature of New Hampshire’s electorate, which lately trends Democratic but still elects Republicans for statewide office, Shaheen believes that she has bipartisan policymaking in her DNA.

“The whole time I was governor, I had a Republican legislature,” she said. “My career in politics has been about trying to work in a bipartisan manner.”

New Hampshire is unique in having an elected Executive Council, also known as a governor’s council. “It’s a carryover from colonial days, and it approves all nominees and all contracts. And the governor and council meet in public session twice a month,” Shaheen said, adding that throughout her tenure as governor, Republicans held nearly all the seats on the council. “So, in order to get anything done, we had to figure out how to work together.”

The senator’s legislating philosophy is similar to her governing philosophy and can generally be summed up by the old aphorism: “Don’t let the perfect be the enemy of good.”

That ethos has guided many of Shaheen’s conversations with fellow Democrats during the second Trump administration. It has also enabled multiple small but meaningful policy wins, such as in summer 2025, when she voted to confirm Mike Waltz as the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations in exchange for the White House releasing $75 million in withheld foreign aid to humanitarian programs in Haiti and Nigeria.

Shaheen also teamed up with Republican Sen. Jim Risch on legislation targeting Russia’s shadow fleet—the aging, reflagged oil tankers that Moscow uses to evade energy sanctions.

Those penalties eventually made it into the massive new Russia sanctions law that Trump signed in September. Shaheen wasn’t the initial sponsor of the broader law—that was the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham—but she played a no less pivotal role in prodding Democrats, who were leery over giving Trump additional powers to impose sweeping tariffs, into holding their noses and backing the legislation to support Ukraine.

“In my mind, it’s a trade-off, and I think the most critical issue right now is putting pressure on [Russian President Vladimir] Putin and trying to do everything we can to end the war in Ukraine,” Shaheen said. “Is it a perfect bill? No. Legislation is never perfect. But would it help us to really put pressure on Putin? The answer is yes.”

With Graham’s unexpected passing, Shaheen stepped forward to shoulder even more of the work of muscling the Russia sanctions legislation through the House and the Senate. As it happened, “the tremendous shock of Graham’s death really crystallized in people’s minds how important it was to get this done,” said Amy English, the deputy staff director for Democrats on Senate Foreign Relations. “This was literally Graham’s final wish.”

Even so, it took Shaheen and her strong working relationships with Republicans such as Sen. Roger Wicker, the chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, and Sen. Katie Britt, to hammer out sufficient agreements on amendments with Republicans and Democrats to clear a procedural path to passage.

“It really does take someone that is absolutely dogged in seizing the moment to push something like this through,” English said, observing that Shaheen cleared much of her schedule last month when the House took up and subsequently passed the Russia sanctions bill.

Short-term waivers are a start, but Congress must act on the full repeal Syria needs to rebuild.

Cutting off independent media abroad leaves the United States vulnerable at home.

A senior member of the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee on Nord Stream 2, Belarus, and Biden’s upcoming summit with Putin.

Advancing global women’s rights has been a passion for Shaheen since her earliest years in the Senate, which she joined in 2009.

When I visited Shaheen’s office in June, I was eight months pregnant and more out of breath than I cared to admit from the short walk from the Uber to her office. Shaheen and her staff greeted me warmly, asking how I was managing in the intense summer heat. If they noticed that, beneath my long dress, one of my swollen ankles had burst the strap of my sandal, they were too gracious to comment.

I later learned from one of her aides that all the staff on the leadership teams in Shaheen’s personal office and on the Democratic side of the Foreign Relations Committee are working moms. “It just tells you about her values,” Durakoglu said.

In the Senate, Shaheen has pushed for the establishment of an ambassador-at-large for global women’s issues and painstakingly secured passage during the first Trump administration of her Women, Peace, and Security Act (WPS), which requires the U.S. government to develop strategies for increasing the role of women in conflict prevention and peace processes around the world.

When Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced in April 2025 that he was ending the Defense Department’s implementation of the WPS law, Shaheen released a statement that accused the defense chief of having “absolutely no idea what he’s doing.”

More than a year later, she is still clearly upset with Hegseth’s decision. But she uses the language of a diplomat to express that dismay.

“It’s frustrating, and I think it’s bad policy,” Shaheen said, citing data she has showing that societies that empower women are more stable and tend to be more democratic. “I think Hegseth and the policies of this administration are…”—here she breaks for a prolonged pause to find the right word—“…not only shortsighted; they’re wrong.”

U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick greets Shaheen before testifying during a budget hearing in Washington on April 22. Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call via Getty Images

For someone just months from retirement, Shaheen doesn’t seem to be slowing down.

After Trump announced on Oct. 9 that he was unilaterally lifting U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel, Shaheen worked quickly with Democrats and Republicans to release a bipartisan statement condemning the move.

“We’re doing so much more than when she wasn’t retiring,” Durakoglu told me. “Part of the reason for that is because, deep down, she probably is worried about what this place is going to look like after her and some of her colleagues with similar mindsets leave. But she wouldn’t be trying this hard and putting herself out there in this way if she didn’t think there was a good chance that her way would succeed.”

The senator’s ability to work with Republicans in specific policy areas such as shoring up support for Ukraine notwithstanding, it’s clear that Shaheen is disappointed with how her GOP colleagues have accepted many of Trump’s foreign-policy moves that they would have surely opposed had they been undertaken by a Democratic president.

Republicans’ failure to conduct oversight of Trump’s nearly eight-month war with Iran, which he launched with little forewarning and no congressional authorization, weighs heavily on Shaheen’s mind. I asked if she thinks that the experience of the Iran war might finally prompt Republicans to reassert themselves to rein in a wayward commander in chief.

She rattled off a long list of what she sees as the war’s strategic failures, from Iran’s increased control of the Strait of Hormuz to having a more hard-line regime in Tehran than there was before the war. “I have not heard one Republican acknowledge that, even behind closed doors,” she said, before adding, “which is shocking.”

I also asked if she sensed in Republicans any greater willingness to defend their constitutional power of the purse.

“They’re really not very willing to engage even in the conversation. It’s more about, ‘Well, that’s Donald Trump. I can’t do anything about him.’ That’s sort of the attitude,” Shaheen said.

In September, the White House canceled almost $1 billion in congressionally directed spending toward programs that mostly benefit refugees and unaccompanied minors crossing into the United States.

“So many of the Republicans who were willing to take a stand against Trump are gone, either voluntarily or like [Sen. Bill] Cassidy, because Trump is opposed,” Shaheen said. Cassidy, who voted to convict Trump in the Senate’s impeachment trial following the Jan. 6, 2021, insurrection, lost in a party primary earlier this year to a hard-line MAGA challenger backed by the president.

Shaheen speaks at the Eleanor Roosevelt Dinner in Concord, New Hampshire, on Oct. 3. Joseph Prezioso/AFP via Getty Images

“My argument is: ‘So you lose your election? What’s more important? Your principles, or staying in office?’ And that argument just doesn’t carry much weight with most people,” Shaheen said.

Polls have been painting an increasingly grim picture for Republicans’ prospects in next month’s midterm elections. If Democrats wind up winning the House and potentially even the Senate, Trump’s war against Iran will have played a significant role in costing Republicans much of their power on Capitol Hill.

Shaheen is hopeful that the November vote could represent a turning point. “It’ll be interesting to see in the upcoming elections if there are any of those states that have historically been Republican but don’t vote Republican this time,” she said. “I think that’s what it’s going to take in order to get people to think about doing more to work together.”

#15. Bari Weiss’ pro-MAGA CBS News pivot is falling flat

When I watched veteran “60 Minutes” correspondent Lesley Stahl report from the West Bank on a recent Sunday night, my first thought was to wonder how the segment had slipped past the watchful eyes of Bari Weiss. Stahl accompanied a group of Palestinians trying to reach their own land, only to be confronted by Israeli settlers clad in black. The Palestinians had approached the settlers with their hands behind their backs to make plain they posed no threat. One man was headbutted in the face and his nose fractured. An Israeli army captain finally defused the standoff, but the Palestinians never reached their property and the settlers appeared to suffer no consequences. It was a riveting piece of television, framed by the Oct. 27 Israeli elections.

The report did not slip past Weiss, of course. Within a day, Oliver Darcy of the Status newsletter reported that screenings of the segment had grown extraordinarily contentious, with the CBS News editor-in-chief taking a “very, very hands-on” role and Stahl, who has been at the broadcast since 1991, privately floating the idea of quitting. Darcy’s sources said Weiss’ objections were not confined to a single factual assertion but ranged far more broadly, and that some on the team were unsure the report would even air at all.

CBS News, for its part, called the Status account a “ludicrous, twisted narrative” and insisted the piece received far fewer edits than most. Perhaps so. But even the network’s version concedes the larger point: A correspondent of Stahl’s stature had to survive an internal fight over an eyewitness account of violence that she and her crew watched unfold.

The former Free Press editor arrived at the network promising to rescue mainstream news from ideological conformity. Yet her tenure has increasingly been defined by disputes over editorial interference, the departure of veteran journalists and a growing perception that certain political narratives receive more scrutiny than others.

That contradiction sits at the heart of the Bari Weiss experiment. The former Free Press editor arrived at the network promising to rescue mainstream news from ideological conformity. Yet her tenure has increasingly been defined by disputes over editorial interference, the departure of veteran journalists and a growing perception that certain political narratives receive more scrutiny than others. As I’ve previously argued, the crisis at CBS News is bigger than one controversial editor. It is about what happens when corporate power no longer values a news organization’s independence as a principle to be defended.

Under the watch of Skydance boss David Ellison and Weiss, whom he handpicked, CBS News’ rightward renovation is running into a problem. The internal revolt at the network has become a daily reality for rank-and-file employees who watched the forced departures of foundational figures like Scott Pelley, Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega. The journalists who remain have not all agreed to become instruments of Weiss’ apparent worldview; many are leaking their misgivings to media reporters. Nor do the audience numbers establish that replacing an investigative institution’s identity with a slickly packaged right-wing populist brand constitutes a successful business strategy. Now the network is caught struggling to hold on to the credibility it inherited while forging the political project its leadership appears determined to impose.

If you want to hear what passes for rigor in Weiss’ newsroom, the tape is available. After Weiss fired London bureau chief Claire Day in April — her offense was apparently coverage of Israel that displeased the new regime — she installed Shayndi Raice as foreign editor. Last week Raice summoned the foreign staff to a virtual meeting and delivered a 15-minute tirade that Status obtained on audio and later released in full. “This is not your publishing platform,” she told the assembled journalists. “This is a company that we all work for, and there’s a hierarchy in place.” Failure to follow that hierarchy, she explained, “is called insubordination, and it’s legal grounds for firing.”

When Holly Williams, the veteran correspondent whose report on the anniversary of the Oct. 7 attacks had been edited to remove the Palestinian death toll, respectfully challenged her, Raice informed Williams that she had gotten her own story “wrong.” Williams, Raice said, does not know it as well as she does. As for the figure itself — more than 74,000 Palestinians killed in Israel’s bombardment of Gaza — Raice waved it off as a “magic number.” Including it in the report, she suggested, amounted to “posturing” rather than journalism.

The same partisan thumb has appeared on the scales in CBS’s domestic political coverage. Semafor’s Max Tani reported that Weiss has taken a personal interest in Michigan’s Senate race, and she has pushed CBS journalists to pursue story after story about Democratic nominee Dr. Abdul El-Sayed and his supposed sympathy for the Muslim Brotherhood, raising the subject on editorial calls and tasking the network’s investigative unit with combing his background for a link to the organization.

The raw material for this enterprise is a 2012 tweet by El-Sayed’s half-sister describing a conversation with their mother about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood in Egypt in the early 1970s. El-Sayed has disavowed the group. He has explained that his parents divorced when he was young and that he was raised by his father and stepmother, and the leap from a mother’s politics in another country half a century ago to a candidate’s secret loyalties is the kind American journalism once required evidence to make.

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only, written by Amanda Marcotte, now also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

To be fair, El-Sayed is a legitimate story. A Senate candidate’s family history is fair game, and there is nothing inherently scandalous in an editor telling reporters to look into it. The scandal, though, is in the selectivity. The same editor who dispatched investigators after a Democrat on the strength of his mother’s biography also tasked staff with pursuing the theory that James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas, had secretly checked into a mental health facility during his nine-day absence from the campaign trail, a claim right-wing influencers manufactured out of a bad case of the flu — and one that collapsed on contact with a hospital’s denial and time-stamped security footage. One CBS staffer told Semafor that Weiss’ story ideas “routinely come from social media influencers or from opposition research that’s been placed in conservative outlets,” and that the resulting reports “usually leave out important context and facts.”

It is worth highlighting what unites the targets: El-Sayed and Talarico are both progressives who have criticized Israel’s conduct in Gaza and the West Bank.

What Weiss is building with her other hand is a stage to platform MAGA. Her signature project is Things That Matter, a town-hall series she devised and launched by interviewing Erika Kirk, the widow of Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk, in a December broadcast that drew 1.87 million viewers, which was notably down 11% from what CBS ordinarily draws in that hour. Of the series’ single-guest town halls since, exactly one has featured a Democrat, Maryland Governor Wes Moore. The segment’s latest installment on Saturday handed a Michigan stage to Vice President JD Vance a little over two weeks out from the midterm elections, in a state where the administration needs every vote it can find.

Ironically, the format’s one unscripted moment came from the audience. Joey Amor, whose wife, Master Sgt. Nicole Amor ,was one of six American soldiers killed in an Iranian drone strike on an outpost in Kuwait in March, asked the vice president when this administration would hold its own officials accountable for the failures that left those troops exposed. Vance pleaded unfamiliarity, explaining that “sometimes information doesn’t filter up to me.”

The irony was abundant: A town hall designed as a coronation had accidentally produced a news story, and the news was that the vice president of the United States had nothing to say to a man widowed by President Donald Trump’s war of choice.

Now consider what the new CBS has gotten for all this friction. “60 Minutes” recently saw the smallest audience of the season and the smallest for a fourth episode in at least a quarter century. The season premiere in September managed 7.94 million, a 21% drop from 2025 and the weakest opening this century.

This is a broadcast that grew 9% last season. Nobody was asking Weiss to fix it.

#17. DOJ charges 28 in California with voting crimes as election tensions escalate

People vote in Norwalk, Calif., during early voting in California's primary election on June 1, 2026. The Department of Justice has charged 28 green card holders in the state for allegedly illegally registering to vote or voting in U.S. elections, in an escalation of a feud with California officials over the state's voting system. Frederic J. Brown/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

The Justice Department announced on Monday it was charging 28 noncitizens with election crimes in California, signaling a further escalation over the state's voting system that looks like it will continue through Election Day and beyond.

The DOJ also filed an emergency request in federal court to stop California from processing ballots returned by people on the voter rolls whom the federal government says are "likely noncitizens." The state has asked for specific information on how the federal government came to its conclusions, but has not received it.

"This Department of Justice will not look the other way while noncitizens vote in federal elections," Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said at a press conference on Monday announcing the election crime charges. "Unfortunately the same can't be said for California and L.A. County."

Noncitizen voting has never been found to be a widespread problem in American elections, but the Trump administration is devoting significant resources to uncovering the ineligible voting that does occur. The DOJ has been announcing handfuls of new charges almost every day as early voting gets underway in many states.

The Justice Department's latest request in federal court is a continuation of a saga that began this summer with President Trump's primetime speech on election integrity. It took a major turn last week with the delivery of a flash drive to Los Angeles County that contained 20,000 names and a 48-hour deadline to investigate them. Local and state officials declined to do so, and the federal government sued.

McCotter escalated the dispute further on Friday by warning California officials in a letter that they could be criminally prosecuted for knowingly processing ballots "cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens." President Trump wrote on Truth Social that evening: "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!"

Taken together, the threats have local officials and election experts worried that the adversarial posture of the Justice Department towards California portends more actions to come aimed at delegitimizing results in this fall's midterms.

"There's a few things to be worried about," said Rick Hasen, an election law expert who runs UCLA's Safeguarding Democracy Project. "One is the risk of disenfranchising eligible voters. The other is the risk that it further undermines voter confidence in the electoral process by making it seem like [noncitizen voting] is a major problem when it is not. And the third risk is that this is going to be used as some sort of pretext to try to seize ballots or interfere after the election is over."

Dana Lewis, the Republican county recorder for Pinal County, Ariz., said local officials nationwide are watching and communicating about what's happening in California, the same way they did when the FBI raided an elections office in Fulton County, Ga. in January.

If those officials are administering a race this fall that is close or contested, they feel they could be next, she said.

"When this impacts another jurisdiction, you automatically have to feel that," Lewis said. "If it's happening in Georgia, if it's happening in Colorado or California, we're all watching."

All 28 people charged in California on Monday are green-card holders, and all appeared on the list of 20,000 names the DOJ gave California officials last week, according to DOJ officials.

A number of them do not appear to have actually voted, and some registered to vote more than 20 years ago. Many are accused of making false statements in their naturalization applications, which ask whether applicants previously registered to vote or claimed U.S. citizenship.

Previous research has shown that when noncitizen voting and registration occurs, it is also often the result of bureaucratic error and not intentional fraud. New Jersey revealed this summer that a software glitch at the DMV registered more than 6,000 people to vote even though they had indicated they were noncitizens.

Bill Essayli, the First Assistant U.S. Attorney for California's Central District, downplayed that possibility on Monday, however.

"It's not something that just happens to you," Essayli said. "They either attested to it when they got a driver's license, or they went out of their way to file a voter registration form, and they swore under oath that they were a citizen."

In the past seven weeks, the Justice Department has charged 113 noncitizens across 20 states with voting and registration crimes, officials said at Monday's press conference.

UCLA's Hasen said the charges seem to be meant to make noncitizen voting "look like a bigger issue than it is."

"Given that there's over 20 million registered voters in California, this is quite a small number of allegations," Hasen said. "And we don't know how many of these allegations will even pan out. And so even if all of these were in fact people who were illegally voting, it's a drop in the bucket compared to the number of voters in California."

Recent polling suggests a sizable portion of the American public thinks immigration enforcement will be present at voting locations this fall, despite federal law banning armed federal agents from the polls. Non-white voters are more likely than white voters to say they fear voting could put them at risk of being questioned by immigration authorities despite being citizens.

In an interview earlier this fall with NPR, Los Angeles County's top voting official, Dean Logan, alluded to those worries.

"Given everything leading up to this election, what we're trying to remind voters is the best way to secure the election is through your participation," Logan told NPR. "Don't be distracted by the litigation. Don't be distracted by the mis- and disinformation. If you have questions, let us know, let us answer them. But don't let this keep you from voting," he said.

"Because if you're not voting, none of the rest matters, right?"

The Justice Department's request that a federal judge block California and Los Angeles County from processing ballots from the list of 20,000 "likely noncitizens" it gave state officials last week is unprecedented and an especially unusual request given that voting is already underway.

California officials have argued that complying with the Department's demand to set the ballots aside would be unlawful and noted the DOJ has not confirmed that the voters on the list are noncitizens.

"The extraordinary measures you demand are contrary to both federal and state law," California Secretary of State Shirley Weber wrote to the DOJ's McCotter on Oct. 13.

"Withholding ballots from some duly registered voters and segregating and refusing to tabulate voted ballots submitted by others, is an unprecedented suspension — and even denial — of voting rights," she wrote.

Los Angeles County's assistant county counsel, Peter Bollinger, wrote to McCotter on Oct. 15: "we are not authorized to, or are prohibited from, taking the actions requested in your letter under both federal and state law. The actions described would disenfranchise those in question without due process." The same letter noted the list of names from the DOJ included voters from outside Los Angeles County, whom the office does not maintain any records on.

Both letters cited the National Voter Registration Act, a federal law that bars states from systematically removing ineligible voters from state voter rolls during the 90 days before an election. The law is supposed to prevent mistakes that could erroneously purge eligible voters right before an election without giving voters time to correct errors.

There are also questions about the methodology the Trump administration used to come up with its tally of 20,000 likely noncitizens and its accuracy. A July letter to California from the Department of Homeland Security alleged the state had a potential of 190,000 noncitizens on its rolls.

In Monday's press briefing, McCotter said the 20,000 figure represented the people the Justice Department had the most confidence were noncitizens after DHS cross-referenced various government databases and other records with identifying information.

McCotter and other DOJ officials blamed California for not handing over its entire voter roll — including partial Social Security Numbers and driver's license numbers — which they said could help shed more light on the citizenship status of these voters. So far 26 federal judges have dismissed DOJ demands for that data across the country.

In the Justice Department's Monday filing for a restraining order preventing California from counting ballots from the 20,000 individuals, the DOJ wrote: "Once illegally cast ballots are counted and commingled with lawful votes, the resulting harm may be impossible to remedy. The urgency is heightened because of the fundamental right to vote and to have one's lawful vote counted without dilution."

A half dozen voting and civil rights organizations filed to intervene in the case last week to argue the DOJ's demands are unlawful.

Election experts have said the DOJ's lawsuit against California seems more about sending a political message or teeing up future challenges than winning this case in court, given that the constitution gives states the authority to administer elections.

"I expect this lawsuit to go nowhere," UCLA's Hasen wrote last week.

NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

#19. North Carolina Republicans battle headwinds in district redrawn in their favor

NEW BERN, N.C. – In the race for control of Congress, Democrats have history and momentum on their side.

But there was no sense of panic among Republican loyalists at a recent campaign rally here in North Carolina’s Inner Banks, where a newly redrawn House seat represents one of the GOP’s best pickup opportunities this year.

Like others in the crowd, Guy Gregg expressed confidence that Republicans will prevail, despite the fallout from soaring prices and an unpopular war.

“If you’re a politician, you’re always scared,’’ said Gregg, a former New Jersey state legislator who’s been active in local politics since moving here about six years ago. “If you’re not, you’re probably going to lose, so it’s good to be a little nervous.”

New Bern, a picturesque retirement spot known as the birthplace of Pepsi and the setting for the novel “The Notebook,” falls within red-leaning turf of Eastern North Carolina folded into the 1st District under the state’s new congressional map. By carving out rural counties in the heart of the state’s Black Belt, the Republican-controlled state legislature shifted the district from one that Donald Trump carried by 3 points in 2024 to one that would have backed him by 12.

Republicans are counting on the new map to help retired Army Col. Laurie Buckhout defy the current political headwinds and become the first Republican to represent the district since 1883. Buckhout is seeking a rematch against Democratic Rep. Don Davis, who beat her by less than 2 points under the old district lines in 2024. Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales rates the race a Toss-up.

The redrawn seat provides Buckhout with “a pretty significant structural advantage,” said Peter Francia, a political science professor at East Carolina University. “In a normal year, she would probably win.”

But Trump’s sinking poll numbers have scrambled the calculus and turned what was meant to be a likely Republican flip into a battleground race. Both sides have poured money into the contest, with outside groups dropping more than $20 million through mid-October.

Speaker Mike Johnson made a quick stop here Thursday to rally support for Buckhout – and convince any naysayers that Republicans will hold their House majority.

“I’m looking right into the camera and telling you the polls are wrong,’’ Johnson declared before several hundred people at a reception hall adjacent to the Neuse River. “If we turn out, we’re going to win.”

Buckhout, an Iraq War veteran, leaned on her military background while framing Davis and his fellow Democrats as champions of progressive causes and advocates for economic policies that tip into socialism.

“Remember how crazy it was when we had Democrats in charge?” she asked the audience. “We don’t want to go back to … open borders. We don’t want to go back to having all these tax advantages we have right now … rolled back and disappear. Crime will run rampant.”

A few hours earlier, Davis was outside a municipal building in New Bern’s historic downtown shaking hands with people lined up for the first day of in-person early voting. Even though this is new territory to him, many voters were familiar with the second-term Democrat.

Davis grew up on a tobacco farm in rural Snow Hill, some 50 miles west of New Bern. He graduated from the U.S. Air Force Academy, served in the state Senate and is a Presbyterian lay minister.

“We’re traveling every mile of the district,’’ Davis said in an interview. “People are tired of all of the fussing, the fighting, the attacks.”

Tyler Scott, a 19-year-old first-time voter, said he’s not following politics closely but recognized Davis from the ads: “He seems like the right guy.’’

Asked about his opinion on Trump, Scott brought up rising prices and the federal immigration crackdown.

“How are you supposed to get to work when the gas prices are so high?” said the teen, who is preparing to start college soon. “And everything that’s happened with [Immigration and Customs Enforcement], it’s just very sad.”

Davis has sought to walk a careful line in this socially conservative district, portraying himself as a centrist willing to occasionally cross party lines. He voted for an early iteration of Trump’s voting bill, now known as the SAVE America Act, and was one of eight Democrats to side with the GOP on a measure that would have required public schools to get parental consent before children could change their pronouns. A CQ Roll Call analysis of 2026 votes on which Trump’s position was publicly known found that Davis sided with the president nearly 70 percent of the time, second among Democrats only to Texas’ Henry Cuellar.

“When you look at the makeup of this district, there are going to be Davis-Trump supporters,” the congressman said. And while Buckhout has Trump’s endorsement, “that doesn’t take away my ability to work with him over the next two years, just as I have over the last two years.”

Buckhout said Davis’ moderation is a mask to cover for a more radical agenda. “He has a reputation as a nice guy,” she told the crowd at the rally. “So here’s what this nice guy did: He voted to keep the border open and to keep criminals pouring through it.”

The race has grown increasingly acrimonious. The pro-Democratic House Majority PAC, is running an ad highlighting Buckhout’s 2017 arrest in Georgia on a charge of driving under the influence of alcohol. (She pleaded guilty to reckless driving.) The spot also cites Buckhout’s recent fine and suspension by the prediction market Kalshi after she bet on her campaign.

Meanwhile, the Congressional Leadership Fund, the top House Republican super PAC, is airing an ad hitting Davis on transgender rights after he launched a commercial stating that the matter ought to be left to the states.

Jennifer Dacey, a Republican seeking reelection to Craven County school board, said cultural issues such as transgender rights motivate Republican voters while also pulling in moderates across party lines.

“It’s just common sense,” she said, “and people across the aisle don’t want that kind of nonsense playing out either. This is a pretty culturally conservative area, and folks don’t want to be on the cutting edge of social democrat policy.”

Republicans said rallying the base was key to winning in this bellwether district, and many were looking ahead to Trump’s visit to Eastern North Carolina on Tuesday.

Steve Stevenson, a member of the Carteret County GOP executive board, said he was fully supportive of the president’s agenda, including the war in Iran, though he felt “the timing could have been a little bit better” given the proximity to the midterm elections.

Gregg, the former New Jersey lawmaker, remained confident that Buckhout will come out ahead.

“If there was a concern, the concern is always energy,” he said. “But we added a whole seat, and we designed the seat, so we damn well ought to win.”

Bill Clark and Ryan Kelly contributed to this report.
