#39. Between the coasts, populist Democrats see room to reclaim lost ground in red states

Sam Forstag poses for a portrait on a ranch outside of Drummond, Montana on October 7, 2026. A former U.S. Forest Service smokejumper, Forstag is trying to flip a House seat in the state's 1st congressional district. Tailyr Irvine for NPR hide caption

WESTERN MONTANA — Voters are angry, and an unconventional crop of Democratic candidates see an opening in this year's midterms to reclaim territory others in the party have given up on.

From the Great Plains and Upper Midwest to the Deep South, campaigns are taking a page from a progressive brand of economic populism that once flourished away from the coasts.

They are betting that harnessing anger at corporate power and both parties might succeed when many voters believe the economy and government are not working for working people.

If successful, they could forge a new playbook to compete again in places Democrats used to win.

In Montana, former U.S. Forest Service smokejumper Sam Forstag is trying to flip a House seat by speaking directly and from his own experience about the economic stress facing many Montana voters.

"I was making 19 bucks an hour jumping out of airplanes for the federal government in a community where you'd be lucky to find a home for a half million bucks," says Forstag, who in 2022 joined an elite team of wildland firefighters parachuting into remote areas. "If a smokejumper is being left behind, a whole lot of other people are being left behind by both political parties."

When President Trump cut nearly 400 Forest Service jobs in Montana last year, Forstag was his union's vice president. Forstag says he tried to reach his Republican congressman, Ryan Zinke.

"Time and time again, I got crickets, so I decided if he's going to come after my coworkers and our members' jobs, I'm going to come and take his," Forstag told a crowd of smokejumpers and wildland firefighters this month at the Great Burn Brewery in Missoula.

Zinke ultimately retired, opening a district that runs some 400 miles between Yellowstone and Glacier National Parks. Trump won the district by double digits in 2024. Now it is considered a toss-up.

A mix of factors are upending the typical political dynamics inside the district.

With an influx of wealthy transplants since the pandemic, the Montana housing market has become among the most unaffordable in the nation. That squeeze has been compounded as the cost of groceries, gas and health insurance have also soared.

Former Montana Senator Jon Tester on his ranch in Big Sandy, Montana on October 6, 2026. Tester says the Democratic brand is not good in Montana, but believes the Iran war and rising costs could prompt some voters to give his party another look. Tailyr Irvine for NPR hide caption

Montana has not usually been thought of as a swing state in recent years. Not long ago, voters here regularly elected Republicans and Democrats. But as the urge for disruption and a strain of populist rhetoric trained on cultural elites and immigrants helped propel Trump to victory in 2016, Democrats increasingly struggled to hang on.

Sandi Ramos voted for President Obama twice before backing President Trump. Still she continued voting for Montana's Democratic senator, Jon Tester.

In the Biden era, Ramos soured on Democrats more broadly. She says overall she is pleased with the job Trump is doing, despite not liking him personally, and says it would be hard to vote for a Democrat, even Forstag.

"I don't think anything could happen that fast to make me vote for him," Ramos says. "Although I really respect him as a person and I like him."

With support from split ticket voters like Ramos, Tester was able to outperform national Democrats for years. But that record of electoral success came to an end in 2024, when he lost his bid for reelection.

Following the Blackfoot River and then crossing the Continental Divide, golden aspen trees give way to wide-open fields for wheat and peas where Tester's family has farmed for over a century.

"Where you're standing right now in 1960 was pretty damn blue," Tester says. "These were the children of homesteaders in the Great Depression. They understand the role government played. Before my grandfather died, he said if it wasn't for FDR, we wouldn't be on this place."

Tester says the Democratic brand here is not good. He believes many national Democrats have written off places between the Appalachians and the Rockies. But as the Iran war and tariffs spike prices for fertilizer and fuel under Trump, Tester says some voters may be willing to give Democrats another look.

Sam Forstag hears from farmers and ranchers at an event on a ranch outside of Drummond, Montana on October 7, 2026. Tailyr Irvine for NPR hide caption

That is one reason Forstag spent a sunny Wednesday afternoon talking with a group of farmers and ranchers gathered at Peterson Angus Ranch. Proprietor Sue Peterson also chairs the small Granite County Democratic Party. Atop a bluff with vistas in all directions, she says she has one theory why Democrats sometimes struggle to connect with ranchers or farmers in places they used to win.

"If you're dealing with animals, you're dealing with life and death all the time and sometimes the decisions are hard and it's hard to relate to someone in a suit," Peterson says.

Forstag says it is frustrating to hear so many Democrats talk about affordability like a novel messaging strategy or a buzzword.

"We don't change this by giving a new term to it," Forstag says in an interview. "We change it by changing who's in those damn rooms. Because there are politicians who have been sitting in those offices for 10, 20, 30 years and nothing has changed."

For Forstag, running as a populist means recalibrating the relationship between the people in power in Washington and the regular people who send them there.

"I'm going to answer to the people I've worked with for the last eight years," Forstag says. "I'm going to answer to people like the kid I was growing up, whose belly is full because of food stamps. It does not feel like that's who Congress is answering to right now."

Forstag poses for a portrait outside of Drummond, Montana on October 7, 2026. He says it is frustrating to hear Democrats talk about affordability like it is a buzzword. "We don't change this by giving a new term to it," he says. Tailyr Irvine for NPR hide caption

With a campaign hyper-focused on answering the economic pain shaping the lives of voters, Forstag has managed to attract endorsements from the party's left flank, like New York Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and also more moderate members of the Blue Dog Caucus in the House.

"Populist language is a way to unify disparate groups who might lean towards or be willing to vote for Democrats, but might have problems with the beliefs or the priorities of one or another constituency within the Democratic Party," says Georgetown University professor Michael Kazin, who studies the history of American populism.

In places like Iowa, Arkansas and Wisconsin this year, candidates are embracing a more specific identity – as prairie populists, a nod to the late 19th century political movement with Great Plains roots that united small farmers and workers against corporate monopolies.

Kazin says it was also a reaction to states in the heartland feeling neglected in favor of more populous, urban states on the coasts. Kazin says claiming this identity today allows candidates to tap into the anger that's fueling anti-establishment campaigns across the country this year, without alienating voters in more conservative-leaning states who might be put off by the party's toxic brand or divisive social issues.

In Iowa, Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek calls himself a "common sense prairie populist" and says his north star is "to go up there and fight for the people that can't afford to make a political donation or afford a lobbyist."

The Democratic candidate for governor, Rob Sand, is campaigning on issues like the big agriculture corporations stymieing politicians from addressing polluted water supplies.

In Kansas, Democrats have nominated the Rev. Adam Hamilton as their candidate for Senate. Hamilton does not use the kind of anti-establishment rhetoric employed by other Democrats showing traction in red states. But he often ends his stump speech citing the Wizard of Oz, which some historians see as an allegory for the 19th century populist movement.

"Do you remember what the scarecrow needed? A brain. And then what did the Tin Man need? The heart. And what did the Cowardly Lion need? Courage," Hamilton tells crowds. "This is what's missing in the United States Senate right now."

Forstag hears from farmers and ranchers at an event on a ranch outside of Drummond, Montana on October 7, 2026. Tailyr Irvine for NPR hide caption

For some Democrats, embracing this ethos is less about a position on the ideological spectrum and more about speaking to voters fed up with the status quo.

"The most common thing I've heard, whether I'm in Kansas or Wisconsin or Michigan, is we want a new generation of leaders and we want big and bold ideas. People are absolutely done with what they've known in the past," Michigan Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin told NPR after stumping for progressive Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed at a local Democratic club this summer in Michigan.

Jane Kleeb, the state party chair in Nebraska where Democrats are backing a mechanic running as an independent and a populist for Senate, says it is perplexing when Democrats complain that the only way to win power in the Senate is to reform its structure. She says the answer is to earnestly compete in more states.

"So trying to focus on eight battlegrounds never made mathematical sense," says Kleeb, who is also a vice chair at the Democratic National Committee.

But if Democrats gain ground in Republican-leaning places, it might not be clear how much of that success is a reflection on the type of candidates and messages or just the deteriorating national environment for Republicans.

GOP candidates are also feeling the pressure to speak to anger over the economy.

Campaigning across the vast district in an RV, Forstag's Republican opponent, veteran Aaron Flint, is promising to "make the Montana dream affordable again." As a conservative radio host, Flint has an intimate relationship with many Montana voters and hears about the challenges they are dealing with.

Aaron Flint, the GOP candidate for the House in Montana's 1st District, speaks ahead of an address by President Trump in Kalispell, Mont. on Oct. 14. Ross D. Franklin/AP hide caption

He is also trying to pierce Forstag's working class biography and effort to appeal to the middle, pointing out Forstag has campaigned with Ocasio-Cortez and lobbied in the off seasons for the ACLU. Flint says if Democrats take power, they will hike taxes and make Montana's problems worse.

"I'm not just running because of deep frustration with the damage that was done to this party by the Democrat party," Flint said in an interview after a stop in the old mining town of Butte. "I'm also running because there's some Republicans back in Washington that aren't doing enough to fix everything either."

Voter Nicholas Babcock is skeptical. He is a mail carrier in nearby Anaconda, where an old smelter for the once behemoth Anaconda Copper Company rises 585 feet above town. Babcock voted for Trump three times. He says the first term was more good than bad.

"The second term is the exact opposite," he says. "We have seen a complete betrayal of almost every campaign promise that was made. It just feels almost like a slap in the face that we were sold one thing and none of it was delivered."

Sam Forstag speaks at a rally geared toward former and current firefighters at the Great Burn Brewery on October 5, 2026 in Missoula, Montana. Tailyr Irvine for NPR hide caption

So Babcock showed up at a Forstag town hall. He says his hero was Charlie Kirk, the conservative activist who was assassinated last year. "He would listen to absolutely anybody, discuss anything with anybody," Babcock says. "I'm absolutely willing to change my mind."

Babcock says Forstag also knows what it's like to punch a clock and thinks he might actually buck the establishment. He hopes this politician will follow through.

With reporting by Barbara Sprunt in Nebraska, Stephen Fowler in Kansas and Danielle Kurtzleben in Iowa.

#41. Ilhan Omar's sister questioned by feds after dramatic DC home raid

Rep. Ilhan Omar's, D-Minn., husband, Tim Mynett, defends her immigration timeline outside their DC residence that Homeland Security Investigations raided on Monday amid a criminal fraud investigation. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

EXCLUSIVE: Rep. Ilhan Omar's older sister was questioned by federal investigators last week in relation to an immigration fraud probe into the congresswoman, Fox News Digital has learned.

Three sources familiar with the investigation said Sahra Noor voluntarily spoke with the investigators after the high-profile Monday morning raid on the residence Omar shares with her husband in Washington, D.C. It is not clear the scope of the conversation Noor had with investigators.

Like Omar, Noor came to the United States as a child fleeing the civil war in Somalia. She currently lives in Kenya, according to her LinkedIn page, but has been in the United States promoting her new book, "Salt in the Snow: A Somali Immigrant Story."

The House lawmaker's sister canceled a Minnesota stop on the book tour last week amid the fallout of the raid and the ensuing interview with authorities.

ILHAN OMAR'S SISTER SKIPS BOOK TOUR EVENT AMID WEEK OF CHAOS FOLLOWING RAID ON PROGRESSIVE'S DC HOME

Rep. Ilhan Omar, left, in patterned hijab and green scarf. Ilhan Omar's sister, Sahra Noor, speaking at an event at the University of Minnesota in 2016. (Stephen Maturen/Getty Images; University of Minnesota)

The book event, which was scheduled for Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, at the University of Minnesota Rochester, was promoted online by Garden Party Books, a local bookstore that listed itself as a "proud supporter" of the event alongside the university and the Rochester Public Library.

A representative from Garden Party Books told Fox News Digital last week that the event was canceled because Noor had a "family emergency." It is now revealed that last week she was questioned by federal investigators.

Omar’s D.C. home was raided by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the chief investigatory body of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), at around 6 a.m. last Monday. Sources confirmed to Fox News Digital that the agency executed a search warrant in relation to an immigration fraud probe.

Specifically, they are probing whether the lawmaker or her father falsified information when filling out her citizenship paperwork.

ILHAN OMAR'S TURBULENT WEEK EXPLAINED: THE DUELING PROBES THAT THREW THE SOMALI-BORN PROGRESSIVE INTO CHAOS

Homeland Security Investigations police search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on Oct. 12, 2026, in Washington, D.C. According to reports, the search is part of an ongoing criminal investigation. (Andrew Leyden/Getty Images)

Border czar Tom Homan revealed over the weekend that if the allegations are proven, they could lead to Omar’s denaturalization.

During the raid, Omar’s personal phone, passport and computer were seized, The Wall Street Journal reported last week. And Omar’s attorneys over the weekend demanded that the Justice Department return some of the property confiscated by HSI.

Additionally, The New York Times reported that about a dozen people, including Omar’s relatives, have been subpoenaed in the case.

Omar has not been seen publicly since before the raid, though her husband has been seen several times walking their dog, taking out the trash and speaking outside the home with one of the congresswoman's aides. Omar has not responded to Fox News Digital's repeated requests for comment, but she did react to the raid publicly on social media.

U.S. President Donald Trump's border czar Tom Homan speaks to reporters at the White House in Washington, D.C., on July 20, 2026. (REUTERS)

"This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," she said in a statement posted to X hours after feds descended on her home.

FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE

"For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," the post continued. "Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies."

In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital last Tuesday, Vice President JD Vance said the investigation is not politically motivated.

"We don't want to be like the Biden administration. We never want to be like that — where they would allow the law to go after their political opponents," he said.

DEMOCRATS' FURY OVER ILHAN OMAR RAID DRAWS STINGING GOP REMINDER ABOUT RAID FROM THE PAST: ‘SET THE PRECEDENT’

"We really want to let the law, the facts drive this," he continued. "And if justice requires something else be done, then, of course, we'll take a step when we have to."

Fox News Digital reached out to Noor, but did not hear back before publication.

Omar's attorneys did not immediately return a comment request.

#42. Trump’s Russia moves could complicate lame-duck agenda

Lawmakers in both parties are assailing President Donald Trump for a series of decisions this month that critics say ally the U.S. government with the Kremlin amid its ongoing war on Ukraine, now in its fifth year.

In the last 10 days, the U.S. government:

Zelenskyy has also said Ukraine is being pressured by U.S. officials to halt strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.

And Ukraine’s president told Bloomberg News over the weekend that the United States is slowing deliveries of U.S.-built Patriot antimissile interceptors already paid for by European nations.

Zelenskyy has publicly criticized these moves with unusual candor. Trump has attacked Zelenskyy, telling reporters earlier this month that the Ukrainians “should get a new president.”

A handful of Ukraine’s Republican allies in Congress, joining with most Democrats, are promising obstacles for the president’s lame-duck legislative agenda if the perceived tilt toward Moscow continues.

Even more resistance on this issue could arise next year if Democrats gain control of the House or Senate in the 120th Congress.

With thin majorities in both chambers for the rest of the year, it would not take many GOP mavericks to threaten, for example, the prospects for the NDAA and the Defense spending bills, among other measures.

On Sunday, Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., a Trump loyalist, said on Fox News’ “Sunday Morning Futures” that there are concerns in House panels such as Intelligence and Foreign Affairs about the president waiving Russia sanctions, and he said more discussions need to occur with the White House on the issue.

Johnson said he told White House officials this past weekend that “we need to talk about it and I think carefully consider the unintended consequences that may ensue” from the waivers.

“Congress voted on this decisively just several weeks ago, and we understand that Putin cannot be trusted,” Johnson said. “He demonstrates that over and over and over.”

Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., who is locked in a competitive reelection battle, pushed back Monday morning against Trump’s Russia moves.

“The United States must provide any and all defensive equipment that Ukraine needs to defend itself,” Fitzpatrick said on X. “The United States must not import a single drop of Russian oil. Sanctions against the Russian regime must be harsher and stronger than they’ve ever been before. Each and every one of these items will be brought to the House Floor — and each and every one of these items will pass on the House Floor by an overwhelming margin.”

Fitzpatrick, a senior Intelligence Committee member, said he plans to speak to Zelenskyy directly this week to assure him that “anyone who attempts to limit the use of Starshield for Ukraine will be fully investigated and will be held fully accountable, to include public congressional oversight hearings, and immediate harsh and punitive budget cuts to any responsible agency or agency head.”

Fitzpatrick had said on Oct. 10 that a measure that would impose an energy embargo on Russia “will be forced to the Floor via discharge and it will pass overwhelmingly.”

Likewise, Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., a member of the Armed Services Committee who is retiring after this Congress, said on X on Oct. 14 that the Trump administration will have legislative difficulties in the lame-duck session if the president continues to do more for Russia than Ukraine.

“The Administration’s decision to reduce intel sharing to Ukraine & access to Starlink equates to aiding the invader & the war criminal who bombs cities,” Bacon said. “Does the Administration think it will get ANY support for the remainder of the 119th Congress? Their agenda is dead unless they change paths.”

Numerous Republican senators have also joined their Democratic colleagues in resisting the president’s softening of sanctions on Russia and apparent withholding of some security help for Ukraine.

Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who serves on the Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, told reporters Monday morning she was “extremely surprised” Trump waived the Graham sanctions.

“You’ve seen opposition across the board, I think, Republicans and Democrats,” Capito said. “This was an act of Congress that we had worked with the White House on. We had timed this to when the president and the White House felt it was a good time to move forward with this, where it could be effective.”

In the House on Monday, Rep. Craig Goldman, R-Texas, also decried the undoing of the Graham sanctions.

“I certainly would be in favor of keeping those sanctions on Russia until the war is over,” Goldman told reporters.

On Oct. 13, 12 senators — six Republicans and six Democrats, including several senior ones from both parties — criticized Trump’s proposal to lift sanctions on purchases of Russian diesel fuel.

For example, on Oct. 15, nine senators from both parties called on the Pentagon inspector general to investigate the reports of restrictions on Starlink and Starshield.

On Satuday, Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C, criticized the administration’s moves on Russia in no uncertain terms.

“It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day,” Tillis said on X.

Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., added his voice to the critique in an appearance on CBS News’s “Face the Nation” on Sunday.

“Capitulating to a bully generally means they’re going to make more demands going forward,” Cramer said. “That’s the problem with taking sort of a business negotiation approach to negotiating with a thug, which is what Vladimir Putin is.”

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said on Fox News on Saturday that he wishes the president had not waived the Graham sanctions law.

Sen. Roger Wicker, R-Miss., chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, has been pushing an arrangement, which he says Zelenskyy has agreed to, under which Ukraine would stop striking Russian energy facilities in exchange for Ukraine receiving U.S. assistance in targeting Russian missile launchers.

Zelenskyy has also offered to withhold such deep strikes in exchange for more Patriot antimissile interceptors.

On Monday, four Democratic senators wrote to Space X’s vice president for legal affairs, Christopher Cardaci, asking for a thorough explanation for the reported scaling back of Starlink and Starshield support to Ukraine.

The Senate signatories were Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the ranking member of the Foreign Relations Committee; Chris Coons of Delaware, the ranking member of the Defense Appropriations Subcommittee; Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island; and Blumenthal.

In the House, 17 Democrats and five Republicans wrote Trump on Oct. 15 urging him to implement the Graham law’s sanctions “to their fullest extent and without delay.”

The letter’s GOP signatories were Bacon, Fitzpatrick and Reps. Michael McCaul, R-Texas, Dan Newhouse, R-Wash., and Joe Wilson, R-S.C.

Another House Republican, Rep. Michael R. Turner of Ohio, called Sunday for a congressional investigation into the throttling of Ukraine’s defensive systems, saying on “Face the Nation” that “lives are at risk, and lives are lost over these things.”

Turner stopped short, though, of saying Trump’s legislative agenda should be halted to secure changes in his Russia policy.

“I don’t think there’s any brinkmanship that needs to have to occur on this,” Turner said.

At the same time, Rep. French Hill, R-Ark., the House Financial Services Committee chairman, called for a classified briefing on the rationale for suspending sanctions, posting on X: “We should be increasing economic pressure on Russia, not easing up.”

Democrats have, with virtual unanimity, condemned the president’s actions.

On Oct. 16, Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said he filed a bill that would block U.S. purchases of Russian energy.

Many Democrats criticized the Graham sanctions bill when it was being debated, partly because of the tariffs power it gave Trump but also because the waiver authority was, in their minds, too broadly worded.

Meeks said Congress must address the law’s perceived shortcomings.

“All of these measures should become law making clear where America stands: with Ukraine and against Putin,” Meeks said in a statement.

On Sunday, though, Trump doubled down on his approach to Russia.

“My decision on Russia is a very simple one,” he said on social media. “I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.”

Meanwhile, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday that Putin is working to secure a summit meeting to resolve the Ukraine war, a conclave that reportedly would exclude Zelenskyy and would comprise just the leaders of Russia, America and China.

That proposal drew a quick rebuke Sunday night from Coons.

“There can be no talks about Ukraine’s future without Ukraine at the table, and there can be no real negotiations as long as Trump signals weakness and servitude to Xi and Putin at every opportunity,” Coons said on X.

All these developments came amid reports of Russian technical support for Iran’s military attacks on U.S. and partner forces and facilities in the Middle East.

The Kremlin is also widely seen as the culprit in a recent spate of sabotage and violence across Europe, which leaders there have ascribed to an attempt to weaken support for Ukraine and intimidate governments.

Moreover, a Russian satellite has recently been spotted suspiciously tracking a U.S.-registered commercial satellite that provides radar data to Ukraine.

#46. Why Is France Perpetually Rioting?

Analysis: Why Is France Perpetually Rioting?

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

When I first started studying contemporary France as a graduate student in 2006, the country was still reeling from a convulsion of urban violence triggered by the deaths of two teenagers in an electrical substation as they were hiding from police. For several weeks in late 2005, the country had gone up in flames as angry young people protested against police violence, racism, social inequality, and the broken promises of France’s social contract.

Fast forward 20 years, and the images of France being broadcast to the world are the same. What began as a protest by high school students has escalated into a nationwide cry of exasperation, punctuated by looting, the ritual burning of public buildings, and a cascade of violence meted out by riot police armed with smoke grenades and tear gas.

When I first started studying contemporary France as a graduate student in 2006, the country was still reeling from a convulsion of urban violence triggered by the deaths of two teenagers in an electrical substation as they were hiding from police. For several weeks in late 2005, the country had gone up in flames as angry young people protested against police violence, racism, social inequality, and the broken promises of France’s social contract.

Fast forward 20 years, and the images of France being broadcast to the world are the same. What began as a protest by high school students has escalated into a nationwide cry of exasperation, punctuated by looting, the ritual burning of public buildings, and a cascade of violence meted out by riot police armed with smoke grenades and tear gas.

No less predictable has been the cascade of hot takes by commentators, politicians, shock jocks, and activists, all looking to capitalize on the spectacle of French people taking to the streets. For the most part, this has involved endless platitudes about the French—who are said to be especially revolutionary or pathological, depending on your view—or outright untruths about a supposed invasion of migrants destroying French and Western civilization.

For those of us who have worked on contemporary France for much of our careers, the rush to commentary is exhausting. But it does at least highlight one of the signature questions of our field: Why is it that modern France seems to be a land of protest? And no less importantly, why does anyone still care about what happens in a medium-sized European country that has long ceased to be a global power?

The answer to the first question—about the omnipresence of protest—does not have an easy answer, but the facts are beyond doubt. According to Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, which monitors political violence and protests worldwide, there have been about 20 protests a day in France in recent years. These are often small and localized, but sometimes they are nationwide, with hundreds of thousands of people taking part.

Crucially, protesting is an activity for everyone in France. The idea that only young left-wing activists march in the streets is wildly inaccurate: Some of the biggest protest movements of the last 50 years have been led by the right, most famously the huge demonstrations against reforms to private schooling in 1984 and same-sex marriage in 2013.

For such a culture of protest to develop across the political spectrum, two basic elements are needed: the politicization of the fight against injustice and a belief in the power of the street. Both of these have been present in France for a long time.

The idea that opposition to any perceived injustice must be politicized—and that any such politicization can take the form of insurrectionary violence—has a long and distinguished pedigree in France. It was the French, after all, who first showed the world what ideology-driven revolutionary insurrection looked like. France also bequeathed to the world the perennial distinction between “right” and “left,” a divide that became the basic coordinates of parliamentary and extra-parliamentary politics worldwide. Time and again, from 1789 onward, the French have made protest more than the sum of its parts.

This politicization of discontent has not translated into stable institutions. France has had multiple republics and dictatorships since the French Revolution; compared with other Western countries, it has had relatively weak intermediary bodies. It is not a land of strong political parties or powerful trade unions. In fact, rates of union membership in France have long been much lower than elsewhere in Europe. Contrary to widely held perceptions of the French as perpetually “on strike,” the speed with which popular protest develops is an indication of the weakness of institutions that might channel discontent.

The presence of a strongly authoritarian, centralized state has not helped. For at least a century, if not more, the French state has been top-heavy and technocratic. Its grand plans for reconstruction after World War II, for instance, were elaborated by the central government with no real popular consultation, and the foundation of today’s constitutional settlement—the Fifth Republic—was explicitly anti-democratic in its elevation of presidential authority and the subservient role given to the French Parliament when it was devised in 1958.

All of which means that protest is one of the few ways in which French people can make themselves heard beyond the ballot box. Memories of earlier struggles are passed down through the generations as older activists tell their youthful comrades stories of their first protest, parents come out in support of their children, and teachers stand in solidarity with their students. As any good French protester knows, the symbols, language, and power of protest resonate across decades and even centuries.

And it sometimes works: Protesters do get their way, and reforms do get reversed. Every French government knows—and fears—the judgment of the street, which can be harsh and uncompromising.

This is one of the reasons that French governments frequently take preemptive action in the form of violent, sometimes murderous, repression. From the crushing of the Paris Commune in 1871 to today’s police violence, the French authorities often shoot first and ask questions later. Remarkably resistant to 21st-century de-escalation strategies, they still operate according to 19th-century ideas about the irrational mob, and they see everyone from schoolchildren to football fans as a potential threat.

Yet this only hardens the resolve of protesters. Some take to outright violence, joining petty criminals in the destruction of private and public property, while others record TikTok videos in front of riot police, lampooning a state that sees its citizens as a perpetual nuisance.

Of course, many contemporary protest movements go through a similar cycle. At the same time as the protests in France were taking place, hundreds of thousands of young Indians were launching their own movement to protest against another authoritarian state—and they met with an equally robust response.

So why do protests in France continue to capture the public imagination?

Some of this no doubt has to do with a tendency, especially in the Anglosphere, to imagine France as a volatile dystopia. Much of 19th-century British politics was built around a myth of stability that was positively contrasted with France’s revolutionary upheavals, and this characterization of France is still very much alive. More recently, the great conservative intellectual Roger Scruton attributed more or less his entire political outlook to his experiences in Paris during May 1968.

But there is something deeper than simply prejudice and national stereotypes. Despite its much-reduced global status, France has managed to maintain its status as the vanguard of European radical politics on both sides of the political spectrum. Protesters in Paris—like the teenager Elwan, whose eloquent paean to left-wing politics quickly went viral—appear to be more articulate than their peers elsewhere, and the intensity of their revolutionary symbolism gives them global appeal.

It is surely no coincidence that much of the protest imagery of the contemporary far left is French in origin. So is one of the biggest slogans of the global far right—the “Great Replacement” theory, which posits that a cabal of liberal elites seeks to replace the native population with migrants.

Although the French do not have a monopoly on protest—far from it—they have spent more time than anyone else packaging it for public consumption, and their ideas continue to shape political movements around the world. This alone makes it worth examining closely what happens on the streets of Paris, Lyon, and Marseille.

Emile Chabal is a professor of contemporary history at the University of Edinburgh and the author, most recently, of The Age of Hobsbawm: The Life of a Revolutionary Historian.

#48. The Limits of American Power

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

The war in Iran is far from the first time that U.S. policymakers have failed to appreciate the limits of American power. But the Trump administration’s use of military force against the Islamic Republic since February 28 offers a particularly glaring example of a mistake that has often characterized American strategy in recent decades. The war was launched without a clear rationale and with a constantly shifting set of objectives—from changing Tehran’s regime and squelching its nuclear ambitions to, more recently, reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which wasn’t closed until the war started. The results, not surprisingly, have been bad both for U.S. interests and for the Middle East.

Still, to focus only on the blunders in Iran is to miss a deeper problem in U.S. foreign policy—one that preceded and will outlast Donald Trump’s presidency. Although the particular missteps in Iran may stem from the shortcomings of this president and the team around him, the overestimation of the potential of military force has been a growing feature of American strategy since at least the end of World War II. A tendency to wish away the limits of power accounted for some of the greatest mistakes of U.S. statecraft during the Cold War, with Vietnam the clearest and most consequential example. Yet despite an apparent commitment to internalizing the lessons of that overreach, this American delusion—our excessive faith in the capacity of military power to achieve victory and thereby fundamentally political ends—has gotten worse rather than better, especially in the past quarter century.

And unfortunately, there is good reason to worry that the delusion will deepen in the years ahead. Presidential power is becoming increasingly personalized as the constraints on it continue to erode. The politicization of the military (along with the diplomatic corps and intelligence communities) is making it less likely that policymakers will receive the best advice, including frank warnings about risks and costs. And the rise of artificial intelligence and new weapons technologies reinforces a sense of complete battlefield awareness and mastery, feeding superpower hubris. The risk of overreach has never been higher, at a time when the damage from overreach is becoming more difficult to repair.

In April 1975, Colonel Harry Summers, a member of the U.S. delegation dealing with postwar issues in Vietnam, was meeting in Hanoi with a North Vietnamese counterpart, Colonel Tu. “You know, you never defeated us on the battlefield,” Summers observed. To which Tu replied, “That may be so, but it is also irrelevant.”

Summers went on to write a seminal book about the war, On Strategy: A Critical Analysis of the Vietnam War. His key takeaway was simple: there are limits to American power that are neglected at immense cost. War is, and always has been, a contest of human will, shaped by heroism and cowardice, fear and elation, chance and uncertainty; no matter how superior a military force, it is not guaranteed strategic victory.

The book became required reading for many military officers, including me. I had joined the Naval ROTC unit at the University of Texas two years before the encounter between Summers and Tu. The draft had just ended, and the fall of Saigon was still to come, but discussion of Vietnam consumed our ranks. As I studied the American failure, I came to see that a great strength had become a fatal liability: our fundamental faith that we, the United States of America, had to win and thus would. We had won World War I, we had won World War II, and we had at least fought to a draw, holding off the North Koreans and Chinese, in Korea. And somehow, at all costs, we would win in Vietnam.

To believe you can win is important. It inspires troops and keeps the public engaged. But when the commitment to winning is not coupled with sound policy judgment, when the principles of war are disregarded in the false belief that technology or firepower can overcome the inherent frictions of combat, when tactical successes are viewed as a guaranteed path to a strategic win, when the cost in blood and treasure rises inexorably while any claim to righteousness collapses, it is essential to reassess. In Vietnam, the answer to mounting losses was simply “more”—more troops, more bombs, more money. To lose the fight was seen as anathema to all we stood for; we would keep fighting in spite of the increasingly evident limits to our power. When the end finally came with the rushed U.S. withdrawal from Saigon in 1975, many military and political leaders could still not understand how the United States had won nearly every skirmish, battle, and fight but lost the war.

The military I entered in 1977 was struggling in the aftermath of Vietnam. The “peace dividend” meant a dramatic drawdown in manpower and money. Readiness was at an all-time low across the services—army enlistment had fallen by 60,000 and the number of navy ships from around 650 to barely more than 500. Meanwhile, the transition to an all-volunteer military had proved challenging: drug abuse and racial tensions were high, morale among senior leaders and young troops alike was low, and new recruits lacked basic skills.

When President Ronald Reagan took office in 1981, he began the largest peacetime expansion of the U.S. military since the Korean War. Over the course of eight years, he increased defense spending by 35 percent. There was a slew of major procurements: the M-1 Abrams tank, the Bradley Fighting Vehicle, the Apache and Black Hawk helicopters, the F-15 and F-16 fighters, the B-1 bomber, the E-3 Sentry. The navy built back toward 600 ships, including 15 aircraft carriers, 100 attack submarines, and cruisers and destroyers equipped with the revolutionary Aegis Combat System. For troops, pay rose, recruiting goals were met, and standards were restored. Just as important, Congress passed the Goldwater-Nichols Act in 1986. It fundamentally changed the military by strengthening the role of the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, establishing the regional combatant commanders as the warfighters, ensuring joint force integration, improving joint planning and procurement, and leading to the establishment of the U.S. Special Operations Command. By 1990, the military I entered in the 1970s had been transformed. Our troops were well trained, well equipped, highly motivated, and, most important, well led.

In July 1990, I left San Diego on a routine six-month deployment to the western Pacific. I was a SEAL task unit commander assigned to Amphibious Squadron Five and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit. Little did I know that this reinvigorated military and our civilian leaders were about to be tested, raising the question of whether the United States had learned anything from Vietnam and the other failed missions of the recent past.

On August 2, 1990, Iraqi President Saddam Hussein ordered the Iraqi army into Kuwait. Within hours of the invasion, the National Security Council convened and options for U.S. action were presented to the president. “This is the first test of the postwar system—as the bipolar world is relaxed, it permits this,” Deputy Secretary of State Lawrence Eagleburger emphasized. “If [Saddam] succeeds, others may try the same.”

Fortunately, American leadership had never been stronger or more experienced—and in wartime especially, leadership matters. President George H. W. Bush was a young navy pilot when he was shot down near Iwo Jima and eventually rescued by an American submarine. Bush understood war. Later in life, he had served as U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, de facto ambassador to China, director of the Central Intelligence Agency, and vice president. No president in American history had come into office with more national security experience. Nevertheless, Bush surrounded himself with some of the most remarkable diplomats, military officers, intelligence professionals, and strategic thinkers of their time: Brent Scowcroft, the national security adviser; Secretary of State James Baker; Secretary of Defense Dick Cheney; Colin Powell, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff; and many more.

U.S. Central Command, which would spearhead the military effort against Saddam, was led by General Norman Schwarzkopf. Schwarzkopf was a Vietnam veteran who had been awarded three Silver Stars for heroism and two Purple Hearts for combat injuries. Upon his return from Vietnam, Schwarzkopf had reflected: “Nobody is more antiwar than an intelligent person who’s been to war. . . . And when they get ready to send me again, I’m going to have to stop and ask myself, ‘Is it worth it?’ That’s a very dangerous place for the nation to be when your own army is going to stop and question.”

Grappling honestly with that question—Is it worth it?—is the imperative of good leadership. Bush carefully weighed the costs and risks associated with confronting Saddam and decided the war was worth it. Together, the United States’ political and military leaders developed a strategy with clear goals and objectives and built both popular and international support for the operations to come. It would prove to be the finest application of political and military power in recent American history—and its success is thus worth lingering on.

The success of the Gulf War rested on several fundamental principles that were at the heart of American strategy. First, that the United States should begin by taking the moral high ground. The high ground implies that you hold a dominant position when facing an enemy. The moral high ground shows that the fight is worth it. With it, leaders can inspire troops, galvanize publics, and rally allies.

Immediately after Saddam’s invasion, Bush ordered the deployment of military forces into the region and worked with Saudi Arabia to establish a footprint in the kingdom in the event military action was necessary. Bush was still hoping to avoid a conflict, but he saw a similarity “between the Persian Gulf and the situation in the Rhineland in the 1930s, when Hitler simply defied the Treaty of Versailles and marched in.” Yet he knew that he had to convince the international community and the American people that any actions he might take would be moral, legitimate, and in the interests of the United States and its allies.

Bush and his team engaged in a full-court diplomatic effort to build support from Arab states in the region, from European allies, and from Moscow and Beijing. Although skeptical of the United Nations, Bush nonetheless sought a variety of UN resolutions that condemned Iraq’s invasion, imposed sweeping economic sanctions, and authorized the use of force if necessary. Simultaneously, he built the case with the American people, a large majority of whom ultimately approved of his handling of the crisis. And although Bush believed he had the authority as commander in chief to commit military forces without congressional approval, he sought and received Capitol Hill’s support.

Second, Bush and his administration recognized the value of building an international coalition, even if the United States had the firepower to go it alone in strictly military terms. This was partly about legitimacy, partly about the chance to send a message. Saddam’s invasion presented an opportunity to shape what some in the administration thought of as a “new world order,” one in which aggression would be met with collective action; major powers would come together despite their ideological differences; and the United Nations and international law would play a critical role rather than be ignored. Bush leveraged the strong personal relationships he had developed over his long career in public service, gaining the support of everyone from Germany’s Chancellor Helmut Kohl and France’s President François Mitterrand, to Saudi Arabia’s King Fahd and Egypt’s President Hosni Mubarak, to Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev. As secretary of state, Baker also embarked on a campaign of shuttle diplomacy that took him across the globe, adding to the coalition.

In the end, the United States did not simply get the support of the international community. Much of the costs of the conflict were borne by others. The allied force ultimately assembled—750,000 troops from 36 countries, including 540,000 Americans—was the largest since World War II. It included, critically, an Arab coalition with forces from Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Egypt, Syria, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Oman, and Bahrain. The coalition was challenging to manage; British Prime Minister Winston Churchill once quipped that “there is only one thing worse than fighting with allies, and that is fighting without them.” But Bush understood that international support brought operational legitimacy and regional stability. It sent a message to Saddam and to the world.

Third, Bush and his advisers were intent on establishing clear goals and objectives, with political and military dimensions aligned. Politically, the purpose was to uphold international law and restore peace in the region. The military objectives supported those political objectives. The coalition would drive Iraqi forces out of Kuwait. But in doing so, it would attempt to minimize friendly casualties, maintain the alliance, and limit the duration of the war. U.S. leaders were clear from the beginning: there would be no push to Baghdad or protracted engagement with the Iraqi army.

Yet even with these limited objectives, neither civilian nor military leaders were under the illusion that success would be easy or cost-free. Driving out a determined enemy that owns the terrain requires overwhelming firepower and a willingness to commit to ground operations. As Carl von Clausewitz stressed in On War, the defense is stronger than the offense, since the defense has only to preserve and protect, while the offense must impose its will on the enemy. He argues that the only way to overcome the inherent strength of the defense is through overwhelming firepower. The Iraqis were prepared to defend the ground they had taken in Kuwait; they owned the terrain, the geography was in their favor, and they had an experienced fighting force after eight years in combat against the Iranians. But Cheney, Powell, and Schwarzkopf understood the principles of war. They had a clearly defined objective. They massed U.S. firepower in the most important areas, accepted risk in less important ones, and were prepared to maneuver against the enemy. And they were committed to leaving when the objectives were reached, not allowing the war to go on too long.

To accomplish these goals meant putting troops on the ground—a lot of troops. U.S. military and civilian leaders understood that defeating the Iraqis would take more than just airpower. Early on, Cheney observed, “The history of air campaigns suggests they are not terribly successful.” Powell agreed: “To further deter Iraqi action with Saudi Arabia would require U.S. forces on the ground. . . . It would mean a major confrontation. Most U.S. forces would be committed to sustain not just for one or two days.”

If I have learned one important lesson in over four decades of military service, it’s that to defeat the enemy, you must stand on the ground he holds dear and own it. It is why Alexander invaded Persia, William the Conqueror crossed the channel to England, Genghis Khan rode into China, Sherman marched to Atlanta, the Allies landed at Normandy, and the United States rolled into Kuwait. (It is why today the Israelis are in Gaza and Lebanon and why the Russians will never be victorious until they hold Kyiv.) But as Cheney cautioned, “We should start this only if we are prepared to see it through. . . . The problem is the American people might have a short tolerance for war.”

Operation Desert Storm began with air attacks at 2:38 AM Baghdad time on January 17, 1991. After 43 days of air operations and 100 hours of ground operations, Washington’s political and military objectives had been achieved. The Iraqi army was ousted from Kuwait, and most American forces were soon on their way home.

“We’re doing something decent and we’re doing something good,” Bush wrote in his diary. “Vietnam will soon be behind us.”

Desert Storm was a reset, but not in the way it should have been. It presented an opportunity to internalize lessons about how to use force effectively and about what military power could and could not achieve. Instead, it spurred a wave of triumphalism. When I returned from Desert Storm, where I’d led a special operations task force, the euphoria was palpable: we were winners again. The victory proved intoxicating, drawing us back into the false belief that our power could do almost anything to shape the world to our liking.

Adding to this euphoria was the technology that had been on display against Iraq. Precision-guided munitions could put a 500-pound bomb on a moving target from 20,000 feet in the air. Tomahawk cruise missiles could be launched from ships and submarines hundreds of miles away. A GPS satellite could guide an infantry battalion across a flat desert at night and get it to exactly the right destination, and the joint surveillance target attack radar system could see the Iraqi army as it maneuvered. Digital command and control systems could provide computerized air-tasking orders, secure satellite communications, and digital planning tools. No military in history had ever commanded the battlespace as precisely as we did during Desert Storm. It made sense to build on this success to spur a revolution in military affairs that would improve the way the United States fought. But the experience also fueled a widespread belief that technology could overcome the inherent frictions, costs, and risk of war.

In the 1990s, U.S. military missions, in line with the confidence that followed Desert Storm and the hopes of the post–Cold War world, were focused on supporting norms and containing humanitarian harms—some successful (Bosnia and Kosovo), some less so (Somalia). But it was after 9/11 that the failure to learn the right lessons from the Gulf War became especially clear, with a persistent misunderstanding of the limits of American power and what the military could and couldn’t achieve. The war in Afghanistan began with the right intentions but devolved into a protracted fight with shifting goals, misaligned military and political objectives, and a determined Taliban force fighting on its home ground. Even after the special operations mission that killed the al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden, the goals and objectives in Afghanistan kept shifting. As always, the strength of the military was our troops: they were courageous, disciplined, technologically savvy. We made mistakes, but there was no lack of fighting spirit or tactical successes. Even public support remained strong throughout most of the war. But we faltered by assuming that the quick victory could extend to the complex task of fighting an insurgency, conducting counterterrorism operations, and building a nation. Lest I appear too righteous in my critique of American strategy, make no mistake: as a combat leader in Afghanistan, I fell into the same trap of believing that more troops, more weapons, and more money could solve some of the most intractable problems. They could not.

The Iraq war, based on a far shakier case at the outset, also degenerated into a counterinsurgency and counterterrorism mission with insufficient forces, a small coalition, and an evolving timeline. Once again, our troops were everything the American people could have hoped for, but our leaders repeatedly disregarded the fundamental principles of war. Our claim to the moral high ground was based on flawed intelligence, our international support was limited, and our goals shifted from removing Saddam to trying to build a Western-style democracy. We may have entered Iraq and Afghanistan with noble intentions, and perhaps in the long term the seeds of freedom we tried to plant will take root. But so far, minimal gains have come at immense cost to our military and our troops, our home front, and our international legitimacy.

Yet even these recent experiences—which several key members of the Trump administration witnessed firsthand in their own military service—did little to instill caution when it came to Iran earlier this year. To be clear, the Iranian regime is despicable. It is responsible for the death of hundreds of American troops. It threatens its neighbors, uses proxies to attack our allies, and has killed tens of thousands of its own people.

Given the fall of the Assad government in Syria, the destruction of Hamas’s power in Gaza, the crippling of Hezbollah in Lebanon, and a weakened supreme leader in Iran itself, it is easy to appreciate the allure of trying to change the Iranian regime. What’s more, coming off the dramatic capture of President Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, where the U.S. military exercised remarkable speed, lethality, and courage to overcome a very sophisticated defense, it was all too easy for U.S. policymakers to assume once again that the power of our technology and the courage and experience of our soldiers made us virtually invincible. But there is a reason no U.S. president has attempted to change the regime in Iran since 1979, and it has little to do with determination or political will. The challenges of legitimacy, coalition building, and geography; the will of the enemy; and the reality that it would be necessary to put American boots on the ground to achieve such an ambitious end all argued against it.

From the start of the Iran war, there was no attempt to build international legitimacy. It began on February 28 with a U.S.-Israeli strike. To make matters worse, an early airstrike went awry and hit an Iranian elementary school, resulting in the deaths of 120 students. Mistakes happen in war, but not acknowledging our error added to the sense of illegitimacy and vindictiveness, losing whatever moral high ground we might have had. The Trump administration failed to notify any U.S. allies of the impending strike, most notably neighboring Arab states, which resulted in a lack of regional trust from the outset. Later, when the president sought allied support to open the Strait of Hormuz, he was met with an international cold shoulder. This refusal came as no surprise: Trump had been notoriously caustic with European leaders.

There was never a clear understanding of the goals. The administration at first said it wanted regime change. But later Trump told reporters that he never cared about regime change. The administration claimed the urgency of preempting an imminent Iranian nuclear weapon. But when pressed, Trump later dismissed such concerns as inconsequential, since there was little left in Iran but “nuclear dust.” After Iran closed the strait, and reopening it to shipping became the primary focus of both military strategy and diplomacy, Trump told the world that it mattered little since the United States didn’t need the oil. The objectives seemed to change by the day. I have no doubt that American military planners understood the limits of airpower when it came to achieving U.S. aims in Iran; this should have been a signal to the White House that unless the military planned to invade Iran, victory was unlikely.

Geography was always going to be a limiting factor. In my almost 40 years of military service, much of that time in the Middle East, no general or admiral I ever met talked about Iran without talking about the Strait of Hormuz. It was the Iranians’ weapon of mass destruction, their bulwark against invasion, their ace in the hole no matter the game. Additionally, the Iranian leadership was in the position of the defenders: they only had to preserve and protect themselves to win. And protect they have. At this point, it is highly unlikely the U.S. military will ever stand on the ground they hold dear and call it our own.

The U.S. war was also limited by the will of the enemy. From 1980 to 1988, Iran and Iraq fought a vicious war claiming the lives of hundreds of thousands of Iranians. It should have been clear from the beginning of this war that the Iranians would fight and fight hard. The zealots in Iran control the narrative, and they are battling for their survival.

Such a grave failure to recognize and appreciate the limits of power is not a new phenomenon in American history, or in military history more broadly. With every revolution in military technology, from mounted cavalry to motorized units, from the single-shot musket to the Gatling gun, from propeller-driven aircraft to jets, leaders desperately want to believe that they can wish away the basic nature of war. As our ability to project power around the globe becomes more formidable, we desperately want to believe that geography is no longer important. As new media allows us to see national outrage among an adversary’s population, we desperately want to believe that we can spur change with little risk or commitment. And as AI speeds up tactical decision-making, we desperately want to believe that the lessons of military experience can be disregarded. These beliefs are illusions.

More concerning, however, is that there are several structural trends in the United States that suggest the problem will get worse rather than better, no matter how vivid the lessons of the Iran war may seem at the moment. The first is the trend toward more personalistic presidential leadership, in which loyalty to the leader becomes more important than loyalty to institutions. When institutions designed to provide a president with the best military, diplomatic, economic, or intelligence advice are led by loyalists, there is a risk that advice will be shaded, inadvertently or intentionally, to reflect the president’s desires. This is a recipe for disaster. A leader needs the unvarnished truth, the best advice possible, regardless of his or her personal position on the issue. The growing concentration of power in the executive branch has unfolded over several administrations, and despite occasional noise from Congress, there is little sign this will change. Here, too, Trump may be a particularly flagrant example, but he’s unlikely to be the last president susceptible to such temptations and operating with few constraints.

The dangers of personalistic presidential leadership are severely exacerbated by more politicized leadership in the military. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s ongoing purge of military leadership will undermine the civil-military dynamic for years to come. Trump and Hegseth have forced out senior officers across nearly every service, including the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the chief of naval operations, and the army chief of staff. Hegseth has intervened to block career advancement in unprecedented ways, personally removing dozens of officers from promotion lists, often with no explanation (although a disproportionate number seem to have worked for leaders who were viewed as obstacles to Trump’s domestic political goals). While remaining military leaders will largely stay committed to serving honorably and providing their best advice to civilian leaders in the Pentagon and the White House, this purge is bound to have a chilling effect on the willingness and ability of senior officers to give frank counsel, especially when it comes to the costs and limits of what force can achieve.

And finally, the rapid introduction of new technologies, from AI and unmanned vehicles to robotics, cyber- and space-based systems, will once again make it all too easy to wish away the fundamentals of war. Technology will always be an important factor in how wars are fought, and every military must seek greater lethality, survivability, and situational awareness. But although these capabilities are necessary, they are not sufficient to overcome the basic principles of war. Leaders must understand technology for what it is—an enabler. It can improve the application of military power, but it cannot compensate for misguided policies that draw us into conflict in the first place.

Today’s U.S. military is the finest, most professional armed force in the history of the world—yes, the history of the world. But that doesn’t mean we can disregard the limits of our power.

We will be limited by moral uncertainty. If the reasons for a conflict are dubious or worse, it will prove challenging to build a coalition, motivate troops, maintain civilian support, and undermine the will of the enemy. Such failures explain why the Greeks defeated the Persians at Salamis, the English defeated the Spanish at Gravelines, George Washington defeated the British, the Russians defeated the Germans at Stalingrad, the Vietnamese defeated the French and the Americans, and the Ukrainians are defeating the Russians today. Although the moral high ground does not guarantee military victory, it is a foundation on which success rests.

We will be limited by geography. No matter the advances in technology, geography will always be a critical factor in determining the outcome of any engagement. Every military leader knows that the terrain dictates how the enemy will fight, where he will position his forces, how he will supply his troops. It is the oceans and the rivers that provide natural barriers to an advancing force, and the terrain and the waterways that will limit the ability of the attacking force to maneuver, hold ground, resupply, and project power. The Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el Mandeb Strait present the same challenges as the English Channel, the Rhine, or the Volga.

We will be limited by the will of the enemy. There is a “sleeping giant” in every population that will rise from its slumber and fight hard, driven by a sense of righteousness, a desire for survival, or both. Invaders, aggressors, and first strikers all elicit a visceral response from the population they seek to mollify. Never underestimate the enemy’s will to fight—a mistake we have made again and again.

We will be limited by our hesitancy to put troops on the ground. No American wants to lose our young men and women on a foreign battlefield, but sometimes it is necessary to achieve the greater good. During World War I, over two million young doughboys deployed to Europe. During World War II, over five million GIs fought the Nazis and island-hopped to Japan. In both cases, mankind was better for their sacrifice. Of course, if there is any doubt about whether we own the moral high ground, leaders will be hesitant to fully commit. In that hesitation comes defeat.

We will be limited by time. This is not a uniquely American limitation, but we seem to suffer from it more than most countries. It has been said that the Russians will eat grass before they capitulate. The United States’ reputation is that sooner rather than later, we will tire of the fight and leave. Much of this reputation stems from the reality that our democracy demands public support to sustain a long engagement. Even with a compelling reason to send our young men and women into battle, the cost in blood and treasure can soon outweigh our collective sense of the necessity of the fight.

Finally, we will be limited by the quality of our leadership, political and military. Without experienced leaders—leaders who understand the need to establish legitimacy, to build coalitions, to have clear and attainable goals, to commit to the task, to limit the duration of the fight to only what is necessary—all the power in the world will be irrelevant.

William H. MCRaven served in the U.S. Navy from 1977 to 2014, including as Commander of United States Special Operations Command from 2011 to 2014. He was Chancellor of the University of Texas from 2015 to 2018.

#50. Top Trump ally warns Republican Party 'dead' if it loses key voting bloc ahead of midterms

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, discusses the Democratic Socialists of America's agenda on 'The Ingraham Angle.'

A top Senate Republican warned that the same voting bloc that has propelled the GOP to power over the last decade is at risk of turning its back on the party during this election cycle.

For decades, White, working-class voters often aligned themselves with the Democratic Party, giving Democrats a stranglehold on Congress until the 1990s and often favoring the Democratic candidate atop the presidential ticket.

President Donald Trump’s entrance onto the political scene and victory in 2016 solidified a shift that was years in the making, giving Republicans a strong base of working-class support. But with the state of the economy, Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, a top ally of Trump’s on Capitol Hill, warned that the GOP’s steady base could head for the exits.

FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS

President Donald Trump arrives to speak during a campaign rally at F&M Bank Arena in Clarksville, Tenn., on Oct. 10, 2026. (Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images)

"This is the whole deal," Moreno told Fox News Digital. "It's the whole deal. If we don't hang on to those working-class voters, we're dead as a party. That's why I say with no hyperbole, if President Trump hadn’t won in 2016, the Republican Party would be dead. Because the Republican Party had abandoned working-class Americans."

"Ironically, the Democrats abandoned working Americans, and there was a void — President Trump filled it," he continued. "That's why he won."

Trump has consistently performed highly with White, working-class voters each time he has run for office, scoring between 66% and 67% of their vote between 2016 and 2024, according to a variety of exit polls.

REDISTRICTING GIVES REPUBLICANS AN EDGE, BUT AFFORDABILITY WILL DECIDE THE MIDTERMS

Some Democrats acknowledged that after the 2024 election, their party had a problem with engaging the working class. Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., circulated a memo that urged Democrats to embrace economic populism following stunning losses across the gamut of power in Washington.

"No one, including me, has all the answers right now, but what we know for certain is that Democrats must reclaim our identity as the party of the working class," Murphy wrote.

Still, Republicans are facing political headwinds heading into this midterm election cycle, in which affordability issues are dominating headlines and voters’ concerns.

FOX NEWS POLL: MOST RATE THE ECONOMY NEGATIVELY, INCLUDING HALF OF REPUBLICANS

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, warned that the Republican Party could be on the verge of losing working-class voters. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

Trump and the GOP again rose to be the dominant party in Washington, D.C., after the 2024 election by pitching a message to rectify the economy that the president charged was "destroyed" by former President Joe Biden.

But a Fox News poll published earlier this month found that nearly 60% of voters said that their top concern was the economy. A separate Fox News poll published in May found that 67% of White voters without a college degree disapproved of Trump’s handling of the economy.

Republicans have hit the trail this fall pitching their economic successes, particularly from the colossal "big, beautiful bill" and trying to instill in voters that the cost of fuel, for example, is only temporary as the war with Iran continues.

Moreno, however, argued that working-class voters "hate" the war.

"They obviously hate gas prices because, look, they're already struggling. I mean, you talk to some of these working Americans, they're an engine failure in their vehicle away from bankruptcy, and that's a disaster."

"So, I think what we have to do is explain, this is a very, very necessary thing that had to happen," he continued. "Iran was attacking us for 47 years, and we didn't take him out. They would have used a nuclear weapon. I don't know that that case is penetrated enough, and this gas price situation will be very temporary."

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

#59. Europe Is Finally Getting Tough on China. Now Comes the Hard Part.
