More than two centuries ago, Franco-Swiss Enlightenment writer Madame de Staël lamented that the German states had neglected “the great national power that had to be forged amid Europe’s colossi.” She was writing about how the politically fragmented German states had failed to combine their economic strength into a national power capable of challenging Napoleon Bonaparte. But the remark could easily apply to all of Europe today. The continent is neither small nor poor, but it has often struggled to translate its economic might into political leverage.

The joint French-German letter and nonpaper sent to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in early October is one encouraging sign that this may be changing. French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz want the European Union to act much faster against persistent market distortions. In service of this goal, they are proposing a new mechanism that could ultimately restrict access to the European single market. Under their proposal, economic measures put forward by the commission could take effect unless a qualified majority of governments opposed them.

More than two centuries ago, Franco-Swiss Enlightenment writer Madame de Staël lamented that the German states had neglected “the great national power that had to be forged amid Europe’s colossi.” She was writing about how the politically fragmented German states had failed to combine their economic strength into a national power capable of challenging Napoleon Bonaparte. But the remark could easily apply to all of Europe today. The continent is neither small nor poor, but it has often struggled to translate its economic might into political leverage.

The joint French-German letter and nonpaper sent to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in early October is one encouraging sign that this may be changing. French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz want the European Union to act much faster against persistent market distortions. In service of this goal, they are proposing a new mechanism that could ultimately restrict access to the European single market. Under their proposal, economic measures put forward by the commission could take effect unless a qualified majority of governments opposed them.

The French-German letter doesn’t name the source of the market distortions that these measures are intended to check. But the unspoken target is obvious: China.

For much of the past two decades, France and Germany approached China from significantly different economic positions. Paris was concerned about a lack of reciprocity, threats to industrial sovereignty, and the risks created by strategic dependencies. German Chancellor Angela Merkel’s China policy was shaped by that firm belief that expanding economic relationships with Beijing remained, on balance, favorable to the German economy. As a result, China became a major source of growth for the German industry—especially cars, machinery, and chemicals—while German companies helped develop the Chinese industrial infrastructure by investing heavily in local production.

But Berlin might have wanted to be more cautious, as the geoeconomic dynamics of the past decade have made its calculations much harder to sustain. German exports to China fell by 9.7 percent in 2025, while imports rose by 8.8 percent. The bilateral German deficit reached 89.3 billion euros. During the first five months of 2026, exports fell another 14.5 percent from the same period a year earlier; imports continued to rise. Unsurprisingly, German motor-vehicle exports have been hit particularly hard.

Those numbers capture more than a growing trade imbalance and point to an uncomfortable truth for Europe—and in particular Germany, the continent’s industrial powerhouse. China has moved steadily from customer to competitor in industries that are crucial to the German economy.

This explains why the Franco-German paper feels somewhat different from previous exercises in European “de-risking.” At last, Berlin accepts a proposition that Paris has pressed for years: Interdependence does create leverage, and Europe would be foolish not to use its own. This is particularly true at a time when large parts of European industry are now at risk of disappearing, with millions of jobs at stake and likely political repercussions that are easy to imagine.

The rest of the continent is not to be outdone. In 2025, the EU imported 559.4 billion euros in goods from China and exported 199.6 billion euros, leaving a deficit of 359.8 billion euros. European exports to China were 37 percent higher than a decade earlier. Imports had risen by 89 percent.

Trade deficits do not, by themselves, necessarily establish strategic weakness. Nor is dependence automatically a problem. But in an age of heightened geoeconomic tensions and coercion risks, European governments find themselves asking whether some forms of interdependence leave them exposed to the agenda of a foreign power—and what assets Europe can mobilize in response. The tone can only be music to France’s ears, as Paris has been pushing for a decade for Europe to use the weight of its market as the foundation of a more integrated form of power.

Call it a continentwide commitment to self-deprecation, but talking about power in Europe usually begins with a list of the continent’s major deficiencies: It lacks U.S. military capabilities, it has fewer large technology firms and lags behind the San Francisco Bay Area in terms of investment capacity, it cannot mobilize industrial policy at a scale and speed comparable to that of China, and so on. The list is almost endless, and many of the specifics are difficult to argue with.

But looking at the glass half-empty can distort the perception of reality and impede strategic judgment. Europe has also been sitting on a massive geopolitical asset for decades. Foreign companies want access to some 450 million relatively affluent consumers operating within an integrated regulatory space. Foreign governments rightfully care about whether their exporters can enter that golden-goose market. European rules already de facto shape corporate behavior well beyond the borders of the EU. This is the so-called “Brussels effect,” whereby companies often adopt EU standards across their global operations rather than run separate systems for different markets.

The Franco-German initiative indicates that some in Europe might actually start using the continent’s strength to defend its citizens and its economy from threats and unfair competition.

The Anti-Coercion Instrument, adopted in 2023, was the first important shift. Its purpose is explicitly as a deterrent: If another country uses economic pressure to force the EU or a member state to alter a policy, then Brussels can respond across a wide array of tools encompassing tariffs as well as services, investment, and public procurement.

When U.S. President Donald Trump threatened 30 percent tariffs on European goods, EU governments approved potential counter-tariffs on 93 billion euros of U.S. exports. France and Germany were the most vocal proponents of putting the Anti-Coercion Instrument on the table, too. This was one reason why Trump ultimately settled for peaceful negotiations with Copenhagen last month, even as European governments remained divided about how far they were prepared to go to deter Washington. Yet the move indicated that some strong political taboos were weakening: It was no longer unthinkable to flex the bloc’s geostrategic muscles to deter any foreign power—even a traditional ally—from using economic coercion against the EU.

Now, the French-German proposal goes one step further. Macron and Merz are contemplating restrictions on market access as a response to persistent distortions and practices damaging Europe’s industrial base and threatening jobs in the industrial sector. German officials have compared the proposed mechanism to the United States’ Section 301 powers and argued that Europe, too, needs to be capable of responding within days.

This is moving closer to economic statecraft, but it will not be enough. Europe has accumulated an impressive collection of instruments in recent years, but political willingness to use them has lagged behind.

One could ask whether this is not just too little but too late. Market power is useful while Europe remains indispensable to the Chinese economy, but the balance is shifting quickly. This is particularly true in some key industries such as batteries, clean tech, and electric vehicles. In other words, indispensability won’t last, and the clock is ticking for the EU to take action while it retains leverage.

Building a more geopolitical Europe does not mean that the continent will eventually turn into a military power comparable to that of the United States, nor that the EU will reach the Chinese industrial scale anytime soon. What’s more, trade defenses alone won’t produce cheaper energy or create technological leadership. Protecting an industry and making it competitive are clearly two different undertakings.

The Franco-German letter is an encouraging sign. But a bigger challenge remains. Paris and Berlin still need to implement reforms to revive their waning competitiveness and declining economies. Once the question of unfair Chinese industrial competition is settled, the real work, the harder work, will need to begin: economic reform at home. Alas, a Franco-German nonpaper on the issue is much less likely.

Grégoire Roos is the director of the Europe, Russia, Eurasia programs at Chatham House and a nonresident fellow at the Columbia University Center on Global Energy Policy.

#60. “Earth Satellites and Foreign Policy”

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

The advent of a new technology invariably comes with strategic implications, raising the question of who will benefit and whether risks can be managed. In 1957, following the Soviet Sputnik launch, U.S. policymakers and analysts recognized that the satellite, as the American physicist and engineer Lloyd Berkner observed in these pages, would bring transformative effects. The United States could not risk losing out, Berkner argued, but nor should governments allow geopolitical tensions to prevent the technology’s broad benefits from emerging.

From the vantage point of 2100 A.D., the year 1957 will most certainly stand in history as the year of man’s progression from a two-dimensional to a three-dimensional geography. It may well stand, also, as the point in time at which intellectual achievement forged ahead of weapons and national wealth as instruments of national policy. . . .

We should not make the mistake of seeing in the satellite merely the symbol of a foreign Power’s military progress. It does, of course, represent important advances in military capability. But quite irrespective of the usual interaction of scientific and military strength, the satellite symbolizes an intellectual attainment that may dominate the period immediately ahead as the most powerful single instrument of national policy. The vital point is not so much that the Soviet satellite preceded that of the United States, heretofore credited as the leader of world technology; it is that the United States, for the first time, finds a challenging competitor in the most advanced scientific fields. The achievement of the Soviet satellite has demonstrated to Americans what they refused to believe before, that they are in a race for intellectual leadership when they hadn’t realized that there was a race, or even that another nation had the capability to challenge their technology. In the complacency of our assumed technological lead, we have confused our high standards of living and material prosperity with intellectual stature. It is an extravagant and dangerous mistake.

Published by The Council on Foreign Relations, Inc.

#61. Security official warns of more suspicious letters to lawmakers

A wave of suspicious letters mailed to members of Congress is likely to continue, House officials warned Monday, describing a white powder in the envelopes.

So far, “none of the letters received by Congressional offices have been determined to contain hazardous substances,” according to a memo sent to members and staff and obtained by CQ Roll Call.

But more offices may receive similar letters “in the coming days,” House Sergeant at Arms William McFarland wrote in the memo.

At least a few dozen House Democrats have already spoken out about receiving suspicious mailings, according to a review of social media posts and statements from lawmakers.

On Monday morning, Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., said his district office in Leesburg was evacuated after receiving a suspicious envelope. “These acts of political intimidation have no place in our country,” he said in a statement.

Last week marked the 25th anniversary of anthrax attacks on the Capitol, and the white powder in the letters had raised fears of a repeat.

The FBI confirmed Thursday it was working alongside the U.S. Postal Inspection Service to investigate “a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices.”

Photos shared by some lawmakers show “DSA” in the upper left hand corner alongside a return address once tied to the Democratic Socialists of America. The group has denied involvement, with a spokesperson telling The New York Times, “D.S.A. did not send these letters.”

Rep. Hillary Scholten, D-Mich., said in a statement Friday that her office received a letter that “made a direct and specific reference to an impending ‘civil war’ beginning after the election.”

Several lawmakers said the similarities between the envelopes had helped their staff identify them before opening them. “A member of our team identified a letter matching the description and return address, immediately secured the envelope without opening it, and called local law enforcement and US Capitol Police,” Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., posted Friday on social media.

While most of those posting about the mailings so far are House Democrats, several senators, including a handful of Republicans, have also described being targeted.

“Today my Omaha office received a letter with a powdery substance. The letter matches the description of letters sent to other congressional and state offices across the nation,” Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., wrote on X Friday.

Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, Mike Rounds, R-S.D., and Susan Collins, R-Maine, similarly announced they were targets of suspicious mail sent to their state offices. A spokesperson for Collins said a letter was also addressed to her Capitol Hill office but was intercepted.

“Despite escalating political rhetoric and harassment, we will continue our work for the people of Maine,” Collins’ chief of staff said in a statement.

“This situation is deeply concerning and follows a trend of intimidating tactics that impact our team members. This has no place in our nation. America is better than this,” Rounds wrote on X on Friday.

After the attacks in 2001, when an intern opened a letter to then-Sen. Tom Daschle and anthrax poured out, security officials made significant changes to how mail is handled at the Capitol, adding offsite screening. But lawmakers also have offices around the country in their home states and districts. Mail arriving there should be “received utilizing established safe mail handling procedures, including the use of SAA provided mail hoods,” according to the memo sent to House staff Monday.

Some lawmakers have described the tense moments after their staff discovered powder in the envelopes, leading to hazmat responses and evacuations.

“An envelope containing a suspicious white powder was delivered to my Santa Cruz district office and opened by staff this morning as part of her normal daily morning routine responding to constituents. Upon realizing that there was powder in the envelope, she immediately put the envelope in the garbage can, cleared fellow staff members out of the office, and called 911,” Rep. Jimmy Panetta, D-Calif., said in a Friday statement.

Gecko Robotics CEO Jake Loosararian says AI-powered inspections can cut repair costs and get warships back to sea faster as the Navy expands the company’s contract ceiling to $300 million.

FIRST ON FOX: The U.S. Navy is quadrupling the ceiling on a contract for AI-powered robots used to inspect warships to $300 million.

Just six months after initially tapping the technology to help get ships through maintenance and back to sea faster, the expanded agreement with Pittsburgh-based Gecko Robotics underscores the importance the U.S. military is putting on tech-based solutions. The initial ceiling for the deal was $71 million, but the Navy is pushing to improve fleet readiness amid a widening shipbuilding gap with China.

"While the U.S. may not be able to out-manufacture faster than China, we can outsmart the ways that we maintain, operate and are ready with our vessels," Gecko Robotics CEO Jake Loosararian told Fox News Digital.

Gecko says its technology can save the Navy up to $8 million in repair costs on a single ship and identify some structural issues up to 50 times faster than traditional inspection methods.

INSIDE TRUMP’S DEAL TO GIVE AMERICAN TAXPAYERS A MASSIVE STAKE IN NEW $6.6B SUBMARINE DEAL

Gecko Robotics uses robotic inspections and AI-powered software to map structural conditions aboard U.S. Navy warships, helping maintenance crews identify areas that may need repair. (Gecko Robotics)

The company is also unveiling a new robot developed specifically for the Navy that can inspect the steel beneath thick coatings on warship decks without first stripping them away.

Dubbed Komodo, the robot scans a ship's deck to map corrosion and material thickness, giving maintenance crews a picture of what needs to be repaired before more invasive work begins.

"It's essentially a CAT scan," Loosararian said. "You're basically understanding exactly what's going on."

Traditionally, determining the condition of steel beneath a ship's non-skid deck coating can require removing material before crews know the extent of the problem. Komodo is designed to gather that information without first taking the surface apart.

"The robots are able to actually understand what's wrong without having to take apart the ship to figure out what to fix," Loosararian said.

In another example cited by Loosararian, an assessment that initially called for roughly 1,200 square feet of repair work was narrowed to about 300 square feet after robotic inspections provided a more precise picture of the damage.

"You reduce and focus the kinds of repairs that you need," Loosararian said. "You're repairing less."

A Gecko Robotics wall-climbing robot scans the surface of a U.S. Navy warship, collecting data on material condition that can be analyzed for corrosion and structural damage. (Gecko Robotics)

CHINA’S LONG-TERM FINANCES ARE ALL WET AS BILL TO MAINTAIN HUGE NAVY COMES DUE IN 2031

The increased ceiling comes just six months after the Navy awarded Gecko a five-year, $71 million contract vehicle to expand the use of its robotic inspection technology across the fleet.

Under the initial agreement announced in March, Gecko was set to begin work on 18 ships in the U.S. Pacific Fleet, including destroyers, amphibious warships and littoral combat ships.

The company's wall-climbing robots crawl across hulls, flight decks, ballast tanks and other difficult-to-access areas, scanning for corrosion, metal loss and other structural problems. The data is fed into Gecko's AI-powered Cantilever platform to help maintenance planners determine where repairs are needed.

The goal is to find those problems earlier, before a ship enters a major maintenance period and crews discover additional work that can extend its stay in the shipyard.

"The biggest savings are just in speed," Loosararian said. "Speed — you can't put a price tag on it, especially if you're in the U.S. Navy right now."

The expansion comes as Navy leaders seek to push fleet readiness toward 80% while maintenance delays continue to sideline ships that would otherwise be available for deployment.

China already fields a larger battle force than the U.S. Navy and can produce vessels at a pace American shipyards cannot easily match. That has put additional pressure on the Pentagon to keep more of the ships already in the American fleet available for operations.

The inspections will focus on destroyers, amphibious warships and littoral combat ships — vessels that form a core part of U.S. naval operations in the Indo-Pacific. (Gecko Robotics)

For Gecko, the longer-term goal is to move beyond finding existing damage and use years of inspection data to anticipate problems before they force ships into longer repair periods.

"You are able to predict exactly what's going to break before it does," Loosararian said, allowing maintenance planners to have workers, materials and repair plans ready when a ship reaches the pier or enters a shipyard.

The technology could also reduce the amount of dangerous and labor-intensive inspection work performed by shipyard workers as the industrial base struggles with shortages of skilled labor.

Loosararian said the combination of robotics and AI is ultimately aimed at allowing a limited workforce to spend more time fixing ships and less time determining what needs to be fixed.

For a Navy racing to keep pace with a rapidly expanding Chinese fleet, he argued, getting more out of the ships already in the water could prove just as important as building new ones.

"While the U.S. may not be able to out-manufacture faster than China," Loosararian said, "we can outsmart the ways that we maintain, operate and are ready with our vessels."

#70. A Better “America First”

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

CHARLES KUPCHAN is Professor of International Affairs at Georgetown University and a Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. He is the author of Bringing Order to Anarchy: Governing the World to Come.

What Trump Gets Right—and Wrong—About Foreign Policy

Critics from across the political spectrum have disparaged U.S. President Donald Trump’s “America first” brand of statecraft—and for good reason. He has alienated allies, appeased great-power rivals, launched yet another failed war of choice in the Middle East, and blundered into trade wars that have worsened the United States’ affordability crisis.

But as debate heats up about what the next administration’s foreign policy should look like, Democrats and Republicans alike must be careful not to throw the baby out with the bathwater. Trump is right to recognize that U.S. strategy is in need of an overhaul. Most of his instincts are sound and align with fundamental changes in the international system and in American public opinion. His “America first” foreign policy is a symptom, not a cause, of global disarray and the public’s turn against the establishment; many U.S. voters have been disillusioned by the country’s chronic overreach abroad and the affordability crisis at home. Trump successfully tapped into these grievances by promising to scale back international entanglements and bring back factories and manufacturing jobs.

These are worthy goals, but Trump’s policies have badly missed their mark. He has started new wars and mostly failed to end old ones, and his tariffs have fueled inflation while doing little to resuscitate the manufacturing sector. Trump has implemented his course corrections with marked incompetence, making policy by impulse, gutting the diplomatic corps, relying on an inexperienced inner circle, and prizing loyalty over fact.

The challenge ahead is not to reflexively restore what came before; liberal internationalism long served the United States well, but during an era that no longer exists. Instead of burying “America first,” Trump’s successor should salvage its best elements and implement them more capably. The next version of U.S. foreign policy should marry the realist impulses that shape “America first” with the liberal cause that remains at the heart of the American experience. That composite strategy would see Washington pare back its commitments abroad, reach across ideological dividing lines to work with great-power rivals, operate through nimble coalitions, and repair the United States’ broken social contract and ailing democracy. Foreign policy starts at home: only by redressing the socioeconomic discontent that has cleaved the body politic into hostile camps can the country recoup the bipartisan centrism and democratic vitality needed to anchor a purposeful and steady statecraft.

Two tectonic shifts are leading to a historic turning point. Power is rapidly shifting from West to East and North to South, as Brazil, China, India, Indonesia, Nigeria, and other large developing countries rise. The United States and its democratic allies, assuming they manage to stay partners, will remain an influential bloc, but no longer a preponderant one. As the diffusion of power fuels geopolitical rivalries, Americans are growing weary of entanglement in a fragmenting world. Meanwhile, technological advances made possible by the digital age have undermined the social contract of the industrial era and hollowed out the middle class. As broadly shared prosperity has given way to economic insecurity and inequality, political cleavages have emerged along socioeconomic, educational, and rural-urban lines. Liberal democracy is in retreat worldwide, including in the United States, where the centrist, bipartisan compact that long anchored U.S. statecraft has collapsed.

Enter Trump. By the time U.S. forces withdrew from Afghanistan in 2021, more than 70 percent of Americans deemed the two-decade war a failure. Speaking to an electorate fed up with the never-ending conflicts in the Middle East, Trump pledged “no more wars” as he ran for reelection in 2024. He began his second term by using force sparingly. The single-night air campaign against Iran’s nuclear installations in June 2025 and the in-and-out raid to seize Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January 2026 succeeded in their narrow aims. Perhaps emboldened by these low-cost wins, Trump then proceeded to launch a full-scale war against Iran in February 2026. By planning for a short conflict and getting stuck in a long one, he fell into the very trap that he swore to avoid.

Given that the United States keeps getting mired in errant conflicts, Congress urgently needs to reassert its constitutional obligation to approve acts of war and oversee retrenchment. The bar for engaging in major conflicts outside the core strategic areas of Europe and East Asia should be quite high. It is past time for Washington to return to its traditional geopolitical vocation: playing the role of great-power balancer in order to preserve stability in the strategic heartland. American strategy toward Europe and East Asia has been a steady and cost-effective success, facilitating great-power peace since 1945. The roughly 150,000 U.S. troops still stationed in these core theaters are a wise investment in extending that track record.

A retrenchment from the Middle East and other peripheral areas does not mean a comprehensive retreat, but it does mean relying far more heavily on diplomacy and economic engagement than on the military. When force is required to counter threats to U.S. interests or allies, the United States should generally limit itself to supporting regional partners and relying on special forces and surgical strikes. As it seeks to end its addiction to military force, Washington could take a page from Beijing: China has spread its influence and maximized its leverage in the global South not through armed intervention but through investments, trade, and the Belt and Road Initiative, the biggest infrastructure project in modern history.

As the United States refocuses its attention and resources on maintaining stability in Asia and Europe, it can nonetheless lighten its load by rebalancing its alliances. Trump made headway by pushing allies to shoulder their fair share of the defense burden; NATO members and Asian allies are substantially increasing their defense budgets. But true to form, Trump has marred this success by taking actions that corrode decades of trust, such as threatening to seize Greenland and repeatedly demeaning allied leaders.

Allies are force multipliers; rather than alienating them, the United States should hold them even closer as they beef up their militaries. Washington should work with allies’ defense industries and military planners to come up with a new division of labor, set force levels, and create a realistic timetable to meet their goals. The United States’ network of defense pacts is poised to get stronger as its allies get stronger, but only if rebalancing occurs with consent, foresight, and respectful treatment of partners.

Adjusting U.S. strategy to the onset of multipolarity also entails building on Trump’s recognition that regional spheres of influence are making a comeback. As power diffuses across the international system, Washington will be neither willing nor able to oversee all the world’s main strategic theaters. Instead, major powers in each theater will play a more prominent role in guiding projects of regional integration, shaping regional order, and providing public goods.

For decades, most American policymakers have denounced spheres of influence. In 2021, Secretary of State Antony Blinken called the concept “a recipe for an international system that falls apart.” Yet since the founding era, the United States has prioritized establishing and defending its own sphere of influence in the Western Hemisphere. During the Cold War, Washington granted the Soviet Union a buffer zone in Eastern Europe while entrenching its own zones of control in Western Europe, Northeast Asia, and the Middle East.

Trump recognizes this double standard. The 2025 National Security Strategy endorses a reassertion of U.S. dominance in the Western Hemisphere and calls on other countries to “assume primary responsibility for their regions.” Trump has exhibited long overdue regard for the strategic interests of other great powers and appropriate caution about the extension of U.S. commitments into their backyards. He has precluded the possibility of Ukraine’s entry into NATO, aware that membership would run afoul of Russia’s legitimate security interests and overextend the alliance. He is also looking for ways to reduce tensions in East Asia, pausing arms sales to Taiwan and canceling military exercises with South Korea.

But even if Trump is right to herald a return of spheres of influence, he has acted with self-defeating excess. In the Western Hemisphere, he has been driving away Canada, treating Venezuela like a U.S. colony, strangling Cuba, ordering strikes of questionable legality against boats allegedly running drugs, and renaming the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario. Instead of working toward a benign sphere of influence that attracts neighbors and promotes stability, Trump has been building a malign sphere of coercion that prompts other countries to run for cover.

Trump is making a similar mess in other theaters. Even if he is right to close NATO’s door to Ukraine, he has failed to convince Russia to end its war of aggression. A vision of a stable security order in Europe is nowhere to be found. And although regional integration offers the best bet for creating the stronger Europe that Trump seeks, he is backing far-right parties hostile to the European Union. Trump’s approach to East Asia is similarly muddled. He holds summits with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and hopes to do the same with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, but his administration lacks a coherent strategy for China or northeast Asia more broadly.

The diffusion of power makes a more regionalized world inevitable, and to maintain order in that world, the United States will need to work with China, Russia, and other countries that hold sway in their neighborhoods. Trump’s successors will need to salvage his defective effort to help guide this transition. Washington needs to exercise a restrained and lawful brand of hegemony in the Western Hemisphere, respecting the sovereignty of its neighbors and pursuing mutual gains. That approach will encourage other powers to do the same in their own neighborhoods. To that end, Washington needs to grant Russia and China more breathing room in return for their readiness to exercise restraint within their regions. Moscow and Beijing might well take a less coercive stance toward their neighbors if the United States were to reduce its own military presence in and designs on their rimlands.

It will be particularly important for the United States to work with China, its only peer competitor, to de-escalate tensions without encouraging Chinese expansionism. On one hand, the United States needs to make allowances for growing Chinese power and ambition. A new regional order in Asia will endure only if the reigning hegemon and rising challenger can come to terms on the distribution of power and influence within the order. On the other hand, Washington cannot allow Chinese aggression against its neighbors. The United States needs to walk a fine line between prudent accommodation and dangerous appeasement. The goal in the long term would be to establish a multilateral system of regional governance—anchored by China but accepted by its neighbors.

Trump’s 2025 National Security Strategy embraces what it calls “flexible realism,” a pragmatic foreign policy that aims to establish good relations with all countries “without imposing on them democratic or other social change that differs widely from their traditions and histories.” This readiness to work across ideological lines is an important corrective to the “democracy versus autocracy” framework that guided the Biden administration’s foreign policy. The United States must navigate the world as it is, not as it would like it to be. Trump is right to reach out to autocracies and set aside the zealous promotion of democracy.

Trump’s flexible realism also entails recognizing the need to form bespoke coalitions of the willing to augment the United Nations and other large multilateral institutions. When it comes to preventing or stopping major conflicts, the UN has largely been a bystander. Support for formal multilateralism has also evaporated in Washington; Republicans, in particular, have embraced a hostility toward institutionalized international commitments. Coalitions of the willing are already emerging as the vehicles of choice for resolving conflicts. China, France, Germany, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States negotiated the 2015 nuclear deal with Iran. Oman, Pakistan, and Qatar have led efforts to mediate between Iran and the United States. Meanwhile, a coalition of Egypt, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and the United States has been working to end Sudan’s civil war.

Yet even if Trump’s brand of realism marks a needed course correction, its implementation has been deeply flawed. Trump’s outreach to Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin occurs in fits and starts and lacks a clear set of objectives. Washington’s unilateralism and fondness for ad hoc coalitions have also gone too far. The UN system admittedly falls woefully short on managing most security issues, but it plays an important role in humanitarian relief, global health, and climate change. By slashing humanitarian assistance and withdrawing from the World Health Organization and the Paris climate agreement, Trump has hobbled effective multilateral initiatives. And even though his signature coalition of the willing, the Board of Peace, has potential, it was thrown together haphazardly. The board’s first mission—to pacify and bring lawful governance to Gaza—has been an utter failure.

Whoever comes after Trump should continue his pragmatic effort to work with autocracies. But that effort must be guided by a clear set of strategic objectives, promote geopolitical stability, and be anchored by the sustained work of experts, not just a handful of financiers. Experienced U.S. diplomats should thoroughly prepare summits and identify concrete deliverables with their foreign counterparts. Summits between world leaders are critical opportunities to advance the cause of global stability and must be treated as such.

Greater reliance on coalitions of the willing is the right move, but they need to be fit for their purpose. The Board of Peace is certainly not. It has over 25 members, including countries that carry little diplomatic weight, such as Kosovo, Mongolia, and Paraguay. Instead, the board should function as a concert of great powers, both democratic and autocratic, tasked with managing crises and overseeing and building consensus on matters of global governance. Unlike the UN Security Council, which is often paralyzed by veto, this steering group would forgo binding rules and formal charters. It would strive for consensus through the give-and-take of diplomacy, providing a venue for sustained engagement that currently does not exist.

Even as it sets up a great-power steering group to manage core security issues, Washington should resume supporting the UN to advance human welfare. The World Food Program, the World Health Organization, and the Paris climate agreement may not be perfect, but Washington should try to make them more effective, not undermine them. And when the United States defects, others follow. France, Sweden, and the United Kingdom all slashed spending on foreign assistance after the United States gutted its own budget. Washington needs to be a leader, not a laggard, on issues of human welfare. Doing so is not only a matter of altruism; the United States itself will have to grapple with migrants fleeing failing states, pandemics, and the dangers of climate change.

Finally, although the United States should continue to practice ideological pluralism and work with autocracies, that effort must be paired with a revival of democracy at home. Americans have no choice but to learn to live comfortably in a politically diverse world. Yet they should do so while upholding the original version of U.S. exceptionalism, which was to spread republican ideals by serving as a democratic exemplar. Americans should not give up on their messianic mission to bend the arc of history toward more freedom. But instead of seeking to foist democracy on others, they should pursue this mission by refurbishing the American experiment and demonstrating that representative government can outperform the autocratic alternatives.

The antiestablishment wave that Trump rode to power in 2016 and 2024 is animated by discontent with the quality of life at home at least as much as overreach abroad. Much of Trump’s voter base feels left behind by automation and globalization, displaced by immigrants, and sidelined by progressive social and cultural trends. Trump has responded by cracking down on immigrants and attacking “DEI”—diversity, equity, and inclusion. At the center of his domestic agenda is his pledge to rebuild the middle class. As he ran for reelection in 2024, Trump promised that higher tariffs would turn the United States back into a “manufacturing powerhouse,” with plenty of factory jobs to go around.

Trump is right to want to tame inequality, scale back some of the excesses of globalization, and secure supply chains of critical goods. But his protectionism won’t revive the manufacturing sector. Automation, not free trade, is the main cause of the decades-long decline in manufacturing jobs. Despite years of tariffs and industrial policy, manufacturing jobs have continued to disappear. And the rate at which machines replace humans will pick up as firms grow reliant on artificial intelligence. Around 80 percent of the U.S. workforce already works in the service sector, and most will not be headed back to the production line. In the meantime, Trump’s tariffs, combined with the supply chain disruptions caused by the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, have significantly raised the cost of living—the main reason that Republicans are heading into the midterms in deep political trouble.

Instead of promising to claw back manufacturing jobs that are gone for good, the next administration should train Americans for the jobs of the future. The public sector must work with the private sector to fashion an education and employment ecosystem fit for the digital age. In the decades ahead, most Americans will work in information technology, data processing, education, finance, health care, travel, hospitality, leisure, and retail. And as AI disrupts labor markets in many different sectors, workers will need transferable skills that will allow them to adapt. Expanding worker retraining programs, investing in the ailing public school system, and improving access to community colleges will do far more than tariffs to rebuild the middle class—and are the first steps in forging a new social contract. A credible plan for getting Americans back on their feet is critical to repairing the nation’s democracy and steadying its statecraft.

Even if the Democrats take back control of one or both chambers in the November midterms—which appears likely—they will struggle to change Trump’s course. He ignores Congress on most issues, but especially on matters of foreign policy, over which the legislative branch has limited power.

Accordingly, Americans have little choice but to ride out the Trump era and try to limit the damage that he does by defending democracy at home. But getting ready for the next administration requires drawing the right lessons from his errant presidency. Trump has begun implementing a needed overhaul of U.S. grand strategy, but he is incapable of turning good instincts into sound policy. It will be up to his successor to better align U.S. grand strategy with a changing world and provide the judgment and competence missing from Trump’s time in charge.

#71. Trump Can Push Past Israeli-Palestinian Paralysis

Argument: Trump Can Push Past Israeli-Palestinian Paralysis

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Three years after Oct. 7, 2023, the prospects for meaningful Israeli-Palestinian diplomatic progress appear worse than ever. Israelis look at the way Hamas celebrated killing innocents and brutalizing hostages and conclude that they could never be safe alongside an independent Palestinian state. Palestinians look at many Israelis’ indifference to their deaths and continued suffering in Gaza and are equally convinced that Israel will never accept their independence or let them live with security and dignity.

Peacemaking in such an environment seems hopeless—and hopelessness provides fertile ground for the extremists to promote violence, claiming the conflict can only end with the destruction of the other side. Which is why, as daunting as the current environment is, it is more important than ever to show that practical, positive changes are possible.

Three years after Oct. 7, 2023, the prospects for meaningful Israeli-Palestinian diplomatic progress appear worse than ever. Israelis look at the way Hamas celebrated killing innocents and brutalizing hostages and conclude that they could never be safe alongside an independent Palestinian state. Palestinians look at many Israelis’ indifference to their deaths and continued suffering in Gaza and are equally convinced that Israel will never accept their independence or let them live with security and dignity.

Peacemaking in such an environment seems hopeless—and hopelessness provides fertile ground for the extremists to promote violence, claiming the conflict can only end with the destruction of the other side. Which is why, as daunting as the current environment is, it is more important than ever to show that practical, positive changes are possible.

First, it is important to recognize that actual cooperation is taking place between Israelis and Palestinians even now, for example, in managing the sewage problem in Gaza. Sewage from Gaza flows directly to the Israeli coastline and, from time to time, has necessitated closing Israel’s nearby desalination plant at Ashkelon. Not surprisingly, there are nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), like the Arava Institute in Israel, that bring Israelis and Palestinians together to work on water, sanitation, health, environment, and related economic issues and challenges.

All this needs to become far more visible. The Trump administration—whether through Jared Kushner’s team or through the State Department’s Bureau of Near Eastern Affairs, or through the U.S. embassy—should promote, participate in, and publicize such meetings. It should also provide funds, or solicit them from partners, for NGOs whose mission is to foster cooperation between Israelis and Palestinians on functional issues.

Second, the realities on the ground must be transformed. In Gaza, U.S. President Donald Trump’s 20-point peace plan produced a cease-fire a year ago and helped secure the release of the remaining hostages. The basic formula built into the Trump plan was the demilitarization of Gaza in return for reconstruction and Israeli withdrawal. A year later, Palestinians in Gaza are still living in wretched conditions, and Hamas coercively controls about 30 percent to 35 percent of the territory, including a vast majority of its population.

The promise of the 20 points remains on paper but not on the ground, where there has been no disarmament, no reconstruction, and no Israel Defense Forces withdrawal. Similarly, the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG)—the 15-member body of Palestinian technocrats designed to govern Gaza on a transitional basis—remains in Cairo, not Gaza. So long as it is not in Gaza, it cannot begin to demonstrate that there is an alternative to Hamas rule. (The initial tranche of Palestinian police who are to provide security for the NCAG also remains in Cairo.) Moreover, the International Stabilization Force (ISF), which is to back up the Palestinian police, monitor Hamas’s disarming, and oversee the borders to prevent smuggling, is only now organizing and will not deploy to Gaza until the NCAG and the Palestinian police are entering the strip.

After long months of talks and prodding, Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace’s high representative, working with Egypt, Qatar, and Turkey, reached agreement with Hamas on a 15-point road map to implement the Trump plan. This agreement, announced on July 30, committed Hamas to a process of decommissioning all of its weaponry in phases. And yet, in no small part because of the October Israeli election and his political base’s opposition to the 15 points, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he did not accept the road map—leading to the plan’s being put on hold until after the Israeli election.

While Israelis are in general skeptical that Hamas will actually disarm, the 15-point road map puts Hamas to the test. It is in Israel’s interest to put the onus on Hamas and not keep it on itself. If Hamas fails to do what it agreed to, Israel will be in a far better position to apply military pressure. But if the plans for decommissioning proceed, that will allow the NCAG, Palestinian police, and the ISF to deploy to Gaza. Then the process of rebuilding Gaza under an alternative to Hamas will finally begin.

Both sides continue to wonder whether the Trump plan and the road map will ever be implemented. Israelis may be skeptical that Hamas will credibly disarm, but Palestinians are skeptical that Israel will allow rebuilding and withdraw. Putting the NCAG in a position where it can begin to deliver portable and pre-fab housing before winter sets in would do wonders for its credibility and buy it time to produce more in terms of governance. Showing that Gaza can be transformed will also have the benefit of restoring a sense of possibility about what might be done between Israelis and Palestinians.

Third, Arab states must play a more active role. Historically, Arab leaders have generally limited their role to offering slogans and saying they would agree to whatever the Palestinians accepted. That was a way to avoid responsibility and leave the conflict to others, such as the United States, to resolve. To make progress, key Arab states—what used to be called the Arab Quint, of Egypt, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar—need to play two roles: In the near term, they should get serious about producing real reform in the Palestinian Authority (PA). This means creating credible standards of reform, providing incentives for meeting them, and making clear they will call out the PA should it fall short.

Arab states also need to create an umbrella of support for the hard decisions the Palestinian leadership will have to take. There is no peacemaking without concessions—and Palestinian leaders will need to cover any steps they take that seem to address Israeli needs. Arab leaders must endorse these hard decisions and defend them.

Key Arab states like Saudi Arabia can play one other role to help Palestinians: They can offer further outreach to Israel in return for concessions to the Palestinians. The Saudis, for example, could allow direct commercial ties with Israeli companies in return for Israel stopping de facto annexation, and modifying the Paris Protocol of 1994 that govern economic ties between Israel and the PA and significantly limit Palestinian commercial and economic activity.

Finally, the Trump administration needs to hold Israel accountable. That starts with insistence that this Israeli government act demonstrably and systematically to stop the extremist attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank. In addition, Trump should make clear that he expects the next Israeli government to do its part to fulfill his plan and the 15-point road map. While insisting that Hamas and the PA must deliver on their commitments, including on de-radicalization, he will want Israeli—and Palestinian—leaders to understand that if Hamas and the PA follow through, Israel will be held to its commitments as well.

The mutual trauma of Israelis and Palestinians won’t go away any time soon. But for now, both sides must again be convinced that change is possible. The Trump administration must push all parties for the practical steps that will end the current paralysis.

Dennis Ross is a distinguished fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy and the author most recently of Statecraft 2.0: What America Needs to Lead in a Multipolar World. Ross served in senior national security positions in  the Reagan, George H.W. The next day, Watters made no bones about El-Sayedâs appeal. âI like him,â he said. âI donât want to like him. I like him for some stupid reason.â

But the reason was obvious. The doctor-turned-politician has an aggressive bro style that appeals to someone like Watters. Quick-witted with bulldog energy, El-Sayed never backs down from a fight. But despite Wattersâ admiration, Fox News has become obsessed with taking El-Sayed down. Itâs not because heâs Muslim, though Republicans are ratcheting up the racism in their efforts to derail his campaign. Itâs because he is a model for how Democrats can escape their reputations for being weak and feckless.Â

El-Sayed has a lot going for him. He spent years running public health services in the Detroit area and speaks eloquently and with authority about peopleâs struggles to afford healthcare, even writingÂ a book about Medicare for All. Most importantly, heâs an excellent communicator who can boil down complex policy ideas into easily digestible concepts without dumbing them down. A video of him explaining to Trump voters why universal healthcare is cheaper than the insurance system went viral for good reason. One can see that, for these voters, itâs likely the first time someone plainly explained how removing executive salaries and profit incentives from healthcare makes it cheaper.Â

Other politicians, like Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., or Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., are good at explaining progressive policy. But what really seems to scare Republicans about El-Sayed is his political persona as a brawler â and for good reason. Vice President JD Vance learned this last week when he lobbed a strange insult at El-Sayed during a rally in Michigan for Rogers. The Democrat, Vance said, is âa little weasel who should shut his mouth and show a little gratitude.â

This is a common and deeply racist attack from Vance, who portrays non-white progressives as undeserving recipients of white peopleâs largesse â a caricature that has no relation to reality. El-Sayed left a position as an assistant professor at Columbia University to work in public health, where he won awards for his success in protecting childrenâs health from environmental pollution. During this same period, Vance worked as a venture capitalist who was close with tech billionaire Peter Thiel.

El-Sayed resisted the temptation to âwell, actuallyâ Vance, and instead hit back by calling the vice president and those around him âcarnival barkersâ who âare small and want to make us small like them.â His response was smooth. âJD Vance called me a little weasel today,â El-Sayed said. âIâm like, âNo, no, no. What youâre talking about is a Wolverine,'â a reference to the mascot for the University of Michigan, where the Democrat got his undergraduate degree.Â

As Salonâs Sophia Tesfaye recently wrote, El-Sayed has been courting Fox News viewers by appearing on the channel and running endless ads on it, all without softening his left-leaning message. He clearly hopes his bravado will woo some of the networkâs audience, just as it won over Watters.Â

For his part, President Donald Trump is worried that El-Sayed is right. Heâs been openly complaining at rallies and on Truth Social about how charming the candidate is in his Fox appearances. In early October, Axios reported that the White House contacted the network to complain about El-Sayedâs coverage. Trump was especially miffed at the Democratâs interview with Martha McCallum, during which the hostâs efforts to bait him into saying something that could be spun as âradicalâ failed. Instead, MacCallum embarrassed herself by defending billionaires hoarding wealth, to which El-Sayed said that heâd rather pay for schools than be so âfocused on allowing a billionaire to make another billion.â

Since then, it seems that Fox producers got the White Houseâs message that they have to do something to dirty up El-Sayed. But theyâve learned the hard way that it wonât work to come at him directly, because he ends up dominating interviews and beguiling those who, like Watters, love his commanding and clever style. MacCallum later tried to redeem herself by interviewing progressive activist Corbin Trent and pretending he was a stand-in for El-Sayed.

At first glance, Trent performed as Fox producers no doubt hoped he might. He took MacCallumâs bait by defending the Muslim Brotherhood, something that the host could not get El-Sayed to do. The problem, though, is that Trent has no discernible relationship to the candidate. While he has worked for other progressives, including Sanders, I found no evidence that he has even met El-Sayed, much less is qualified to speak for him.

This attempt to hobble El-Sayed was revealing; itâs clearly all Fox News has. If the network tries to bring El-Sayed on again to ask him the same questions, they know from experience that heâll probably just win over even more of their viewers. This isnât idle speculation. MS NOW recently conducted a focus group with regretful Trump voters in Michigan and found that five out of the six are voting for El-Sayed. Republicans should be worried about the young male demographic in particular. Trump won male voters under 30 by a narrow margin in 2024, but they are jumping ship and now strongly favor Democrats.

El-Sayed is a compelling model for a new kind of Democrat. Polling by Strength In Numbers/Verasight shows that even Democratic voters take a negative view of the party, but not because they think their leaders are too progressive. â[T]he single most common complaint about their own party is that it is too weak, too cautious, or not fighting hard enough,â writes G. Elliott Morris in an analysis of the poll.

The Democratic base wants the party to take a more aggressive stance toward their GOP opponents, which will be key to building a more lasting coalition â especially one that includes younger and more male voters. El-Sayed is doing just that, and it has the right scared.

#73. Data center anxiety plays out in Senate campaign debates

In debates and advertisements ahead of the midterm elections, Democratic candidates for Senate are consistently pressing their opponents on artificial intelligence data center policy, often as a proxy for voter fears about the economy and local impacts.

In Ohio, former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is fond of calling Republican incumbent Sen. Jon Husted “the face of data centers.”

Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., tied the vote by opponent Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., for the Republican “One Big Beautiful Bill” health and tax cuts measure last year to data centers.

And James Talarico is accusing his opponent in the race for the Senate, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, of “selling off Texas” to data center firms.

In addition to attacking each other’s policy positions on tech, candidates of both parties are attacking each other’s campaign donations from Big Tech groups and investments in data center companies. Both pro-AI and regulation-focused groups are spending millions on Republican and Democratic candidates.

As Democrats have sought to put Republicans on the back foot by tying data centers to rising energy costs and the larger issue of affordability, polling data appears to support the choice.

A Pew Research Center survey conducted in July and August found that 50 percent of U.S. adults think data centers are “mostly bad” for home energy costs, compared with 38 percent in January.

Those polled have also gotten more pessimistic about data centers’ effects on the environment, jobs, tax revenue and quality of life for those living nearby.

Dan Cassino, a professor of government and politics at Fairleigh Dickinson University, said because voters believe data centers are the cause of their higher electricity bills, the construction projects are part of affordability concerns.

“President [Donald] Trump campaigned for office in 2024 saying he was going to make things more affordable, was going to break down inflation, and he hasn’t delivered on that,” Cassino said. “And that means it’s a real point of vulnerability for Republicans.”

As a result, Cassino said, Democrats are “hitting Republicans really hard” on the need to regulate data centers.

In a Georgia Senate debate earlier this month, Ossoff used last year’s budget reconciliation bill, which included tax breaks that Ossoff said are being used by data center companies, to criticize Collins.

“Just think about this, when you are paying more for your health insurance, when a hospital in your community is closing down,” Ossoff said. “Mike Collins voted to take that money out of your pocket and out of your community and give it instead to data center developers.”

Collins, in turn, said he favored “local control” over data center decisions.

Data center attacks may work differently, however, against sitting members of Congress. Cassino posited that candidates like Collins who have already been on Capitol Hill may have an easier time on this issue than their counterparts coming from state and local government. “They might have been doing something indirectly, but they weren’t on zoning boards,” he said.

Talarico’s race with Paxton highlights the local nature of the data center backlash, with ads tying data centers both to the cost of living and to accusations of corruption against Paxton.

“The data centers bankrolled Paxton, they get tax breaks and you get stuck with the bill,” Talarico said in one ad. In another, he promised that if elected he would “take on the data centers raising our costs.”

Husted, as well, is being challenged for actions during his time in state government. He served as lieutenant governor before his appointment to the Senate early last year when fellow Republican JD Vance became vice president. In an ad, Brown pointed to tax breaks his state agreed to for tech companies building data centers.

Husted “gave away two and a half billion dollars to these out-of-state corporations and billionaires,” Brown said in the advertisement. “He gave up Ohio’s money, our tax money, to Meta, a company worth $2 trillion, to make sure they come to Ohio.”

Other Brown ads connect data centers to rising residential electricity costs. He also pledged to “require the data centers pay the full cost of their electricity, not you.”

While Husted’s own ads don’t seem to mention data centers, his work in the Senate has.

He sponsored the Senate version of a bill, dubbed the “Ratepayer Protection Act,” that would encourage states to adopt standards to make data centers take on the cost of electrical grid upgrades needed to meet their new energy demand. The House-passed version stalled on a procedural vote last month on the Senate floor after Democrats said it wasn’t strong enough.

In a debate last week between Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, Collins responded to Jackson’s data center attacks by pointing to her support for the Husted bill.

She also said that “guardrails” on energy use are particularly important because of Maine’s high energy prices, which she blamed on Jackson, who previously served as state Senate president.

Jackson agreed on the need for “real guardrails” to ensure that data centers don’t cause higher electricity costs for other consumers or hurt local water quality.

Democrats’ data center arguments, while not the central issue of most campaigns, seem to be part of a successful strategy. Inside Elections rates Georgia as Lean Democrat, while Maine, Ohio and Texas, all seats currently held by Republicans, are rated as Toss-up.

As sitting senators talk about the Ratepayer Protection Act bill, Cassino cautioned that voters may not care about Capitol Hill procedural votes.

“Anything incumbents say about, ‘oh, this is what I’m doing to protect you,’ is going to ring hollow because everyone sees their electricity prices going up,” Cassino said.

Ray La Raja, a professor of political science at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and co-director of the UMass-Amherst Poll, said that Republicans also aren’t likely to see success arguing that data centers are needed to beat China in a race over artificial intelligence.

“When people see these huge constructions in their backyard, that is much more tangible than any … economic, national security competition with China,” La Raja said.

He also said that with less than a month to go, “this election is baked in,” including the Democratic advantage in talking about data centers. But he sees a possibility for Republicans to develop a long-term strategy to tell voters why they support data centers.

“If you want to allay people’s fears… be very concrete about the benefits that are going to be coming into the community,” La Raja said, adding that benefits could include subsidies or promises that “you’re going to keep your … energy prices below this level, we’re going to build new facilities that serve the community, recreation.”

In the Michigan Senate debate earlier this month, Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers tried a version of that tactic.

“If a community wants one of these facilities … every dollar of the generated property tax should go to defray the cost of everyone that lives in that municipality,” Rogers said. “Dollar for dollar, it should go down.”

Rogers has previously expressed support for Michigan taking a one-year pause on data center construction. His Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, said at the debate that he supports “terms of engagement” for data centers, though he did not specify what those terms should be.

Inside Elections rates the Michigan Senate race as Tilt Democratic.

Looking beyond the midterms, Darrell M. West, a senior fellow in the Center for Technology Innovation at the Brookings Institution, said this year’s vote could be “very formative.”

“If the candidates who were supporting data centers end up losing, that’s going to encourage the critics to enact even tougher rules,” West said. If things go the other way, it could “take the wind out of that sail.”

But any federal restrictions in the next Congress would be up against Trump’s firm support for AI and data centers.

West said that support is making things even more complicated for Republicans running this year.

“They’re getting local pressure to slow down the development of data centers, and Trump is telling the country, ‘don’t worry about this, data centers are not a problem,’” West said. “And voters don’t believe that anymore.”

#78. The real reason it's going to take a while to know who won in some midterm races

Election workers process ballots for the California state primary at the Los Angeles County Ballot Processing Center on June 5. California's relatively slow vote count has put "a big target on its back," one expert told NPR. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images hide caption

Stephen Richer no longer runs elections in the fourth-largest county in the country.

But for the rest of his life, he'll remember the feeling when polls closed on an election night.

More than a million ballots staring at him and his staff. Every moment that passes without them fully counted means another conspiracy theory sprouting online.

"Those days, those were hell for me," said Richer, a Republican who served as the clerk and recorder for Arizona's Maricopa County. "You'd have a limited number of workers, and you'd have a limited amount of space, and you'd be doing everything that you possibly could. … And yet you have everyone blowing up your phone, everyone saying that you're incompetent or corrupt or worse."

This midterm year, election officials in competitive congressional districts will face that same pressure.

But they will also face a hard reality: that those races might not be called until days after Election Day.

Here's an FAQ on why that is, and what it could mean this year.

Which sounds strange, since who wins an election and by how much shouldn't impact how long it takes election officials to count ballots.

But the reality is what most Americans think of as "election results" — the winners announced on election nights across TV networks and social media — are not the result of all ballots being counted, but rather, races being called by news organizations that determine the winners based on a state or district's demographics and initial returns. (NPR relies on The Associated Press for its race calls.)

Those determinations come a lot faster when races aren't close.

"Margins matter," said Richer, who noted that in recent elections, there has been a lot less scrutiny on Utah than there has been on his home state of Arizona, or certain contests in California, despite the states counting votes at similar speeds.

"In Utah you can call all the races very quickly because the Republicans there have high margins," Richer said.

That gives the illusion of elections there being complete, but no state is done counting ballots on election night, even if it seems that way because notable races are called early.

The closer the race, the more election analysts need to see before they can make a call. So the faster states count ballots, the faster those determinations can be made.

This is why the longest wait times every election usually come from places that have competitive races and which also count slowly.

Exactly. California has become the poster child for long results times because of both those factors: a bevy of competitive congressional districts, which help determine the balance of power in the U.S. House, and a vote count that's been among the slowest in the nation.

Add in that President Trump, the most prominent purveyor of election misinformation in the country, has long targeted the liberal California, and experts see a perfect storm for false voting narratives.

"It's progressive, it likes mail ballots, it gets [postmarked] mail ballots after Election Day," Richer said. "It just all adds up to a fairly incendiary situation."

Charles Stewart, an elections expert at MIT, put it more simply.

"California just has a big target on its back," said Stewart.

Kim Alexander is cautiously optimistic that won't be the case.

She runs the California Voter Foundation, which has been advocating for ways to speed up California's vote tally without giving up the state's generous voting access policies, like mailing every active registered voter a ballot.

"We have all these amazing rights and opportunities that we give to our voters, and the price we're paying is a longer vote count," Alexander told NPR. "But that doesn't mean that it has to be this long."

An election worker processes ballots for the California state primary at the Los Angeles County Ballot Processing Center on June 5. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images hide caption

The single biggest cause for California's slow count comes from a phenomenon Alexander calls "the pig in the python" problem: a logjam of millions of vote-by-mail ballots getting returned on Election Day that need to be processed.

Those ballots take longer to count than in-person votes, as officials need to deal with envelopes and verify signatures to make sure mail ballots are cast by the people they're supposed to be cast by.

Some counties see up to 50% of their vote-by-mail ballots turned in on Election Day, Alexander said, which means processing work doesn't even begin until later in the week.

"I can't tell you how many people who are informed and engaged and … when I tell them that the cause for the long vote count is voters holding on to their ballots to Election Day and turning them in, they look at me and they're like, 'That's what I do,'" Alexander said. "And I'm like, 'I know! You're part of the problem!'"

The state allocated $40 million to speeding up its counting this year, and part of that money is going to voter education.

Alexander is optimistic that once voters learn they can play a role in speeding up the process by voting earlier, or by utilizing other voting methods that allow for quicker counting, they will respond.

"California has been beaten up by this president for over a decade over our election process, and it's gotten pretty worrisome," Alexander said. "I think that California voters, if they feel they can do something to respond to that, many will take action."

To that point, research conducted earlier this year found that when voters in California's San Joaquin County received postcards urging them to vote earlier, they were more likely to meet the recommended deadline that allowed for election-night counting.

Alexander noted one more change that could mean less spotlight on California this year: fewer competitive House districts.

Ahead of the 2022 elections, the state had nine districts that the Cook Political Report considered competitive. But this year, in part because voters approved a mid-cycle gerrymander to respond to gerrymanders in Republican-controlled states, the state has just three.

That makes it less likely the entire country will be waiting on California to know who controls the House.

Using the formula discussed earlier (competitive races + slow vote counting), it's impossible not to look at Alaska.

According to data from the MIT Election Lab, Alaska was the last state in 2024 to reach 95% of its ballots counted.

Election Day was Nov. 5 that year, but the state's lone House race — which Republican Nicholas Begich won by fewer than 10,000 votes — wasn't called by the AP until Nov. 20.

This year, polling shows a tight Alaska Senate race. That means, if results fall a certain way in other states, the entire country could be waiting weeks to know which party will control the U.S. Senate next year.
