#79. Food safety fears are bipartisan. Trust in oversight isn’t

A Crunchwrap Supreme and a bag of supermarket salad generally appeal to rather different notions of a good lunch. One offers the architectural pleasure of a crunchy tostada tucked inside a warm tortilla; the other, the satisfaction of having arranged to eat vegetables without chopping any. This summer, however, both came with a less welcome consideration: iceberg lettuce.

A massive cyclospora outbreak linked to shredded iceberg from Taylor Farms de Mexico prompted recalls extending from Taco Bell kitchens to supermarket produce aisles. Shoppers began trying to determine which seemingly unrelated groceries shared a supplier; someone even made a barcode-scanning app for precisely this purpose. (Such was the broader atmosphere of suspicion that an entirely unsupported rumor about the Trump administrationâs promised bargain beef being horse meat eventually inspired online guides for distinguishing one animal from the other.)

And according to a Gallup poll published October 8, Americans emerged from it considerably more cautious about what they eat. Nearly three-quarters now say they have avoided buying certain foods because of recalls or government advisories, up from 53% in 2024. This newfound vigilance crosses party lines: 81% of Democrats and 63% of Republicans report having taken such precautions.

What it did not produce was much agreement about the people responsible for keeping the lettuce safe.

In 2024, when Joe Biden occupied the White House, 74% of Democrats and 50% of Republicans expressed confidence in federal food-safety oversight. Two years and one change of administration later, those figures stand at 30% and 70%, respectively.Â

A 24-point Democratic advantage has become a 40-point Republican one, a remarkable 64-point reversal.

Ahead of the midterms, the findings illustrate a curious feature of American political life: People can encounter the same dangers, take similar precautions and nevertheless arrive at radically different conclusions about the institutions responsible for protecting them. And if there were ever a summer when one might have expected a little consensus about the importance of competent food-safety oversight, surely it was this one.

The outbreak, the largest recorded cyclospora outbreak in U.S. history, sickened nearly 13,000 people across 21 states, hospitalizing 570 and killing two. The recall included lettuce served at Taco Bell and Marketside iceberg salad sold at Walmart. Taylor Farms maintained that its own branded salad kits were unaffected, a distinction that mattered scientifically, if not necessarily psychologically, to shoppers eyeing the refrigerated wall of greens.

The trouble with becoming an amateur food-safety inspector is that the job is never quite finished. You can establish that the blueberries in your refrigerator havenât been recalled, but this tells you remarkably little about the blueberries youâll purchase next Thursday. You can discover who owns the company that packaged your broccoli, though what to do with that information is another matter. Every new discovery yields a little more knowledge, if not necessarily a corresponding increase in certainty.

Want more great food writing and recipes? Sign up for Salonâs free food newsletter, The Bite.

There was a policy dimension to this uncertainty, too. In March 2025, the FDA announced plans to delay compliance with its Food Traceability Rule, which requires businesses handling higher-risk foods, including leafy greens, to maintain records that help investigators identify and remove contaminated products more quickly. Originally scheduled for January 2026, the compliance deadline was proposed to be extended to July 2028; Congress subsequently directed the FDA not to enforce the rule before then. The agency said businesses needed additional time to coordinate their systems.

The delay did not cause the summerâs outbreak. Still, there is something peculiar about postponing industry-wide traceability requirements while ordinary shoppers are left scanning their broccoli with smartphones, hoping to learn something useful about where it came from.

During Bad Lettuce Summer, even the official answers required some translation.

In July, the FDA announced that a lettuce sample had tested positive for cyclospora, then corrected the finding as a false positive. Taylor Farms emphasized the correction; federal investigators maintained that their broader epidemiological and traceback evidence still implicated the companyâs shredded iceberg. Subsequent environmental testing strengthened that evidence, without conclusively establishing how the contamination occurred.

One could read the competing statements carefully and emerge with some more information, but not much more confidence about dinner.

Then came the political subplot. As the investigation intensified, Taylor Farms representatives met privately with White House officials. The company and its leadership had donated substantial sums to Republican-aligned political groups, including $1 million to the pro-Trump super PAC MAGA Inc. Rep. Robert Garcia, the ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, subsequently sought answers about whether the company had attempted to influence the investigation. The White House denied compromising public safety, and no evidence established that political access changed the FDAâs findings.

Still, it is an extraordinary distance to travel from wondering whether the lettuce in your taco is safe to wondering who has the ear of the White House.

The Gallup numbers do not establish why Americansâ confidence has diverged so dramatically. Someone may distrust the industrial food system while enthusiastically supporting an administration promising to reform it. Someone else may have specific objections to that administrationâs regulatory decisions. But the speed of the partisan reversal suggests that who runs Washington matters enormously to how Americans evaluate its institutions â though there is a certain irony to this in the age of Make America Healthy Again, which has elevated suspicion of the conventional food system into something approaching a civic virtue.

Its influence has extended all the way to the fast-food fryer: Steak ân Shake announced that it had âRFKâdâ its French fries by replacing vegetable oil with beef tallow, a development Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. celebrated over burgers and fries during a televised appearance with Sean Hannity. The nationâs health secretary had become a verb, and the French fry a political statement.

It is, admittedly, easier to stage a photo opportunity around a basket of fries than a database of food-traceability records. Both involve questions about what Americans eat, but investigating foodborne illness requires a rather different kind of governmental attention.

Of course, Americans did not suddenly begin losing confidence in food-safety oversight under Trump.Â

Gallup found that overall confidence has fallen from 85% in 2004 to just 47% today. And recalls themselves contain an uncomfortable ambiguity: They reveal that something dangerous entered the food supply, but also that someone detected a problem and warned the public. The same event can look like evidence of a system working or a system failing, depending on which part of the story one chooses to emphasize.

With the midterms approaching, that distinction matters. The lawmakers elected in November will have a say in how federal food-safety agencies are funded, scrutinized and held accountable when the next outbreak arrives. Yet Americans are approaching that election with increasingly different assessments of the institutions charged with protecting them, even as their own precautions suggest a broadly shared sense of vulnerability.

The next outbreak, unfortunately, will not wait for everyone to agree on whom to trust.

#81. China Is a Peer Competitor in a Dangerous Space Race

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Analysis: China Is a Peer Competitor in a Dangerous Space Race

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Washington may be focused on the battle over artificial intelligence, but China is also ready to compete among the stars. The rapid progress of China’s space program may not yet be seen as a “Sputnik moment,” but Beijing is a full-spectrum peer competitor with Washington in everything from planned moon bases each powered by nuclear reactors to space weapons.

Space, with an already crowded low Earth orbit (LEO) and few rules, is another bifurcated realm of conflict-prone rivalry that brings, like maritime clashes or the future of AI, systemic challenges to the U.S.-China relationship. From potential nuclear warfare in space to competition over real estate on the moon, China’s ambitions are multifaceted and often in direct competition with those of the United States.

Washington may be focused on the battle over artificial intelligence, but China is also ready to compete among the stars. The rapid progress of China’s space program may not yet be seen as a “Sputnik moment,” but Beijing is a full-spectrum peer competitor with Washington in everything from planned moon bases each powered by nuclear reactors to space weapons.

Space, with an already crowded low Earth orbit (LEO) and few rules, is another bifurcated realm of conflict-prone rivalry that brings, like maritime clashes or the future of AI, systemic challenges to the U.S.-China relationship. From potential nuclear warfare in space to competition over real estate on the moon, China’s ambitions are multifaceted and often in direct competition with those of the United States.

A key part of Beijing’s ambitious strategy is building an integrated satellite network that rivals U.S. capacities. To capitalize on technological breakthroughs, such as Chinese start-up LandSpace’s reusable rocket, China has built a vertically integrated manufacturing base for its space industry, similar to its approach to electric vehicles.

China views space competition holistically, with manufacturing speed and capacity conceived of as a comparative advantage enabled by behemoth aerospace state-owned companies and state support and encouragement for a burgeoning commercial industry where more than 500 players are already competing. Since it is a key national security industry dominated by military-directed state-owned companies, it is a less fiercely cutthroat competitive environment than those for EVs and solar energy—at least for now.

The United States remains largely ahead of China in several key areas, including satellites in orbit, LEO broadband capabilities, and space situational awareness (SSA)—the tracking, characterizing, and predicting of the movement of satellites, debris, and natural objects in Earth’s orbit. The United States still has some 10 times more satellites in orbit than China, and while China’s launch cadence is rising, the country’s 92 total space launches in 2025 were still well below the 165 launches of SpaceX alone.

SpaceX’s September launch of Starship, intended to propel the United States back to the moon, is another measure of U.S. commercial superiority. Given their existing constellations, launch costs, and technological advancement. U.S. LEO broadband providers still represent a standard that Chinese competitors strive toward.

U.S. SSA systems are robust, including the NASA-designed Space Traffic Management (STM) architecture, the Traffic Coordination System for Space, and U.S. Space Force’s satellite catalogue. That coordination system now covers 11,345 satellites, including from 10 foreign governments, compared with some 1,500 Chinese satellites. Although China is beginning to develop its own comprehensive SSA capabilities, these efforts are not yet capable of realizing their goal of independence from U.S. SSA systems. Moreover, China lacks a comparable global network of ground radars and will likely lean more heavily on space-based SSA plays as it builds is own STM system. China’s efforts to develop its own STM system is still in an embryonic stage.

In sharp contrast, U.S. Space Force’s Space Surveillance Network, with ground-based-radars, optical telescopes, and space-based sensors, is state of the art, despite needing upgrading. It tracks and monitors all man-made objects in space, including some 47,000 pieces of fast-moving, dangerous space debris that could cripple orbiting satellites, warning in cases where debris threatened satellites

Despite these U.S. advantages, China has already achieved peer status or surpassed the United States in other areas, such as positioning, navigation, and timing; remote sensing and satellite imaging; and anti-satellite capabilities. These functions underpin myriad fundamental services and would be critical in wartime. While GPS encompasses 31 satellites, all in medium Earth orbit, China’s BeiDou system has 56 satellites spanning three orbits, making it a more diversified and resilient global positioning, navigation, and messaging services provider than GPS.

China has progressed significantly in remote sensing and surpassed the United States in visible, radar, and hyperspectral imaging and anti-satellite capabilities. China’s remote sensing and imaging lead is, again, partially due to ambitious constellation layouts—groups of satellites working together—and a greater emphasis on achieving broad, highly resilient coverage.

Beijing is not only placing its own satellites but also thinking about how to attack the satellites of others. The United States is already highly concerned by Chinese ground-based anti-satellite missiles, directed energy weapons, jammers, and on-orbit capabilities such as complex multi-satellite rendezvous and proximity operations and moving satellites with robotic arms. China’s progress may be one reason why the United States recently revealed that it has weapons in space.

Perhaps the most consequential gap China is narrowing is in reusable rockets and launch technology. On July 10, China recovered a Long March-10B carrier rocket with a net-based capture on a sea platform, a global first for this recovery method and China’s first controlled recovery. On Aug. 19, LandSpace achieved China’s first controlled land recovery with its Zhuque-3 rocket using landing legs.

These two successful recoveries catapult China past a critical bottleneck and threaten a key U.S. technological superiority. LandSpace’s August recovery closely resembled SpaceX’s Falcon-9 method, making it just the third company to achieve this feat. A widely read WeChat article points out that the July net capture represents China’s capacity to not just replicate but also innovate. Other commercial firms may follow suit, including Orienspace, a Shandong-based firm planning to launch its Gravity-2 reusable rocket late this year. Beijing will now eye utilizing its manufacturing base, AI application potential, and industrial infrastructure to scale quickly and improve launch costs and frequency.

China and the United States’ respective space stations are also moving in opposite directions. The United States plans to retire and deorbit the International Space Station (ISS) by 2030, hoping that private space firms will replace it. Meanwhile, China is expanding its manned Tiangong space station. Tiangong, fully operational since 2022, conducts science experiments with 17 countries, and Beijing is adding three new modules, doubling its size. This will boost China’s global space status among prospective partners and accelerate its space industry’s growth.

All these developments pose enormous challenges to U.S. plans for, as a 2025 Trump executive order put it, “Ensuring American Space Superiority.” The order’s goals include establishing “initial elements” of a permanent lunar outpost with nuclear reactors by 2030; detecting and countering the full range of security threats to U.S. space interests; spurring the private sector to create a “commercial pathway to replace the International Space Station by 2030”; and fostering a vibrant private space sector.

Only the latter goal seems assured, with an already dynamic private space industry of more than 1,000 firms commanding 65 percent of the global launch market and 69 percent of satellite production, though Beijing is beginning to challenge both.

The increasingly frantic race to establish a permanent presence on the moon, a pivotal goal of both nations’ space programs, is among the most ostentatious and intense competitions of the zero-sum space race to stake claims, for prestige, and for broader space operations. One reason for the fierce rivalry is that real estate on the moon is only 25 percent of that on earth, much of which is pockmarked with craters. The prime areas are the north and south poles, which have water. After a previous NASA head predicted last September that China would beat the United States back to the moon, then-acting NASA Administrator Sean Duffy said he’d “be damned” if China got there first.

But don’t underestimate China. Beijing has initiated the International Lunar Research Station (ILRS), a project to establish a crewed base presence at the moon’s south pole by 2035, along with its main partner, Russia, and 17 cooperating nations and international organizations. ILRS’s intense competition with NASA’s Artemis program, which plans to send humans back to the moon and then to Mars, represents the decline of space as a global commons since post-Cold War U.S.-Russia ISS cooperation.

The one foundational treaty governing space activities is the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which 118 nations e, including the United States, China, and Russia, have ratified. The treaty defines space as one of the global commons and says exploration and use of outer space “shall be carried out for the benefit and in the interests of all countries” and “shall be the province of all mankind.”

However, the policies and actions of the United States, China, and Russia highlight how modern technology and geopolitics have overtaken the Outer Space Treaty. The treaty doesn’t address current realities, including a crowded LEO with more than 16,000 satellites, space debris, and anti-space weapons. Great-power competition and withering international rules are not conducive to updating global norms. A 2020 Trump executive order directly declared that space was not a global commons. The legal basis of building bases on the moon or granting private firms mineral mining rights remains fuzzy—like staking gold claims in the Wild West. The 2011 Wolf Amendment, which bans NASA from cooperation with China, constrains effort to coordinate solutions.

The ILRS has only published terms of cooperation for its partners and no detailed space activities or STM principles. The U.S. Artemis Accords, introduced in 2020, offer an elaborate set of principles to govern civil exploration and activities in space. The accords, which claim to be consistent with the Outer Space Treaty, have been signed by 76 nations, including most major space actors except China and Russia.

They detail areas and terms of cooperation, from information and data sharing to deconflicting activities to declaring “safety zones” where nations are building bases or doing scientific activity. Had the Artemis Accords not been drafted unilaterally and presented as a fait accompli, they would be a solid starting point for negotiating a global treaty. But given that the United States rejects the premise of space as a global commons and that the Outer Space Treaty says celestial bodies are not subject to “national appropriation by claim of sovereignty,” on what basis do nations build bases, nuclear plants, or extract resources on the moon, asteroids, or Mars?

This uncertainty creates risks, such as the 2021 incidents when China’s space station had to maneuver to avoid a collision with Starlink satellites. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk reportedly warned China, but they failed to respond, according to industry sources. Afterward, Beijing filed a complaint, to the UN, but expressed an openness to establishing lines of communication, and the U.S. Space Surveillance Network has asionally warned China of debris threats on an ad hoc basis. This is obviously one area requiring U.S.-China coordination and deconfliction of STM. The system does not work if only your friends stop at red lights.

Coordination and deconfliction are vital, even between suspicious opponents. Risk-reduction steps such as pre-notification when satellites are moved, collaboration on space debris monitoring and early warning, and coordination and deconfliction on STM are needed. A starting point for these issues would be to repeal or revise the Wolf Amendment so U.S.-China dialogue can include space.

It may take a catastrophic event in space before the reality of mutual vulnerability overcomes deep distrust and suspicion enough to define the terms of coexistence.

Robert A. Manning is a distinguished fellow with the Strategic Foresight Hub at the Stimson Center, where he works on its strategic foresight and China programs. X: @Rmanning4

Nick Hawkins is a research associate with the China program at the Stimson Center.

#82. Europe’s Credibility Gap

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

CLAAS MERTENS is a Research Fellow at the Blavatnik School of Government and Worcester College, University of Oxford.

NGAIRE WOODS is Professor of Global Economic Governance and Founding Dean of the Blavatnik School of Government at the University of Oxford.

Dependence on America Has Left It With Little to Offer Would-Be Partners

The second Trump administration’s National Security Strategy declared that “the days of the United States propping up the entire world order like Atlas are over.” That sentiment has animated much of the administration’s foreign policy over the past two years, and its approach to Europe has been no exception. In 2025, the United States suspended military aid to Ukraine, and in May of this year, it announced it would remove 5,000 troops from Germany. President Donald Trump has threatened to seize Greenland, the territory of a fellow NATO country, and promised to levy tariffs against member states that opposed the effort. When the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February, they neither consulted nor warned European powers, which have been left to face the war’s economic consequences largely alone.

Europe has not stood idly by amid this onslaught. It stepped in to fill the gaps left by the United States’ withdrawal of financial support for Ukraine in 2025. During the Greenland episode, European countries facing tariffs convinced Trump to back down by threatening massive retaliatory trade measures against the United States. And the continent has begun to deepen its other relationships. The EU has set up a $168 billion defense-loan scheme, with Canada as its first non-European member. Earlier this year, it finalized the largest trade agreement in its history, with India, and signed a long-delayed deal with the South American economic bloc Mercosur.

These measures have been encouraging departures from the bureaucratic indecisiveness for which the EU has frequently been criticized. But despite its leaders’ newfound interest in self-sufficiency, Europe remains dependent on the United States. In fact, some of its attempts to stand on its own have made it more dependent on the United States. European defense planning, command, nuclear deterrence, and military enabling systems still rely on American capabilities. Increased defense spending buys American weapons. As of 2025, the United States supplied more than half of the EU’s liquefied natural gas imports. Many of the continent’s most promising technology firms still move to New York or San Francisco.

This continued dependence has in turn weakened Europe’s credibility with other countries seeking new security, technology, and economic ties of their own. For decades, the European offer to these countries relied on the continent’s relationship with Washington. As long as the United States underwrote European security and welcomed Europe’s integration with its economy, that offer was an attractive one. Now that Washington has begun to treat both arrangements as negotiable, however, it no longer is. The weaker the transatlantic relationship becomes, the more Europe needs other countries’ export markets, raw materials, defense industrial capacity, and solidarity against coercion—and the less able it is to convince those countries of its worth as a partner. Europe needs a better offer, grounded in its own capabilities rather than those of its mercurial ally.

European countries have long presented themselves as leaders on issues such as the environment, consumer protection, and high regulatory standards. To neighboring countries, Europe dangled membership in and association with the EU. Beyond the continent, it promised developmental and humanitarian partnerships in the form of aid through the EU and national agencies. Until recently, these were appealing terms: 13 countries have joined the EU since 2004, and more than 140 countries accepted some form of aid from EU or member state programs.

The United States upheld the underlying security and economic order that made these offers possible. EU aspirants could count on Washington to underwrite Europe’s defense through NATO, and and non-European countries could count on a U.S.-led rules-based economic order, within which they could easily access European aid, markets, and investment.

But the U.S. retrenchment has accelerated the emergence of a more bellicose “might is right” disorder in which different needs have risen to the fore. Countries are now seeking security partnerships to shore up their defense capabilities, stable trade relationships to protect against economic warfare, and financing to make up for cuts in aid and increases in the costs of government borrowing.

For example, when Ukraine turned to Europe in the early 2010s, it did so because of the prosperity and modernization that economic integration promised. But Kyiv now needs intelligence and weapons to fend off Russia, which Europe can deliver only through the United States. For countries similarly seeking security assistance and cooperation, dependence on such a fickle partner is a liability.

Partners hit by Trump’s tariffs need access to reliable markets to export goods and services once destined for the United States. But Europe has felt the need to defend its own economies instead of opening up its markets to them. For instance, the European Commission drastically increased tariffs on steel and reduced its quotas for duty-free imports, blocking India, South Korea, and Turkey from selling into the European market—precisely as those countries were searching for alternative markets to the United States.

Other countries need financing for infrastructure and the energy transition. Europe has the firepower to meet these countries’ needs, but its commitments take far too long to be realized as completed projects. And as in security, the U.S. withdrawal has left Europe adrift. Joint G-7 packages to finance clean energy buildouts in Indonesia, South Africa, and Vietnam, for example, suffered when Washington withdrew its support in 2025.

Europe has lately shown some ability to rise to the occasion. In 2025, EU member states’ combined annual military expenditure was approximately $461 billion, less than the United States’ $954 billion, but higher than China’s $336 billion and Russia’s $190 billion. When the United States wound down its aid to Ukraine in 2025, European governments made up most of the shortfall and have since committed to financing Kyiv’s war effort through 2027. The continent also has an existing defense industrial base, two permanent UN Security Council seats, and nuclear forces. Partners just beyond the core add more: Ukraine has a battle-tested army and an innovative drone industry, and Turkey has NATO’s second-largest army and access to the strategically important Black and Mediterranean Seas.

There is similar cause for optimism in trade and finance. The EU’s 2026 trade agreement with India removed nearly all tariffs for both parties, reduced nontariff barriers to trade, and made it easier for Indians and Europeans to temporarily work in each other’s markets. The EU’s Global Gateway investment program, Europe’s answer to China’s Belt and Road Initiative, passed its $335 billion mobilization target ahead of schedule.

These individual successes show that Europe has the potential to present partners with a more compelling offer. Yet much of that potential remains unfulfilled.

Europe has substantial assets across security, trade, and finance, but it lacks the internal cohesion needed to bundle them into a comprehensive package to attract other countries and bolster its own autonomy. When Europe could fall back on the United States’ leadership in institutions such as the World Trade Organization and NATO, internal disunity was less of a problem: American military commanders not only supported but organized European defense, and U.S.-backed rules governing global trade opened foreign markets to European exports, reducing the need to negotiate bilateral agreements. Without that leadership, the continent has been left to overcome its internal fragmentation on its own.

Nowhere is that fragmentation more apparent than on security. European leaders have committed to improving the continent’s defense in response to Washington’s wavering on NATO, but defense budgets, industries, and forces remain primarily national. As governments prioritize negotiating the best deals for domestic firms and other constituencies, conflicts arise: joint projects fail, purchases overlap, redundant R & D efforts waste precious resources. These frustrations have ultimately led the continent to simply purchase more U.S. systems. The EU’s Security Action for Europe loan program aims to reverse this trend by financing member states’ joint purchases of European equipment. But loans alone will neither overcome distributional conflicts nor create common command structures, standards, and logistics.

Europe does negotiate its trade deals with one voice. But many agreements need to be ratified in each country, leaving them at the mercy of domestic lobbies, from farmers to automakers, which seek to protect their markets at the expense of the continent’s collective interest. More than a decade after Canada and the EU negotiated the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, for example, just 17 of the organization’s 27 member states have ratified it. The 2026 trade deal with Mercosur, in the works for decades, was immediately contested, politically and legally, by individual member states and their representatives in the European Parliament.

On finance, Europe does not lack money but channels it through a byzantine set of EU instruments, member-state agencies, development banks, and changing flagship initiatives. Partners are left to navigate this morass of funding sources, each with their own procedures, timelines, and conditions. In Ghana, for example, Europe is present through EU programming, member-state development agencies, the European Investment Bank, and Global Gateway initiatives. When the Trump administration’s cuts to the U.S. Agency for International Development hit Accra, a more coordinated Europe might have been able to make its finance more visible, usable, and politically credible.

Many of these challenges predate the U.S. retrenchment. But they were less damaging to Europe’s other relationships as long as Washington upheld an imperfect but generally secure global order. Now that U.S. leadership is no longer part of the European offer, though, they loom much larger for potential partners.

The United States is not the only great power to have weaponized its chokepoints. Beijing and Moscow have also used their dominance over important industries coercively. Europe’s problem is that attempts to reduce the continent’s exposure to Russian and Chinese chokepoints too easily increase its dependence on the United States. Weaning itself off Russian pipeline gas means buying American energy. Procuring rare-earth elements outside China’s supply chains means cooperating with Washington on critical mineral exploration. When, for instance, Beijing weaponized its demand for French cognac by imposing duties on the liquor in October 2024, the industry’s best alternative was the U.S. market—until the Trump administration levied tariffs of its own. A more enticing offer to other partners must be built on economic ties and capabilities that are not beholden to American commitments.

To make such an offer, Europe must first reduce its reliance on U.S. defense commitments and equipment, moving toward becoming a more equal partner within NATO. Although Europe is unlikely to replace the United States as a global security guarantor, it needs to be able to offer third countries viable security partnerships, sustained deterrence in its neighborhood, and the ability to act with coherence when American priorities shift.

It can begin by working faster and more efficiently with its current friends. Since 2022, Poland has bought South Korean tanks, howitzers, aircraft, and rocket artillery; more recent agreements have moved beyond off-the-shelf purchases toward technology transfers that enable production, service, and repair in Poland. Japan has joined with Italy and the United Kingdom to develop a next-generation combat aircraft through the three countries’ collaborative treaty-based Global Combat Air Programme. The EU-India Security and Defense Partnership signed in January 2026 provides a framework for cooperation spanning maritime security, emerging technologies, and the defense industry. Europe should build on this approach, making use of its partners’ strengths to benefit both their and its own security.

European dependence goes well beyond security, however. Europe has the scale, capital, universities, industrial base, and regulatory capacity to be a tech power. But a lack of later-stage financing, fragmented product markets, and shortages of specialized talent and compute have too often driven European entrepreneurs, including the founders of such high-tech leaders as Hugging Face, Arm, and Wise, to start, expand, or list their companies in the United States.

These companies might be persuaded to remain in Europe if they could count on investments and a truly single market. But only a tiny percentage of European pension fund assets are currently invested in venture capital. The EU has announced a slew of initiatives to increase venture capital funding, but it still lacks anything comparable in size to the biggest U.S. funds. The harder tasks are to integrate capital markets, reduce regulatory differences between member states, and dismantle barriers to cross-border investment and commerce. A Europe-wide financial system and consumer market would make investment more attractive, keeping the continent’s most promising innovators from crossing the Atlantic in search of funding and customers. A competitive tech apparatus would give Europe not just control over the leading technologies it produces but also the ability to offer partners a viable alternative to the U.S. innovation ecosystem.

Europe must also reduce its energy and raw-material dependence. As the war in Iran has shown, exposure to volatile fossil fuel markets can harm overreliant economies. The International Energy Agency has noted that renewable energy has partly insulated European economies from truly disastrous fossil fuel price shocks. But the risk of shortages of refined petroleum products, especially diesel and jet fuel, is a daily reminder of the continent’s ongoing reliance on imports over which it has no control.

Integrated energy markets offer a way to prevent such dependence from forcing U-turns on foreign policy. After Russia’s February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Germany, which in 2021 had imported more than half of its gas from Russia, initially opposed an embargo on Russian oil and gas before reversing course in May of that year. When Russian gas subsequently stopped flowing, Berlin was spared shortages and a more severe economic crisis largely thanks to other European countries, which provided emergency supplies. The continent seems to have learned the right lessons from the episode: the European Commission’s 2026 work program, its annual legislative agenda, explicitly commits to building a “genuine Energy Union” through electric grid upgrades and the removal of cross-border bottlenecks. The more resilient its energy system becomes, the more reliable a partner Europe will be.

In raw materials, on the other hand, it has little hope of achieving self-sufficiency. The European Commission’s planned Critical Raw Materials Centre will gather market intelligence, coordinate joint purchasing, and facilitate stockpiling. But demand-side measures alone cannot produce the raw materials the continent needs. Europe could start to build a global network of partner countries by creating the conditions for investment in mines and refineries across Africa, the Americas, and Asia. Because mines, processing plants, and the infrastructure to transport their outputs require long planning horizons and prices are volatile, joint actions could make projects more financially attractive and less risky and would ensure the minerals produced have a market.

Finally, Europe needs the ability to retaliate when China or the United States threatens to choke it. Europe’s response to U.S. tariff threats exposed how difficult it can be to get European powers to agree to retaliate. But it does have a powerful tool at its disposal. In 2023, Europe created its Anti-Coercion Instrument, a bundle of economic countermeasures, including tariffs and restrictions on imports or exports and restrictions on access to EU public procurement, foreign direct investment, and intellectual property rights, that in essence permits European countries to weaponize other countries’ dependence on economic interactions with them. A global ACI, expanded to pool non-European partners’ resources for more powerful joint retaliatory measures, would not solve every problem for Europe and its partners, but it could swiftly convert some of Europe’s strongest assets into a partnership offer with real security benefits.

Europe’s relationship with the United States was founded on shared values, mutual reliance, and reciprocity. It enabled European countries to focus on rebuilding their economies after World War II and on building institutions to avert future wars on the continent. The tumult of the last two years has revealed that Europe took the benefits of that relationship for granted. Today, the continent faces different threats than it did 80 years ago, and it can no longer count on the United States to come to its aid. Rather than mourn the loss of its partner in Washington, Europe must find new ones built on the recognition of a different kind of mutual reliance: that most countries have little hope of resisting great-power coercion if they go it alone.

Building these new relationships to reduce European dependence on the United States would not mean shutting out Washington entirely. Both sides would still benefit from security cooperation through NATO, from continued trade and investment, and from an integrated international financial system. Cooperation with the United States would remain valuable but no longer indispensable. Europe will get better deals from the Trump administration and its successors if it can negotiate from a position of strength, undergirded by more diverse partnerships.

Those partnerships will not emerge overnight. Nor will a new coalition become a unified strategic actor immediately. But an improved European offer will set that coalition on the right path. As with all important endeavors, the hardest part is getting started.

How Europe Can Take More Responsibility—Without Starting an Arms Race

#83. Leadership barnstorming continues ahead of midterm elections

Speaker Mike Johnson is trying to rally the Republican faithful — and keep them from staying home in the midterms — arguing that polling is bad and the party of President Donald Trump can still defy political gravity.

“Even even some of our own candidates who are doing internal polling, even they have a hard time getting Republicans to respond to polls because Republicans don’t trust pollsters anymore,” Johnson, R-La., said on a podcast hosted by the Family Research Council’s Tony Perkins. “And they can’t discern when they get a call who’s originating the call, and that is affecting the outcome of the polls.”

Johnson has been among the congressional leaders from both the Republican and Democratic parties on a campaign, fundraising and media blitz. His schedule included a visit to North Carolina last week.

“I’m traveling nonstop. Forty districts across 22 states this month alone. I’m going to the swing districts. I’m going to the places that the pollsters and the pundits say we’re going to lose,” Johnson said in an interview that aired Sunday on the Fox News Channel. “They are wrong. We have incredible turnout.”

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has been hitting the trail as well, including a visit to Toledo, Ohio, in support of Rep. Marcy Kaptur, who is in a tight race for reelection against Republican Derek Merrin.

Despite Ohio lawmakers redrawing Kaptur’s district to make it more friendly to Republicans, her race is rated as a Toss-up by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales.

“We are working hard across the country, continuing to make the case that we need dramatic change as opposed to the status quo,” Jeffries told The Associated Press on Sunday, “and that Democrats are going to be the only ones to fight to make this country affordable.”

House Democratic Whip Katherine M. Clark of Massachusetts — who’s in line to be majority leader if her party wins control of the House — will be continuing on the road as well. She is expected to be in Florida this week, including campaigning for Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff and congressional staffer running in the open 7th District.

Clark’s visit could be a sign of where Democrats believe the map is trending just over two weeks out from Election Day. Inside Elections rates the open-seat race to replace GOP Rep. Cory Mills as Likely Republican.

But, as Gonzales wrote last week, House Republicans appear to have a problem with open seats.

President Donald Trump heads to Kansas on Monday, where Republicans are trying to shore up support for Sen. Roger Marshall, the incumbent Republican facing an unexpectedly strong challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton.

At least when it comes to the Senate, Trump’s travel schedule has him playing defense more than offense this week. He’s scheduled to make stops in North Carolina, South Carolina, Iowa, Florida, Georgia and Michigan.

Each of those states has a Senate seat on the ballot, but only in Georgia and Michigan are there Democratic incumbents.

Georgia has been seen as less competitive as of late, and Inside Elections rates the race between Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff and Republican Rep. Mike Collins as Leans Democratic. The same rating applies to the open Senate contest in North Carolina, where Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper is facing former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley.

In the Michigan race, Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers is running against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. Inside Elections currently rates the race as Tilt Democratic.

Vice President JD Vance is also scheduled to be in North Carolina this week, along with stops in his home state of Ohio and in Nebraska.

#87. Rogers argues El-Sayed is vulnerable with 2 traditionally Democratic blocs as Obama heads to Michigan

Michigan GOP U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers discusses the final stretch of his campaign against Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed and the influence of Democratic socialism on ‘Hannity.’

Republicans made their pitch to Michigan voters at a Fox News town hall Monday night, with GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers arguing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is vulnerable among Black and Jewish voters as one of the nation's most closely watched Senate races enters its final two weeks.

Fox News host Sean Hannity also spoke with Republican gubernatorial nominee Rep. John James and House GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain, R-Mich., as the candidates sought to tie Michigan Democrats to government spending, socialism and the party's progressive wing ahead of Nov. 3.

Early on in the night, Rogers argued that his opponent, El-Sayed, could underperform among a handful of key demographics that traditionally support Democratic candidates, presenting political opportunities for Republicans.

EL-SAYED GRILLED ON PIKER, ISRAEL AND SOCIALIST TIES AFTER MIKE ROGERS SKIPS SENATE DEBATE

Hannity pressed Rogers about El-Sayed's past criticism of former President Barack Obama, whom El-Sayed described as "not the right choice" to advance a progressive agenda following Obama's 2012 re-election.

"He is dismissive in Detroit. We have just dozens of Black pastors that we have talked to, neighborhood leaders in the city of Detroit that we’ve talked to. They’re looking for a change," Rogers said.

Notably, Obama is scheduled to campaign with El-Sayed in Detroit on Oct. 24 and has released a video urging voters to support the Democratic nominee.

ROGERS WARNS MICHIGAN VOTERS AGAINST EL-SAYED’S ‘EXTREME’ AGENDA AHEAD OF ELECTION

Rogers argued the Jewish community could present a unique opportunity for Republicans amid El-Sayed's criticism of Israel.

Recently, El-Sayed declined to answer whether he viewed Iran or Israel as a greater threat.

"I think both of them have proven dangerous in their own way. One, at risk of attacking us. One, getting us into wars we have no business fighting," El-Sayed said in a recent debate.

Rogers noted that if only half of Jewish Democratic voters in Michigan felt alienated by El-Sayed’s remarks enough to support his campaign, it would provide a significant boost.

"There are about 70,000 Jewish Democrats. If we get half of them to vote for us, which we think — we had an event last night. Had over 1,000 people at it. We’re fired up and excited and scared for their children, by the way. They’re afraid for their children. They’re with us, and they’re going to vote, we think, 35,000 votes out of the Jewish Democrat — these are normally solid Democratic votes."

"That’s changing the dynamic," Rogers added.

MINNESOTA FRAUD SCANDAL WILL HAUNT FLANAGAN IN HIGH-STAKES SENATE RACE, TOP HOUSE REPUBLICAN WARNS

Rep. John James, R-Mich., the state’s Republican candidate for governor, also appeared with Hannity, presenting his pitch to attendees on what he would do differently if elected.

Alongside promises to reshape education, James promised to create more scrutiny around government programs and expenses.

"Michigan is spending 50% more right now under Gretchen Whitmer than we spent under Rick Snyder’s administration, the last Republican, and $20 billion more per year than at the height of the pandemic."

"Michigan does not have a taxation problem. Michigan has a spending problem," James added.

James also raised concerns about potential fraud in Michigan, drawing comparisons to Minnesota's sprawling taxpayer-funded fraud investigations.

"If a 19-year-old journalist named Nick Shirley can find $9 billion of fraud in Minnesota, a state with 50% of our population and 60% of our budget, what do you think he can find here?" James said, referring to a videographer who had become famous for investigating Somali fraud rings.

Shirley drew national attention to suspected fraud involving Minnesota childcare providers, although he did not uncover $9 billion in fraud. That figure came from former federal prosecutor Joe Thompson, who estimated last year that fraud across 14 high-risk Medicaid programs could total $9 billion or more. Minnesota officials have disputed the estimate. Federal and state investigators in Minnesota have uncovered fraud involving taxpayer-funded childcare, food assistance and healthcare programs, including schemes in which defendants allegedly billed the government for services they never provided.

OBAMA'S STAR POWER GETS A REALITY CHECK FROM BLACK VOTERS IN CRUCIAL SENATE RACE: 'IT'S A TURNOFF'

At the close of Hannity’s town hall, Rep. Lisa McClain, R-Mich., the House GOP conference chair, accused Democrats of hiding their true character.

"I don’t even call them Democrats anymore; it’s the Communist Party," McClain said.

"They want to pack the Supreme Court, they want to abolish the police, they want to let people out of prisons."

With primaries in the rearview mirror, Michigan heads to the polls alongside the rest of the country on Nov. 3.

Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

#89. “You Can See Everything” and the tragedy of Elizabeth Holmes

In the first episode of his hit HBO series, âThe Rehearsalâ â a show about evaluating the outcomes of hypothetical real-life situations â comedian Nathan Fielder admits, âIâve been told my personality can make some people uncomfortable, so I have to work to offset that.â For Fielder, who is equal parts lovably strange and dryly hilarious, offsetting other peopleâs discomfort can be a sizable task. Itâs not easy to go through life in a double consciousness, hyperaware that oneâs behavior might offend or unease. âHumor is my go-to instinct,â Fielder says about trying to reassure others. âBut every joke is a gamble.â

Consider, then, the overlap between Fielder and someone like Elizabeth Holmes, founder of the bogus blood-testing company Theranos, who was convicted of swindling hundreds of millions of dollars from investors with her purportedly revolutionary blood-analysis device. Even before her downfall, Holmes drew the mediaâs attention with her wide, unblinking eyes, bold red lip, deep voice and stilted speech â all of which became parody-ready upon her indictment. But all the more perplexing was Holmesâ reticence to admit guilt when caught with hands as red as her lipstick, talking herself in circles in pursuit of her truth. Her statements always seemed misaligned with the evidence, as if she were so convinced of her companyâs virtue that she didnât care about the eerie dissonance between her reality and the worldâs. If Holmes was indeed playing a character she made up, as many people speculated, she was a skilled method actor.Â

As Fielder gains steady footing on the margin dividing observation and manipulation, aiming the camera at either side, he uncovers something deeply, cosmically sad: Holmes canât seem to tell the difference between the two.

Sitting just inches apart around a San Diego beach rentalâs dinner table in Fielder and co-director Lance Oppenheimâs magnificent new documentary, âYou Can See Everything,â Fielder and Holmes look decidedly comfortable with one another. They share an ease and rapport neither has readily exhibited on camera before â certainly not around virtual strangers. But while they may not share many overt similarities, the strange duo align in their mutual slipperiness.Â

Before them lie components of Theranosâ blood-analyzer, which Holmes hopes to turn into a new product after her 11-year prison sentence, set to start 34 days after filming begins. Trying to explain the device, and how her claims of its efficacy were misread by investors and the public, Holmes once again canât translate her thoughts into words that make sense to Fielder. Instinctually, Fielder makes a joke. âIsnât it funny that I hosted a show about business scams, and now youâre in trouble for a business scam?â Holmes remarks that she hadnât thought about it until now, and the tension lifts as her frustration dissipates. Despite his well-intentioned wisecrack â or perhaps because of it â Holmes can relate to her new associate. Somehow, Fielder can see her.

But which version of her Fielder â and, by extension, the audience â sees, and which version is the truest, remains up for debate. The title âYou Can See Everything,â taken from a text Holmes sent to Fielder during production, is an obvious red herring. This documentary is about a woman notorious for her deception. We, of course, canât really see anything.Â

And yet, itâs all on display. Fielder, Oppenheim, and the viewer share the task of putting those pieces together legibly, to tell Holmesâ story in a way that hasnât already been done for her by the media, Huluâs limited series âThe Dropout,â and Holmesâ muddled observations. As the film plays out, its three-hour runtime gliding by in a flash, it becomes painfully clear that this is what Elizabeth Holmes has wanted all along: for someone to tell her story in a way she canât â not because she doesnât want to, but because she herself is unclear about what that story is. Breaking through Holmesâ tight circle of dubious companions, Fielder pulls at every thread he can, attempting to unravel a greater truth from lifeâs gnarled yarn. As he gains steady footing on the margin dividing observation and manipulation, aiming the camera at either side, Fielder uncovers something deeply, cosmically sad: Holmes canât seem to tell the difference between the two.

That does not, however, mean she doesnât want to try. Holmes is intent on letting the cameras see as much of her life as possible, not only to prove the innocence sheâs maintained all along, but to show that she has nothing to hide. She understands that the world sees her a certain way, a way she doesnât understand â or, in the case of the infamous photo of her holding a vial of blood between two fingers, outright refutes â but that peopleâs perception is entirely out of her control. Maybe emerging from hiding for the first time in seven years with a full-scale documentary team isnât such a bad idea. Five weeks out from a decade in prison, whatâs the worst they could uncover?

âYou Can See Everythingâ isnât so much about big, jaw-dropping revelations as it is about the people behind them, and the assortment of personality and/or neurodevelopmental disorders fueling their actions. Holmes raves about her husband, San Diego hotel-chain heir William Evans, whose ego takes up most of the space in their beachside rental. When Fielder asks how he and Holmes met, Evans relays murky details of a 2017 party where the two spoke for an hour before he realized who Holmes was, even though heâd toured the former Theranos building the day before.Â

Later, during a visit from Holmesâ parents, Fielder asks Holmesâ father, Christian, about her former lover and Theranos business partner, Sunny Balwani. Evans immediately interjects, trying to halt and redirect the conversation. Persisting, Fielder asks Christian to pinpoint a turning point in his daughterâs life. âThatâs an easy one,â Christian says, confessing that the turning point came when Holmes was sexually assaulted at 19, a crossroads that Holmes admits had a hand in her dropping out of Stanford and starting Theranos.

Want more from culture than just the latest trend? The Swell highlights art made to last. Sign up here

When Evans derails the conversation again, a new question pops up â an occurrence in this film as natural and frequent as breathing. Is Holmesâ husband trying to maneuver the situation because he cares for his wife, or because his behavioral patterns mirror those of Balwani and Holmesâ assailant? All three men directly impacted Holmes at vulnerable points in her life, and from the filmâs outset, itâs clear Evans savors controlling the narrative, whether through Holmesâ lifeâs work or simply the way she whisks eggs for scrambling. Whatâs constantly baffling is how much affection Holmes has for her repugnant husband, no matter how much he twists stories or alienates the film crew. One could say the two share a talent for deception, but it always feels more complex and tricky than that, as if it would be too easy to say that Holmes and Evans get along because theyâre both hucksters, skilled in fabrication. They both get something out of this relationship. Whether itâs love is anyoneâs guess.Â

Whatâs brutally, painfully clear, beyond a shadow of a doubt, is that Holmes has not yet learned how to use her own voice. She knows how to speak, dictate orders and ideas. (And, obviously, how to fool powerful people.) But Holmes doesnât grasp where her ideas end, and someone elseâs influence begins. She personifies a complete lack of identity, so irrevocably tied to her inventions, physical or otherwise, that, compared to Fielder â whose work is marked by his own keen self-awareness â she looks like the diametrical opposite. Holmes is the tragedy to his comedy. Naturally, the two are intrinsically connected.

Many things about Elizabeth Holmes arenât certain. But whatâs irrefutable is that she knows how lonely it is not to be able to communicate the world inside her head, and how painful it is not to understand others the same way. Itâs no wonder that, when she meets someone who can bridge that gap, she wants to make a monument of it.

All of the questions about whoâs running Holmesâ show take new, thorny form as the film blossoms in its latter half â the portion that, thanks to a surprise guest, makes the movie one of the most startling and memorable exercises in metafiction ever concocted. But the filmâs most heartbreaking and pivotal scene comes in its first third, before Holmes surrenders for her prison sentence, when Fielder gathers her and Evans on the couch to show them Abbott and Costelloâs famous âWhoâs on First?â act.Â

Fielder tells Holmes that he was reminded of the bit the day before, when Holmes tried to describe the science and intention of Theranos in front of its deconstructed prototype. Holmes has never seen the routine, and gives it a few chuckles. But when Fielder asks her to explain the joke â that âWhoâ is the name of the baseball player on first base, yet sounds like a question, confusing the two men â and why itâs funny, she canât. As Fielder clarifies the punchline, Holmes breaks down in tears across from him, frustrated that she canât understand.

In this moment, Fielder conjures a world of empathy for his subject, again posing questions about what gets lost between two people who believe theyâre being perfectly clear, yet arenât making sense to one another. Many things about Elizabeth Holmes arenât certain. But whatâs irrefutable is that she knows how lonely it is not to be able to communicate the world inside her head, and how painful it is not to understand others the same way. Itâs no wonder that, when she meets someone who can bridge that gap, she wants to make a monument of it â be it a business, a marriage, a film or a profession of love.

Though the questions persist: Is this all part of Holmesâ master plan? Is she letting the cameras in to dupe us, to make us feel sorry for someone whose actions caused real harm? Maybe. Those seeking clear answers will leave with nothing more than new questions, but thatâs the glorious part of âYou Can See Everything.â In an era when documentaries are made for everything and nothing, itâs critical to remember that searching for reason in something as immense as the human condition is a foolâs errand.Â

Fielder might be fascinated by motive and rationale, but heâs primarily interested in circumstance, and he understands Holmesâ circumstances perfectly. His film is a self-reflexive study of the inability to act as people expect â of masking and deception. How much of life is a performance? Can anyone truly be themselves when societyâs bylaws not only dictate proper human behavior but also how successful anyone can be in something as complicated and unknowable as life itself? In seeking the truth, all one finds is more differences, more judgment. Sure, we can see everything. But whether we really should is another question entirely.
