#92. The Iran War Has Changed the World Forever

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Essay: The Iran War Has Changed the World Forever

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Many of the immediate consequences of the Israeli-American war with Iran are already clear. The further emergence of drones and missiles as dominant weapons of war; the danger to the global economy from the threats to vital chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb; and the inadequacy of U.S. weapons procurement, among other issues, have garnered widespread and entirely merited attention.

Yet as important enough as those developments are, the Iran conflict could also have far wider and longer-term implications—changes that could be truly transformative for the Middle East region and the rest of the world. Decades from now, we might look back on this conflict as a watershed event that fundamentally reshaped what had been bedrock principles of modern geopolitics.

Many of the immediate consequences of the Israeli-American war with Iran are already clear. The further emergence of drones and missiles as dominant weapons of war; the danger to the global economy from the threats to vital chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb; and the inadequacy of U.S. weapons procurement, among other issues, have garnered widespread and entirely merited attention.

Yet as important enough as those developments are, the Iran conflict could also have far wider and longer-term implications—changes that could be truly transformative for the Middle East region and the rest of the world. Decades from now, we might look back on this conflict as a watershed event that fundamentally reshaped what had been bedrock principles of modern geopolitics.

While it would have been better to have discerned these potential break points before the war, there may still be time to take action to try to steer them in favorable directions. As always, the first requirement is to recognize the possible seismic changes that may already be underway.

A satellite view shows a major fire following an Iranian drone strike at the Port of Salalah oil storage tanks in Oman on March 11.Gallo Images/Orbital Horizon/Copernicus Sentinel Data 2026

There has been no shortage of commentary on the new technologies of combat highlighted by the Iran war, with the United States having been mostly focused on defensive systems. Americans have both marveled at the superb performance of Western interceptors and hyperventilated over their dwindling stockpiles of them. However, the Persian Gulf states—and likely many other threatened middle and smaller powers—have taken another lesson from the conflict: The best defense is a good offense.

U.S., Israeli, European, and South Korean interceptor munitions have performed brilliantly, shooting down Iranian ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones. Coupled with the ability of Western fighter aircraft to shoot down drones and cruise missiles—and to suppress the launches of ballistic missiles—Iran has done far less damage to its targets than would otherwise have been the case. In short, air and missile defenses have performed extremely well so far. That’s not nothing.

The problem is that it has not proved to be anything close to enough. Because drones; cruise missiles; and even, to a considerable extent, ballistic missiles are so much cheaper, easier to produce, store, hide, and launch than most of the interceptors that the United States and its allies use against them, Iran has been able to keep making more and launching them at targets across the Gulf, Jordan, and Israel. Even though the defenses are stopping roughly 90 percent of them, the 10 percent that are getting through are 100 percent too many.

Only the Israeli population is inured enough and its infrastructure hardened enough to prove undaunted by Iran’s counterstrikes. In stark contrast, the same levels of damage have proved catastrophic for the Gulf states. Energy companies, shipping companies, and insurance companies are all balking at the prospect of functioning with the residual threat of constant Iranian attacks, even if more than 90 percent are defeated. The 10 percent that have gotten through have done significant physical damage and far greater psychological damage. They called into question the current and planned future socioeconomic model of the Gulf states.

All of the modern Gulf economies were built in the expectation that their lands would be peaceful havens for commerce, hydrocarbon production, rest, and relaxation. Iran’s drone and missile attacks have shattered that, undermining the energy, manufacturing, trade, finance, investment, and tourism industries of the Gulf.

Who is going to want to invest, manufacture, or vacation in countries that are periodically subject to missile and drone attacks, even if nearly all of them are intercepted? Who wants to conduct business, import oil, invest money, trade goods, or take a vacation in a place where, a few times a week (or day), you hear explosions overhead, even if they are the sound of defensive systems successfully intercepting attacking munitions?

Tehran has long called for greater cooperation among Muslim states. The Mecca pact is not what it had in mind. By Saeid Jafari

At some level, the Gulf governments understood this. However, what they assumed before the war was that the threat of massive retaliation by the United States (or Israel, after the Abraham Accords), would limit the size and scope of Iranian missile and drone attacks—enabling their defenses to defeat any small retaliations that Tehran thought necessary for honor’s sake.

They were counting on the restraint that Iran had consistently shown in the past, including as recently as the short June 2025 war, because Iran had always feared that a larger response would trigger a U.S. bid for regime change.

Of course, in this war, by trying—and failing—to achieve regime change and then taking it off the table altogether, the United States has turned that logic on its head. Iran now has the ability to threaten both the Gulf economies directly with missile and drone attacks and the global economy by throttling tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz without fear of a U.S. effort to overthrow its regime. Americans know that they can’t achieve regime change by air power alone and (so far) lack the political will to employ the ground forces that would be necessary to do it for certain. With the threat of regime change gone, it is Iran that has demonstrated that it can deter U.S. and Israeli attacks at least as effectively as the United States and Israel can limit Iranian attacks on the Gulf.

This state of affairs—in which the Gulf states now have such reservations about relying on the United States (or Israel) to deter Iranian attack—is intolerable. It is why they are all purchasing or contemplating acquiring fleets of drones and missiles of their own. Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and Kuwait are all purchasing Turkish drones, while the Saudis are working with U.S. corporations to begin to build thousands of their own. Likewise, the UAE is trying to acquire drones and drone manufacturing capabilities from Israel, China, and Ukraine. Qatar and Bahrain are in talks to do the same.

Bayraktar AKINCI unmanned aerial vehicles in Elazig, Turkey, on Sept. 23.Bestami Bodruk/Anadolu via Getty Images

While it could prove that a balance of terror will impose a wary peace on drone- and missile-armed adversaries on both sides of the Gulf, just as the Cold War did for the United States and Soviet Union, that outcome is much less likely in this instance. As Bernard Brodie famously said back in 1946, what made a nuclear balance so effective at keeping the pace was the unmistakable power of nuclear weapons. No one could misunderstand what would happen if even a single nuclear weapon—let alone several dozen—were detonated in their country. When both the Gulf states and Iran possess thousands of conventional drones and missiles, that certainty of incalculable damage will be absent.

Instead, the arsenals will probably serve as a spur to further warfare. Iran will see the Gulf states attempting to build offensive strike forces of their own and will want to demonstrate that these will not be enough to deter Iranian attacks. The hard-line fanatics now in charge in Tehran will want to ensure that the conservative Gulf monarchs believe that Iran can take far more punishment than they can, and so Iran will look for opportunities to strike the Gulf to prove it.

In turn, the Gulf states will feel the need to retaliate to establish that they won’t be bullied and can give as good as they get. And the United States may well choose to keep out for fear that coming to the defense of the Gulf states will cause Iran to shut down the Strait of Hormuz again. All of this portends multiple missile and drone exchanges as each side seeks to bolster its capabilities, find weaknesses in the other side to exploit, and demonstrate its resolve.

As bad as this is likely to be, there is one more unfortunate development to consider. Once the Gulf states acquire the capacity to project power beyond their borders—something that none of them has had for roughly a century—they are likely to start using it and using it to do things that the United States won’t necessarily like.

This, too, has been the history of the Gulf. In the 1970s, when the United States armed the Iranian shah in hope that he would relieve some of Washington’s defense burden in the region, he began using his new military to do all kinds of things that the United States did not like, from backing the Kurds against Saddam Hussein to seizing Gulf islands from the UAE. Likewise, over the past decade, at American urging, the UAE has developed modest power projection capabilities of its own, which it has been using to pursue its interests in Yemen, Libya, Sudan, and the Horn of Africa, often in opposition to U.S. policies.

The Gulf is acquiring offensive military capabilities for the first time in modern history. We can call it burden-sharing, and perhaps it will mean that the United States will no longer have to defend them and their invaluable energy exports. But it seems far more likely to provoke greater conflict in the region, and to convince other states in other parts of the world that they should and can do the same.

A cargo ship carrying Chinese trucks for export to Middle Eastern countries sails in the waters of Yantai, Shandong province, China, on July 20. Costfoto/NurPhoto via Getty Images

For roughly the past four decades, China has been the ultimate free rider in the Middle East. Beijing has relied on Washington to keep the region stable by dealing with its endless security problems—from interstate wars to intrastate wars—and allow China to concentrate on enriching itself through favorable trade, investment, and infrastructure construction.

In their defense, the Chinese haven’t been subtle or bashful about it. I once had the Chinese vice minister for foreign affairs berate me for the United States’ failure to keep the peace of the region on China’s behalf. He literally shouted at me that China did not understand the Middle East, with its religion and “craziness,” and so it was Washington’s responsibility to keep things quiet—a responsibility that he felt Americans were failing at. I wasn’t even in the U.S. government at the time.

Moreover, the Chinese certainly weren’t the first, even if they may have been the most blatant. For almost a century, the United States played China to Britain’s United States. Beginning in the 19th century, American merchants plied the waters of the Gulf in search of lucre, deliberately disdainful of local politics and conflict, leaving all of that to the British until London withdrew its forces from the region in the early 1970s. Even then, the United States did not fully take on the role of regional hegemon until the 1990s, after the Iranian revolution, the Iran-Iraq War, and Saddam’s invasion of Kuwait convinced Washington that the region would not remain stable on its own.

So, like the United States—and even to a lesser extent, Britain—before it, China has been allowed to ignore the constant problems of the Gulf by leaving them to someone else. However, the events of the past decade, more so the past three years, and even more so the past six months, have been calling the viability of this arrangement into question.

China’s permanent representative to the United Nations, Fu Cong, votes during the U.N. Security Council meeting on a draft resolution on Strait of Hormuz at the U.N. headquarters in New York City on April 7.Liao Pan/China News Service/VCG via Getty Images

Whereas before Oct. 7, 2023, China was the talk of the Gulf, almost immediately after the horrific Hamas attack, it fell from the conversation almost entirely. What all of the countries of the region realized was that China had no capacity to project power into the Middle East. And in a time of war, its vast economic involvement in the region counted for little, if anything. China could not defend its regional friends against attack. China could not threaten regional enemies. U.S. military operations such as Rough Rider, Midnight Hammer, and now Epic Fury were entirely beyond Chinese capabilities.

About the most that the Chinese have been able to do is to encourage their Pakistani allies to act as intermediaries between Tehran and Washington, but even months later, this has not ended the conflict, and there is no sign that Chinese interests are being considered in the negotiations.

The Iran strikes will convince Beijing to double down on military growth. By Deng Yuwen

Without firing a shot, Beijing gained a freer hand in the Gulf, a boost for its industries, and new credibility. By Fareed Zakaria

And therein lies the rub. China has very considerable interests in the Middle East. China is the biggest oil importer in the world, and it relies on the Gulf for up to 50 percent of its imports. Chinese trade with the Gulf states has been growing at a torrid pace, now accounting for more than $500 billion annually, and it is expected to reach $800 billion by 2030. The Gulf region is also a critical market and transshipment point for Chinese goods flowing onward to Europe, western Asia, and Africa.

So, the great question here is whether the carnage wrought by three years of warfare across the region, punctuated by the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran this year, all of which threaten Chinese interests, will prompt Beijing to reconsider its powerlessness and willingness to rely on others to secure its vital interests in the Middle East. Will Beijing choose to make a determined effort to build a capability to project power into the Gulf so that it can demand compliance with Chinese needs, from both the locals and extraregional actors such as the United States?

If Beijing chooses that pathway—and the aircraft carriers that it is now deploying have always seemed far more useful in the Indian Ocean and North Arabian Sea than in the South China Sea—it will be a major change in the military balance and security relationships of the Middle East.

Destroyed buildings in the southern Lebanese town of Kfar Kila, as seen from across the border from northern Israel on March 8. Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images

Before the Iran war, in late 2024, I traveled to Israel with a small group of American military experts for extensive conversations with senior serving and former Israeli military officers.

As part of these discussions, the Israelis laid out the new defense doctrine that they were developing in response to the shock and horror of the Hamas attacks on Oct. 7, 2023. They intended to occupy buffer zones along their borders in Lebanon, Syria, and Gaza and then conduct constant military operations against Hamas, Hezbollah, the Islamic State, and other Arab extremist groups (or states) beyond those buffer zones to ensure that none of them were ever able to develop the infrastructure or field forces to mount a major attack on Israel ever again. It is exactly what Israel has been pursuing ever since.

At the time, I observed that what the Israelis were proposing was something akin to the defense doctrine of the Roman Empire. The Romans also frequently established buffer zones—with friendly tribes or denuded territory—just across their borders and then conducted constant military operations against the barbarian tribes beyond to punish them, weaken them, and prevent them from mounting major military operations against the Roman territories themselves. It was a doctrine of constant warfare beyond the empire’s frontiers to ensure peace within them.

I pointed out that prosecuting that doctrine would require a very different Israel from the one that existed before Oct. 7. The superb military analyst Aaron MacLean, host of the School of War podcast, was also part of that U.S. team, and he put a fine point on it: He wondered aloud whether the “start-up nation” culture could be consistent with a military doctrine of Roman frontiers.

For Israel, adopting the Roman frontiers approach will require a reversion to something like its original defense doctrine—and the national culture that supported it. From its founding in 1948 (and arguably before then) on up to the 1973 Arab-Israeli War, Israel’s defense doctrine emphasized preemptive or even preventive offensive operations to eliminate potential military threats before they could be employed and fight battles on the enemy’s territory, far from Israel’s own vulnerable population centers.

For Amman, Israeli annexation of the West Bank looms as an existential risk. By Sean Yom

It required a population both trained and committed to long-term reserve military service, to enable a small country to maintain a large enough field force to defeat its more populous adversaries. It required a people ready to make constant individual sacrifices—including the supreme sacrifice—for the good of the nation. A defense doctrine of Roman frontiers will require the same.

But slowly after 1973, as it became ever clearer that neither the Arab armies nor the anti-Israeli terrorist groups no longer posed an existential threat to the state, Israeli culture changed. As one of the most insightful studies of the changing relationship of the Israeli people to their armed forces put it, they shifted from a culture of self-sacrifice to one of self-actualization. This shift gained further steam as Israel’s economy began to boom in the early 2000s, to the point where ever more young Israelis disdained service in the armed forces, let alone a military career, and it became harder and harder to get the older generations to take their reserve duty seriously.

To hear Israelis talk, Oct. 7 changed all that. They insist that they are again ready to return to the total self-sacrifice for the sake of national security that made the original defense doctrine possible. The Roman frontiers approach represents the 21st century version of that strategy. But it remains an open question whether that spirit will persist for decades—and if it does, whether it will suck the energy and creativity from Israel’s private sector that made the “start-up nation” such a wonder.

An Israeli army vehicle patrols the northern border with Lebanon in the Upper Galilee on June 18. Jalaa Marey/AFP via Getty Images

In addition to the potential demands on Israeli society and culture required to enable it, the shift to Roman frontiers poses other dilemmas for Israel. In particular, the economic boom that came from the country’s internet entrepreneurship required a high degree of connectivity with the rest of the developed world. However, the security policies associated with Roman frontiers in Gaza, Lebanon, Syria, and elsewhere have steadily eroded goodwill toward Israel in many of those same states. A number have considered or even imposed (relatively circumscribed) sanctions on Israel in response. The harder that Israel hews to this defense doctrine, the more that these same ties may come under strain.

Nowhere is this stress more important to Israel than in the United States, where shocking numbers on both the far left and far right have turned against the U.S.-Israel special relationship. Here as well, the aggressive military operations required of the Roman frontiers approach have alienated many otherwise sympathetic Americans and provided the perfect excuse for the anti-Zionists (and antisemites) on both political extremes to demand an outright abrogation of the alliance. If these trends continue, Israelis may soon face a fundamental choice between their cherished relationship with the United States and their new approach to their own security.

Iranian Army servicemen stand at attention during the opening ceremony of a camp for ”self-sacrificing” forces in downtown Tehran on Oct. 3. Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images

Still another great question that only the future can answer is whether a war meant to retard Iranian hegemony in the Middle East has instead enabled it. The United States and Israel attacked Iran in hope of overthrowing its odious regime and, if that failed, cutting it down to size by eliminating the means that it employs to project power across the region.

Of course, the initial strikes did kill much of Iran’s top leadership, including Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei himself, but that did not lead to the downfall of the regime—at least not yet—and in the short term has left Washington to face a worse version of it.

In killing Khamenei, Israel and the United States removed a monstrous leader, but one who was conservative, cautious, and extremely wary of U.S. military power. He has been succeeded by a leadership that is far more hard-line, aggressive, belligerent, and risk-tolerant.

Indeed, as best we understand it, Khamenei consistently limited Iran’s conventional military actions against the United States and Israel because he feared that escalation would beget escalation and eventually trigger a determined U.S. effort to kill him and overturn his regime. He repeatedly prevented Iran’s hard-liners from indulging their preference for more violent attacks on Israel and American interests. These same hard-liners are now in charge in Tehran and unsurprisingly waging a far more aggressive campaign against the United States, unconstrained by Khamenei’s worries.

As for Iranian military power, the war has almost certainly set back the country’s ballistic missile and drone production program for months, possibly longer, although the Iranians are not only rebuilding but also improving the quality of their systems with Russian and Chinese help. The war may also have further set back Tehran’s nuclear program, although that is even harder to tell. And it did eliminate some Iranian power projection capabilities—its navy and air force—although these were not particularly important elements of either Iran’s threat or its defense. Yet rather than diminish the country’s ability to use force to influence regional and global affairs, the war could end up enhancing it.

Tehran seems to have embraced a pair of policies that existed only in theory beforehand. First, Iran now knows that it can attenuate or even choke off shipping through the Strait of Hormuz without triggering a massive, globally backed, U.S.-led military campaign to reopen it and overthrow the Iranian regime. That was the fear that had kept Iran from doing so since 1979. (It is worth noting that, contrary to common misperceptions, Iran never actually tried to shut down the strait during the Iran-Iraq War. It had far greater capabilities to try to do so, but it used only a tiny portion of them to harass maritime traffic, mostly in the Persian Gulf to drive up the price of oil to increase the value of its exports and convince the United States and the Gulf states to end their support for Iraq.) Second, Iran learned that it can lob thousands of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones at the United States’ Gulf allies with outsized impact compared to the actual damage inflicted.

Iranians walk across a street painted with a U.S. flag in Tehran on May 5. AFP via Getty Images

Moreover, we should remember that many of those now in charge in Tehran opposed the 2015 nuclear deal because they wanted war, not negotiations, with the United States, and they wanted a nuclear arsenal to prevent the United States either from attacking them or preventing them from attacking other countries. By placing them firmly in charge, at least for now, the war has probably made a new nuclear deal with Iran an even steeper climb than it was beforehand. It may well have convinced a group that already wanted nuclear weapons that such an arsenal is the only way to prevent still more U.S. and/or Israeli attacks.

Finally, the war has so far tightened cooperation between Iran, Russia, and China. That pseudo-alliance had frayed considerably during the June 2025 conflict because neither Moscow nor Beijing did much to help Tehran, leading many Iranian hard-liners to question the extent of the “alliance.”

However, this time around, both Russia and China have furnished Iran with considerable material and informational assistance—providing air defenses, missile and drone components, targeting data, and other forms of help in rebuilding and improving Iran’s arsenal. Consequently, Iran could emerge from the war with a more meaningful partnership with Russia and China than it had when the war began.

It is for all of these reasons that the war must end with the United States having demonstrated to the Iranians that they cannot interrupt shipping in the Strait of Hormuz or take potshots at the Gulf states with impunity. If it ends in such a way that the Iranians can resume either, let alone both, then the war will have rendered Iran far more influential than it was beforehand, regardless of the damage to its missile, drone, air, and naval forces.

The Iran war is, and always was, about regime change. By Ali Hashem

History’s most dramatic changes are always clearest in the rearview mirror. The great trick of policymaking is to recognize them in the present—or anticipate them in the future. It’s also the hardest thing to do.

Nothing is ever crystal clear in the moment, and denial is one of the most powerful factors in human psychology, individual and collective. There are always countervailing trends. People who do not want to believe that trends will continue will insist that they won’t, and they will grasp at the inevitable evidence to do so. Recognizing the signal in the noise is always hardest when it would be the easiest to respond to the signal.

None of us can say for certain that any of the possible changes that I’ve sketched out above will come to fruition. But their seeds are already there in the course of the United States’ ongoing war with Iran. It’s not too soon to recognize them and to start to consider how Washington might act to avert the worst and prepare for whatever it cannot prevent.

Kenneth M. Pollack is the vice president for policy at the Middle East Institute. He is a former CIA Persian Gulf military analyst and a former director for Persian Gulf affairs at the National Security Council. His latest book, The Iraq Wars, will be published in February.

#94. The Axis of Upheaval Goes to War

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

ANDREA KENDALL-TAYLOR is Senior Fellow and Director of the Transatlantic Security Program at the Center for a New American Security. From 2015 to 2018, she was Deputy National Intelligence Officer for Russia and Eurasia at the National Intelligence Council.

RICHARD FONTAINE is CEO of the Center for a New American Security. He has worked at the U.S. Department of State, on the National Security Council, and as a foreign policy adviser to U.S. Senator John McCain.

How Battlefield Cooperation Is Binding Together America’s Adversaries

Andrea Kendall-Taylor and Richard Fontaine

On July 17, an Iranian missile struck Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, killing three American soldiers and wounding four others. The strike was unusually precise. In the weeks that followed, U.S. officials discovered that before the attack, Tehran had received high-resolution satellite images of the base that could aid its targeting. Afterward, Iran obtained more imagery, potentially helping it assess the damage and hone future attacks. The images came from Chinese entities.

China is not alone in assisting Iran. Russia, too, has helped Tehran find and hit American and allied targets. Two days before the March 27 attack on Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia that wounded 12 American personnel, 14 Russian spy satellites passed overhead. U.S. officials later concluded that Moscow had fed Iran satellite intelligence that aided Iranian precision strikes. Moscow has also provided Iran with weapons and military expertise, including upgraded versions of Iranian drones refined on the battlefield in Ukraine, and Russian engineers are helping Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles that could evade U.S. and Israeli air defenses.

Neither Russia nor China has directly entered Iran’s war with the United States. They haven’t needed to. By providing intelligence on American targets, military technology and components, and economic and diplomatic support, they can give Iran what it needs without joining its war.

The United States entered the conflict with advantages its adversaries lacked: a vast network of formal allies, military bases, intelligence-sharing arrangements, defense partnerships, and interoperable forces spanning Europe, the Middle East, and Asia. Yet many of Washington’s traditional partners were reluctant to associate themselves with the campaign, and some denied the United States specific forms of military access, at least for a time. Others publicly resisted U.S. calls to help secure the Strait of Hormuz.

The contrast illustrates a striking shift since we first described Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea as an axis of upheaval in Foreign Affairs two years ago. The United States’ adversaries began this war with this weaker network, and Washington with the far stronger one. But after helping Russia fight its war in Ukraine over the past few years, members of the axis are now finding ways to make their network work in a new theater. They are fine-tuning their cooperation to make their partners more resilient—and more dangerous to the United States—while limiting costs and risks. Washington, for its part, is creating friction in many of its partnerships instead of deepening them, and risks squandering its network just as its adversaries are learning to make more of theirs.

Much has changed since 2024. Most obviously, the United States itself has become a source of upheaval in the international system. The Trump administration has challenged international institutions, strained traditional alliances, and adopted a more transactional approach to foreign policy. It has upended trade agreements, threatened the sovereignty of allies such as Canada and Denmark, and embraced unpredictability. It has also pursued improved relations with China, North Korea, and Russia while seeking to weaken Iran. None of this has loosened the ties among the United States’ adversaries.

Early in the Trump administration, U.S. officials expressed hope that normalizing relations with Moscow might peel Russia away from the group. Yet President Donald Trump’s oft-expressed bonhomie toward the Kremlin has opened no gaps with the other three. As seen from Moscow, the administration has been unable to deliver a deal on Ukraine, and any Trump-driven rapprochement with Washington is unlikely to endure: Congress continues to pressure Russia, and a future administration may well adopt a tougher approach.

More fundamentally, attempts to weaken the axis misunderstand what holds it together. Its members object to an international order that they see as enshrining Western dominance at their expense. But more pointedly, they oppose the United States’ extraordinary power to constrain, isolate, and punish them, and potentially to threaten their regimes. Recent U.S. actions have only rekindled those concerns. The United States’ capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and the killing of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei reinforce long-standing fears in Beijing, Moscow, Pyongyang, and Tehran about U.S. intervention and regime security.

The axis countries may moderate their anti-American rhetoric when doing so is tactically useful, but their motivation to reduce their vulnerability to American power remains. The Trump administration’s own skepticism about international order will not ease minds in axis capitals. On the contrary, Trump’s efforts to create a more transactional and coercive world may increase the value of their partnerships. As rules and institutions constrain less and brute power matters more, countries will seek partners to help them blunt sanctions, access critical technologies, compensate for military weaknesses, expand their room for maneuver, and resist isolation. Axis cooperation is evolving to meet the moment.

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, cooperation among the four countries was relatively easy to map. Iran provided Russia with drones, and North Korea sent ammunition, ballistic missiles, and later, troops. China became Moscow’s most critical lifeline, buying Russian oil and supplying the machine tools, microelectronics, and other components it needed first to sustain and then to expand its military production. Russia, in turn, transferred increasingly sophisticated military technology to its partners.

These exchanges were consequential, but they could still largely be understood as a series of bilateral transactions focused on Russia’s war. That is becoming less true. Cooperation is increasingly networked and geared toward solving new problems in new regions.

Russia’s drone program illustrates the change. Iran initially sold Russia its Shahed drones and then helped Moscow establish production at home. Russia did not simply replicate what it received; it incorporated Chinese components and continually modified the drones’ navigation, communications, payloads, propulsion, and tactics in response to Ukrainian defenses. New military units fed successful modifications back into production, generating an unusually rapid cycle of battlefield adaptation. Russia’s Unmanned Systems Forces, a drone-and-robotics branch of the Russian armed forces, was established last year to help institutionalize this cycle. The combination of domestic adaptation and axis partnership has proved effective. Russia’s latest jet-powered Geran drones, for instance, are faster, carry larger payloads, and are significantly harder for Ukrainian forces to intercept than earlier variants.

Russian improvements do not stay in Russia, either. They circulate through the axis network. For Iran, the technology that originally flowed to Russia is now returning, along with tactical advice drawn from Russia’s experience in Ukraine. If Russia’s jet-powered drones also show up in the Middle East, as they likely will, Iranian attacks on U.S. forces and regional energy infrastructure will become harder and costlier to defend against.

North Korea and China are also benefiting. According to Ukrainian reports, Russia struck a deal to help North Korea expand production of its Shahed-type drones. North Korean engineers have learned from time spent working in Russia’s massive Yelabuga drone factory, and North Korean forces fighting alongside Russia have gained firsthand experience in integrating drones into modern combat. Chinese military personnel have received training in drone warfare from Russian forces, and Chinese suppliers are gaining valuable information about how their technologies perform in combat. Beijing is thus seeing gains from the evolution of drone warfare that began with Iranian technology and has been refined in Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Two years ago, it was not clear whether partnerships among the four members of the axis could outlast the war that accelerated their formation. If the Ukraine war ended and Russia no longer needed Iranian drones, North Korean ammunition, or Chinese economic and technological support, the relationships might lose momentum.

Yet the war did not only create an immediate need for cooperation. It has also provided proof of concept for what these partnerships can accomplish, beyond what any country might attain on its own. Ukrainian defenses, Western sanctions, U.S. military supplies, and diplomatic isolation have all been less effective than would be the case if Russia were operating alone. By helping one another withstand pressure, the axis countries make it harder for the United States and its allies to compel them to change course.

Iran is now showing that the model can travel. Russia’s support for Tehran has been operationally meaningful but carefully bounded. Even as it fights its own war in Ukraine, Moscow has found ways to help Iran strike American targets and sustain the fight through diplomatic cover and material support while stopping short of actions that could draw Russia into direct conflict with the United States. China has been even more cautious, but its sharing of dual-use electronics and purchases of Iranian oil have similarly enhanced Iran’s ability to withstand U.S. pressure.

Such restraint is not evidence that the axis is weakening but rather a defining feature of how these partnerships work. With the striking exception of North Korean soldiers deployed on Russia’s behalf, the axis countries have generally avoided fighting one another’s wars. Instead, they provide political backing, economic support, intelligence, technology, and limited military assistance when doing so advances their own interests at manageable risk.

The wars in Ukraine and Iran have taught the axis another lesson: supporting a fellow member does not merely strengthen the recipient. Conflict in one theater can also create opportunities for partners elsewhere. Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz, for example, sent oil prices soaring, delivering a windfall to Russia and prompting Washington to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian oil exports. Iran’s war thus generated resources Russia could use to sustain its own.

Before attacking Iran, the United States redeployed key military assets, including air and missile defenses, from the Indo-Pacific to the Middle East. As the fighting continued, U.S. forces put two aircraft carriers in the region, leaving none in the Indo-Pacific. China gains operational freedom from a thinner U.S. military presence in the western Pacific and is less vulnerable when U.S. munitions stocks are depleted. If Washington settles into a prolonged strategy of containing Iran, as it did with Iraq in the 1990s, Beijing could enjoy the advantages of those diversions for years.

The experience of the axis of upheaval shows that the size and strength of a network matter less if its members cannot turn their individual capabilities into collective power. The United States and its allies start from a position of considerable advantage: greater economic and technological resources, more capable militaries, and a far larger network of allies and partners. The question is which network can make better use of its assets.

That starts with leadership. For decades, the United States favored an international order that forbade wars of conquest, upheld freedom of the seas, maintained a generally open global economy, and allowed populations to exercise democratic rights, even if autocracies remained. Washington coupled this vision with an implicit bargain: any country that wished to join the order could do so. Upholding the order’s basic principles conferred benefits, including from the United States: trade relations, diplomatic preferences, sometimes military alliances.

For countries that rejected the open international order, as the axis countries do today, the benefits were far fewer and the penalties considerable. The United States sanctioned, pressured, and sometimes went to war against rogue states, and it resisted the establishment of competing orders such as the Cold War communist bloc. U.S. foreign policy started from the seemingly uncontroversial premise that Washington should befriend like-minded countries and treat them better than rejectionists.

The Trump administration demonstrates, at least at times, something like the opposite inclination. The U.S. ambassador to China recently said that Trump offered to sell Beijing weapons, while stalling arms sales to Taiwan. The president has expressed greater interest in and affection for North Korea’s dictator, Kim Jong Un, than for South Korea’s democratically elected president, Lee Jae-myung. The administration has also intermittently pressured Ukraine to cave in its war of survival against Russian aggression. And Trump has threatened to bomb Oman, a longtime partner. Such moves both strengthen the axis countries and weaken the cohesion of the network best positioned to confront them.

Doing no further harm would be a good start in dealing with the axis. Beyond that, Washington should help its partners grow stronger. Just as the axis countries are helping one another work around sanctions, preserve access to critical technologies and components, and sustain their economies under pressure, the United States should aid its own network. That means strengthening supply chains that run through trusted partners, sharing technology, and encouraging allies to take on greater security burdens. Washington must take care, however, not to transfer defense responsibilities faster than allies can develop the capabilities to assume them—and not to do so in ways that erode trust, interoperability, and coordination. Otherwise, the United States and its allies could become individually more capable but collectively less effective.

The United States should also reverse policies that undercut its own network. Tariffs and other protectionist measures harm allied economies and their industrial bases. Expressing a desire to seize allies’ territory and attempting to undermine their political leaders do not make for a more capable international network. Washington should project vision and leadership to its friends, not jarring uncertainty and bullying transactionalism.

Even if the United States changes course, American and allied policymakers should prepare for a long struggle. As the unsuccessful regime-change effort in Iran demonstrated, there are no shortcuts to besting the axis countries, together or individually. The contest of networks will be nearly global, waged in multiple domains, with huge stakes riding on the outcome. The United States and its allies have the capacity to prevail. They should demonstrate the will.

How the Search for Economic Security Will End in Geopolitical Calamity

Henry Farrell, Abraham Newman, and Yeling Tan

Why the Future of War Can’t Escape the Past

Dependence on America Has Left It With Little to Offer Would-Be Partners

How Europe Can Take More Responsibility—Without Starting an Arms Race

How Beijing Is Challenging Washington in Outer Space

#96. ‘Red to Blue’ Democrats rake in more than GOP rivals in third quarter

In their quest to flip the House, Democrats have sought to expand the battleground map by targeting seats in red-leaning terrain, and their candidates in these races dominated third-quarter fundraising, new filings show.

But many of their Republican opponents, including vulnerable incumbents, entered October with larger bank balances, according to a CQ Roll Call analysis of the reports filed with the Federal Election Commission, as the fight for the House heats up in the campaign’s closing weeks.

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has 46 candidates in its “Red to Blue” program for top recruits. And the average candidate in the program outraised their Republican opponent roughly 2-to-1 between July and September — $2.1 million versus $1 million.

Related: Senate Democratic candidates in red states dominate third-quarter fundraising

In total, 40 of the “Red to Blue” Democrats outraised their GOP rivals, including former California state Sen. Richard Pan, who’s challenging Rep. Kevin Kiley, an independent who caucuses with Republicans; and independent candidate Bill Hill, who has the DCCC’s backing as he takes on Alaska’s Republican freshman Nick Begich.

Reps. Eli Crane of Arizona and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania and Tennessee candidate Charlie Hatcher, who knocked off Rep. Andy Ogles in an August primary, were among the six Republicans who outraised their Democratic opponents. Additionally, three GOP self-funders also posted bigger quarterly hauls: New York’s Anthony Constantino, who loaned his campaign $5 million, Florida’s Casey Askar and Nevada’s David Flippo.

Among the top Democratic fundraisers in the “Red to Blue” group were those running in some of the most competitive House races this year: New York’s Cait Conley (who raised $5.4 million), Colorado’s Manny Rutinel ($4.2 million), New Jersey’s Rebecca Bennett ($3.9 million), Wisconsin’s Rebecca Cooke ($3.7 million), Arizona’s JoAnna Mendoza ($3.4 million), Texas’ Bobby Pulido ($3.3 million) and Arizona’s Amish Shah ($3.2 million).

Still, a majority of Republicans facing “Red to Blue” challengers closed the quarter with more cash on hand for the campaign’s final stretch, according to CQ Roll Call’s analysis of the latest filings.

For example, while Conley outraised GOP Rep. Mike Lawler in New York’s 17th District in the third quarter, the congressman began October with $2.9 million on hand to the challenger’s $1.2 million. Similarly, Democratic former Rep. Elaine Luria outraised Republican incumbent Jen Kiggans in a rematch of their 2022 race for Virginia’s 2nd District, but Kiggans had nearly $1 million more in her account on Sept. 30.

Several recent additions to the “Red to Blue” list, including Wisconsin’s Mitchell Berman, who is challenging Rep. Bryan Steil; Arkansas’ Chris Jones, who is running against Rep. French Hill; and Colorado’s Dwayne Romero, who faces Rep. Jeff Hurd, outraised their opponents in the third quarter, but all began October with less in their campaign coffers.

Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales rates all the “Red to Blue” races as competitive, with the exception of a pair of contests in Tennessee: Hatcher’s race for the 5th District against Democrat Chaz Molder; and the redrawn 9th District race, which pits Republican Brent Taylor against Democrat Justin Pearson.

The GOP counterpart to "Red to Blue” is the National Republican Congressional Committee’s "MAGA Majority" program, which also includes several races on the Democratic list.

GOP candidates in this group saw their Democratic opponents raise nearly twice as much as them in the third quarter, with the average Democrat hauling in $1.6 million compared with $867,000 for the Republican.

Nevada state Sen. Carrie Buck was a rare “MAGA Majority” Republican to report a larger third-quarter haul than her opponent. She once again outraised Democratic Rep. Dina Titus, $638,000 to $439,000. Titus had a slight cash-on-hand advantage at the end of the quarter.

Additionally, Republican Anthony DiLorenzo outraised Democrat Stefany Shaheen in New Hampshire’s open 1st District, though his $2.7 million haul included a $2.3 million personal loan.

Most of the 27 Republicans in the "MAGA Majority" program ended September with less cash banked than their Democratic opponent, though seven had more on hand.

They included Florida’s Mike Beltran, who is challenging Democratic Rep. Kathy Castor in a seat redrawn to favor Republicans; New Mexico’s Greg Cunningham, who is taking on Democrat Rep. Gabe Vasquez; and Washington’s John Braun, who is vying for the seat of Democratic Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Pérez.

#97. Zelenskyy warns: “We will not prevail” if U.S. backs Russia

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed Sunday that the United States temporarily interrupted intelligence-sharing with Ukraine, as a Republican congressman demanded an investigation into separate disruptions affecting Ukrainian battlefield communications.

Speaking on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” Zelenskyy said American intelligence used to detect incoming Russian missile strikes had been restored after a brief interruption.

“We are very thankful for this,” Zelenskyy said. “Now it works.”

President Donald Trump previously maintained that intelligence-sharing had never stopped, despite Ukrainian officials reporting that some Russian attacks occurred without warning.

Zelenskyy also criticized the administration’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports and waive new sanctions targeting Moscow, warning that Washington’s actions could undermine Ukraine’s defense.

“If the United States will officially take the side of Russia … we will not prevail and we will not be able to stand,” he said.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, appearing on the same program, declined three times to directly answer whether the United States considers Ukraine an ally.

“I’m not the secretary of state. I’m not the president,” Bessent said after repeated questioning by moderator Kristen Welker.

Bessent pointed to continued American intelligence and military assistance, arguing that Washington was seeking a negotiated end to the war.

Start your day with essential news from Salon. Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

Meanwhile, Rep. Mike Turner, R-Ohio, called for a congressional investigation into disruptions involving SpaceX’s Starshield satellite communications system, which Ukrainian forces rely on for battlefield operations.

On CBS’ “Face the Nation,” Turner rejected Secretary of State Marco Rubio‘s explanation that the slowdown occurred without a White House order.

“Absolutely not,” Turner said when asked whether Rubio’s explanation was sufficient. “There needs to be a congressional investigation.”

Turner warned that interrupted communications could endanger Ukrainian lives and urged Trump to reconsider waiving sanctions on Russia.

The tensions also provided material for Saturday night’s “SNL UK,” which spoofed Zelenskyy’s meeting with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

James Austin Johnson, reprising his Trump impersonation from the American “Saturday Night Live,” crashed the meeting as the fictional Zelenskyy pleaded for restored Starlink access. Johnson’s Trump offered to help Ukraine with anything, “provided it’s not help with war.”

#101. How Congress Fixed Social Security During Its Last Crisis

Analysis: How Congress Fixed Social Security During Its Last Crisis

Social Security faces a major fiscal challenge. The program, which has provided retirement, survivor, and disability benefits to millions of Americans since its creation in 1935, is projected to soon cost more than its total income. The budgetary shortfall is already prompting the government to draw down reserves, which will reach unsustainable levels by the early 2030s. As more baby boomers retire, the number of beneficiaries is rising faster than the number of workers contributing payroll taxes. A September report from the Congressional Budget Office warned that, without reforms, benefits may have to be cut by 26 percent.

Although the program’s creators in 1935 envisioned building up reserves, Social Security has been financed largely on a pay-as-you-go basis since Congress enacted changes between 1939 and 1950. The payroll taxes collected from current workers and employers, together with taxes on benefits and interest income, finance the benefits of current retirees.

Social Security faces a major fiscal challenge. The program, which has provided retirement, survivor, and disability benefits to millions of Americans since its creation in 1935, is projected to soon cost more than its total income. The budgetary shortfall is already prompting the government to draw down reserves, which will reach unsustainable levels by the early 2030s. As more baby boomers retire, the number of beneficiaries is rising faster than the number of workers contributing payroll taxes. A September report from the Congressional Budget Office warned that, without reforms, benefits may have to be cut by 26 percent.

Although the program’s creators in 1935 envisioned building up reserves, Social Security has been financed largely on a pay-as-you-go basis since Congress enacted changes between 1939 and 1950. The payroll taxes collected from current workers and employers, together with taxes on benefits and interest income, finance the benefits of current retirees.

What will Congress do? In a hyperpolarized environment on Capitol Hill, with a president who has shown little concern about governing, the prospects for a resolution remain uncertain. The stakes are high. Millions of Americans depend on this program for their retirement income. After paying taxes throughout their time in the labor force, retirees expect the benefits they were promised. Allowing this pillar of the social safety net to collapse would be disastrous for U.S. workers and the broader economy.

In the early 1980s, Congress faced a similar crisis and acted. Although the solution that a bipartisan coalition put into place in 1983 has itself contributed to the challenges policymakers face today, the political approach they took remains instructive. Indeed, it is the only viable path forward. At a critical moment, elected officials from both parties demonstrated that they could forge an agreement necessary to govern.

Congress created Social Security in 1935, and was paid for through an earmarked payroll tax that funded the benefits of retirees. President Franklin Roosevelt supported the tax because he wanted workers to see Social Security as a “contributory” system rather than public welfare. “With those taxes in there,” Roosevelt later said, “no damn politician can ever scrap my social security program. Those taxes aren’t a matter of economics, they’re straight politics.”

Under the original plan, workers and employers would begin paying Social Security taxes in 1937, while monthly benefits would not be distributed until 1942. The delay would allow the government to build reserves that would be invested in government bonds. Initially, the program covered primarily industrial and commercial workers. Domestic and farm workers, the self-employed, government civil servants, and other categories of work would be incorporated over time.

With the Social Security Amendments of 1939, Congress accelerated the distribution of benefits while extending coverage to survivors and dependents. Policymakers also scaled back the plan to build a large reserve, in large part because they feared that old-age assistance, a means-tested welfare program funded through general tax revenues (also part of the Social Security Act of 1935), was far more popular in the states. Economists were also concerned about the consequences of accumulating an enormous federal reserve fund. The Social Security Amendments of 1950 further entrenched a shift toward a pay-as-you-go system, in which payroll taxes finance monthly benefits. The program’s actuaries make recommendations based on 75-year projections.

The program continued to grow over time and to become popular among Republicans and Democrats. In 1954, Republican President Dwight Eisenhower, who was no radical, wrote, “Should any political party attempt to abolish social security, unemployment insurance, and eliminate labor laws and farm programs, you would not hear of that party again in our political history.”

Congress continued to expand the program over the next decade, with both parties regularly agreeing to increase benefits. In 1965, Congress created Medicare, raising payroll taxes to finance hospital insurance for the elderly in a program connected to Social Security. In 1972, Congress passed additional Social Security amendments, which indexed benefits to inflation by tying them to the Consumer Price Index. A flaw in the new formula, “the double-indexing” problem, however, produced benefit increases that were larger than lawmakers had anticipated.

During the 1970s, Social Security entered a period of financial crisis. High inflation drove up benefits, while high rates of unemployment reduced the number of workers paying into the system. In 1977, Congress attempted to address the short-term crisis by raising payroll taxes and correcting the technical error in the 1972 law.

But the Social Security Amendments of 1977 did not resolve the program’s financial challenges. By the early 1980s, policymakers recognized that Social Security faced a short-term financial shortfall that could hit by 1983, caused by stagflation as well as a long-term imbalance stemming from the anticipated retirement of the baby boom generation and longer life expectancy.

The path toward a resolution was contentious, partisan, and grueling.

In the spring of 1981, President Ronald Reagan’s first attempt to address the problem turned into a political disaster. His administration proposed deep reductions in early retirement benefits. It separately supported eliminating the minimum benefit, a cut that made it through Congress in 1981 before being reversed later that year. Rumors circulated in Washington about additional reductions that he intended to pursue.

Democratic Speaker of the House Tip O’Neill saw an opening to attack the conservative president, leading a coalition that charged the administration with trying to dismantle the cherished program. The charge had some foundation, given that conservatives such as Republican presidential candidate Barry Goldwater in 1964, for whom Reagan had campaigned, had talked for years about making Social Security voluntary.

The Republican-controlled Senate rejected Reagan’s proposal, and the president backed down. The battle reinforced the idea that Social Security was a “third rail” in U.S. politics: Politicians who touched it risked political electrocution. Democrats made Social Security a major issue in the 1982 midterms, when they gained 26 seats in the House.

Still, Social Security’s fiscal problems did not disappear. Reagan, in consultation with congressional leaders, established a 15-member bipartisan National Commission on Social Security Reform, headed by the economist Alan Greenspan, who had chaired the Council of Economic Advisers under President Gerald Ford and advised President Richard Nixon. The commission included representatives from the worlds of politics, labor, and business, and its ultimate report received widespread praise. However, getting there wasn’t easy. After an initial deadlock, but with broad agreement on the nature of the problem, a smaller group of officials and congressional negotiators met privately at the home of White House chief of staff James Baker. As reality that a financial reckoning was looming soon set in, the commission reached an agreement in January 1983, and its recommendations became the basis for congressional action.

The Social Security Amendments of 1983, which the president signed into law on April 20, accelerated payroll tax increases, raised contributions from the self-employed, delayed cost-of-living increases, and subjected a portion of the benefits received by higher income beneficiaries to income taxation. The law also brought several categories of workers into the system and gradually raised the full retirement age from 65 to 67. Republican Rep. Barber Conable Jr. told his colleagues: “This is not a work of art. But it is artful work.”

In the end, many believed that the realization the program could implode propelled the last-ditch compromises. Both parties made concessions to reach a deal. Democrats accepted the six-month cost-of-living delay and new taxation for higher income recipients while Republicans accepted additional revenues, including the accelerated payroll tax increases.

Upon signing the bill on a stage decorated with red, white, and blue bunting in front of 400 people, Reagan said: “This bill demonstrates for all time our nation’s ironclad commitment to social security. It assures the elderly that America will always keep the promises made in troubled times a half century ago. It assures those who are still working that they, too, have a pact with the future. From this day forward, they have one pledge that they will get their fair share of benefits when they retire. And this bill assures us of one more thing that is equally important. It’s a clear and dramatic demonstration that our system can still work when men and women of good will join together to make it work.”

Today, there is considerable nostalgia for the 1980s as a golden era of civility and bipartisan cooperation, a memory that obscures the bitter partisan divisions of the Reagan years. Yet the Social Security Amendments of 1983 remain an important testament to what the nation’s political parties can achieve when they turn their attention to governing rather than endless warfare.

The final bill was far from perfect. The changes did not permanently resolve Social Security’s long-term fiscal challenges, including those associated with the retirement of the baby boomer generation. Nor did legislators anticipate how growing wage inequality would create additional financial pressures on the program.

The governing environment has since become considerably more difficult. Hyperpolarization has made bipartisan agreements harder to reach, while today’s media ecosystem, characterized by openly partisan outlets and unfiltered social media awash in disinformation, has largely eliminated the closed spaces in which party leaders once negotiated agreements that risked angering constituents.

The Republican Party has also shifted much further to the right since the 1990s, demonstrating a greater willingness to cut core social safety net programs, including those that benefit working-class Americans whom President Donald Trump helped bring into the GOP.

Nonetheless, leaders in both parties understand that Social Security remains enormously popular. That political reality explains why Trump has remained opposed to cutting Social Security benefits, even as he has targeted almost every other part of the federal government.

If Democrats retake control of Congress in the midterms, strengthening Social Security will have to be a top priority. They will test the insightful scholarship of political scientists such as Princeton’s Frances Lee and Philip Wallach of the American Enterprise Institute, who have published forceful arguments about how Congress can and still works. If Democrats take on that challenge, as they must, they will learn whether there is any room to work with Republicans in Congress and the White House to secure a program that has saved millions of elderly Americans, and their families, from the devastation of poverty.

Julian E. Zelizer is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a professor of history and public affairs at Princeton University. He is the author of The Long View, a newsletter putting the news in perspective. In 2027, Norton will publish his new book, Rumble on the Promenade: The Clash of Justice and Power at the 1964 Convention. X: @julianzelizer
