#156. The Empty Classrooms of ‘American Hagwon’

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Review: The Empty Classrooms of ‘American Hagwon’

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

One of the first places I was made aware of my race was the classroom. Placed in a cohort for so-called gifted children, I quickly understood that while my white classmates were considered gifted because they were naturally inclined or exceptionally hard workers, my academic aptitude was seen as a facet of my ethnic background.

My classmates’ parents would pry, asking about my standardized test scores only to wave them off as a result of my supposed cultural upbringing. Friends assumed my Japanese mother was a tiger mom hounding me to finish my homework, when in fact it was my white father who pushed me academically.

One of the first places I was made aware of my race was the classroom. Placed in a cohort for so-called gifted children, I quickly understood that while my white classmates were considered gifted because they were naturally inclined or exceptionally hard workers, my academic aptitude was seen as a facet of my ethnic background.

My classmates’ parents would pry, asking about my standardized test scores only to wave them off as a result of my supposed cultural upbringing. Friends assumed my Japanese mother was a tiger mom hounding me to finish my homework, when in fact it was my white father who pushed me academically.

There were many things in my life that I saw as part of my Asianness: the food I liked, the manga I read, the language I spoke at home. But at school, I learned that there was nothing as Asian to my classmates as my grade point average. Americans expected Asians to care deeply about school, to excel no matter the cost.

American Hagwon, Min Jin Lee, Cardinal, 656 pp., $36, September 2026

The novels of Korean American author Min Jin Lee’s planned diaspora quartet, whose previous installments include Free Food for Millionaires and Pachinko, attempt to distill various facets of the diasporic Korean experience. Lee’s hotly anticipated third novel, American Hagwon, tries to untangle the essentialization of education, asking why diasporic Asians pin their hopes on it and what they get in return.

American Hagwon spans 1992 to 2007, following John and Helen Koh as they struggle to keep their family afloat. Their three children, Bo, DH, and Mido, follow their parents from South Korea to Australia to the United States, growing from schoolchildren into young adults trying to support their parents financially. Sudden job loss, infidelity, poverty, illness, and even the 1997 Asian financial crisis buffet the Kohs as they claw their way to stability on scarce funds.

Lee’s novel is ambitious, taking a panoramic and fulsome view of its characters’ lives. But its pulsing heartbeat, and the core of her vision of the Korean diaspora, is the hagwon: a private, for-profit cram school where children ostensibly go to get ahead. These are not trivial after-school activities: As of 2022, 78.3 percent of South Korean elementary-aged students attended private hagwons. In the United States, hagwons are less prevalent and often attached to Korean American churches, a familiar locale in Lee’s novels.

South Korean students study a map of the United States as to practice their English language skills in Seoul on Dec. 10, 2004. Chung Sung-Jun/Getty Images

Lee treats these cram schools as arenas of conflict, reckoning, and rote labor in American Hagwon. The Koh children attend hagwons when they are young, and Lee casts them as places where a student’s sense of self is built up and broken down—an academic forge where they test their mettle against the demands of a stratified society.

Bo, for example, chooses to live near his hagwon even after his family leaves South Korea for better economic prospects, and studies for the Suneung—the grueling, nine-hour university entrance exam. Later, youngest child Mido puts her own college education on hold to work at a hagwon in the United States under a maverick owner nicknamed Lion, whose approach puts students’ wellbeing ahead of test scores. (It still delivers college admissions results.) There, Mido falls in love, grieves family tragedy, and begins to find herself.

So many of the characters’ formative moments happen in or around the hagwon that it functions as a synecdoche for the novel—as if to say, Look how much time these Koreans spend in this temple for educational advancement. See their single-minded dedication.

It should come as no surprise that Lee imbues the hagwon with so much meaning. She is, after all, an ethnographic novelist whose worlds are baroque yet entirely pleasurable to sink into. Each new setting, drama, and side character’s yearning culminates in a larger comment on a social question, much like Charles Dickens and poverty or Leo Tolstoy and Russian class dynamics. (In interviews, Lee talks about her great love of the 19th century social novel, and it shows.)

Pachinko, Lee’s second novel, was celebrated for its life-like portrayal of Korean migrants in Japan. The author told a polyphonic, affecting story of resilience and memory, asking how we ought to remember those whom history would rather us forget. To achieve that granularity, she populated the book with meticulously researched settings, animated by heroines and villains who drew sympathy from even the most stoic of readers.

Beijing long promoted novels about working-class travails. What happens when authors point fingers at the state?

The Homeric scholar’s new book on translation is bitingly smart.

The debut novel “Venus, Vanishing” is a fast-paced tale of deception, forgery, sex, and escape.

American Hagwon attempts the same, and its worlds feel real, from the sumptuous rooms of a luxury apartment in Seoul to the dingy back kitchen of a seafood joint in southern California. The novel clearly knows the sociology of its setting, describing the inner machinations of late ’90s Korean American community politics with an insider’s ease.

But against this impeccably painted backdrop, the people who inhabit the rooms feel flimsy. There are moments, especially in the latter half of this almost 700-page novel, where one can’t help but feel that character complexity is sacrificed for social commentary about Asians and education. Yes, American Hagwon is interested in nuanced questions about education, wisdom, and what it means to live a meaningful life. But its characters start to flag under the weight of those questions.

Pupils raise their hands during class at the Jongno Academy in Seoul on Aug. 10, 2016.Yelim Lee/AFP via Getty Images

Take Danbi, the book’s consummate villain. Unlike the antagonists in Lee’s previous novels, there is very little to like about Danbi. She is conniving and promiscuous, a liar and a cheat; there is no attempt to complicate her or redeem her. It is as if the book has made her the emblem of an unmeaningful life. This simplification is puzzling given the novel’s insistence on a systemic view of society.

If American Hagwon wants to examine the pitfalls of South Korea’s emphasis on education, surely the book’s ultimate antagonist should be societal as well—inequality, poverty, or lack of access to higher education, for example. Instead of an unlikable person struggling to survive in a hypercompetitive system, we get a jezebel who causes the downfall of not one but three separate men—a narrative with a predictably damning tenor.

Other characters suffer under the book’s desire to make a point rather than tell a story. Mido, ostensibly a heroine, is presented as an intriguing child: quiet and shy, but determined. One would expect to see her become more layered as the novel progresses. In adulthood, though, Mido is relentlessly, tediously good. She never attains conventional success in school, but she becomes a hardworking and sought-after hagwon instructor. She is appropriate to a fault, less a character than a vehicle for a moral.

Perhaps Mido is meant to be the anti-Danbi, proof that one can lead a meaningful life even without an Ivy League education. As a hagwon instructor, education is still certainly the yardstick of her life’s worth. And like Danbi, she is uncomplicated: moral, doe-eyed, and an embodiment of the message that good things happen to good people.

What, then, is the moral that Lee is so intent on promoting? Despite the black-and-white characters and their dime-novel outcomes, it’s hard to say.

On one hand, American Hagwon is curious about the Korean diaspora’s relationship to education, particularly what it means to parents hoping to claw their way upward in a hostile society. On the other, it seems to question whether it is ultimately for the betterment of South Korean children to be so focused on schooling, even as its main characters find success teaching in cram schools.

Of course, novels don’t need to deliver a thesis, nor is an author required to give a simplistic final take on their subjects. But this book’s threads are so discordant that it is hard to see where the reader is meant to arrive without Lee weighing in conclusively. This ambiguity is doubly frustrating when so many characters are reduced to caricatures in service of the message.

Perhaps some of the muddiness reflects the increasingly fraught relationship between Asian Americans and the U.S. education system. In 2023, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in favor of a coalition, led by a coalition of Asian American students, backed by conservative activists, that struck down affirmative action.

An anti-affirmative action activist with the Asian American Coalition for Education protests outside the U.S. Supreme Court building in Washington on June 29, 2023. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

The coalition argued that Asian Americans were being punished by policies meant to account for the systemic hurdles to higher education faced by other minorities, and that they should be rewarded for their intense focus on academics rather than filtered out because too many of them did well. In the years since, data has shown that the ruling has not done much to help Asian American college applicants, with little to no change in their overall rates of enrollment at Ivy League institutions.

Which is all to say, though American Hagwon tries to unravel the essentialization of Asians and academic excellence, it ignores how that essentialization has been used to disenfranchise other minorities seeking educational advancement. The novel’s fretting over what education is for and how one attains wisdom—Lion’s voice in his hagwon comes to mind—starts to feel stale, if not slightly sinister, when we consider how the Asian American pursuit of education has been used as a cudgel to dismantle education for all.

Lee’s fans know that her opening lines offer an emotional thesis for the novel that follows. “History has failed us, but no matter,” opens Pachinko, defiant in its tale of resilience against Japanese erasure. “Competence can be a curse,” starts Free Food for Millionaires, as it plots its heroine’s struggle to free herself from the trappings of capitalism.

A young attendee waits for then-U.S. President Joe Biden and first lady Dr. Jill Biden to welcome then-South Korean President Yoon Suk-yeol and first lady Kim Keon-hee to the White House in Washington on April 26, 2023. Kent Nishimura/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images

American Hagwon begins: “The rules of engagement have changed already.” The line points to the tempestuous winds of fortune and failure that follow the Koh family from continent to continent and job to job, as its members hold on to school as their only hope. It also rings true of the book’s most damning weakness. The Asian relationship to education is no longer an innocent thing. The rules of engagement have changed, and this novel doesn’t seem to have noticed.

#157. The Real Lesson of the Iran War

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

JUSTIN BRONK is Senior Research Fellow for Airpower and Technology at the Royal United Services Institute.

For months, Iran’s resilience in its war with two of the world’s most capable militaries has perplexed many politicians and confounded public expectations. Israel and the United States have hit thousands of Iranian targets, systematically destroying much of the country’s military infrastructure and killing many of its top leaders. Yet the Islamic Republic has not only survived but also continued to maintain significant offensive capabilities. To account for this, some have pointed to Iran’s effective deployment of low-cost precise mass weapons, such as the Shahed-136 one-way attack drone. Others have looked at the decentralized and self-replacing nature of the regime itself.

Although these and other factors have played a part, there is a more straightforward reason for Iran’s staying power: the American and Israeli decision to rely on a sustained air and stand-off naval campaign to bring the regime to its knees. This approach did not come out of nowhere. Air supremacy has been the defining tenet of U.S. and wider Western military strategy for decades. In the post–Cold War era, the United States has perfected the art of airpower—winning control of the skies so that enemy armies, navies, and territory can be bombed at will—to a degree that no country or even alliance of countries has matched. When pitted against an adversary’s deployed ground forces, this strategy has consistently yielded impressive results. The U.S. ability to achieve rapid air superiority has also long served as a powerful deterrent to would-be aggressors.

Yet there are few examples in history of adversaries conceding to maximalist demands in the face of punitive bombing campaigns alone—even by the world’s greatest air force. Indeed, Operation Epic Fury is only one of several recent or current conflicts—including Russia’s war in Ukraine and international responses to the Houthi threat in Yemen—that have exposed the drawbacks of relying heavily on airstrikes to try to unseat a government or to defeat insurgent forces. For American strategists, then, it will be crucial to distinguish the different uses of airpower. The Iran campaign has been a disastrous misuse of military resources, and it showcases the policy limits of what airpower can achieve. Yet it would be a mistake to conclude that the United States should shift away from its doctrine of prioritizing air superiority, as it prepares alongside NATO and Asian allies for very different threats in the coming few years.

During the major wars of the twentieth century, U.S. and Allied air superiority was critical to successes on the battlefield. But airpower still failed to force political capitulation by adversaries. In World War II, Nazi Germany fought to the very end despite the Allies’ systematic bombing of its cities, its industrial base, and its transport and fuel networks. In the Korean War, North Korea fought the United States and its allies to a standstill, even as fleets of U.S. bombers obliterated most of its cities and infrastructure. And in Vietnam, the North Vietnamese outlasted the United States, despite the U.S. military dropping more than a million tons of ordnance on cities, factories, and supply routes, in successive punitive air campaigns.

In the defining counterinsurgency conflicts of the twenty-first century, there is little evidence to suggest that air superiority proved any more effective. In Afghanistan and Iraq, the United States and its allies quickly established total air superiority over the enemy and were able to call in precision airstrikes at will, giving allied troops a huge advantage in combat. Yet in both cases, these campaigns also ultimately failed to achieve their political objectives.

Despite near-daily barrages of Ukraine’s cities, power infrastructure, and industry, Russia is no closer to vanquishing the country more than four and a half years after its brutal invasion began. In Iran, there has been little sign that U.S. and Israeli airstrikes have fueled popular pressure to end the war. This is despite major antigovernment protests throughout the country shortly before the campaign began, which were stamped out only after mass state violence. Indeed, inflicting hardship on the population seems especially unlikely to change the calculus of the Iranian regime, given its willingness to kill thousands of protestors to stay in power.

If anything, there is reason to think that it may be even harder today to win wars than in the twentieth century. Because of the increasingly multipolar nature of the world order, countries can often rely on international support to mitigate the damage from a sustained enemy strike campaign. In Ukraine, this can be seen in the influx of American and European weapons and economic, military, and technological support into the country since Russia’s 2022 invasion. This assistance has not prevented Ukrainians from experiencing terrible loss and hardship, but it has enabled the Ukrainian economy to continue functioning and its military to consistently replace lost and expended equipment and ammunition over time.

For Iran, China has provided a stable market for Iranian oil and gas exports, which helped keep Iran’s economy afloat until the imposition of a U.S. naval blockade in April. More recently, Beijing has also provided military support in the form of short-range air defense systems, which will sustain and improve Iran’s capability to pose a pop-up threat to U.S. and Israeli aircraft loitering to seek targets at medium or low altitudes. Russia also remains a key Iranian ally, providing Tehran with intelligence to target U.S. forces in the Gulf and helping it develop new military capabilities, such as supersonic antiship missiles. In both wars, external support has made sustained air and missile strike campaigns far less likely to result in political capitulation, or economic or military collapse.

Despite the poor record of punitive bombing campaigns in forcing political capitulation, air superiority has proved decisive in many wars through its impact on the battlefield. The U.S. military’s overwhelming success against the well-equipped and battle-hardened Iraqi army in Operation Desert Storm, in 1991, was, perhaps, the defining example of how an air-centered approach can be effective. The initial U.S. air campaign in January and February 1991 sufficiently degraded Iraqi forces and command and control capabilities to allow coalition ground forces to decisively defeat the Iraqi army in less than 100 hours of ground combat operations.

Other partial successes include NATO’s intervention in Kosovo in 1999, in which a 78-day air campaign led Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to withdraw his forces. Yet another was the European-led air campaign against Muammar al-Qaddafi’s forces over Libya in 2011, which rapidly destroyed government tanks and artillery attacking the city of Benghazi, and facilitated a subsequent rebel advance to Tripoli with further airstrikes. In each of these cases, air superiority made the battlefield situation untenable for enemy ground forces and forced them to retreat. The fundamental difference that distinguishes this effective use of airpower lies in the objectives that the enemy was seeking to achieve. When an adversary is pursuing goals that require the significant deployment of ground forces—such as an invasion to seize the territory of a neighboring state—establishing air superiority over that adversary almost always confers a decisive military advantage.

In World War II, the Anglo-American combined bomber offensive against German cities and industry failed to force Germany to surrender. But once the Allies established air superiority in any given theater of operations, the operational defeat of Axis armies in the field was only a matter of time. In the Western Desert, and then in Italy, Normandy, and Germany itself, roving Allied fighter-bomber patrolsrapidly rendered movement by armored vehicles and supply columns by day prohibitively dangerous. They also could provide devastating close air support whenever Allied ground units met strong Axis positions or units.

In 1991, Saddam Hussein’s objectives required the Iraqi army to hold territory in Kuwait against U.S.-led ground forces, and U.S. tactical airpower rapidly made that impossible, by destroying Iraqi air defenses and then conducting a massive interdiction campaign against armored vehicles, logistics convoys, bases, and communications infrastructure. In Libya in 2011, Qaddafi’s forces deployed tanks and artillery around Benghazi to bombard rebel forces and civilians, but these were easily found and destroyed by European combat aircraft, as were units that Qaddafi deployed to try to stop later rebel counterattacks toward Tripoli. The ultimate rebel victory and killing of Qaddafi did not deliver long-term policy success in Libya as the Western world would define it. But Qaddafi’s military forces were decisively defeated by Western airpower and his objective of crushing a popular uprising by force was rendered impossible.

In Afghanistan and Iraq, by contrast, none of Washington’s adversaries needed to field regular military forces in the open to achieve their objectives. Simply by maintaining a steady tempo of IED strikes and ambushes against U.S. patrols, and then melting back into the wider civilian population, these groups were able to deny coalition forces the security they needed to foster democratic state building. Of course, whenever militant groups attempted larger operations designed to overrun bases or towns, they were met with ferocious firepower, much of it delivered by airstrikes, thanks to ubiquitous U.S. and coalition air superiority. But just as in Vietnam, victory in most major battlefield engagements was not enough to secure the political objectives that the United States sought. All that the Taliban in Afghanistan or militant groups in Iraq had to do was to maintain a security vacuum for long enough to exhaust U.S. and European patience with discretionary “forever wars.”

Although every war is different, the United States confronts a similar problem in Iran: it is trying to use airpower to achieve maximalist aims against an enemy that can largely afford to keep its conventional military forces dispersed, hidden, or underground. The initial U.S. and Israeli campaign to establish air superiority was very successful, and in general, the advanced aircraft and tactics the two militaries deployed worked as intended. But although subsequent months of airstrikes have destroyed some of Iran’s enormous ballistic missile arsenal, most of the country’s significant remaining stocks and production capacity are in deeply buried “missile cities,” out of reach of almost all conventional bombs and missiles. Because of the earlier 12-day war, in June 2025—when U.S. airstrikes targeted Iran’s nuclear infrastructure with highly specialized 30,000-pound bunker-busting bombs—the bulk of Iran’s remaining highly enriched fissile material, movable equipment, and scientists were likely dispersed and hidden from further airstrikes long before Operation Epic Fury began.

To defeat U.S. war aims, therefore, the regime does not have to deploy regular armed forces in the open. It simply has to maintain control of the Iranian population, which the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps is well placed to ensure through widespread day-to-day repression. And in Hormuz, Iran can easily conceal the small boats it needs to drop mines, its antiship missile launchers, and its drone launch positions along the extensive and rocky coastline. Airpower alone is unlikely to deliver a victory against Iran, despite Israel’s and the United States’ ability to functionally strike almost anywhere in the country, at will, for months on end.

This is in fact the same problem that has frustrated earlier attempts by the United States and its allies to stop antiship drone and missile strikes by the Houthis in Yemen. Airpower can be and has been used repeatedly to destroy any Houthi forces identified in the open, but it cannot prevent the group from posing a sustained threat to commercial shipping with concealed missile and drone launch sites in coastal territory that they control.

The war in Iran has significantly tarnished the global aura of U.S. airpower. It is unlikely that the Trump administration would have launched Operation Epic Fury if it had known that seven months later it would still be facing an inconclusive slugging match—one that has wasted a huge part of Washington’s complex munitions stockpile and come at exorbitant economic and geopolitical cost. Alongside the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine, in which neither side has been able to achieve air superiority, there is a real risk that policymakers and the public lose faith in advanced air capabilities as the central pillar of American and wider Western military advantage.

That would be a huge mistake. The first lesson of the war against Iran in 2026—as in numerous other wars, including Vietnam, Iraq after 2003, and Afghanistan after 2006—is that conventional military superiority gained through overwhelming airpower will not be enough to achieve unrealistic political goals. But the second lesson is that this failure is not about weaknesses in U.S. air capabilities themselves. On the contrary, airpower remains the most potent piece of the United States’ conventional forces, as well as its main source of both deterrent capacity and warfighting advantage against conventional aggression by hostile states. If the U.S. goals for Operation Epic Fury had been to defeat an Iranian invasion of a neighboring country, then the air campaign would almost certainly have done that within a few weeks.

That hypothetical scenario is highly relevant because it bears on the most significant nondiscretionary threats that the United States may be forced to deal with in the coming few years. In the case of a Russian invasion of a NATO member state in eastern Europe or a Chinese move to take Taiwan, the enemy would need to make large deployments of regular ground forces to seize and then hold territory. In either case, advanced U.S. and allied airpower capabilities would be absolutely essential to defeating them quickly. As with Saddam Hussein’s invasion of Kuwait, both actions could be rendered militarily untenable if NATO or U.S. forces could rapidly win and exploit air superiority over the territory that had been invaded.

To prevent larger, far more costly wars between Western powers and either China or Russia, then, it will be vital to convince both adversaries that NATO forces in Europe and U.S.-led forces in the Pacific can rapidly establish and leverage air superiority should either power decide to attack. To do so, the United States will need to make the right investments and force decisions. Especially urgent priorities include restocking and improving U.S. air-launched munitions, ramping up production of missile interceptors to defend airbases and naval task forces, and accelerating the development of next generation fighter, bomber, and enabler aircraft.

Although establishing air superiority over an area contested by Chinese or Russian forces will be far more difficult than doing so over Iran, it is an essential task for the United States and its allies if they want to maintain conventional deterrence and avoid a major great-power conflict. Air superiority cannot win all wars. But if it can be credibly achieved, it all but guarantees deterrence by denial against state opponents considering territorial aggression of their own.

Why the Future of War Can’t Escape the Past

How the Search for Economic Security Will End in Geopolitical Calamity

Henry Farrell, Abraham Newman, and Yeling Tan

Dependence on America Has Left It With Little to Offer Would-Be Partners

#160. Pamela Voorhees has a point, and Peacock’s “Crystal Lake” proves it

I canât remember the last time a catch-up phone call with a confidante didnât include one of us marveling that we havenât caught an assault charge. If any law enforcement happens to be reading this, I want to make it clear that will never happen.

Well, letâs call it a non-zero chance. At the end of the day, I am a realist; anything can flip a personâs switch from off to blackout rage. However, I have decades of practice holding back my inner She-Hulk. So do most women.

Every day, we wake up in a nation controlled by a convicted felon accused of multiple sexual assaults, while a college student seeking justice after alleging she was gang-raped at a fraternity party is doxxed and swatted. We are not taken seriously in politics or at work. The manosphere has poisoned our water coolers and social media feeds.

Women have had it, including with each other. Aspiring tradwives and âLive, Laugh, Loveâ Karens selling out everyone else to keep up their manicures are legion. They threaten to run you down in crosswalks and refuse to bow out gracefully when told, for instance, that a pretty mechanical bird mounted on a boutiqueâs wall isnât for sale.

Ladies, look to your left. Now look to your right. One of you is dying to knife somebody. Only Pamela Voorhees, brought to life by Linda Cardellini in âCrystal Lake,â has the guts to act on that impulse. Her bloodlust coats her skin in the crappy opening scene of this âFriday the 13thâ prequel, after sheâs dispensed with two goons who make the fatal blunder of invading her home and taunting her. One goes down with a swift nick to the jugular. The other loses half his face to the Voorhees familyâs machete.

The thing is, by the time weâre assaulted by all that, we understand that Pamela has had it, too. She lost her gentle son, a boy born with hydrocephalus, a birth defect in the brain, who is endlessly bullied until he drowns at camp. The town moves from pitying her to whispering that sheâs crazy, leaving her rutted in the anger stage of the grieving process. As she chops away at the men who attack her, I found myself muttering, âYes. Get him. Again. Again!â

Donât confuse this for an endorsement. Please donât. âCrystal Lakeâ is a barely watchable gorefest, with a plot riddled with more seeping holes than Pamelaâs victims. (Of course, if youâre into that kind of thing, which I am not, I guess that counts as a recommendation.) What passes for story amounts to little more than a two-dimensional cartoon rendered in human-flesh puppetry, courtesy of actors capable of much better, Cardellini included.

Even so, itâs kind of great to watch one of TVâs most enjoyable performers massacre a gaggle of sex-crazed hippies, or knock an abusive parent into a deep fryer for stress relief.Â  Few of us can claim to have never daydreamed about, say, an anvil dropping from the clouds to erase some menace from our lives, whether itâs an entitled relative or an idiot comedian. Jason Voorheesâ mom simply prefers a hands-on approach.

I understand why the many chefs who mucked up the âCrystal Lakeâ cauldron, starting with Bryan Fuller, were compelled to fill in the blanks of Pamelaâs origin story. The beauty of the character, once her truth was revealed in the original 1980 movie, is her relative mystery. Who would suspect a frumpy matron in a humble sweater could wreak such unhinged havoc? Other women, thatâs who. Weâve always suppressed murderous desires. (See: âDateline,â âSnappedâ and rest of the Oxygen channelâs true crime lineup.) Only recently have we taken to saying that out loud.

Long before the medical and pharmaceutical industries made perimenopausal rage fashionable, Pamela Voorhees was a genre outlier, especially in a cultural climate that had already started retreating from a decade of legislative gains for womenâs rights.

Now, in this post-Roe v. Wade world of ours, feminine wrath must be mansplained to be taken seriously. While women have produced excellent recent examinations, including âFuriousâ and âEast of Eden,â the brutal truth is that the âFriday the 13thâ movies are IP recognizable to hockey-masked trick-or-treaters too young to watch them.

So it falls to âCrystal Lakeâ to tell most of us why the mother of slasher cinemaâs patron saint was driven to kill, kill and kill again in the first place. But it also helps us understand why a crumpled sock in the middle of the living room or dirty dishes on the kitchen counter makes the exhausted woman in your life crash out.

Letâs assume that if youâre reading this far, you already know the first movieâs big twist: the real killer wasnât Jason Voorhees, but his mad mama. If not, I mean, what gives? Did you see that picture of Cardellini and wonder what cool-as-a-cuke Lindsay Weir from âFreaks and Geeksâ has been up to? With regret, I present this as your answer.

But as any old-school porn hounds skilled in fast-forwarding through âthe plotâ will tell you, thereâs merit in skipping straight to the action â meaning, Pamela destroying fools with something more cutting than wit.

Maybe Fuller, the guy who classed up âHannibal,â could have done something brilliant with Pamela. But he exited the project early due to creative differences, leaving âIt: Welcome to Derryâ showrunner Brad Caleb Kane to expand the legend of a woman whose motives were fairly basic. I mean, if your kid died because two horny teen counselors shirked their lifeguard duties to bone in a shed, you might harbor a few homicidal compulsions too.

Alas, in these days of milking dormant franchises for every drop of ichor, a simple explanation isnât enough. Therefore â and this will either save you the trouble of enduring all eight episodes or spoil them â Pamela Voorhees is revealed to be a victim of a patriarchal industrial plot.

The former professional singer gets knocked up by her lover, Elias (Hamish Linklater), who works for a company called Bellflower. When she nearly miscarries, he convinces her to marry him and move to his companyâs sponsored enclave thatâs popping with pregnant women like her. Once sheâs settled in, her husband plies her with Bellflower-manufactured TV dinners and happy pills, occasionally shuttling her to the doctor to be pumped full of mystery muck. Truly a MAHA conspiracistâs nightmare.

Sometime later, Jason arrives and demonstrates a knack for reviving from naps the average human wouldnât wake up from. So father secretly subjects son to all manner of mad science, including massive radiation exposure. Once Pamela discovers this, she rescues Jason, turning the skull of the man who gets in her way into soup, and they escape to Crystal Lake.

Want more from culture than just the latest trend? The Swell highlights art made to last. Sign up here

Cardelliniâs Pamela Voorhees is what happens when women drinking from a bottomless well of contempt and human carelessness hit their limit. The writers, in their clumsy way, cater to that idea by having her dispose of her first slaughter by slathering the bodies in a deconstructed tonnato sauce of canned fish and honey, and standing by as a massive bear lumbers up to feast.

Before the animal takes a bite, it sizes up Pamela, sniffs her tears, and leaves her be. You could view this as one predator recognizing another. To women of a certain mood, though, it confirms what we already know: that a bear is preferable company to thoughtless, dangerous people. Plus, itâll help rid you of pesky evidence without asking questions, which only a true, understanding friend would do.

All episodes of âCrystal Lakeâ are streaming on Peacock.

#162. Reporter’s Notebook: Senate sneaks in one last political play before voters have their say

Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on Senate Democrats blocking data center legislation and a bill barring members from stock trading on ‘Special Report.’

In politics, you sometimes just do what you can.

All 100 duly chosen and sworn U.S. senators understood why the Senate met for a week at the end of September.

Yes there was the college sports bill. Yes there was the confirmation of Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling. Yes there was a big hearing with former special counsel Jack Smith.

But you’d be badly mistaken if you thought both sides were really there to hammer out a package to bring down the cost of living for Americans.

Don’t take my word for it. Take the word of the senators.

REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: A GUIDE TO THE COLLEGE SPORTS VOTE AND SENATE’S OHIO SHOWDOWN

Former Special Counsel Jack Smith testifies during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing in the Hart Senate Office Building on Sept. 29, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Getty Images)

You are correct to say that Democrats blocked two bills that Republicans say voters really want. One was a measure to diminish the costs consumers pay for data centers and a plan to restrict stock trades by lawmakers. The latter bill even included a voter ID requirement – crucial to the GOP and its base. But Republican senators knew that Democrats wouldn’t accept these proposals.

And Democratic senators wouldn’t accept any of the GOP’s legislative propositions, either.

So let’s start with the Ratepayer Protection Act.

Both sides know that voters are tripped out about AI and utterly losing it when it comes to data centers. An internal GOP memo in August revealed that the party was especially leery of what this meant for Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio Republican Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine appointed Husted to the Senate last year to succeed Vice President JD Vance. Husted helped foster development of data centers as an official back in the Buckeye State.

So, the final week of the Senate’s session before the midterms crawled with politics.

REPUBLICANS FEAR THEY ‘HAVEN’T DONE A DAMN THING’ TO LOWER PRICES AHEAD OF MIDTERM RECKONING

The U.S. Capitol building is seen on Aug. 7, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

Republicans aimed to curb skyrocketing utility costs associated with the construction of data centers.

"(People) ought to be guaranteed no electricity bills will go up by a cent because of a data center," said Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo. "It sends a clear message that these AI companies and these data centers can't just come into local communities and strip mine out (land). Raise the electricity rates. Kick people off the grid. Take their water."

But Democrats say the bill didn’t compel compliance by AI firms. This was just a suggestion that those who build the data centers help foot some of the bill.

"It is a sham. A charade because it has no enforcement," said Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.

"Everything in that bill can already be done by a state regulator. Or it can already be done by a data center developer. And the bill requires nothing of them," argued Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va.

I pressed Kaine on if "something was better than nothing."

"No. You shouldn't trick people. And this is not even something," replied Kaine. "It's nothing,"

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., piled on with, "The Ratepayer Protection Act is a fraud. It does not require any protections at all. While Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, Republicans are offering a toothless messaging bill."

The bill is laced with midterm politics. Democrats claim Republicans called the vote to throw a lifeline to Husted.

Many Senate Republicans were ready for the Senate to leave town for the midterms. But they hedged their bets around the data center bill. And, Husted.

"Can you say 110 precent this is not a vote to help Jon Husted in Ohio?" yours truly inquired of Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D.

"I think it will help him," replied Hoeven. Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., agreed with Hoeven.

"The one thing I'll just say is that this is clearly a political ploy," said Kim. "This is not something that's good for the American people. But it's certainly good for Sen. Husted."

DATA CENTERS COULD BE THE SLEEPER ISSUE OF THE 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS

Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, spoke to Fox News Digital about Republican efforts to keep Ohio red in a challenging political landscape. (Fox News Digital/Andrew Mark Miller)

The tilt between Husted and former Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio, is one of the nation’s most contentious Senate contests.

"I don't think that there's a secret that Sen. Husted is trying to pass a piece of legislation so he could go home and run a campaign ad," said Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M.

"We gave everybody a chance to do something about affordability and the Democrats blocked it. So we'll go campaign on it," said Husted.

So yes. The Senate’s last week of session was about the midterms.

"Has there ever been a late September or October before an election that wasn't all politics?" asked Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C.

The evolving positions on the data center bill by Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., may be an example of that.

Welch was a yea when asked about the legislation on September 23 , after it overwhelmingly cleared the House.

"I support it and I'd be glad to vote on it," said Welch.

But the Vermont Democrat flipped to nay when the issue approached a roll call vote on the floor.

"Well, two things. One, they won't allow us to have an amendment. And the problem with this bill is that it has no teeth," he replied.

So the question is whether the sides prefer action. Or, if they’d rather have the issue. In fact it could be argued that Husted may have scored some political capital, deploying the blocked bill as a foil in an effort to contrast himself to Democrats.

"It ought to be something that should be a no brainer here on the floor of the Senate," said Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D.

TRUMP’S DATA CENTER PUSH FRACTURES CONGRESS AS LOCAL ANGER EXPLODES: 'GRASPING AT STRAWS'

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks at a press conference with Senate Republican leaders following a policy luncheon at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on April 21, 2026. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)

It’s rare that competitive Senate contests pivot on a solitary issue. And certainly an individual debate or vote. Democratic Maine Senate nominee Troy Jackson is pushing Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, on her vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh in 2018. It was one of the most factious confirmation battles in history. But Collins won reelection in 2020. That vote was eight years ago.

A vote like the one on the data center measure just before the election can plant a seed in the mind of voters. And since Republicans were struggling on affordability – and then AI and data centers emerged as an issue – forcing this vote was probably the best political play the GOP had at its disposal. In campaigns, you do all you can.

Let’s say for a moment that Husted loses narrowly to Brown in two weeks. And maybe Republicans would have held the Senate had Husted prevailed. Perhaps exit polling reveals that voters wished Republicans had done more on affordability. Party insiders would then accuse the Senate GOP brass of political malpractice by denying Husted a chance to make his case.

It was the best Husted could do. And the best Senate Republicans could do.

It may not work. But at least Republicans can say they did what they could.

Chad Pergram currently serves as Chief Congressional Correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in September 2007 and is based out of Washington, D.C.

#163. Sending Syrian Soldiers to Yemen Would Be a Mistake

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Argument: Sending Syrian Soldiers to Yemen Would Be a Mistake

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

In June, U.S. President Donald Trump floated an extraordinary proposal to deal with Hezbollah: Syria should enter Lebanon and finish off the group. Few leaders had more reason to oblige than Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa. Hezbollah had spent years fighting alongside Bashar al-Assad’s forces. Even after Assad’s fall, the group continued to sow instability across Syria’s western border. Damascus had every reason to settle the score, and Sharaa still refused. He insisted that his government sought cooperation with Syria’s neighbor, not another war.

Four months later, Sharaa appears to be contemplating a foreign intervention, this time more than a thousand miles from home. Following Sharaa’s Oct. 6 meeting with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh, Axios and Reuters reported that the Saudis were seeking Syrian military assistance against the Houthis in Yemen, where Saudi-backed forces have been battling the group since early September. This reporting suggested that Sharaa, with U.S. approval, might be inclined to accept the Saudi request and deploy as many as 20,000 soldiers, including troops for offensive operations. Washington is said to have approved of the plan. Other sources have claimed that approximately 1,500 Syrian fighters have already arrived in Saudi Arabia and that Syrian drone operators are present in the southern coastal city of Aden.

In June, U.S. President Donald Trump floated an extraordinary proposal to deal with Hezbollah: Syria should enter Lebanon and finish off the group. Few leaders had more reason to oblige than Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa. Hezbollah had spent years fighting alongside Bashar al-Assad’s forces. Even after Assad’s fall, the group continued to sow instability across Syria’s western border. Damascus had every reason to settle the score, and Sharaa still refused. He insisted that his government sought cooperation with Syria’s neighbor, not another war.

Four months later, Sharaa appears to be contemplating a foreign intervention, this time more than a thousand miles from home. Following Sharaa’s Oct. 6 meeting with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh, Axios and Reuters reported that the Saudis were seeking Syrian military assistance against the Houthis in Yemen, where Saudi-backed forces have been battling the group since early September. This reporting suggested that Sharaa, with U.S. approval, might be inclined to accept the Saudi request and deploy as many as 20,000 soldiers, including troops for offensive operations. Washington is said to have approved of the plan. Other sources have claimed that approximately 1,500 Syrian fighters have already arrived in Saudi Arabia and that Syrian drone operators are present in the southern coastal city of Aden.

Syria’s fractured and under-equipped military is unlikely to change the course of the war in Yemen. Still, its participation could have profound consequences at home: exposing Damascus to retaliation by Iran and its regional allies, undermining the government’s promise to keep Syria out of foreign conflicts, and threatening the country’s economic recovery. Rising energy prices are already fueling domestic protests, while the country remains desperate for foreign investment. The irony is that the countries investing in Syria may now be pushing it into a war that could jeopardize its stability.

Damascus is susceptible to this kind of pressure because its recovery from more than a decade of civil war depends on the goodwill of its partners. Saudi Arabia has emerged as one of Syria’s most important political and financial backers, pledging billions of dollars in investment. Riyadh’s partners in the Mecca Pact also provide the support Damascus desperately needs. Turkey is helping to rebuild the Syrian military, while Pakistan has reportedly become a supplier of weapons to replenish an arsenal devastated by Israeli strikes after Assad’s fall in December 2024. These partnerships have helped Sharaa rebuild Syria’s regional standing, but they have also left Damascus increasingly dependent on these countries.

Since taking power, Sharaa’s foreign policy has focused on balancing regional powers. Syria is drawing closer to Saudi Arabia but continues to maintain a strong relationship with the United Arab Emirates. Syria is deepening military cooperation with Turkey while signaling to Israel that it wants a comprehensive peace agreement. Damascus’s logic is to court competing powers without committing to one camp. At the same time, it seeks to benefit from these relationships without becoming entangled in their rivalries.

But that flexibility is becoming harder to sustain as the countries financing Syria’s recovery and rebuilding its military begin to expect something in return. For Riyadh, a Syrian deployment to Yemen could serve as a test of how far Sharaa is willing to go in supporting Saudi security interests. After investing considerable political and economic capital in Syria, Riyadh now expects Damascus to show it’s aligned with Saudi regional security interests and willing to repay the support it has received.

There is also a military calculation for Saudi Arabia in having Syria join the fight in Yemen. Despite their superior weapons, resources, and manpower of around 300,000 fighters, the Saudi-backed forces have struggled to dislodge the Houthis from their strongholds or achieve decisive territorial gains. Syrian fighters, particularly the battle-hardened formations that spearheaded the offensive against Assad, may offer what the Saudi-backed forces have lacked.

But winning a war in Syria does not mean knowing how to fight one in Yemen. The fighters who toppled Assad were operating on familiar terrain against a demoralized army. In Yemen, they would confront a Houthi movement that has spent years fighting on its own territory and has entrenched itself in mountainous strongholds. Syrian forces have no comparable experience in Yemen, lack much of the heavy equipment needed for a sustained campaign, and would face an enemy with a decisive terrain advantage.

The first casualty of a Syrian intervention could be the foreign-policy restraint that Sharaa has championed since Assad’s fall. After years of civil war, the leadership promised its people that it would “remain outside any conflict.”

Assad’s defeat dealt Iran one of its greatest strategic setbacks; after spending $50 billion supporting the regime, Tehran lost its strategic foothold in Syria, and its vital weapons corridor to Hezbollah was compromised. Sharaa has since sought to keep Syria out of a direct conflict with Iran and its proxies in order to avoid a confrontation that could give them pretext to destabilize his country. Joining the Saudi-led campaign against the Houthis would likely place Syria back in Iran’s crosshairs.

In March, the Iraqi Resistance Coordination Committee, an umbrella grouping of Iran-backed militias, warned Sharaa that Syrian involvement against Iran’s allies would amount to “a declaration of war against the entire Axis of Resistance.” The group threatened to turn Syria into an “open battlefield.” In July, a former Iranian official went further, threatening that intervention against Hezbollah in Lebanon would invite Iranian missile and drone attacks against Syria.

As reports of a possible Syrian deployment in Yemen began circulating, those warnings became more direct. Former Iraqi Interior Minister Baqir al-Zubaidi, a former member of the Iran-aligned Badr Organization, threatened that if Sharaa deployed troops, Syria could face “devastating Houthi strikes” and attacks “from other fronts.” The Houthis have already begun preparing the narrative for their confrontation with the Syrians. A Houthi-aligned Yemeni outlet portrayed the possible arrival of Syrian soldiers as a tool to transform the conflict into an “existential sectarian confrontation.”

Syrian government troops fighting the Houthis—who follow Zaydism, a branch of Shiite Islam—would offer the movement an opportunity to recast the conflict over territory as a sectarian struggle against foreign Sunni extremists. The arrival of Syrian fighters could become a powerful recruiting and mobilization tool. Pro-Iranian axis accounts have already depicted Syria’s military as a mercenary force available to whichever foreign government is willing to pay, a charge with implications for Syria’s reputation across the region.

Already, the prospect of sending troops to Yemen has unsettled Syrians themselves. Some have undeniably welcomed the prospect of intervention, arguing that Syrians and Yemenis were fighting the same Iranian-backed forces that had devastated their countries. But many others, including those who have little sympathy for Iran or the Houthis, are concerned. “Syrian blood is … not for sale,” one Syrian commentator declared, calling the proposed deployment “unacceptable.” Another raised the specter of Iranian retaliation: “If we fight the Houthis and Iran responds by bombing us, who will stop it?” Or as yet another declared on X: “This is sheer stupidity to enter a war that is none of our concern.”

There is no available polling that directly captures Syrian attitudes toward a military intervention in Yemen. But existing surveys show that reluctance to fight another war extends beyond online spaces. An April poll found that 63 percent of respondents opposed Syrian military intervention in Lebanon. A February survey revealed that only 5 percent of Syrians favored a military response against Israeli incursions in southern Syria.

Trump has repeatedly pledged to give Syria a “chance at greatness,” remove all barriers to rebuilding Syria, lift all sanctions, and let foreign investment pour into the country, betting that economic recovery will create the stability needed to transform Syria into a dependable partner. Yet Washington is now appearing to jeopardize that progress for the prospect of a few thousand soldiers fighting the Houthis. U.S. officials may see the Syrian deployment as a chance to strengthen the Saudi-led campaign without committing U.S. forces. But the military benefits of Syrian participation are uncertain, and the costs of a regional confrontation and instability could undo one of Washington’s most significant achievements in Syria.

The same applies to Saudi Arabia. Riyadh has pledged billions of dollars toward Syria’s reconstruction, betting that the country’s recovery will create new economic opportunities. Yet these investments will only return if stability holds.

This is a true foreign-policy test for Sharaa; his decision will ultimately define what kind of regional partner he wants Syria to become. He has worked to convince foreign governments that Syria is a country worth investing in, but that will be harder if he begins sending troops into wars far beyond its borders.

Ahmad Sharawi is a research analyst at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, focusing on Middle East affairs and the Levant.
