#177. Iran’s Theory of Victory

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

NARGES BAJOGHLI is an anthropologist and Associate Professor of Middle East Studies at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies. She is the author of Iran Reframed: Anxieties of Power in the Islamic Republic.

VALI NASR is Majid Khadduri Professor of International Affairs and Middle East Studies at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies and the author of Iran’s Grand Strategy: A Political History.

Tehran’s Fight for Great-Power Status in the Post-American Middle East

When it comes to Iran, the Trump administration has a decidedly dismal record. It failed to wear down the Islamic Republic with months of intense bombings. It could not bend Iran’s will at the negotiating table. Yet despite seven months of setbacks, U.S. officials believe that they have turned the page. They have implemented fresh sanctions while maintaining the existing American blockade of the country’s southern coast, throttling its access to outside commerce. As a result, they have concluded that the Islamic Republic will soon either concede or be downed. “We are going to economically asphyxiate this regime,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent declared on September 1.

There is no doubt that Washington has dealt significant damage to Iran. But the Islamic Republic does not believe it is unraveling. In fact, Tehran thinks that it will defeat the United States—and it isn’t hard to see why. The Iranian government did not merely survive the U.S.-Israeli bombardment. It retaliated ferociously, damaging American military bases and obstructing the Strait of Hormuz. Its people are paying a hefty economic price thanks to damage caused by the war and Washington’s cutoffs, but much of the population has rallied around the flag and seems to accept that hardship is necessary if Iran is to defend itself. As a result, Tehran has been emboldened. Its officials may not see eye to eye on each tactic. But they share the same ambitions: evicting U.S. forces from the Persian Gulf, forcing Washington to remove all its sanctions, and getting the United States to accept that Iran is a great power.

This agenda might sound overly audacious, given that Iran has been materially weakened. But the Islamic Republic thinks its aims are within reach. It believes its military can drive U.S. troops from the Persian Gulf by continuing to strike American bases directly and by getting Arab countries to push the United States to leave. It thinks that by wreaking havoc on energy markets, it can force Washington to lift economic restrictions, as well. Tehran’s theory of victory, in other words, is that it can hold out and inflict enough pain that the United States will end its containment of Iran.

No one doubts that Iran has been battered by war. Months of American and Israeli bombs have damaged the country’s industries and infrastructure, spiking unemployment and pushing more Iranians into poverty. Washington’s sanctions and naval blockade have caused rampant inflation. And the American and Israeli militaries can count many tactical successes, including the assassination of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.

But strategically, the conflict has been disastrous. U.S. officials believed that punishing aerial bombardments and sweeping efforts to degrade the Iranian economy would bring the Islamic Republic to its knees. They didn’t. Washington hoped that assassinating Khamenei would prompt a mass antigovernment uprising. That scheme also failed. Instead, Khamenei’s death brought out the Islamic Republic’s ardent supporters. They marched every night in the country’s main cities and were eventually joined by Iranians of other political hues, who rallied in support of their homeland. When the war started, Turkey planned to accommodate 70,000 Iranian refugees. But few people fled. In fact, as the war progressed, many Iranians living abroad returned home, including long-exiled cultural figures, journalists, and politicians, such as the singers Mohsen Namjoo and Bijan Mortazavi.

This surge in nationalism is not an endorsement of the Islamic Republic. Many Iranians remain deeply unhappy with the country’s leadership. But the anger at their government has been subsumed by their anger at Washington. Previously, most Iranians were skeptical of the Islamic Republic’s claim that the United States was bent on their country’s destruction and in fact hoped Tehran would seek better relations with Washington. But the bombings of Iranian cities and U.S. President Donald Trump’s repeated threats to annihilate the country’s civilization (saying, for example, that he might “blow the entire nation up” and drive it “into hell with no chance of survival”) have changed attitudes. Iranians across the political spectrum now do think that the United States wants to obliterate their country—or at least make it capitulate to every American demand.

This conclusion was apparent in our lengthy conversations with Iranians of all ideologies, which we started conducting when Washington first bombed Iran, in June 2025, and have continued to the present, tracing their political attitudes over that period. The vast majority expressed deep distress and anger at their government after the massacres that took place in response to January’s mass protests. But we found that political opinions have shifted drastically as the war has dragged on and as Trump has upped his annihilatory rhetoric. “We believed so much in the American promise,” Ali, a 45-year-old long-time dissident who has spent years in prison for his activism on social and political issues, told us. “Yet with this war and everything that Trump and his administration have said and done, it’s obvious the Americans sold us a false bill of goods. They want nothing but Iran’s total submission, and that’s not acceptable to us.” Mahsa, a writer and artist in her 30s, relayed similar sentiments. “Everything we believed the [United States] stood for, freedom and respect and democracy, I now see as lies,” she said. “As angry as I’ve been at our state over the years, this is our homeland, and no outside country has the right to kill our leaders and drop bombs on our children and attempt to destroy us.”

Little wonder, then, that Khamenei’s July funeral procession drew millions of mourners, even though the country was in the midst of conflict. At the event, people handed out red flags, symbolizing their desire for bloody vengeance. Shortly after, Iran attacked commercial vessels crossing the Strait of Hormuz, unraveling the precarious cease-fire the country had struck with the United States three months earlier.

Many U.S. officials seem to think that stiff economic pressure will ultimately prompt a shift in opinion—that if they suffer enough, Iranians will decide to try overthrowing their government or that the Islamic Republic, fearing for its survival, will submit to American demands. But this is magical thinking. Iran has spent the past 15 years developing an economy specifically designed to withstand American economic warfare. Iranian officials, for instance, have forged strong relations with neighboring traders and made the country nearly self-sufficient when it comes to food. As a result, even though Iran’s economy is hurting and inflation is high, cities and towns have had no shortages of important goods or services to date. “It’s incredible how well-run everything has been inside of the country,” Hamid Reza, an engineer who regularly travels between Isfahan and Tehran for work, said. “Things are expensive, but there have been no shortages whatsoever across the country. Everything has been managed internally with a lot of care.”

That is not to say that Iranians feel optimistic about their country. They are anxious about the future, and they yearn for a return to calm and economic relief. But they do not see the U.S.-Israeli war as liberating. Instead, they see it as gratuitous aggression, and the resulting nationalism has blurred the lines between political factions and diminished the likelihood of another political uprising. The war, then, has strengthened the Islamic Republic.

Much like its population, the Iranian government has adopted a more hostile view of Washington since the conflict began. The country’s new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, has moved trusted lieutenants to key roles (even as he himself remains in hiding), and they are largely hard-line figures tied to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. These people, including Mohsen Rezaei, the national security adviser, and Hossein Taeb, the commander of Iran’s main domestic paramilitary forces, think deterring further attacks requires a decisive, aggressive response to any provocations. They are skeptical that Washington is serious about diplomacy. They point out that the United States has twice attacked Iran amid negotiations and then walked away from the memorandum of understanding it signed with Iran in June—and thus argue that it cannot be trusted. In fact, they believe that if the United States shows interest in talks, it might even be planning for renewed attacks, as it was in June 2025 and February 2026.

Iran’s relative moderates feel somewhat differently. These elites, which include Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Speaker of Parliament Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, former President Hasan Rouhani, and former Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, have consistently argued that Tehran should keep looking for a diplomatic solution to the conflict. Pezeshkian and Ghalibaf have highlighted the economic hardships facing ordinary people. But the distance between them and the country’s hard-line leaders is not as great as it might seem. As one analyst familiar with these figures told us, “No one is saying Iran should surrender.” They may see economic relief as a top priority, yet their solution is to force the United States to implement the memorandum of understanding it signed in June. That deal, in Iran’s view, committed Washington to unfreezing all of Iran’s assets, lifting all sanctions, never striking the country again, and paying reparations in exchange for nothing more than a cease-fire and renewed commerce through the Strait of Hormuz (on which Iran could still charge fees). Since the end of summer, Rezaei and Ghalibaf have declared that diplomacy must start with the United States returning to the memorandum. As the same analyst told us after recent UN meetings in New York, these figures think that “Trump is not ready” for real talks. Instead, they believe that Trump will return to this deal only if he comes to terms with Iran’s victory, and that means increasing the war’s costs for the United States.

Iran’s behavior will therefore be unrestrained and disproportionate. If the war resumes, it will attack across the whole region, not just in the country’s immediate vicinity. The dominant view in Tehran is that prudence and predictability will only invite greater U.S. pressure and will do nothing to advance its main military goals: making Washington pull all its troops from the Persian Gulf and accept Iran’s primacy. Iran’s repeated attacks on American military bases and facilities in Jordan, Syria, and across the Persian Gulf are already aimed at this objective. To an extent, they have succeeded. The strikes have seriously damaged several U.S. assets, forcing the United States to move many of its operations and military resources to Israel and Jordan and rely on a base in the central Indian Ocean for logistical support. The threat of Iranian attacks has even pushed Washington to withdraw all its B-1 bombers from a base in the United Kingdom.

Tehran is simultaneously trying to get Washington’s Gulf partners to close U.S. military bases in their countries. To do so, it has openly declared that peace and security in the Persian Gulf will depend on pushing out the American military and has repeatedly bombed Gulf states it suspects of aiding the U.S. war effort. Iran is ultimately unlikely to end the United States’ military presence in the Gulf region. But it has done enough to make Arab states think twice about relying on the American security umbrella, which could mean a smaller U.S. military footprint in the region.

Iran, of course, could force the American military out of its neighborhood without obtaining economic relief. In fact, the Trump administration announced “economic D-Day” in part because the military was fatigued and because Iranian attacks on the U.S. Navy have forced Washington’s ships farther away from Iranian shores. But Iran believes it can coerce its adversary into some kind of economic understanding by causing sufficient financial suffering. To that end, Tehran has worked to drive up the price of oil, gas, diesel, jet fuel, and other oil derivatives by attacking several energy facilities in the Gulf region, including Qatar’s Ras Laffan gas field (in retaliation for an Israeli attack on Iran’s South Pars gas field) and oil facilities in the United Arab Emirates’ Fujairah port. Iran is also striking tankers ferrying oil and natural gas. And it is trying to consolidate its control over the Strait of Hormuz, which it sees as sovereign Iranian territory. Washington has fought back hard against this effort, and has recently succeeded at helping tankers pass through the chokepoint. But these operations have required enormous naval resources, and the United States cannot sustain them forever.

Iran’s regional partners are also lending it a hand. Iranian-backed Iraqi forces have attacked a vital oil pipeline carrying Saudi Arabia’s oil to facilities on the Red Sea, which will markedly reduce global oil supplies for months. Its Houthi allies in Yemen have also consistently attacked Saudi oil facilities. The Houthis have even captured vast new territory and reached the Bab el Mandeb Strait, helping them menace the Red Sea—through which 12 percent of world trade passes. These attacks also showed that, although Iran’s network may be battered in Lebanon and Syria, it remains quite capable overall.

The United States may think that it has cornered Iran. But Tehran disagrees. It does not see itself as on its heels or out of options. Instead, it believes that it has won great-power status. It is proud of its military performance and feels as if it commands newfound international respect. Officials in Tehran cheered images of Iran’s delegation being enthusiastically received by member states at the September meetings of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and the non-Western BRICS consortium.

Iran is still facing monumental challenges, and it has not found a way to turn what it has won in the war into enduring, peacetime gains. But it is ready to fight on, if and when it needs to. The government believes, as one Iranian senior analyst close to the country’s policymakers put it, that the Iranian people “are willing to endure economic pain and the suffering, if it means that [they] are going to win.” And its elites have coalesced around a shared strategy. Tehran, in other words, is confident that it can prevail by staying the course. No compromises are necessary.

#180. I miss the restaurant pager

At 16, I was entrusted with one of the most important pieces of technology at a suburban Chiliâs: a wire rack full of restaurant pagers.

The restaurant occupied a sprawling shopping center alongside an Olive Garden, a Cabelaâs and a Costco, making it something of a regional mecca for homecoming dinners, birthday parties and Little League victories. The air smelled perpetually of tortilla chips, and the soundtrack was an agreeable mixture of Matchbox Twenty and sizzling fajita platters.

I liked the job. I liked asking people what brought them in, hearing about their celebrations and making small talk while consulting my restaurant map and section list. On busy nights, Iâd estimate the wait, scribble down a last name, party size and pager number in black pen, then hand over a pleasantly hefty plastic puck.

âYou can wander as far as your car,â Iâd explain.

âOpe! Was hoping to make a Costco run,â some dad would inevitably reply. I laughed every time. It was a very reliable joke.

Every five or 15 minutes, another pager returned to the host stand, blinking and vibrating in the hands of a customer whose table was finally ready. I particularly liked watching one go off. A group could be deep in conversation when the puck sprang to life, producing a brief, collective flicker of delight. Dinner!

They were not beautiful objects. One woman who came in weekly after church complained that hers was ugly and bulky, then set it on the red pleather waiting bench so that it would vibrate against the upholstery rather than any part of her body. Occasionally, someone stole one, apparently deciding that a restaurant pager belonged in the same category of souvenir as a pebbled Coke glass. Sometimes the rechargeable batteries flagged, and weâd pull a pager out of rotation.

There was a reason these contraptions belonged to the Chiliâs end of the dining spectrum. You wouldnât mistake one for fine-dining theater. But they had an appealingly limited set of ambitions. They buzzed, they blinked, and when the wait was over, we took them back. The technology stayed at the restaurant.

I donât remember exactly when the pagers mostly disappeared. There was no retirement ceremony, no last call for the little plastic puck. I began noticing their absence most acutely when restaurants reopened after the first wave of the pandemic. Minimizing shared surfaces made sense then. Why distribute and disinfect pagers when customers already had phones in their pockets? Digital waitlists predated COVID-19, of course, but for me, that was when the phone began to feel less like an option and more like a condition of dining out.

And it rarely stops at the host stand. Your phone tells you the table is ready. It may supply the menu via QR code, take your order and settle the bill. Hours later, another text arrives asking you to rate the experience.

At some point, the meal has ended, but the restaurant apparently hasnât finished with you.

None of this is inherently awful. Some of it is useful. But every time I wake my phone to perform one of these little tasks, Iâm also opening the door to everything else it contains: emails, notifications, messages I wasnât planning to answer over lunch. What was supposed to simplify dinner can turn it into another administrative process requiring a charged device and a willingness to look at it.

Restaurants are hardly alone in this. I reach for my phone to ride public transit, pay for parking, produce concert tickets, check in at the doctorâs office and occasionally prove to one website that I am the person trying to sign into another. Each request arrives dressed as a convenience. Together, they have made the phone feel less like a personal possession and more like mandatory civic infrastructure.

Want more great food writing and recipes? Sign up for Salonâs free food newsletter, The Bite.

And mandatory infrastructure really ought to work.

For a while, I happily used the Ventra card on my phone to ride Chicago public transit. One less thing to carry! Then, for a miserable stretch, several Red Line stations I frequented seemed to stop recognizing it. One morning, I joined a small congregation of commuters attempting to convince the turnstiles that our phones were, in fact, perfectly legitimate fare payment.

âIt worked yesterday!â one man exclaimed.

âThe terminals are old! They werenât meant for this,â a tired CTA employee explained, kindly ushering us through the stroller entrance as the next train rumbled toward the platform.

The backup plan wasnât faring much better. Around the same time, the ticket machines were proving similarly unreliable about accepting credit cards. A little queue had formed at the station ATM, where commuters were withdrawing cash to buy physical transit cards so they could get on the train.

We had arrived at the future, and it required a trip to the cash machine.

After a few weeks of this, I surrendered. I now carry a physical Ventra card, load $20 onto it when necessary and go about my business. It gets me through the turnstile without involving my phone. A modest pleasure, but one Iâve come to appreciate.

The trouble isnât that every digital convenience is destined to malfunction. Plenty work exactly as advertised. Itâs that weâve become so accustomed to conducting ordinary life through our phones that we rarely stop to consider whether theyâre necessary to the transaction in the first place.

Consider, for instance, a recent brunch in which absolutely nothing went wrong.

Recently, my husband and I went to a brunch spot I love in Chicagoâs Andersonville neighborhood. The front-of-house staff always seem to be navigating the aftermath of a complicated breakup between two polycules, but the breakfast sandwich Â is truly good enough to make the interpersonal intrigue part of the charm. I wanted to do very little beyond sit somewhere pleasant, eat something delicious and enjoy being newly married. There was a short wait. The host asked for my number; I provided it, then sat with my husband in two lobby chairs. We chatted. We waited. We did not move.

I looked up. The host stand was approximately two feet away.

The system had worked flawlessly. Somewhere, a piece of restaurant software had facilitated communication between two people who could reasonably have passed each other a saltshaker. The host hadnât done anything wrong, and neither had I. But a moment that might once have involved someone looking up and saying, âYouâre all set,â now required me to be reachable by a device I had no particular desire to consult.

I understand the alternative. A digital waitlist lets you wander around the neighborhood, browse the shops, maybe get a head start on another errand. Sometimes thatâs a genuine gift. But Iâm not convinced that being able to do two things at once means enjoying either one more. And sometimes I donât want to wander. I want to be there, waiting for brunch, with the reassuring knowledge that the restaurant is handling the details.

Thatâs part of the pleasure of hospitality, isnât it? For a little while, someone else tends to the logistics. You donât need to manage every notification or keep every system running. You can just be a guest.

I donât expect restaurant owners to read this and order a fresh shipment of vibrating pucks. If texts work best, fine. Iâd simply like us to question whether requiring a phone is always an improvement, and remember that convenience isnât much of a convenience when opting out stops being possible.

Maybe the pager never comes back. I can live with that. Iâd just like to be able to let my phone die in my bag and still be called to breakfast.

Though I will say this for those ugly little pagers: At least you could hand one back.

#185. The GOP candidates walking back some of their abortion stances

This story was originally published by The 19th.

This story was originally reported by Shefali Luthra of The 19th. Meet Shefali and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.

Republicans running for governor across the country are backing away from abortion bans they once endorsed.

U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican candidate for governor in Wisconsin, calls his state’s 20-week abortion limit “settled law.” Just three years ago, he co-sponsored a bill that would have banned abortion six weeks into pregnancy.

Stacy Garrity, the GOP’s candidate in Pennsylvania, has said during her campaign that she would “respect” the state’s current law, which allows abortion until 24 weeks of pregnancy. Four years ago, she called on abortion opponents “to engage and make a difference” in state laws after the fall of Roe v. Wade.

In Kansas, where abortion is legal until 22 weeks, Republican Ty Masterson has demurred when asked if, as governor, he would support a statewide referendum to eliminate the Kansas constitution’s abortion protections. Masterson had previously spoken at protests in opposition to reproductive rights and won the backing of state and national anti-abortion groups.

The candidates’ retreat suggests that, even as reproductive rights fade from the national spotlight and polls show voters are far more likely to prioritize cost-of-living concerns, the political ramifications of pushing for new abortion restrictions remain substantial. The rhetorical distancing also moves political conversations away from an issue that overwhelmingly energizes Democrats.

“That might be their strategy there, to try to demotivate Democratic turnout in the state to take abortion off the table as a voting issue,” said Ashley Kirzinger, a pollster at KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research, polling and journalism organization. That’s especially true in tighter races such as those in Wisconsin and Kansas, she said.

Tiffany’s, Garrity’s and Masterson’s campaigns did not reply to requests for comment. The 19th contacted multiple Republican-aligned pollsters who also did not immediately respond.

Start your day with essential news from Salon. Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

About 60 percent of Americans believe that abortion should be legal in most or all cases, including about two-thirds of independents, according to a poll from The 19th and YouGov.

That said, pushing for abortion restrictions has never been broadly popular. Even before Roe v. Wade was overturned in 2022, Republicans seeking general election typically would not campaign overtly on abortion bans, said Molly Murphy, a pollster and president of Impact Research, a Democratically-aligned polling firm.

“It would get discussed in donor meeting hot mics, endorsement questionnaires, etc, but candidates wouldn’t run on the fact that they’d ban abortion,” she wrote in an email.

Voters largely don’t consider abortion to be “settled law,” said Celinda Lake, a longtime Democratic pollster, noting that the share of voters opposing abortion bans has increased since the fall of Roe. “They feel like, ‘Wait a minute, it can be taken away again.’”

In some races, Democrats and their allies are trying to push abortion rights back under the microscope — a strategy geared toward energizing liberal voters, Kirzinger said.

Wisconsin’s Democratic nominee for governor, David Crowley, has said that, if elected, he would work with the state legislature to enshrine abortion rights into the state constitution — though it’s not clear how expansive that protection would be or whether it might supplant the state’s 20-week cutoff.

Pine Tree State Prosperity, a political action committee associated with the national Democratic Governors Association, is running advertising in Maine that highlights anti-abortion remarks made by Bobby Charles, the state’s Republican pick for governor. The Democratic nominee, Hannah Pingree, has led by double digits in recent polls. Charles’ campaign did not reply to a request for comment.

Planned Parenthood’s super PAC, called Planned Parenthood Votes, has focused its resources in states such as Michigan, where the Republican candidate, U.S. Rep. John James, has said that abortion is “decided.” Four years ago, James said he opposed abortion in all cases, and he has compared the practice to genocide. His campaign did not reply to a request for comment.

James’ running mate, Jay DeBoyer, recently suggested leveraging a state constitutional convention to enact a 12-week abortion ban in Michigan, according to recordings of the remarks reported by The Detroit News and Michigan Advance. DeBoyer has since said publicly that abortion is a “settled” issue in Michigan, where voters in 2022 amended the state constitution to protect abortion before fetal viability.

Some gubernatorial candidates are still pushing for abortion restrictions, albeit far less ambitious ones.

In New Mexico, where Democrats are expected to keep control of the governor’s mansion and already control both legislative chambers, Republican candidate Gregg Hull said he was “fully committed” to working with Texas Gov. Greg Abbott to reduce the number of Texans coming to the neighboring state for abortions.

Hull has repeatedly called himself “pro-life” but also said that he would not change the state’s abortion law, which imposes no time limits on the procedure, without legislative support. His campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

Abortion opponents are trying to revive the issue in a handful of states. SBA Pro-Life America, one of the nation’s leading anti-abortion groups, is pushing ads that characterize Democratic candidates for governor as well as the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives as extreme on the issue, including in Ohio, Wisconsin and Michigan.

But generally, voters are less likely to trust conservatives on abortion, Lake said. And talking about abortion, she added, is more likely to generate enthusiasm among key Democratic voting blocs, particularly young women and college-educated women, who typically support reproductive rights.

“We have in our research people who say, ‘I used to be pro-life, I didn’t support abortion, I would never get one, but I think this is a decision that needs to be made by a woman and her doctor,’” Lake said. “People now feel this is just way too dangerous. This has gone way too far.”

#187. Ukraine Resumes Strikes on Russian Oil Refineries

Understanding the conflict four years on.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Ukraine defying U.S. President Donald Trump’s demand for an energy cease-fire, calls for Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign, and a new border crossing between China and North Korea.

Despite the White House repeatedly urging Kyiv not to target Moscow’s energy infrastructure, Ukrainian forces resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries on Thursday. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told the Financial Times on Thursday.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Ukraine defying U.S. President Donald Trump’s demand for an energy cease-fire, calls for Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign, and a new border crossing between China and North Korea.

Despite the White House repeatedly urging Kyiv not to target Moscow’s energy infrastructure, Ukrainian forces resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries on Thursday. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told the Financial Times on Thursday.

U.S. President Donald Trump has faced growing pressure to tackle rising fuel prices inflamed by the wars in Ukraine and Iran ahead of next month’s U.S. midterm elections. In a bid to bring down energy costs, Trump had urged Zelensky to halt all strikes on Russian oil refineries, and on Friday, he suspended U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel exports.

Then, on Sunday, Trump unilaterally declared an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine while also calling for Zelensky’s removal. Ukraine agreed to the truce and suspended such strikes for three days. However, during those three days, Russian forces launched dozens of ballistic missiles at critical Ukrainian energy infrastructure, plunging around 600,000 people in Kyiv into darkness on Wednesday.

According to Zelensky, the decision to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries was made in response to several controversial decisions out of Washington. They include U.S. military officials reportedly threatening to withhold intelligence if Ukraine continues to hit Russian energy targets, new restrictions on Ukraine’s Starlink access (which SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has accused the Trump administration of orchestrating), the White House’s apparent eagerness to ink business deals with Moscow, and Trump’s repeated admiration of Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“Putin is an enemy for us, and he’s the real evil of today. Absolutely,” Zelensky told the Financial Times. “How can Trump be friends with him?”

Some experts suggest that by bucking Trump’s demands, Zelensky risks widening the rift between them. Trump has long had a rocky relationship with Zelensky, going so far as to berate him during a White House summit in February 2025 and repeatedly parroting Kremlin talking points that question the Ukrainian president’s legitimacy.

Despite the risks, many of Ukraine’s European allies have backed Zelensky’s decision. “The faster all the Russian refineries and ability to sell energy will be blown to smithereens, the better, because Russia is funding the war with that,” Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said.

Rama stands firm. Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama defied calls to step down on Thursday amid sweeping student-led protests demanding his resignation. “My responsibility ‌is to listen, address ‌legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward,” Rama told Reuters. “The alternative would be a betrayal ‌of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on European Union membership.”

Youth-led demonstrations in Albania, dubbed the Flamingo movement, have accused Rama’s government of widespread corruption, specifically concerning the controversial development of a luxury resort linked to Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner. In recent months, protesters have also adopted calls for education reform, citing limited job prospects for recent graduates, high tuition fees, and poor conditions in university building.

As rallies in the capital this week took a violent turn—with protesters attacking government buildings, banks, and businesses—Rama has doubled down on his mandate, insisting that his administration is best poised to bring Albania into the European Union’s fold. “Corruption must be ⁠confronted and, as the EU itself has recently reaffirmed, Albania is ​tackling it as ​never before,” Rama said. The EU’s delegation in Tirana, meanwhile, called on demonstrators to “exercise restraint and to refrain from any acts of violence.”

New border crossing. China and North Korea unveiled the largest border crossing between their two countries on Thursday in a sign of ongoing efforts to bolster bilateral trade. The four-lane New Yalu River Bridge spans nearly 2 miles and connects the Chinese city of Dandong to the North Korean city of Sinuiju. Its opening comes barely a month after Pyongyang opened a similar but smaller pass across the Tumen River into Russia.

Construction of the New Yalu River Bridge was delayed for more than a decade. However, the project was accelerated after North Korea opened the bridge to Russia. Analysts believe that the move may have made Chinese officials uneasy as North Korean leader Kim Jong Un draws closer to Moscow; China has long been North Korea’s biggest trading partner.

Pyongyang, though, remains dedicated to countering international sanctions by fostering closer trade ties with both Beijing and Moscow. Experts believe that the bridges into China and Russia could be used to deliver fuel imports into North Korea as well as circumvent prohibitions on North Korean coal and labor exports.

More time off. Brazil’s Senate approved a constitutional amendment on Wednesday that will shorten the workweek from 44 hours to a maximum of 40 hours. Affecting some 37 million workers, the legislation is the country’s biggest labor rights overhaul in decades, and it delivers a major political win to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva less than two weeks before he faces far-right Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro in a presidential runoff.

“Those who build Brazil every day also deserve time to live,” Lula wrote on X on Thursday.

Bolsonaro, the son of imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro, had initially opposed the legislation, arguing that it was designed to improve Lula’s presidential bid; however, he ultimately reversed course after it became clear that public opinion overwhelmingly favored the bill. Only one senator rejected the legislation: former Vice President Hamilton Mourão, who served under the older Bolsonaro.

Lula is expected to sign the legislation into law next week, giving businesses 14 months to comply with the new mandate. Among Lula’s other recent reforms, he has announced new fuel tax cuts, extended existing subsidies designed to lower energy costs, vowed to pardon the debts of more than 3.6 million small businesses, and boosted welfare payments for university students.

From Charles Dickens to Madonna to King Edward VII, London’s oldest restaurant has long catered to a diverse clientele. This week, the building’s owner, J-P Mayhew, made the decision to ensure that tradition carries on long into the future. Mayhew donated 34-35 Maiden Lane in Covent Garden to the United Kingdom’s National Trust on Wednesday in an effort to safeguard “its bricks and mortar, its famous interior, and its invisible atmosphere.” Along with the building itself, which hosts the historic Rules restaurant, established in 1798, the donation also includes menus, visitor books, photographs, and other memorabilia.

#191. After that disastrous debut, Katie Zacharia is already history

This article has been updated to include breaking news.

Donald Trump’s new White House “pep secretary,” Katie Zacharia, introduced herself to America in the Brady Briefing Room this week, to anticipated criticism from Democrats and some unexpected criticism from Republicans.

At first, the press pool acted like that was just business as usual. It didn’t last long. As of Friday afternoon, multiple news reports indicate that Trump has already seen enough, and has asked Zacharia to step down from her role at the White House after just five days on the job.

According to a post on X by reporter Aaron Rupar, Trump told the press corps he had said to Zacharia that “she was treated very, very unfairly by the news. Let’s call it the fake news. I said, ‘Katie, do you need this? I don’t think you need this.’ We’re talking about doing something. I want her to have a good life. She’s being brutalized by the media.”

In all likelihood, that will end one of the shortest tenures of any Trump White House official, only about half the length of the notorious Anthony Scaramucci during Trump’s first term.

Maybe Zacharia was just unlucky. After all, she made her debut on Oct. 13. She showed up 15 minutes late. She spent the next eight minutes telling us how great Trump was. She took questions from just three people. She was gone 15 minutes later. In her praise of Trump, Zacharia sounded like former press secretary Sean Spicer talking about Trump’s inaugural crowds nearly a decade ago as she made dubious claims about the number of attendees at the president’s recent campaign rallies in high school gymnasiums and small arenas.

“Attendance is at record highs as enthusiastic, hard-working Americans are lining up and packing arenas to support President Trump,” she said with a straight face. Yep. The lies have already begun. Don’t act surprised.

When she finally took questions, only Breitbart (which lavished her with praise for allowing them in the building), Fox News and the Daily Mail got to ask questions. She dropped one legitimate piece of news: The president had asked for Kimberly Guilfoyle’s resignation as U.S. ambassador to Greece, based on her evident corruption and widely reported misbehavior, which even Trump didn’t try to defend. The punchline to that incident came a short time later as Trump was departing the White House, when he barely acknowledged Guilfoyle’s existence: Kimberly? Kimberly who?

A handful of defenders noted that the new press secretary had only a day to get ready for her debut. “Katie Zacharia had less than 24 hours to prepare for her inaugural briefing, as she juggled a cross-country move, and only received briefing materials this morning,” the Wall Street Journal reported. OK, so who forced her to go on stage, and why?

She could have taken all the time she needed. It’s not like we were getting press briefings every day anyway, and Trump always says he’s his own best press secretary. So there was no pressure from the press, although more reporters than usual showed up to be part of Zacharia’s inaugural standup routine.

Zacharia didn’t take the time to get to know us, and as a result we once again got a low-grade sideshow at the White House. Don’t expect anything more, and don’t expect the press to push back.

I’ve worked with incoming press secretaries at all levels, from City Hall to the White House. The best of them took the time to study policy briefings, meet department heads and the most active beat reporters before holding their first briefing. By doing that, they avoided being criticized for a lack of preparation and having to look for names on an index card. They also got a feel for the issues and questions they needed to address. Getting to know someone is the key to any long-term relationship, whether professional or personal.

That sort of protocol has long since been forgotten and abandoned, at least at the White House. Today we can’t get into the upper press area of the West Wing to talk with the press secretary. She didn’t take the time to get to know us, and as a result we once again got a low-grade sideshow. Don’t expect anything more, and don’t expect the press to push back. The White House Correspondents’ Association is in “go along to get along” mode. It’s cringeworthy to watch and heartbreaking to endure.

There was no reason to expect much of Zacharia’s first staged appearance, and that’s why no one should be surprised to see her draw as much criticism for her attire and demeanor as for the content of the information she provided. She appeared nervous, at one point calling her husband “my president.” She giggled at herself for that: “That’s a good one.”  That was self-deprecating, which I appreciate. As for her attire, it was professional, but not something I would wear. As for being nervous, that’s to be expected. But again, why did she feel the need to brief us on her first day in the office?

She called on Trump-friendly media exclusively, and then excused herself, saying she had to travel to Alaska with the president, who’s hoping to shore up support for incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, one of many struggling Republicans this fall.

Mind you, if Zacharia had arrived on time, she could have doubled her time with us. Why start late and then cut it short? If she knew she was going to leave with Trump, there was no reason to soil her laundry doing a shortened briefing. Either show up on time or do it upon your return, after you get settled. Nobody would have said anything about that — and nobody would care if they did. That might have given the president another excuse to belittle the press.

I know some Republican lawmakers and even some reporters who believe that Trump set up Zacharia for failure by ordering her first appearance. That certainly isn’t beyond Trump. He’s the best when it comes to lowering expectations.

Those expectations at the moment are so low as to defy measurement.

Just this week Trump has announced his pleasure with a DHS investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar’s immigration papers, a deal to import diesel fuel from Russia, and possible new air strikes on Iran, while Vice President JD Vance made a weird homophobic joke about Texas Senate candidate James Talarico and Speaker Mike Johnson claimed to have no idea why gas prices are spiking. Meanwhile, Trump blamed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for not ending a war that began with Russia’s invasion of his country.

Of course, none of these issues were brought up in the new pep secretary’s very short briefing, the strangest of those issues being the bizarre deal made with Russia. In an attempt to lower prices at the pump, which have spiked because of the war Trump started, the president now says he’s ready to buy diesel from Vladimir Putin’s government.

In essence, Trump has agreed to pay an enemy government that is helping those trying to kill Americans in a war that’s entirely his doing. All to eradicate a supposed threat that he claimed he had “obliterated” a year earlier.

Just to refresh everyone’s memory, Russia is backing Iran in its war with the U.S., reportedly providing intelligence on U.S. bases to the Iranian military. In essence, Trump agreed to pay an enemy government that is helping those trying to kill Americans in a war that’s entirely his doing. And all this to eradicate a supposed threat that Trump had claimed didn’t exist at all because he “obliterated” Iran’s nuclear program a year earlier.

Come to think of it, a two-hour briefing on just that subject wouldn’t have been enough to explain that insanity. How do you tell the press that we’re paying our enemies to attack us?

Even so, that wasn’t the peak of insanity this week.

A few days earlier, a judge in Virginia ruled that the Trump administration had misled the public with a long list of false accusations about Mary Comans, the former chief financial officer of FEMA.

“Armed only with false statements, high-ranking government officials undertook a premeditated campaign to impugn the personal and professional integrity of Ms. Comans, a non-partisan, career public servant,” U.S. Magistrate Judge William E. Fitzpatrick said. “Their intent was to disseminate false and derogatory information about Ms. Comans as widely as possible.”

Comans was accused of money laundering, willfully violating a presidential executive order, undermining public safety and misspending federal funds. As the judge found, none of that was ultimately true. He added that “high-ranking” government officials accused her of such things while “knowing they were false.”

Dealing with that insanity might also require a two-hour press briefing.

Finally, there’s the matter of the lawsuit filed by CNN, MSNOW and Politico against the Trump administration. Judge Timothy Kelly ruled Tuesday night that the temporary restraining order preventing Trump from banning those outlets from the White House would remain in force while their lawsuit proceeded.

Trump had also engaged in “unlawful viewpoint discrimination” by banning those reporters, Kelly said. The president also apparently never gave those news organizations any meaningful list of standards they had to comply with or risk losing their press passes. Trump’s actions, the judge said, “likely did not … come close to satisfying Karem.”

Yes, that’s me. He was referring to the Karem v. Trump case in 2019, when I beat the administration in court on three occasions and got my press credentials back. And the judge is right, by the way: Trump’s actions don’t satisfy me. But unpacking my own victory over Trump would be a tough task for the best press secretary. So would dealing with any of this week’s issues, let alone dealing with a president who seems to have reached peak insanity, especially for a brand new press secretary who just moved to town with questionable credentials.

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only by Amanda Marcotte, also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

To be completely fair, Trump threw Zacharia to the dogs with no prep time, no knowledge of the issues she would have to handle and no readiness to handle even the straightforward questions about her own legal background. (She graduated from law school but is not a licensed attorney in any state.)

Zacharia read a bunch of lies off a written statement, smiled at us and got out of there. It now seems possible that her first day briefing the White House press will also be her best day, as well as her last day. The aforementioned Anthony Scaramucci publicly mused that she may not last as long as he did at the White House (which was 11 days). I’ve heard some reporters saying they won’t even bother to learn how to spell her name.

But what we saw in the briefing room this week was far more troubling than one woman falling on her face. It was a panicky president approaching peak insanity throwing a scapegoat on stage in an effort to deflect attention from his ruthless and corrupt conduct. True to form, the press corps took the bait, and seemed more interested in what Zacharia was wearing and whether she’d exaggerated her qualifications than in the important issues facing this country as a result of the president’s insanity.

I have plenty of empathy for anyone working in the Trump White House, but no sympathy for anyone who willingly joins the lunacy, particularly at this late date.

The midterm elections are at hand. Trump is criminally negligent and mentally unwell. Anyone who goes to work for him now is just asking for trouble.

Just ask Katie Zacharia. If you can find her.

from Brian Karem on the Trump White House

#192. Can Ukraine Afford Its Own Defense?

Understanding the conflict four years on.

In a month littered with dark spots for Ukraine, a bigger, slower-moving storm cloud is drifting toward the embattled nation: the chance of a budget shortfall of tens of billions of dollars if Kyiv fails to pass reforms needed for continued European financial support.

Ultimately, experts believe that Ukraine will likely still be able to count on major European backing. But the saga of the budget gap, as well as tough economic conditions for 2027 and beyond, suggests that Ukraine will increasingly have to walk a fine line to maintain funding for its defense as the war stretches into a fifth year.

In a month littered with dark spots for Ukraine, a bigger, slower-moving storm cloud is drifting toward the embattled nation: the chance of a budget shortfall of tens of billions of dollars if Kyiv fails to pass reforms needed for continued European financial support.

Ultimately, experts believe that Ukraine will likely still be able to count on major European backing. But the saga of the budget gap, as well as tough economic conditions for 2027 and beyond, suggests that Ukraine will increasingly have to walk a fine line to maintain funding for its defense as the war stretches into a fifth year.

“I think substantial European support will continue, but we should not think that any future programs are definitely secured or guaranteed,” said Sergiy Tsivkach, former head of the national investment agency UkraineInvest.

Ukraine’s budget has long been under pressure: The country’s gross domestic product contracted by nearly 30 percent in 2022, the first year of Russia’s invasion, even as spending on military equipment and salaries rose 640 percent. With financial support from the United States, Europe, and others, though, Ukraine squeaked through without too much concern each year—until now.

In August, Ukraine’s officials announced they urgently needed $27 billion more for their defense budget, reportedly causing shock among officials from Europe, which has supplanted the U.S. as Ukraine’s biggest financial supporter. Ukrainian officials said the budget gap was partly the result of the decision to increase military salaries, as well as the cost of drone procurement. Ukraine in September reduced the gap to $20 billion in part through austerity measures.

To fill the remainder, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky urged the European Union to disburse money early from a loan originally meant to be spent in 2027. The bloc balked at this and instead has reportedly pressed Ukraine to pass anti-corruption and tax reform legislation to unlock $38 billion already on offer. The demand comes amid an ongoing corruption scandal that has seen investigations into officials close to Zelensky as well as many lawmakers.

Ukraine is voting this week on some of that legislation, and on Thursday Ukraine’s parliament passed one key revision, thereby unlocking some EU aid. But it’s unclear whether all of the required reforms will pass, and if not, what the EU response might be. Ukrainian society is staunchly opposed to corruption. In a September poll, 50 percent of respondents said corruption was their top concern, higher even than Russian attacks. Yet Ukraine’s elected officials have shown a lack of urgency on the EU’s required reforms. Ukraine’s presidential administration, meanwhile, has reportedly struggled to work with parliament, in part due to personnel shifts within Zelensky’s team.

Zelensky’s office may believe that “some partial implementation [of EU requirements] will be counted as full implementation” said Olena Prokopenko, a senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund think tank. “But I think that approach is a very dangerous game.”

Ukraine must “build the engine while it’s driving the car,” said Vitalii Kim, the country’s new veterans’ affairs minister.

Trump’s diesel-deal feud with Zelensky obscures a more important effort.

Kyiv’s energy war on Russia may hurt on the margins, but the real culprit is Trump’s war on Iran.

Even if Ukraine pulls itself out of the hole this year, though, the joint pressures of Russian attacks and European demands for reform mean that the budget issue is far from settled for the years to come.

Ukraine’s 2027 budget already faces a gap of $32.6 billion, according to the Kyiv School of Economics. In part, Ukraine’s budget woes are due to Russia’s increasingly successful targeting of the country’s top industries: steel and grain. Ukraine’s GDP is expected to rise just 1.2 percent this year and 1.5 percent next year, according to a World Bank report.

And the situation could get even worse. Increased Russian attacks, among other factors, could lead to a further loss of 450,000 jobs and a further loss of as much as $4.9 billion in tax revenue, the Kyiv School of Economics reported. “I think the trend will probably head towards the war becoming more and more expensive,” Prokopenko said.

Russia’s economy is also struggling, with expected growth of just 1.1 percent this year, thanks in part to U.S. and EU sanctions as well as Ukrainian strikes on its energy industry. But energy revenue—including a pending sale of diesel to the U.S. announced last week—has kept Russia rich enough to keep prosecuting the war.

As Russia applies more pressure on Ukraine, cracks could appear in European support, which largely expires by 2027 under the terms of two programs, the $56 billion Ukraine Facility program and the $100 billion Ukraine Support Loan.

After that, Ukraine may have to deal with new governments that are potentially more skeptical of Kyiv’s requests. Between 2026 and 2027, four of the EU’s major economies—Spain, France, Poland, and Italy—will hold elections. In France, Marine Le Pen, the front-runner in the presidential election, has said she would stop financial aid for Ukraine. And although there are no national elections coming up in Germany, the Ukraine-skeptic party Alternative for Germany made major gains in state elections in September.

Still, experts are so far cautiously optimistic that some form of support will endure. In part, that’s because Ukrainian security is increasingly viewed as key to European security, said Prokopenko. “Europe cannot afford leaving Ukraine without sufficient capacity to defend itself and by extension defend Europe,” she said.

Support for Ukraine also shouldn’t be too much of a stretch for the EU’s finances, at least at current levels, said Charles Lichfield, an expert at the Atlantic Council think tank. “Another 90 billion [euros] wouldn’t be a big risk,” he said.

Ukraine’s own economy, while battered, is also far from helpless. “If Ukraine can protect economic activity inside the country, this will by itself decrease the demand for international support and decrease budgetary gaps,” Tsivkach said.

Until the introduction of new jet-powered drones, Ukraine was regularly shooting down most long-range drones fired by Russia. On Monday, former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov announced that a new interceptor drone had successfully taken out two of the new Russian drones.

Ukraine also has yet to tap its biggest potential source of funds: the $235 billion in Russian assets frozen in European financial institutions, a policy that Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha pushed for on Monday in an op-ed. The plan has repeatedly been shot down by Belgium, where most of the assets are held, but has previously been supported by some EU members.

And if all else fails, Ukraine can also rely on nations outside the EU, such as Japan, the United Kingdom, Canada, and Norway—the Scandinavian country alone is set to give Ukraine $9 billion in 2027.

“It’s hard to imagine a scenario where everything goes wrong,” Lichfield said.

Sam Skove is a staff writer at Foreign Policy. X: @samuelskove

Ukraine must “build the engine while it’s driving the car,” said Vitalii Kim, the country’s new veterans’ affairs minister.

#196. Katie Zacharia was too incompetent even for Trump

Well, that didn’t last too long. Katie Zacharia became White House press secretary just five days ago, but after President Donald Trump told reporters she should “reconsider,” the New York Times reported she’d been fired Friday afternoon.

Zacharia held the position for less than a week, but generated considerable controversy in that short time. Her first briefing on Tuesday lasted only 14 minutes as she took questions from just three reporters at Breitbart, Fox News and the Daily Mail, appearing flustered and disorganized. Meanwhile, questions about her credentials took center stage, as she identified herself as a lawyer but in fact had never passed the bar exam. Her long history of pushing far-right conspiracy theories like QAnon also resurfaced.

Then, Zacharia made two appearances on Fox News, both of which did not seem to go well. Sean Hannity grilled her on her false credentials Thursday night and told her, “I can give you some unsolicited advice. That’s never going to be a friendly room to you,” referring to the White House press pool. The next morning, she appeared on “Fox and Friends” and was asked if she still had the “confidence” of the president. “I-I-I’m standing here and I was able to travel with him through all of the midterm convention — or, excuse me — the midterm rallies, and I hope to be able to build the trust and confidence of everyone around me,” she replied.

#198. USAID’s Destruction Left Nepal Dangerously Exposed

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Analysis: USAID’s Destruction Left Nepal Dangerously Exposed

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Nepal was already confronting the growing challenges of preparing for disasters that are becoming more extreme and difficult to predict and responding to them with fewer resources. But after catastrophic flooding hit the country twice since August, another missing piece has been exposed: the absence of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), once a steadfast partner in Nepal’s disaster risk reduction and humanitarian response.

Development workers say that the U.S. response to the flooding along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers has been limited compared to past disasters, including the devastating 2015 earthquake, when USAID worked with multiple organizations in rescue and relief operations and served, in one advisor’s words, as the “lead U.S. government agency for coordinating foreign disaster relief.”

Nepal was already confronting the growing challenges of preparing for disasters that are becoming more extreme and difficult to predict and responding to them with fewer resources. But after catastrophic flooding hit the country twice since August, another missing piece has been exposed: the absence of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), once a steadfast partner in Nepal’s disaster risk reduction and humanitarian response.

Development workers say that the U.S. response to the flooding along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers has been limited compared to past disasters, including the devastating 2015 earthquake, when USAID worked with multiple organizations in rescue and relief operations and served, in one advisor’s words, as the “lead U.S. government agency for coordinating foreign disaster relief.”

“Compared to the 2015 response, the difference is night and day,” Santosh Gyawali—the former Nepal representative for USAID’s Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance, which oversaw disaster response coordination—told Foreign Policy. “The U.S. Disaster Assistance Response Team arrived for search-and-rescue operations and did quick assessments on building safety and saved lives. They worked as auxiliary to the Nepal government. We see that missing now,” Gyawali added.

USAID was effectively destroyed in July 2025 following months of funding freezes and mass layoffs conducted under the Trump administration’s Department of Government Efficiency. The dismantling of one of the world’s largest humanitarian agencies drew widespread condemnation, sending ripples across developing countries where U.S. assistance had long provided lifesaving programs—from improving maternal and child health to providing malaria and HIV medications.

In Nepal, U.S. assistance had helped build disaster response capacity for decades, including the Program for Enhancement of Emergency Response, which created a network of trained personnel across borders in the Himalayas and beyond “who spoke the same disaster language,” Gyawali said. USAID also partnered with Nepal’s National Society for Earthquake Technology for various preparedness programs and conducted Community Action for Disaster Response trainings.

“Our topology and terrain are such that it will take time for people to arrive here,” Gyawali said. “In any disaster, the first responders are the community. We were training first responders in the community and within the security forces, and with USAID pulling the plug, all these efforts have also discontinued.”

Funding cuts are already affecting disaster monitoring. One casualty, ended in January 2025, is SERVIR-Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH)—a joint initiative of USAID, NASA, and the Kathmandu-based International Center for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD)—which helps monitor floods, landslides, and other hazards intensified by extreme weather.

Birendra Bajracharya, the project’s former director at ICIMOD, said initiatives such as SERVIR are crucial for developing customized applications that translate satellite data into actionable information. Mountainous areas, in particular, are difficult to access but highly prone to climate change-driven events. Researchers can use satellite imagery to continuously monitor glacial lakes, landslide-prone areas, and other risky landscapes to strengthen disaster monitoring, early warning, and forecasting.

“The USAID funding was pivotal for research and technology,” he told Foreign Policy. “Although it will not have an immediate impact on the ground, it will affect innovation that would have helped us predict certain weather-related events better in the future. The program also helped in training communities to use our tools and share information. The funding cut has discontinued them.”

While some tools for assessing extreme weather and forecasting river flows remain functional on ICIMOD’s servers, Bajracharya said their upgrading and engagement with users have stopped, which limits the effective use of information and raises concerns over the tools’ long-term sustainability.

A U.S. State Department official told Foreign Policy that the SERVIR-HKH program concluded in January 2025, before the USAID reorganization, and that its tools and services remain active. The official added that the U.S. government continues to support Nepal’s flood-warning capacity through the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and a grant to the World Meteorological Organization.

However, people familiar with SERVIR-HKH said, speaking on background, that the program’s contract was originally due to run through 2026, but that its work was cut short as early as January 2025.

Climate change is making the Himalayas increasingly fragile, with rising global temperatures posing a risk of accelerating glacial melt and increasing the risk of glacial lake outburst floods that can inundate downstream communities. In 2020, ICIMOD identified 47 potentially dangerous glacial lakes in Nepal, India, and China. The growing risks have also raised concerns among climate analysts about the U.S. rollbacks on its climate commitments and consequences for countries on the front lines of climate change.

Just as Nepal has been recovering from the August floods, the country has experienced multiple disasters in its aftermath. In late September, dramatic footage showed a large section of a mountain crashing into the Kali Gandaki River and briefly blocking it in the Mustang region, located in the north-central part of the country, causing devastating floods. On Sunday, another rock-ice avalanche—similar to the August event, though smaller in scale—resulted in a flash flood, sweeping away houses, bridges, and trekking trails in central Nepal’s Gorkha district, though no fatalities have been reported so far.

A report published in September by Washington, D.C.-based advisory firm One Earth Partners noted that USAID’s dismantling has “resulted in the immediate loss of $1 billion per year in direct funding for biodiversity, climate, clean energy, and pollution reduction programs across more than 100 countries.”

Erin Coughlan de Perez, a climate scientist and associate professor at Tufts University, said that satellite-based monitoring and early warning systems are critical infrastructure that requires significant investment across all aspects of early warning systems, including monitoring, forecasting, and communication. She added that the “international community should be providing substantial support for climate-vulnerable countries like Nepal.”

Gyawali, who had worked with USAID for 32 years, said that the agency had provided such support for decades.

In 2014, USAID supported the establishment of an early flood-warning system in eastern Nepal’s Kankai River Basin, which Gyawali said largely helped prevent casualties along the riverbanks. Before its departure, the agency disbursed more than $30 million through Tayar Nepal, its flagship disaster risk-management program, between 2020 and 2024, government data shows.

Tayar worked with Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, local governments, and communities to improve both disaster preparedness and emergency response through local risk assessments, simulation exercises, and disaster drills.

“USAID was not only providing technology but also transferring knowledge, engaging and empowering communities, and giving ownership to the people,” Gyawali said. “That’s all lost now. And sadly, after USAID’s exit, we did not continue many of the programs ourselves.”

Disaster risk reduction experts such as Gangalal Tuladhar, who is also a former education minister, see the lack of ownership of projects after completion as a problem.

“Donors like USAID have helped build capacity, but our institutional memory is very weak, and when the projects ended, the technology transfer and knowledge also ended with them,” he said. “This is also a weakness of our public institutions and the government and reflects our poor work attitude.”

Tuladhar said that Nepal’s local and provincial governments could play instrumental roles in disaster preparedness without donor assistance if they “mobilize funds from the government coffers efficiently and work honestly.” However, rehabilitation and recovery, as well as investments in technologies to monitor climate hazards, would require more bilateral assistance.

The United States has provided about $36 million in assistance—compared to more than $130 million after the earthquake—along with drones and forensics support following this year’s floods. Development workers have questioned whether the amount is sufficient.

A former top USAID official, Mark Ward, described the initial U.S. contribution of $500,000 as “embarrassing,” adding that the assistance would have “been a lot more” if USAID was still running and equipped to conduct a better ground assessment. But other U.S. and Nepali officials, speaking on background, argued that the scale of last month’s disaster was smaller than the earthquake, accounting for a reduced contribution.

U.S. State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told Foreign Policy that Washington’s disaster response has been based on requests from the Nepali government and that “we have proactively offered more assistance than they requested.”

“In reality, by reforming our assistance programs, we have been able to respond faster to crises, as demonstrated across the world,” he said.

Nepal’s disaster risk management authority has estimated the reconstruction bill from the floods at around $4.7 billion, with roughly 65 percent of that amount required to rebuild infrastructure. That figure is likely to rise after the latest flooding.

Many climate activists, meanwhile, are demanding that the world’s largest emitters—including the United States— compensate countries such as Nepal that are bearing the brunt.

Gyawali said that USAID’s absence will further strain government coffers at a time when other Western countries—including the United Kingdom and several European states—are prioritizing domestic needs over foreign assistance.

And while dwindling funds could hamper Nepal’s recovery, experts warn that they could also weaken the systems needed to prepare for the next disaster, including programs such as SERVIR that monitor hazards and help improve forecasting and early warning.

“It’s difficult for the government alone to maintain such systems, and we need donor funds to help customize such technology to our local context,” Bajracharya said. “But development can’t just depend on donor funding, and with more and more international donors downsizing or pulling out, the [Nepali] government and nongovernment organizations need to think about how to design our programs effectively, with clear sustainability plans.”

Bibek Bhandari is a journalist based in Kathmandu, Nepal.

#200. The Ilhan Omar raid makes me fear for my family

When Donald Trump clinched the presidency in 2016, my wife broke into tears on camera as a local journalist interviewed patrons at a bar in Queens that had advertised a presidential watch party, complete, in its wide-eyed audacity, with Clinton cocktails. As an immigrant and Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipient who had to navigate the cruel vagaries of the U.S. immigration system, she grokked then what it would take many people years to understand. Not long after, Trump attempted to dismantle DACA, the executive order that defended immigrant children in lieu of the DREAM Act. While my wife is now a citizen, the raid of Democratic Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home is a reminder that not even U.S. citizenship guarantees the safety of immigrants in Trump’s United States.

The case against Omar worries me, not only because it’s bald-faced political vengeance, a grim milestone in our collective lurch toward fascism, but also because of what it means for naturalized citizens in the United States — people like my wife, my sister and my mother. Attacks on citizens who did not arrive on the Mayflower or through Ellis Island is an extension of the Trump administration’s remorseless persecution of immigrants in the U.S. Child of immigrants? Side eye. Naturalized citizen. Well, let’s revisit that paperwork, shall we?

On the first day of his second term, Trump attempted to end birthright citizenship, how I became a U.S. citizen, via executive order. Over the summer, the Supreme Court ruled against the president, but a month later, he signed two more executive orders targeting so-called birth tourism and birthright citizenship. As this latest attack on immigrants faces fresh challenges, the Department of Homeland Security is focusing on denaturalization.

In June 2025, DHS issued a memo about “prioritizing denaturalization,” a process that enables the federal government to strip people of their citizenship, which historically was reserved mostly for Nazi war criminals. At the time, I worried the memo signaled the escalation of an effort to broaden the discretion of the federal government to determine, even retrospectively, who deserves to be a U.S. citizen. Given Monday’s sweep of Omar’s Washington, D.C., home by Homeland Security Investigations agents, my fears appear to be well-founded.

The federal case against Omar follows years of accusations and innuendoes — and even a review during Trump’s first term that reportedly found no issues with her citizenship. But the president has still repeatedly called for her denaturalization and deportation, saying on social media earlier this year that she “should be in jail” and “sent back to Somalia.” He has called people from Somalia “scammers” and “lowlifes.” Vice President JD Vance has also suggested that Omar is likely guilty of immigration fraud. But what is the actual case against her?

Unfortunately, the judicial warrant is sealed, and as usual, the Department of Justice hasn’t revealed much information except to say that it is an “ongoing criminal investigation.” The involvement of Immigration Customs and Enforcement in the search, however, gives weight to comments made by public officials about potential immigration fraud. Is there any merit to the accusation? Not really.

The U.S. government granted Omar’s family, refugees from Somalia, asylum in 1995. Five years later, Omar became a U.S. citizen via a law in which minors are eligible for citizenship once their parents naturalize. Some critics have suggested without evidence that Omar was born a year earlier, which would have made her ineligible for citizenship through the aforementioned law. The bigger question is: Why now?

It’s been over 25 years, and the federal government happened to unearth “incriminating” evidence of a vocal Trump critic three weeks before the midterm elections? It’s dubious at best, and a rank abuse of power at worst.

It’s been over 25 years, and the federal government happened to unearth “incriminating” evidence of a vocal Trump critic three weeks before the midterm elections? It’s dubious at best, and a rank abuse of power at worst. Even in the worst-case scenario, Omar was a girl at the time, so any fudging of numbers would have been done by her late father, who filed the paperwork.

But this is nothing new for Trump. Casting doubt on a political adversary’s right to be in the U.S. was how Trump made his presidential bones. His 2011 birtherism tour, in which he suggested President Barack Obama was not born in the United States but rather in Kenya, was his beautillion ball, laying the groundwork for what would become his primary political strategy: Attack with conspiracy theories. Never bother to substantiate. Repeat ad infinitum. The difference now is that he has a loyal Justice Department and DHS at his back.

The birtherism lie was not unlike the current mudslinging campaign against Omar. But between then and now, a couple of major changes have taken place. One, Trump became president, and two, in his second term, he has, through a series of executive orders, communiqués and personnel rejiggering, weaponized DHS, Customs and Border Protection, ICE, Border Patrol, U.S. Marshals and other federal agencies by affording them a dangerous amount of latitude.

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only, written by Amanda Marcotte, now also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

A salient example is the expanded 287(g) program, which allows ICE to deputize local law enforcement, thereby entangling local and federal police, effectively eliminating a peacekeeping backstop against federal overreach. Congress established the 287(g) program in 1996 through the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act, but in Trump’s second term, the program has so far ballooned from 140 memorandums of agreement to 2,660 agreements in 38 states and two U.S. territories.

Combine that with $70 billion in immigration funding, donning masks, failing to produce identification and eschewing judicial warrants in favor of administrative warrants — nothing more than a performative gesture — and Trump has effectively created a paramilitary domestic force that does his bidding, including going after political foes with impunity.

Denaturalizations are up, owing to this administration’s expressed priority, and naturalizations are down 75%, a consequence of intimidation tactics and the practice of federal agents ambushing immigrants at green card and naturalization hearings.

Omar’s case will be a litmus test for this administration’s authority, both in terms of carrying out political vendettas and processing denaturalization. Even if Trump’s DHS fails to denaturalize and expel the congresswoman from the country, the mere attempt sends a chilling message to naturalized citizens across the country, including my own family: You’re not safe in Donald Trump’s America.

In January, my wife and I will return to the U.S. for the first time in 15 months — the longest time we’ve been away from the country. Before becoming a U.S. citizen four years ago, my wife hadn’t left the country since she arrived as a toddler. Suddenly, she was free to come and go as she pleased, so when her postgraduate program in Versailles accepted her application, we went. Now, as our return to the U.S. approaches, a worm of doubt squirms within us. We’re both U.S. citizens, safe on paper, but what if the value of our papers has changed? What if the manner by which we obtained our citizenships — birthright and naturalization — now invites skepticism and scrutiny?

Before we moved to Europe, we went on a weekend trip to Montreal. Ahead of our return, prompted by horror stories I had seen in the news about people being detained for something as innocuous as a meme, I deleted media on my phone that could be construed as critical of the Trump administration, and I turned my phone off while going through customs. It was the only time in my life I’ve done that.
