#207. Elon Musk is the donor behind Senate Republicans’ massive rescue mission for Ken Paxton

This article originally appeared on The Texas Tribune.

WASHINGTON — After months of being outspent by Democrat James Talarico on the airwaves, Republicans launched a massive rescue mission for Ken Paxton in September, dropping over $200 million to boost their U.S. Senate candidate in Texas.

New campaign finance filings revealed that much of the advertising flurry was funded by one highly motivated donor: Elon Musk, the world’s wealthiest man.

Musk, who lives near the SpaceX Starbase facility in South Texas, appears to have poured nearly $190 million into the U.S. Senate race in his adopted home state. His role in financing Paxton’s air support was disclosed in reports filed Thursday to the Federal Election Commission by Senate Leadership Fund, the Senate GOP’s main super PAC and the biggest spender in Texas’ Senate contest.

On Sept. 9, the first day of the GOP midterm convention in Dallas, Musk gave $75 million to SLF. The next day, SLF put $75 million into a new entity called Texas PAC. By the weekend after the convention, the new super PAC was up on the air with a positive spot about Paxton’s work on sex trafficking and a negative ad attacking Talarico as being for “they/them, not you.”

Two weeks after cutting his first check, Musk gave an additional $83 million to SLF, according to the group’s filing. Sure enough, SLF deposited $83 million into Texas PAC’s coffers the following day.

Musk’s donations armed Senate Republicans to take over the airwaves in Texas. Using Texas PAC as the vessel to book airtime, SLF has thus far spent over $159 million on TV, radio and digital advertising, double the outlay from Talarico’s campaign, according to media tracking firm AdImpact.

SLF backed Sen. John Cornyn in the primary, estimating that a Paxton candidacy would require $150 million to $200 million to retain the seat — money that could come at the expense of other states. While the prediction proved prescient, Musk’s investment has changed the calculus.

“Thanks to some generous investors who have dedicated money to an affiliate, Texas PAC, we’ve been able to go in and support Ken Paxton,” SLF executive director Alex Latcham told Bloomberg TV Wednesday. “We’ll spend nearly $200 million in that race. But again, thanks to Leader John Thune and the Republican caucus and our fundraising, we haven’t had to subtract resources from other states to do so.”

Start your day with essential news from Salon. Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

The Tesla and SpaceX founder got involved in the race after his political team reached out to Senate Leadership Fund, the Senate GOP’s main outside campaign group, to voice Musk’s concerns about Paxton’s standing in the race, according to a person familiar with the conversations. That led to an agreement between Musk’s orbit and SLF — Musk would provide $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, the main outside group boosting Paxton, if SLF gave $5 million and the PAC raised an additional $5 million. The details of the conversation were first reported by Axios.

That windfall was badly needed. Lone Star Liberty PAC had only $35,000 in the bank at the end of June, having drained its coffers on Paxton’s hard-fought primary win over Cornyn. Talarico, meanwhile, was continuing his torrid fundraising pace and was poised to keep dominating the political ad spending battle if help did not arrive for Paxton.

Talarico posted another record quarter amid Paxton’s SLF-powered ad surge, hauling in $64 million between July and September — a third-quarter record among all U.S. Senate candidates. The Austin Democrat has maintained a polling lead for months in averages of nonpartisan public surveys, an alarming sight for a Republican Party whose unbeaten streak in Texas statewide races spans more than three decades.

With Musk’s donation and the matching funds, Lone Star Liberty PAC spent $17.5 million on broadcast TV advertising in early September, by far the most significant pro-Paxton ad buy of the general election. By the end of the month, a handful of outside groups led by SLF had dropped over $217 million on ads in the Texas Senate race.

Paxton has not commented publicly about Musk’s support.

In the past, the attorney general has praised Musk for backing Republicans in 2024. He spent hours at Musk’s home two days before that year’s election hearing Musk recount all his efforts to boost GOP candidates, Paxton said at Turning Point USA’s AmericaFest in 2024.

“Aren’t you all glad he’s on our side?” Paxton said to cheers. “I am convinced that whatever he did, whatever rocket science thing he did, made a huge difference in this election.”

Paxton has also aligned himself with Musk through his role as Texas attorney general — and largely skirted scrutinizing Musk’s companies as his office has increasingly taken on Big Tech.

In 2022, as Musk sought to buy Twitter, Paxton opened an investigation into the social media company for how it reported the number of accounts on the platform that were fake or bots — inspecting whether the service was inflating the number of its actual users to boost its value for revenue. At the time, Musk was raising similar questions. He ultimately bought Twitter and renamed it X.

In 2024, Paxton opened an investigation into World Federation of Advertisers, an organization that represents marketers, to assess whether its members were conspiring to boycott specific social media services. TechCrunch reported Musk’s X, which had filed an antitrust suit against the group, was likely among the social media platforms.

Meanwhile, Paxton has taken on tech giants including Netflix, WhatsApp, Discord, and Meta — probes he has touted on the campaign trail.

“As attorney general, I’ve sued some of the largest companies in the world … for taking advantage of our kids by exposing them to dangerous, addictive material,” Paxton said after defeating Cornyn in May. “In Washington, I will not stop fighting to protect Texas children from Big Tech.”

But Paxton has taken arrows from critics who’ve accused him of turning a blind eye to X and Musk. In January, a group of Democratic state representatives demanded the attorney general investigate the platform’s artificial intelligence agent, Grok, and its creation of exploitative content about children and women. Paxton did not respond to the letter publicly.

The same month, a group of attorneys general from across the country sent Musk’s company a letter demanding that it address its AI agent’s creation of child sex abuse content. Paxton was not among the signatories.

Musk’s political operation is also deeply involved in the Republican ground game in Texas, from canvassing to mailers, across several key races. America PAC, which he seeded with nearly $90 million last quarter, had pumped $18.8 million into the Senate race through Tuesday, per FEC filings, which capture efforts like text messaging, mailers and ads but not in-person canvassing such as block-walking and phone-banking. Over 80% of that money has gone to anti-Talarico messaging.

The tech mogul has significant business interests in the Lone Star State. Musk has moved the state of incorporation for many of his companies to Texas in recent years. Boring Company and X are headquartered in Bastrop, SpaceX is near Brownsville and Tesla’s corporate headquarters is now in Austin.

And it’s not just the Senate race. Musk’s PAC has spent about $800,000 boosting Republican candidates in the five most competitive U.S. House races in Texas. The biggest share has gone to the 35th Congressional District, a San Antonio-area seat Republicans redrew last summer with the intention of flipping, but which has proven highly competitive.

Musk spent hundreds of millions in 2024 to boost Republicans, including Donald Trump’s presidential bid. Trump rewarded Musk by tapping him to lead the controversial Department of Government Efficiency initiative. The two had a public falling out later that year, when Musk disparaged the president’s signature legislative effort and alleged Trump was in the Jeffrey Epstein files.

The dustup did not appear to sap Musk’s appetite for bankrolling Republicans’ political spending. The world’s wealthiest man has already surpassed his 2024 political spending this cycle, with Texas the largest focus of his operation.

Other GOP groups are fundraising off of Musk’s Texas spending bonanza as well.

“Elon Musk understands what it’s like to live under far left Democrats,” reads one National Republican Senatorial Committee fundraising email, which notes that Musk has spent $276 million in the midterms and directs readers to a WinRed fundraising page. “He fled an oppressive regime in California that crippled the state with a radical agenda before finding a new home in Texas. But now, the same Far Left Democrats that ran California into the ground are coming to SEIZE Elon’s new home!”

While far from reaching Musk’s investment levels, some prominent Texas GOP donors also came off the sidelines for Paxton in recent months, new filings show.

West Texas oil billionaire Farris Wilks, who has supported Paxton in his state campaigns and directed millions to hardline Republicans, donated $250,000 to one of Paxton’s joint fundraising committees in mid-August, his first federal expenditure of the cycle.

Amarillo billionaire Alex Fairly, meanwhile, had maxed out to Paxton’s direct campaign account with a $7,000 donation in the spring; in late August, he gave $274,300 to Paxton’s joint fundraising committee.

Paxton also received large sums this quarter from the Dallas Cowboys brass. Team president Stephen Jones and chief sales and marketing officer Jerry Jones Jr. gave $122,000 and $100,000, respectively. Their father, Cowboys owner Jerry Jones, donated a six-figure sum in the second quarter.

#210. Alex Gibney’s “Musk” asks why we gave Elon Musk so much power

From the moment Alex Gibney announced he was working on âMuskâ in 2023, it became one of the most anticipated documentaries around â and a source of trepidation for its titular subject, tech mogul Elon Musk. But we may have underestimated how far the worldâs wealthiest man and his ilk would go to prevent audiences from seeing it.

Weeks before âMuskâ hit theaters, its distributor, Bleecker Street, couldnât buy ads on TikTok, YouTube, Mark Zuckerbergâs Meta-owned Facebook and Instagram or, hereâs a shocker, Muskâs own X. A Hollywood Reporter story published on Sept. 25 made YouTube and Meta reverse course â a rare case of two media giants shamed into living up to their free-speech claims.

But this attempted media suppression shows âMuskâ has struck a nerve, despite its namesake dismissing it as a âhit piece that misses.â

It was not lost on Gibney that at the same time that was happening, Zuckerberg, Musk and Washington Post owner Jeff Bezos were dining with Donald Trump and Chinaâs Xi Jinping at the White House. Heâs confronted gravely perilous corruption and dangerous figures in previous, fearless documentaries such asÂ  2019âs âCitizen K,â about a Russian oligarch who was crushed by Vladimir Putin, and 2015âs âGoing Clear: Scientology and the Prison of Belief.â

What happened to Bleecker Street, then, is both familiar to Gibney and extraordinarily alarming. âYou can see how a few platforms coalescing around the endorsement of what these tech viziers are doing decide that a criticism of tech power is somehow political and canât be allowed in terms of open discourse on their platforms,â Gibney told Salon. âSo that was really disconcerting.â

Itâs shaping up to be a dark autumn for Silicon Valleyâs villains. In early December, Luca Guadagninoâs âArtificialâ turns our attention to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, played by Andrew Garfield.Â Â

Meanwhile, âMuskâ was recently joined in theaters by Aaron Sorkinâs âThe Social Reckoning,â in which Jeremy Strong portrays Zuckerberg as a soulless ghoul prioritizing clicks over user safety. In âYou Can See Everything,â notorious prankster Nathan Fielder shadows notorious (for different reasons) Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes in the days before she went to prison.Â

Gibney also profiled Holmes in his 2019 work âThe Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley,â which adds another layer of coincidental symmetry: Fielderâs film hits theaters on Oct. 16, the same day âMuskâ opens nationwide.

But âMuskâ is unquestionably a tougher watch, and given its subjectâs extensive integration into the second Trump administration, it canât help but be political.

Of course, âMuskâ isnât campaigning for anything except our need to confront the existential threat posed by one man exercising significant control over our media and our military.

A chorus of testimony from people who were once closest to Musk builds a profile of a megalomaniacal con artist. Two of Muskâs most incisive critics, his ex-wife Justine Musk and former right-wing influencer Ashley St. Clair, describe him as a gaslighter and a nuke, respectively.Â

But perhaps the most damning testimonial comes from Musk himself â or rather, existing audio recordings of Musk delivered by a CGI version of the Tesla and SpaceX CEO, since he refused to participate.

All of it boils down to simple questions Gibney poses at the filmâs outset: How could Musk assume so much power, and why have we given it to him? I discussed those questions with Gibney, and what they taught him about Musk and our penchant for enabling men like him, in a wide-ranging conversation transcribed below.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Salon: Youâve done a documentary on Putin. You did one on Scientology, a famously litigious organization. You have a vast filmography featuring subjects who might have taken issue, or have taken issue, with what was said in your documentaries. Where does this rank in terms of threat level, legal or otherwise?

Gibney: Well, high. I mean, when just before âGoing Clearâ was released, the Church of Scientology took out full-page ads in the New York Times and the L.A. Times with a big picture of me, sort of denouncing me. And there were people, you know, who would pop up in dark parking lots, you know, sort of accosting me, trying to kind of destabilize me psychologically. But I think in this case, heâs the richest man in the world. He has a lot of resourcesâ¦ And he has this platform, Twitter, which has become a kind of Thunderdome of hate and vitriol, and that activates, you know, unpredictable characters who sometimes act on their ownâ¦

That said, I donât want to exaggerate whatâs happened to me so far. Other people put themselves at greater risk than I, in the sense that they came forward and appeared on camera.

One of the things that you said in other interviews, and I think you actually said this in the documentary as well, is that you used to be a fan of Elon Muskâs products.

I mean, I looked at him from afar. I have some history on this whole electric car thing because I was brought in long ago to help with the editing of a doc called âWho Killed the Electric Car,â which is about GMâs first foray into the world of electric cars. A woman I met on that film, Jessie Deeter, later produced a film called âRevenge of the Electric Car,â and Elon Musk is in that.Â  And Jessie, when she worked with him on that, was a big fan. [Deeter is also a producer on âMusk.â]

(Courtesy Bleecker Street Film / Gregg Segal)

So, you know, I had a certain connection to him. And Iâm a big electric car guy. I own one â not a Teslaâ but I own one, and I had a Tesla Powerwall in my house. I also sort of liked the kind of mumbling charisma that he had for a while, because he seemed like very much a regular guy. He was joking with people around on Twitter and stuff like that.

That said, he could also do unpredictable, chaotic and sometimes offensive things. But largely speaking, my view of him was positive. But I was interested in the fact that he accumulated so much power, and so that was the basis on which I dug in back in 2022.

Do you think that his ability to amass this much power is related to the fact that he is doing it in the American capitalist system, or do you think he could have done it in any other place in the world?

Well, I mean, there are a lot of intersections of opportunities for Elon Musk, and I also think he discovered, to use a phrase of his, the anomaly in the matrix for the American system. And that is money. He discovered that not only can you get a lot of money from the federal government, but if you have a lot of money, you can use it to influence sometimes how much money you get from the federal government or state governments. So I think there was that.

The other big thing is that in America we also have a kind of grudging admiration for the P.T. Barnum-like qualities of certain larger-than-life entrepreneurs, you know, and you see that a lot in Silicon Valley . . . That is a kind of cultural trope in this society for which I think we have a weakness. We sort of like to see them trick us all, though we also do like to see them go down after theyâve tricked us. So I think for all those reasons that maybe Elon was able to succeed here in a way that really exploited some of the flaws in our system and our psyche.

Thereâs also a propensity in our culture to believe in some superhuman aspect of genius, which I think your documentary gets at very well.

Yeah, itâs also that our weakness for money, or the power of money, in this culture also causes us somehow to think that if youâre wealthy, youâre also wise rather than just ruthless, right?

I often think of that famous line from âCitizen Kane,â where Orson Welles is joking with somebody, you know, having been very successful playing this William Randolph Hearst character, who said, âItâs no trick making a lot of money if all you want to do is make a lot of money.â Meaning,Â  if youâre ruthless and determined, you can make a lot of money. Doesnât mean youâre a genius, and it doesnât mean that youâre a tech genius either.Â

I also think Elon Musk, having seen the ascent of Steve Jobs, was sort of defining himself in that way too â or going back to Thomas Edison, who had his own P.T. Barnum-like qualities in terms of inventing a character for himself to play. Itâs not just the investor; itâs the inventor.

âMuskâ runs for almost four hours. Did you always know it would be that long?

No. In fact, I had a cut of the film in the spring of 2024 that was under two hours. We were moving to release that and put it into the fall festivals. Then, in Butler, Pennsylvania, Trump is nearly assassinated, and Musk hitches his wagon to the Trump train. And my friends at HBO said, âYouâre not done. You have to follow this story because it could go to places that you donât expect, and having spent as much time as you have, you have to follow it to at least a moment of greater conclusion.â

So I did, and that ended up being the reason that itâs at such a length. You see patterns from the first film that then repeat themselves, but on a much larger scale, in the second film. Suddenly economic power meets political power, economic and technological power meets political power, and that is the making of an epic story.

(Courtesy Bleecker Street Film / Ken Cedenoupi / UPI Alamy News) Elon Musk

In addition, it just so happened that as he embarked on his political project, a lot of people that I was talking to in the background, trying to persuade them to come forward, did come forward because they saw some of the more problematic aspects of Musk wielding power as part of MAGA world. That gave the story a kind of human dimension as well.

Weirdly, you know, I was having trouble kind of putting it all together, and I didnât really get a sense of how to shape it until I watched Guillermo del Toroâs âFrankenstein,â which in itself was a kind of take on the tech bros. That helped me kind of find a way forward in terms of what became a kind of epic narrative.

Well, you know, you start with a scientist who wants to do something big and important. And thereâs even a sense of idealism about his ambition. But then he literally creates a monster, and the whole enterprise becomes utterly reckless and irresponsible and all about his own sort of grandiosity. Rather than a mission that might help people, it becomes about him.

What are you hoping this documentary will do in terms of making people a little bit more aware of who Elon Musk is and getting at the man behind the curtain, so to speak?

Well, I mean, it is an agent provocateur. I donât provide a solution, but I do provide, I think, a pretty compelling story, which asks the kind of fundamental question I posed at the beginning, which is, how did this guy get so much power, and why did we give it to him? Because itâs both about him and itâs about us, and it asks some discomforting questions about how literally existential power rests in the hands of one man who is increasingly chaotic, unhinged, and seemingly pursuing power without reason. Thereâs a chilling moment at the end of the film where somebody asks him, âWhy have you accreted so much power?â And he literally canât answer the questionâ¦

Heâs a very peculiar character whoâs a chaos agent. But weâve allowed him to become normalized in a way.

I remember writing about him being on âSaturday Night Liveâ and people shrugging it off, like, âOh, itâs not that big of a deal.â But it was a very big deal. Those kinds of things make him into a character when the reality is he has massive access to power.

And heâs saying things, even on âSaturday Night Live,â that were patently untrueâ¦ Even when he says, âDid you think I was going to be a chill, normal dude?â Well, thereâs a funny hidden message there, which is kind of discomforting if you really think about it. Like, if you want to drive a Tesla, be prepared to endure a lot of performative cruelty from me, including cruelty that may end up killing people. . .Â  Thatâs a pretty brutal message, honestly, for âSaturday Night Live.â But it was a joke, right? And thatâs the genius, in a way, of Elon Musk: heâs constantly saying stuff that is deadly serious and a joke at the same time.

Speaking of that, the images and the joke, letâs talk about using the [CGI] avatar. I remember when the news first broke about that, someone said, âWell, I wonder if thatâs Alex kind of trolling Musk back.â

I mean, itâs kind of a troll-back, yeah. In a way, itâs kind of investing in him, playing in his sandbox, because he didnât agree to appear.

And I should make it clear, as I tried to do in the film, that what we hear from him are actual audio recordings of him. In other words, theyâre not AI-confected answers. We didnât ask AI what Elon would say. Weâre taking real audio recordings, but how to couch that visually? And we took our cue, having done all this research into stuff that Elon said, from something he kept going over again: This idea that weâre likely living in a simulation. So I thought, OK, how about a simulated interview?

And yes, heâs famous for trolling people. Heâs famous for creating memes. What was it he said in 2020 on Twitter? He said, you know, parodying âDune,â he said, âHe who controls the memes, controls the universe,â right? OK, well, hereâs a meme for you, Elon, of you.

Want more from culture than just the latest trend? The Swell highlights art made to last. Sign up here

What, if anything, about this documentary may help illuminate a few things for people, regardless of their political leanings, as we approach the midterms?

I mean, this should be our concern, whether youâre from the left or the right, is giving people unaccountable power. Also, this whole idea that our politics and, indeed, our Department of Justice and our Department of Defense can be utterly transactional.

Weâre not getting the best that money can buy. Weâre getting what money can buy. Period. In other words, the military stuff that youâre seeing is a third-rate frontier AI technology being fully integrated into our Department of Defense. And why is the worst technology being integrated? Because Elon Musk is literally paying for political advantage. So itâs a payback system, and we should all be outraged about that, left, right, or otherwise.

And now youâre seeing him trying to buy the midterms. Heâs spending way more now than he did for the presidential campaign in 2024, and in part thatâs to get more money for himself in the form of military contracts. But also, he knows that a reckoning is coming for him if the Democrats take over the House and the Senate, and thereâs going to be a lot of investigations into him for corruption and abuse of power, taking our information, particularly possibly relating to DOGE, and doing God knows what with it.

Our whole system is built on a system of checks and balances, and the idea that the government is our instrument for making a better world, rather than, you know, making a few people richâ¦

But I think that whatâs changed now with Trump is that the Department of Justice has become a protection racket for those who flatter and ally themselves with the president, and an instrument of revenge for those who oppose the president. You canât depend on it as a kind of law-enforcing mechanism, and that may be the scariest thing of all. . . What weâre talking about is Putinâs Russia here, right? And if people want to avoid that, then I would strongly urge them to go out to the polls. Because this is a rogue administration that goes beyond any kind of sense of party affiliation. Itâs a rogue administration thatâs literally destroying our democracy.

âMuskâ is playing in theaters nationwide.

#212. Why Spain Is Standing Up to Trump

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Q&A: Why Spain Is Standing Up to Trump

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

No audio? Hover over the video player, and tap the Click to Unmute button. Subtitles are also available. Closed captioning provided by Vimeo and may contain minor inconsistencies.

Register now to watch this on-demand recording.

Countries around the world employ a variety of strategies to navigate the Trump White House. Some try flattery and appeasement. Others keep a low profile. Spain has chosen a path of frank disagreement. Under Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, Madrid has refused to follow Washington’s call for NATO members to increase defense spending to 5 percent of GDP and has rejected President Donald Trump’s request to use Spanish bases in the war with Iran. On issue after issue, from immigration to the Israeli-Palestinian dispute, Spain’s left-wing government has publicly forged a path that runs counter to a global trend of right-wing policies.

But now Sánchez’s government faces elections in November, and Spaniards will decide whether the country’s foreign and domestic policy is something they see as reasonable. I spoke with Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares on the latest episode of FP Live to find out how Madrid thinks about the trade-offs in following its progressive agenda while risking the ire of the world’s biggest economy. The full interview is available on the video box atop this page or on the FP Live podcast on Spotify, YouTube, or Apple. What follows here is a lightly edited and condensed transcript.

Countries around the world employ a variety of strategies to navigate the Trump White House. Some try flattery and appeasement. Others keep a low profile. Spain has chosen a path of frank disagreement. Under Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, Madrid has refused to follow Washington’s call for NATO members to increase defense spending to 5 percent of GDP and has rejected President Donald Trump’s request to use Spanish bases in the war with Iran. On issue after issue, from immigration to the Israeli-Palestinian dispute, Spain’s left-wing government has publicly forged a path that runs counter to a global trend of right-wing policies.

But now Sánchez’s government faces elections in November, and Spaniards will decide whether the country’s foreign and domestic policy is something they see as reasonable. I spoke with Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares on the latest episode of FP Live to find out how Madrid thinks about the trade-offs in following its progressive agenda while risking the ire of the world’s biggest economy. The full interview is available on the video box atop this page or on the FP Live podcast on Spotify, YouTube, or Apple. What follows here is a lightly edited and condensed transcript.

Ravi Agrawal: Let’s start with relations between Madrid and Washington. In July, U.S. President Donald Trump called Spain a “wasted cause” and a “terrible partner” in NATO. He threatened to cut off trade. In September, he predicted that “Spain will be a ruined country.” So I have to ask you, is the relationship between Madrid and Washington broken?

José Manuel Albares: The relationship is fluid. We see this at all levels. I have contact with U.S. Secretary of State [Marco] Rubio. I’ve met with him on different occasions—in NATO ministerials, for instance—and I’ve had different conversations with him at the ambassador and embassy level, both here in Madrid and in Washington, and everything goes well. Above all, people to people, the reality of the relationship between the two countries is really good.

The United States is the historical and natural ally of Spain and of Europe. Spain is one of the few countries with which the United States has a surplus in trade. The same is true when we look at investment. We are great investors in the United States, and the United States is a great investor here in Spain. We are one of the main buyers of liquefied natural gas [LNG] from the United States. In Spain, we have two military bases—of Spanish sovereignty but used also by the United States—that are key to trans-Atlantic security. If you look at the exchange of students, businessmen, and tourism between Spain and the United States, you see the depth of our relationship.

RA: But I think the Trump administration will point out that Spain has not helped the United States, for example, in the war in Iran, by withholding its bases from U.S. use. This is a fairly transactional administration. If they were to ask, “What good is the Spanish alliance to the United States?” what would you say?

JMA: Two military bases with no cost for decades that are essential for trans-Atlantic security and therefore for the security of the United States; a surplus in trade; a lot of Spanish investment, buying a lot of U.S. LNG; and all of the cultural and educational exchange that we have—all of this is the reality of our relationship, and I would say that is positive for both Spaniards and Americans. If you look at trade, for instance, the relationship is even more positive for the United States than it is for Spain.

RA: Especially by Trump’s calculations, given that he likes an American surplus.

But I have to say, many European governments have chosen to manage their relationship with President Trump quietly. They often turn to flattery or grand displays or gifts. Spain is quite alone in being as outspoken as it is, especially in Europe. I can see that it is electorally beneficial, but there are also costs in the form of having a fairly powerful enemy. For example, last year at a White House Ukraine summit, it was notable that Spain was not represented. You lose something by not being at the table. So I’m curious, how do you weigh the trade-offs of Spain’s stance, specifically with the Trump administration?

JMA: We have a coherent foreign policy that stands for the same values and objectives everywhere in the world, whether in Ukraine or the Middle East. We believe in international law. We believe that war shouldn’t be a tool used to achieve foreign-policy objectives. We believe in the principles of the U.N. Charter, in the protection of civilians. That’s how we conduct ourselves in the world and in foreign affairs, and nothing about what we do diminishes our friendships and alliances. We continue participating in NATO and a very strong trans-Atlantic bond for both security and trade.

When it comes to the different crises going on around the world, Spain is always a decisive actor. In Ukraine, we have been backing the government of President Volodymyr Zelensky and the sovereignty of Ukraine since the very beginning of the war. We support the European project and efforts to make it strong. In the Middle East, we’re trying to push forward the two-state solution, which we know is the only solution that will bring peace and stability to everyone in the Middle East but especially to Israelis and Palestinians. Today, Spain not only has a coherent foreign policy with its own voice but is also recognized and welcomed by all countries in the world.

RA: But even supporters of your policies, while agreeing with much of what you’re saying, will point out that the one thing that sticks out is that Spain has refused to join the calls to spend 5 percent of its GDP on defense. I’m curious how you explain that because on the face of it, one of the easiest things to do that would be coherent would be to join these other European countries that are trying to defend Ukraine from Russia while ensuring that Moscow in the future wouldn’t try to attack other NATO states.

JMA: Two things: Spain has delivered all the capabilities that have been requested by the organization, and we are already spending 2 percent. I wish all the allies could say that. So the day all the allies are at 2 percent of expenditure—which is not the case—the day all the allies have delivered the capabilities that are requested by NATO—

RA: But they’re committing to 3.5 percent—

JMA: One thing is words. Another thing is the facts.

And the second thing: What’s the real commitment? The real commitment is the capabilities, the deployment of troops. We are deploying a historical amount of troops. Three thousand Spanish soldiers are on the eastern front, in Estonia, Slovakia, and Romania. We have troops, we have airplanes, we had ships when they were requested. We are commanding the NATO mission in Iraq and many others under the EU and U.N. flag. At the same time, we have been backing Ukraine since the very beginning of the war of aggression.

When it comes to trans-Atlantic security, Spain is always in the forefront. And the way we view things is more than talking about a percentage. We look at the threats, we decide what capabilities are needed to meet those threats, and then we quantify them.

In the Iran war and beyond, Madrid has often done a better job looking out for U.S. interests than Washington.

Madrid is preparing for one of the most ambitious regularization schemes in European history.

Why Spain’s Sánchez has succeeded while Britain’s Starmer floundered.

RA: Well, I’ll just point out that they [NATO members] have committed to 3.5 percent in spending and another 1.5 in infrastructure. Assuming they eventually reach that point in a few years, Spain will be behind that trend line. You can agree or disagree with whether that’s a good thing, but it will make for slightly tougher relations, I think, with the rest of NATO. And I do wonder how you marry that with the idea of a standing army for Europe, which you’ve called for—a common EU force. Do you see that as something that is diminishing NATO?

JMA: Certainly, we will not diminish NATO. NATO remains the key organization for trans-Atlantic security, and I’ve always been very clear that I really believe in the trans-Atlantic bond for security and for trade. But we have to accept that the U.S. administration is inviting us to take deterrence and security in our own hands. We have to do it, and we have to accept that we have threats that are very pressing right now in Europe.

Therefore, we need to advance our common European defense. The idea isn’t new; it has been there since the very beginning of European projects—the objective of having a European army that will not substitute the national army but if the scope of the threat is European, it will deter at the European level. It will be part of the European pillar of NATO, not against NATO, in the same way that having a strong American army doesn’t diminish NATO but reinforces NATO. Having a strong, common European defense will never diminish NATO or weaken NATO. It will make it stronger.

RA: I’m lingering on your words where you said the United States is inviting Spain and Europe to take security in your own hands. When I add to this the fact that in April, you went with Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to Beijing and signed 19 agreements, I’m curious if Spain is hedging toward China—and more broadly, are you derisking from the United States?

JMA: We don’t have to mix things. Most of the European presidents go to China. President Trump invited President Xi Jinping to Washington, and no one thought that they were changing one relationship for the other. The United States is an ally. We are a very solid partner in the European project, but we talk to the main actors in the world. It’s impossible to have a global foreign policy without having a dialogue with China, just like President Trump and all the European presidents do. We are talking about a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council, a great power, whether you look at it economically, demographically, or militarily.

At the same time, we have a huge trade deficit with China, the highest that we have in the world, and we have to really balance that. So we need to make a balance in that trade deficit, and we ask China to allow our companies to go into China in the same way that they come to Europe when it comes to public procurement or technological transfer. But we are committed, above all, to European construction and also to the trans-Atlantic bond, which is where Spain stands very firmly.

RA: I’m going to turn now to the Middle East. Your government has also been quite outspoken on Gaza, another area of stark difference with the Trump administration. You’ve called what is happening there a genocide. You’ve imposed an arms embargo and banned imports from settlements. Spanish-Israeli diplomatic relations were downgraded. The Spanish ambassador to Israel was permanently recalled. Yours is a relatively lonely stance in Europe. Tell me, what do you realistically hope to accomplish with your approach to Israel?

JMA: We are not alone in Europe. We started a movement of recognition of the state of Palestine that was followed by many countries today. More countries in Europe recognize the state of Palestine than not. And when we meet in the European Council, we continue to back the two-state solution every year. That’s where our policy is. It’s a policy that believes in peace and peaceful coexistence. And we think that the only solution that will guarantee peace and security for everyone in the Middle East—but also for the Israeli people because none of what we do or say goes against the state of Israel—is the two-state solution. A state of Palestine, guaranteeing mutual security and prosperity and living in a good neighborhood with the state of Israel. Of course, Israel has a right to have a state of security, prosperity, and peace, but the Palestinian people have the same right to the same type of state.

RA: Minister, all of that sounds good, but do you see that as realistic anymore given what the Trump administration is doing and moving ahead with on the Board of Peace?

JMA: It’s the only realistic possibility. The other one is accepting that for some reason, the people in the Middle East—especially Israelis and Palestinians but all of them—only have one way to relate to each other: through violence and war. For me, that’s unacceptable. They are not different from us. They don’t wish, for them and for their children, different things than we do.

In Europe, we spent centuries waging war on our neighbors. The border was a real curse: Having a border meant that the other side of the border was where your enemy was. Then we went for the European Union, which showed that we could transform the border into a symbol of cooperation and that the people on the other side of that border were the people with which you were going to do everything to achieve peace and prosperity. Why couldn’t the Middle East be the same?

RA: They say that foreign policy begins at home. Your country’s heading into elections in November. Given everything we’ve been discussing about the Middle East, about international law, about Ukraine and defense spending, and relations with the United States, how do you explain why your foreign-policy decisions matter to the Spanish people?

JMA: The Spanish people realize that today, no country in the world, not even the most powerful one, can take all the decisions internally, within the government or in our parliaments. They realize that we need to work and cooperate with others and that there are decisions that are taken in Brussels at the EU level, and in New York at the U.N., that have a direct impact on their well-being.

When we see war in Ukraine, it’s not only about Ukraine; it has an impact on us. What happens in Hormuz has an impact on the pockets of Spaniards. If we don’t stop climate change, it will have an impact even in their lifetimes—we see it more and more with fires and peaks of heat during the summers that cause the deaths of many people. So, for all those reasons, they realize that to have well-being internally—in Spain or in any country—the government has to perform well in foreign policy. It’s important because in the end, foreign policy is about defending the interest of your citizens and of projecting their values.

Ravi Agrawal is the editor in chief of Foreign Policy. X: @RaviReports

#214. Kate Berlant’s great American clown show

In a digital flyer promoting the stand-up shows that would culminate in her new HBO comedy special, “Parmesan,” comedian, actress and one of America’s greatest working artists, Kate Berlant, posed an important question: “HAVE YOU SEEN THIS CLOWN?” In one photo, Berlant, fresh from glam, seduces the camera; in the other, her face contorts into a rascally grin, eyes half-crossed for effect. No dichotomy better represents Berlant’s razor-sharp, thoroughly tasteful wit, which sits halfway between refined humorist and go-for-broke court jester.

If you haven’t seen this clown, there’s no better time than the present. Like most of Berlant’s work — from her extensive collaborations with best friend John Early to her unforgettable one-woman show, “KATE” — “Parmesan” is a masterful send-up of a time when we’re all doing character work. What begins as an honest account of modern life’s bleak state is distorted alongside Berlant’s malleable expressions, slowly blossoming into something life-affirming, like a diamond among the rubble. Some comedians like to say they give their audience a “night off” from the world. Berlant, on the other hand, relishes the chance to remind her audiences of just how blissfully hysterical the world can be.

Everyday life, in the Berlantian sense, is driven by affection for both the mundane and the surreal in equal measure. In the joke that inspires the special’s title, she measures an Instagram comment’s subzero value in a wide scope, lampooning the communal yet cartoonish nature of our endless scroll. Elsewhere, Berlant gets more personal than she ever has on stage, using the relatively recent discovery that she isn’t straight as the springboard for bits about how embracing queerness later in life can be as beautiful as it is uniquely mortifying.

But with Berlant, it’s not just about the jokes; it’s about the rhythm and physicality that accompany them. No one understands their audience better than she does, knowing comedy relies as much on observation as on good, old-fashioned slapstick. Berlant’s a tenured professor at the Make-‘Em-Laugh Institute, and “Parmesan” proves her research-driven thesis statement time and again: There’s no bad mood a good clown can’t improve.

#215. The real reason MAGA fears Ilhan Omar

Donald Trump and his MAGA followers are obsessed with Somali-Americans. The president frequently rants about immigrants from the easternmost African country and their children, using racist rhetoric that would not be out of place at a Ku Klux Klan rally. At a campaign event Monday in Ohio, ostensibly to boost Sen. Jon Husted’s campaign against Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown, Trump fixated at length on Somali-Americans. They “don’t have pants to wear,” he claimed, but then he also expressed anger that they drive “Mercedes Benz and BMWs.” He accused them of being “low IQ” and alleged that they “plundered, ransacked and destroyed” Minnesota, a state with a large Somali immigrant population.

The president’s remarks followed past comments in which he called Somali immigrants “garbage” and said they “aren’t people that work.” Last week, Trump demanded on Truth Social that Minnesotans “fight back,” saying, “Somalians should not be allowed to get away with what they are doing.” Just in case his violent implications weren’t clear enough, Trump promised “the Federal Government will come to your rescue” should anyone follow his instructions.

It’s worth remembering Trump’s history of condoning violence. In January 2025, on his first day back in office, the president pardoned people convicted of violent crimes during the Jan. 6 riot at the Capitol. A year later, his administration took pains to shield officers responsible for the shooting deaths of pro-immigrant protesters Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis.

So it wasn’t too big a surprise when Homeland Security officials raided the home of perhaps the most famous Somali-American in the country, Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on Monday. The action is part of an all-hands-on-deck effort to prove a conspiracy theory that has been percolating on the right for years now, accusing Omar and her family of falsifying her documents to become a U.S. citizen when she was 17. The administration hopes it can denaturalize and deport the progressive lawmaker, whom Trump has deemed “deranged and sick,” repeatedly calling for her to be ejected from the country.

Odds are that the Trump administration has no case at all against Omar — as is true of thousands of other cases it has lost against immigrants so far. Instead, the raid on the Minnesota congresswoman’s home must be understood more as a campaign stunt by a president desperate to distract from his economic failures and the disastrous war in Iran. Omar herself called the raid “pointless” and “the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies.” This isn’t even the first time Trump’s goons have gone hunting for evidence that Omar’s citizenship is illegitimate. On Thursday, the Washington Post reported that, during his first term, Trump made the same demand of immigration officials, but they found “insufficient evidence of wrongdoing” and “eventually abandoned” the search.

No matter how many insults or threats Trump flings Omar’s way, he cannot hide that the congresswoman is exactly the opposite of the racist stereotypes he traffics in. She is smart, beautiful and hard-working. Unlike Trump, who grew up a spoiled rich kid in Queens, Omar has overcome steep odds to be where she is. At only eight, she fled war-torn Somalia with her family after gunmen attacked their home and lived in a refugee camp in Kenya for four years. Whatever one’s views of her politics, there can be no denying that everything Omar has attained, from her education to her career, has been earned against high odds.

Trump’s accusations against Omar and Somali-Americans in general have more than a whiff of psychological projection to them.

Trump’s accusations against Omar and Somali-Americans in general have more than a whiff of psychological projection to them. He calls her “crooked” and “terrible,” but in reality it’s Trump who was convicted of defrauding New York State to the tune of half a billion dollars. It’s Trump who tried to steal the 2020 election, and it’s Trump who is using gerrymandering and frivolous lawsuits to try to cheat his way out of Republicans losing the midterms. It’s Trump who has amassed over a billion dollars in shadily sourced wealth as president through cryptocurrency schemes. He even regularly cheats at golf because he’s so incapable of playing fair.

But that all underscores the greater truth about the administration’s attacks on Omar and her fellow Somali-Americans. The success of the congresswoman and her fellow immigrants handily disproves the claim that non-white people are inferior, and instead proves that progressives are right — that the U.S. is better off for allowing people from around the world to live here. For MAGA, the fear of immigration is not about feeling contaminated, but being shown up and exposed as mediocrities in comparison to industrious newcomers.

Trump’s attack on Omar is reminiscent of his previous accusations that Barack Obama was not a real U.S. citizen. In 2011, Trump, who was then a host on NBC’s “The Apprentice,” started a noisy public campaign demanding the then-president produce his Hawaiian birth certificate, implying that Obama, whose father was Kenyan, could not be a legitimate citizen. Obama eventually did release his birth certificate, but that ultimately didn’t matter to Trump and others who promoted and believed the birther lie, because this was never about the legal definition of “citizen.” It was about the way that the erudite, charismatic Obama revealed the insecurities of the people who, only a few years later, would call themselves “MAGA” by disproving their hopes that whiteness confers an excellence that they, on their own merits, could never produce.

Want more Amanda Marcotte on politics? Sign up for her free newsletter, Standing Room Only, now also on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

Trump made this especially clear by also trying to prove Obama secretly had bad grades in college. The president’s psychological projection isn’t subtle. Unsurprisingly, he has not been keen on releasing his own grades and test scores, but he is quick to assure us he’s a super-genius because he was able to tell the difference between a man and a woman on a medical exam to diagnose dementia.

Another pointed reminder of MAGA’s true fears came recently when Bo French, the Republican nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner, tweeted a photo of non-white students celebrating a University of Texas football win and complained, “The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.” He later whined about the university accepting foreign students, though he had no evidence these young people in the photo were born outside the country and neglected to offer any rational arguments for why the school should discriminate against worthy students from overseas.

French’s outburst kicked off a debate among right-wing commentators about what they crudely called “the Indian question,” an apparent nod to a Nazi euphemism for antisemitic ideas that eventually led to the Holocaust. This revealed an unbelievably noxious racism, and also served as a tacit admission that concern about immigration is not, despite all the “garbage” talk, about immigrants dragging down the country. The MAGA coalition’s fear is that immigrants will make it a lot harder for mediocre white people to compete for plum jobs and school admissions. While decades of right-wing blather about meritocracy was always a lie, now conservatives are basically admitting it: Racism is a protection racket to shield white D-level students from the consequences of their own laziness.

This understanding exposes why Trump and MAGA have it in for Somali-Americans. Like any group of people, the Somali immigrant community contains good and bad people in it, but on the whole, their very existence is a testament to human tenacity. Like so many waves of refugees before and after, these are people who took huge risks to survive, and many of them, like Omar, are thriving. Even though the community suffers from extensive poverty due in part to discrimination and the few resources refugees from a war-torn country are able to marshal, it has also produced a large number of entrepreneurs. Somali-Americans have higher than average rates of labor participation and contribute an estimated $8 billion a year to Minnesota’s economy alone. Like many immigrant communities, such as Irish and Italians in the early 20th century, the second generation is doing much better economically than their parents.

In other words, Somali-Americans are living the industrious values that a lot of MAGA types valorize but at which many, especially rich boys like Trump, fall short. This, too, would be fine, if only conservatives could just relax. Part of the American dream is being able to move beyond working that 60-hour week that so many recent immigrants have to put in to survive. There is nothing wrong with being a C student — as long as you don’t take your insecurities out on the A students who just so happen to have darker skin. That’s what makes this racism so baffling. It’s not just that it’s immoral. It’s also a waste of a one precious life to be so angry that someone who looks a little different might be better at some stuff.

#217. How a foreign government helped accused Saudi spy's family flee US after OpenAI bug scandal

Fox News chief correspondent Jonathan Hunt details the arrest of a Saudi OpenAI employee accused of secretly placing a recording device inside a San Francisco conference room. Hunt discusses the alleged security breach, how the device was discovered and OpenAI’s response to the incident.

A former OpenAI engineer accused of secretly planting listening devices inside the artificial intelligence giant's facilities was communicating with Saudi royalty and searching company records involving the Kingdom before his arrest, according to federal prosecutors who are investigating whether his alleged surveillance was intended to benefit a foreign government.

In a detention filing Sunday, prosecutors revealed that Saudi government officials helped arrange international travel for Abdulrahman Alfozan's wife and three-month-old son shortly after his arrest.

They also raised concerns about Alfozan's potential access to foreign government assistance if released.

Prosecutors disclosed that Alfozan had been in frequent contact with a member of the Saudi royal family who sought to recruit him for a Saudi artificial intelligence initiative. The filing does not allege that Saudi Arabia directed his alleged surveillance.

A man described as Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national formerly employed as an OpenAI engineer, looks behind a television where a recording device had been placed at a conference room in OpenAI offices, in a still image from surveillance video. (Reuters)

TRUMP INTEL CHIEF WARNS AI FIRMS ON HACKS, SAYS NEW DEPARTMENT IS THE 'COP ON THE BEAT'

The investigation remains ongoing and "may result in additional serious charges," prosecutors said. Investigators are examining whether Alfozan sought to record sensitive OpenAI meetings to advance his own business interests, aid a foreign government or both.

According to the filing, Alfozan spent weeks researching how to construct an encrypted recording device with live-listening capabilities and where inside OpenAI he could capture sensitive conversations.

He allegedly used an internal OpenAI tool to identify meeting rooms used by company executives and outside partners before concealing a customized audio recorder behind a television in an executive conference room in late September.

The room regularly hosted leadership meetings, technical and product discussions, and briefings with government officials and business partners. Conversations frequently involved proprietary research, OpenAI's technical capabilities, strategic decisions, government engagements and commercial relationships, according to prosecutors.

Government officials met with OpenAI executives in the room around the time of the alleged surveillance, prosecutors said, warning that Alfozan's conduct "could pose a danger to the national security of the United States."

Investigators also uncovered evidence suggesting his alleged surveillance extended beyond a single device.

OpenAI security personnel discovered a second similar recorder inside a bag Alfozan left in a printer room. Searches of his home and electronic devices subsequently uncovered similar components and photographs that appeared to show reconnaissance of other locations inside OpenAI, including another conference room used for sensitive meetings.

President Donald Trump and Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia pause for photographs along the West Wing Colonnade at the White House on Nov. 18, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Getty Images)

Investigators say Alfozan was also showing particular interest in OpenAI's dealings with Saudi Arabia.

His browsing history showed that he accessed a folder titled "Saudi Gov Docs" on Oct. 4, 2026, and used an internal OpenAI tool to search for engagements involving Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Communications and Information Technology.

Among the subjects he searched were planned OpenAI visits to Saudi Arabia, an upcoming visit by the Saudi ministry and a meeting labeled "HUMAIN x MCIT @OpenAI," according to prosecutors.

At the same time, Alfozan maintained frequent contact with an unidentified member of the Saudi royal family, including just four days before his arrest.

"Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!" the royal told Alfozan in May, according to the filing. Alfozan responded "100," which prosecutors interpreted as agreement.

The royal repeatedly tried to recruit Alfozan for an artificial intelligence initiative in Saudi Arabia and asked when he planned to leave OpenAI. Alfozan said he would not leave until his stock vested, according to prosecutors. He was also allegedly pursuing other opportunities in Saudi Arabia, including applying to the Mohammed bin Salman Foundation's "2030 Leaders" program.

GOOGLE ENGINEER STOLE AI SECRETS FOR CHINA, SENATE HEARS IN EXPLOSIVE TESTIMONY

The Saudi connections have become a focus of prosecutors' argument that Alfozan poses a serious flight risk.

At the time of his arrest, Alfozan had one-way tickets from San Francisco to Riyadh for Oct. 12, 2026, and was scheduled to begin two months of parental leave from OpenAI. The FBI arrested him Oct. 9, 2026.

The accused's wife and infant son initially had a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia booked and paid for by the Saudi government, prosecutors said. Then a Saudi military official purchased business-class tickets for the pair en route to Qatar. They departed San Francisco roughly 36 hours after Alfozan's arrest.

Prosecutors cited the travel arrangements as evidence that Alfozan could receive substantial assistance from the Saudi government if released.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Saudi Embassy, OpenAI and Alfozan's attorney for comment.

Man accused of attempting to 'bug' OpenAI offices had ties to Saudi government, prosecutors say. (Kenneth Cheung/Getty Images)

The government also pointed to a previous federal case in which prosecutors alleged that a former Twitter employee received Saudi assistance leaving the United States after being confronted over his access to internal user data.

After Twitter confronted employee Ali Alzabarah in 2015, prosecutors alleged, calls were exchanged with a Saudi foreign official and the Saudi consul general in Los Angeles to coordinate a flight to Saudi Arabia the following day.

Alzabarah later went to work for the Misk Foundation, according to the filing. Charges against him remain pending.

Prosecutors argued that Alfozan similarly has access to "considerable support from a foreign government" with no extradition treaty with the United States and the resources to provide extraordinary travel assistance.

Alfozan, a legal permanent resident, was earning $385,000 annually at OpenAI and had received a $2.2 million equity grant, according to prosecutors. OpenAI fired him following his arrest.

He is charged with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications. Prosecutors are asking a federal judge to keep him behind bars pending trial, arguing that he poses a serious flight risk and an ongoing danger to the community.

Additionally, Jeanine Pirro, U.S. attorney for the District of Washington, D.C., announced her office was investigating Omar's financial disclosures, which had previously been subject to public scrutiny and congressional oversight, but never by authorities.

Omar has defended herself on social media in recent days.

"This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," Omar's office said in a statement.

"For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back. Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies."

Fox News Digital’s Stephen Sorace and Peter D’Abrosca contributed to this report

Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter from Pasadena, California, who has been with Fox News Digital since 2021. You can reach him at AndrewMark.Miller@fox.com.

#234. Booker rival who ‘shoots from the hip’ hopes viral debate moment can break GOP’s Senate drought

New Jersey GOP nominee Justin Murphy drew national attention after urging Trump to "finish" the Iran war, prompting Booker's stunned reaction.

A New Jersey attorney and former municipal official who made waves during his debate with Sen. Cory Booker, D-N. J., said his unscripted style may be the secret sauce to making history and ending a Republican Senate drought in New Jersey that stretches back more than half a century.

Justin Murphy, a Navy veteran and former deputy mayor of Tabernacle in the state’s Pine Barrens, stunned his incumbent Democratic opponent when, in response to a question about the Iran war strategy, he bluntly said President Donald Trump should forcefully "finish it."

"I don’t have a speechwriter. There’s no teleprompter — I shoot from the hip because I want people to see a very sincere, genuine and authentic Justin Murphy," Murphy told Fox News Digital.

BOOKER 'WOWED' BY GOP CHALLENGER'S BLUNT MESSAGE TO TRUMP

Winner of the Republican U.S. Senate primary in New Jersey on Tuesday, June 2, 2026. (Jersey Justin For Senate)

"This came up. And I had no idea it would become as viral or explode as it has on social media. It's what I felt. I meant what I said. I said what I meant. It wasn't planned to try to spark the reaction that we got … through social media."

Clifford Case, the last Republican to represent the Garden State in the Senate, was last elected in 1972 – the same year Giants Stadium broke ground, years before the Jets joined the Giants in New Jersey and before NJ Transit was created.

Murphy said that in his 60 years, he cannot remember a time when Iran’s support for terrorism, "export" of assassination or killing of its own people was not a feature of the nightly news.

"I think we have a president now that is breaking from the past, and he's no longer kicking the can down the road. And I think that's important that our young people know tomorrow that they will not have to worry about what the words ‘Strait of Hormuz’ mean when this is over."

TRUMP IS DISMANTLING IRAN’S WAR MACHINE, BUT AMERICA STILL NEEDS AN ENDGAME

Senator Cory Booker (D-N.J.) speaks alongside Democratic Senate Judiciary Committee members during a news conference on the nomination of acting Attorney General Todd Blanche on Capitol Hill on July 15, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Eric Lee/Getty Images)

Asked how his message on Iran can overcome concerns about the war’s effect on energy prices – including among Republicans and independents in the crucial Philadelphia metro area where he lives – Murphy said it is important to offer a vision focused on long-term national and energy security.

The "long-term" aspect of his message is twofold, he said, noting that he was in first grade in the Philadelphia suburb of Collingdale, Pennsylvania, the last time New Jersey elected a Republican to the Senate.

"Number one — it’s time for a change. We had a good cordial debate with [Cory Booker] but he’s been a senator for 13 years — he’s been [in Washington] longer than Donald Trump."

"I don't think he gets to blame Donald Trump for anything. He's part of the branch of government that passes our country's laws and writes our tax codes and passes our budgets. I'm wondering what he's willing to take responsibility or blame for."

"So what I tell people is that we need a new generation of Americans to serve in Washington, a new day in New Jersey politics, and our working and middle class New Jersey desperately need a voice in the U.S. Senate, and my campaign represents all three of those."

Looking to that "better tomorrow," Murphy said he understands concerns about the Iran conflict’s effect on gas prices in his area, which he put at $4.20 per gallon as of Wednesday and which have become a major point of criticism of the current administration.

RNC THREATENS LEGAL ACTION AGAINST NEW JERSEY OFFICIALS OVER NONCITIZENS ON VOTER ROLLS: 'ON NOTICE'

"If they're upset at gasoline at $4.20 … you were paying over $5 a gallon with Joe Biden with a 9% interest rate, with a 20% cumulative inflation rate, with an open border, rising crime rates, declining wages and an 8% interest rate that is a full point or two higher than it is now," he said.

Murphy said those concerned about prices should also look to domestic energy production and support policies that increase refining capacity to reduce exposure to global oil markets.

He also pointed to legislation introduced moments before the interview by "Squad" member Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., to dismantle the Department of Homeland Security.

"This is madness and insanity, and it's not the tomorrow that Americans want or can build together," he said.

Murphy was also asked about election security in New Jersey, where hundreds of noncitizens have been found to have voted in recent elections as the Sherrill administration pushes back on federal efforts to crack down.

"Election integrity is extremely and critically important, not only to me and my campaign, but to the country. We're designed as a representative government, a constitutional republic, and we need to know our elections are secure — We know we have contaminated rolls in New Jersey," he said.

Murphy stressed that he does not want an election system that benefits Republicans, as critics claim, but one that is fair, accurate and reflects the will of American voters. He also called Trenton’s immigration enforcement posture "utter insanity."

For Murphy, the debate’s viral "Wow" moment was more than a campaign breakthrough. He sees it as a test of whether an unscripted message on national security can cut through voters’ immediate concerns about gas prices — and give Republicans a path to end their decades-long Senate drought in New Jersey.

Booker's campaign did not respond to a request for comment on the exchange.
